4.2.2.2.3.2.2.2.1. Training in the causes that sustain the awakening mind in this life

d.div: de nas 'jig rten lhar bcas phyag 'os dang / / 'khor bsgyur srung [88] ma nyis gyur gyis bsrung [89] dang / / rig sngags 'grub cing dngos grub rnam gnyis ster/ / bskal pa du mar rab dgongs mdzad pa yi/ /[229]
thub dbang rnams kyis 'di nyid phan par gzigs/ / 'di yi bsod nams gzugs gyur nam mkhar lhag / gal te 'di nyams ngan 'gror ring 'khyams pas/ / skad cig mi 'dor nyin re'ang lan drug bzung / /[230]

229 [With bodhicitta] you become worthy of the homage of gods and men. You are watched over by twice as many protectors as a universal sovereign. Mantra [recitation] is effective and confers the two kinds of attainments.[209] “After deeply pondering the matter for many eons,

230 the buddhas saw its unique benefits.”[210] If the merit of it were to materialize, it would fill the sky and beyond. Since its decline would mean wandering long in unfortunate realms, do not abandon it even momentarily and recommit to it six times daily.
[88] bsrung / rda sa shes dpar/
[89] bsrungs/ rda sa shes dpar/

[209] The two kinds of attainments, or siddhis, are the ordinary ones (thun mong gi dngos grub), such as long life, great wealth, clairvoyance, and flying, and the supreme attainment (mchog gi dngos grub), buddhahood. Excellent realizations such as the awakening mind and the understanding of emptiness are also placed in the latter category.
[210] Although Gomchen does not explicitly state it, these two lines are from Śāntideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva Way, 1.7ab.

f.d: gnyis pa skye ba gzhan du de dang mi 'bral ba'i rgyu la bslab pa
4.2.2.2.3.2.2.2.2. Training in the causes that prevent its loss in subsequent lives
['di ]la gnyis/ nyams par byed pa nag po'i chos bzhi spang ba/ mi nyams par byed pa dkar po'i chos bzhi blang ba la bslab pa'o/ /
This has two parts: training in giving up the four dark deeds that weaken it and practicing the four light deeds that prevent its weakening.
dang po nyams par byed pa nag po'i chos bzhi spang ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.2.2.2.2.1. Training in giving up the four dark deeds that weaken it

d.div: mkhan slob phan 'dogs yon gnas brdzun dbu 1bskor/ / dge byas 'gyod mi ldan la 'gyod 2bskyed dang / / byang sems mi snyan brjod nas don go ba'o/3 / lhag bsam min pas gzhan la g.yo sgyus spyod//[231]
rang gi nyes pa thabs kyis mi mngon byed/ / med bzhin yon tan yod ston g.yo sgyur gsungs//
232 Deceit and hypocrisy are explained [respectively] as using tactics to conceal your faults and affecting possession of good qualities that you lack.
[211] “Celebrants” (mchod gnas), literally “recipient of offerings,” typically means ordained or lay officiants who are requested to perform prayers and rituals in people’s homes.

f.d: gnyis pa mi nyams par byed pa dkar po'i chos bzhi blang ba la bslab pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.2.2.2.2.2. Practicing the four light deeds that prevent its weakening

d.div: de bzhi las bzlog dkar po'i chos bzhi ste/ / de yang brdzun spang drang po'i bsam pas gnas//[232]
byang sems rnams la ston pa'i 'du shes bskyed/ / smin rung sems can rdzogs byang 'dzin 'jug pa'o/ / 'di brgyad phyi mar sems mchog mi 'bral rgyu//[233]
Contrary to these four are the four light deeds: abstaining from lies; maintaining honesty;

233 consciously regarding bodhisattvas as your spiritual teachers and encouraging sentient beings so inclined to develop the aspiration to complete enlightenment. The eight prevent the loss of the supreme aspiration in future lives.

f.d: gsum pa nyams na phyir bcos pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.2.2.3. Restoring the vow if it declines

d.div: nyams na slar yang blang rung theg 'di'i khyad/ / 'jug sdom btang yang smon sems gnas kyi bar/ / smon sems gtong dang sems can blos spong gnyis/ / ma gtogs byang sems bslab bya gzhan 'gal na/ / bar dge khas blangs nyams pa'i nyes spyod 'gyur//[234]

234 Being able to take it again if it declines is unique to this vehicle. You might break your vow of engagement, but as long as you maintain aspirational bodhicitta and neither give up aspirational bodhicitta nor abandon a sentient being, then transgressing any other bodhisattva precept is only a fault that damages the virtues to which you have made a commitment.[212]
[212] The implication is that if you do not transgress your aspirational bodhicitta precepts, you can renew your vow of engaging in the awakening mind by retaking it.

f.d: sems bskyed nas spyod pa la bslab tshul la/
gsum pa sems bskyed nas spyod pa la bslab tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3. Having generated the awakening mind, how to train in bodhisattva practice
['di ]la gsum/ sems bskyed nas bslab pa la slob dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan/ thabs shes re re ba la bslabs pas sangs rgyas mi 'grub par bstan pa/ bslab pa la slob pa'i rim pa nyid bshad pa'o/ /

This has three parts: having generated the awakening mind, why it is necessary to train in the [bodhisattva] precepts; showing that by training in method and wisdom separately, you do not achieve buddhahood; and explaining the process of training in the precepts.
dang po sems bskyed nas bslab pa la slob dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.1. Having generated the awakening mind, why it is necessary to train in the precepts

d.div: smon sems bskyed tsam phan yon che mod kyi/ / de bas sgrub pa snying por byed pa mchog / sgrub pa'ang sdom bzung [90] bslab bya slob nyid yin/ /[235]
235 Although simply producing aspirational bodhicitta already carries great benefits, making it your core practice is best. Its practice consists of taking the vow and observing its precepts.[213]
[90] sdom gsum/ rda sa shes dpar/

[213] The vow is to refrain from eighteen major transgressions and forty-six secondary ones. The precepts are the threefold bodhisattva ethic: the ethics of abstaining from wrongdoing (which includes refraining from eighteen major transgressions and forty-six secondary ones), accomplishing virtue, and fulfilling the welfare of sentient beings.

f.d: gnyis pa thabs shes re re ba la bslabs pas sangs rgyas mi 'grub par bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.2. Showing that by training in method and wisdom separately you do not achieve buddhahood

d.div: thabs shes ya bral sangs rgyas mi 'grub ste/ / ma nor tshang ba'i thabs shes zung 'brel bslab/[91] / 'di yi thabs ni sngar bshad sems bskyed dang / / shes rab yin lugs phu thag chod pa'i lta//[236]

236 As buddhahood cannot be achieved by either method or wisdom in isolation, train conjointly in unmistaken and complete method and wisdom. The method in question is the awakening mind explained above; wisdom is the view that penetrates the ultimate mode of being.[214] [48]
[91] 'brel bslob/ rda sa shes dpar/
[214] Yin lugs, “things as they are,” refers to things’ ultimate mode of existence, emptiness.
stong nyid sgom tshe sems bskyed rtsis zin dang / / sbyin sogs 'jug tshe'ang shes rab rtsis zin nyid/ / 'dir ni thabs shes ya bral min pa'i don/ / kha cig so sor rtog pa'i shes rab kyis//[237]
yin lugs gtan la phab pa'i lta thog tu/ / bzhag nas gzhan gang yid la mi byed par/ / rtse gcig 'jog pa yin lugs sgom yin zer/ / 'o na khyod nyid gang 'dod dris pa'i tshe//[238]
rnam dag rigs pas gtan la phab pa yis/ / don la 'jog rgyu med kyi sems cir yang / / mi rtog 'jog pa'i rtsom 'jog nyid bzang ste/ / lta ba 'di yis zin na nyes spyod kun//[239]
sangs rgyas rgyu ru bsgyur nus zhes kyang smra/ /

237 When meditating on emptiness, imbuing it with the awakening mind and, when practicing generosity and the rest, imbuing them with wisdom — this is what is meant by practicing method and wisdom conjointly. Some say that by means of discerning wisdom,

238 you are to establish the ultimate mode of being and then place [the mind] on this view and think of nothing else, calling this one-pointed mental placement “meditation on the ultimate mode of being.”[215] [Others] when asked, “In what do you believe?” say,
239 “Excellent logical reasoning cannot determine any reality, so the mind too should conceive nothing; remaining in a state of suspension is best.[216] By holding this view, all kinds of wrongdoing
can become causes of buddhahood.”

[215] Jé Tsongkhapa’s Great Treatise (trans., 3:331–39) refutes four major philosophical views. Gomchen first mentions the fourth: the confusion between placement or tranquil abiding meditation and analytical or insight meditation on emptiness.

[216] This corresponds to one of several views propounded by the Chinese master Heshang, discussed here in verses 239–45 and refuted by Jé Tsongkhapa in his Great Treatise (trans.), 2: 87ff. and 3:331–38. The view mentioned in this verse is that logical reasoning cannot determine what is or is not, and that is the way things exist ultimately. The mind should therefore not apprehend anything and should simply abide in a state of nonmentation (ci yang yid la mi byed pa), which constitutes meditation on emptiness. The same view is mentioned in verses 395–97. One implication of this view is that wrongdoing and afflictions can at times become causes of buddhahood and their opposites can hinder its attainment. See Great Treatise (trans.), 2:94ff.
'o na so sor rtog pa'i shes rab kyis/ / dpyad cing bsgoms na khyod la nyes cir 'gyur/ / 'di'o snyam pa'i rtog pa thams cad ni//[240]
'khor gsum rtog pa'i chos kyi bdag 'dzin yin/ / de phyir 'khor ba'i rgyu las ma 'das so/ / skyabs 'gro bshes gnyen yon tan dal 'byor sems/ / 'chi ba dran dang ngan 'gro'i sdug bsngal dang //[241]
byams dang snying rje byang chub sems sbyong dang / / 'jug sems bslab bya slob sogs thams cad la/ / 'di dang 'di zhes nges pa drangs dgos pas/ / 'di dag shes sgrib yin par smra nus na//[242]
240 [Question] Well then, for you what is wrong with meditating analytically by means of discriminating wisdom? [Answer] “All conceptions that think ‘this is this’ are instances of apprehension

241 of the self of phenomena and conceptions of the three spheres, owing to which one fails to eliminate the causes of cyclic existence.” [Question] Then since contemplating refuge, spiritual teachers’ qualities, and leisure and opportunity, practicing mindfulness of death and the unfortunate realms’ sufferings,

242 cultivating love, compassion, and the awakening mind, and training in the precepts of engaging bodhicitta must each be ascertained individually, you dare assert these are all obstructions to omniscience?
chos kyi bdag med ji tsam sgom pa nyid/ / skyabs sogs 'di dag nyams pa'i rgyur 'gro bas/ / lta spyod tsha grang lta bur ma song ngam/ / 'di dag sangs rgyas rgyur 'gro mi srid na//[243]
khyod kyi lta bas zhe sdang la sogs pa/ / nyes spyod sangs rgyas rgyu ru 'gyur [92] ba mtshar/ / gal te go cha'i sgrub pa ji bzhin du/ / gcig thub 'di la thams cad tshang zhe na//[244]
ba yi gci [93] ba chur bcas sbyin pa ste/ / zhes sogs gsungs pa de yis cis mi chog / de nyid tshig yin don la mi gnas na/ / khyod kyi smras de don gnas sgrub byed gang //[245]

243 If this were the case, then since the more you meditated on the selflessness of phenomena, the weaker these good qualities of refuge and so forth would become, would not view and conduct then become as incompatible as hot and cold? And if these [good qualities] did not serve as causes of buddhahood,

244 it is indeed strange that according to your view misdeeds like anger can serve as causes of buddhahood! If you assert that it is like armor practice[217] — all-inclusive — and that this [meditation] includes all the rest,

245 then why could not [a single practice of] generosity as in statements the likes of “anointing [a mandala] with cow dung and urine”[218] also be enough on its own? If, for you, this is just verbiage and not in fact true, what arguments can you put forth then to justify your assertions?
[92] 'gro ba/ rda sa shes dpar/
[93] lci ba/ rda sa shes dpar/

[217] This is a reference to first of “thirteen practices” (sgrub ba bcu gsum) presented in the first chapter of Maitreya’s Ornament of Realizations. The “all-inclusive” aspect of this “armor practice” (go cha’i sgrub pa) is that it ensures that one’s practice of each perfection includes the other five perfections as well. The opponent here is claiming that this one practice of nonmentation is a kind of panacea that encompasses all the bodhisattva practices.

[218] Gomchen refers here to a passage found in certain rituals, also quoted in the Middle-Length Treatise on the Stages of the Path, in which a mandala is offered after anointing the base with cow dung and urine, which in Indian culture is considered to have a cleansing effect. The example is given to illustrate an act of generosity in which the five other perfections are included. See Tsongkhapa, Middle-Length Treatise (trans.), 234.
gzhi yi bden gnyis skyon med 'jog shes na/ / lam gyi thabs shes 'bras bu'i sku gnyis kyang / / blo gros yangs la phyogs tsam bstan pas go/ / de phyir dngos rnams rang bzhin gyis med dang //[246]
rgyu 'bras cung zad ma 'chol nges ston pa'i/ / dmigs med thugs rje can la skyabs su mchi//

246 At the initial [learning] stage, if you know how to correctly establish the two truths, then, [when practicing] the path, method and wisdom will [be correct and] produce their results, the two kāyas.[219] Even a partial explanation will allow those of vast intelligence to understand this. Thus I pay homage to those endowed with objectless compassion,
247 who decisively teach existents’ lack of inherent nature without it contradicting cause and effect to the slightest degree.
[219] These are the two main “bodies” or facets of buddhahood: the truth body (dharmakāya) and the form body (rūpakāya).

f.d: gsum pa bslab pa la slob pa'i rim pa nyid bshad pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3. Explaining the process of training in the precepts
['di ]la gnyis/ theg chen spyi la bslab tshul/ khyad par rdo rje theg pa la bslab tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: how to train in the Great Vehicle in general and how to train in the Mantrayāna in particular. [49]
dang po theg chen spyi la bslab tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1. How to train in the great vehicle in general
['di ]la gsum/ byang sems kyi bslab pa la slob 'dod sbyang ba/ sbyangs nas rgyal sras kyi+i sdom pa bzung ba/ bzung nas ji ltar bslab pa'i tshul lo/ /
This has three parts: cultivating the desire to train in bodhisattva precepts; having cultivated it, taking the vows of the buddhas’ children; and having taken these, how to train in the precepts.
dang po byang sems kyi bslab pa la slob 'dod sbyang ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.1. Cultivating the desire to train in bodhisattva precepts

d.div: sngags dang so thar 'dul ba rang rang gi / sdom pa ma bzung bslab bya bslab mi rung //[247]
'dir ni sngon du bslab byas rgyud sbyangs nas/ / sdom pa blangs te shin tu brtan pa'i thabs//
Without having taken the mantra vows or those of individual liberation, it is not appropriate to train in those precepts.
248 Here, however, you first familiarize yourself with the precepts and then take the vows, a method that makes them very firm.

f.d: gnyis pa sbyangs nas rgyal sras kyi+i sdom pa bzung ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.2. Having cultivated it, taking the vows of the buddhas’ children

d.div: len tshul tshul khrims le'u'i rnam bshad blta//
For the way to take them, refer to the explanation found in the Ethics Chapter.[220]
[220] Gomchen is referring to the eighth chapter in Asaṅga’s Bodhisattva Grounds (Bodhisattvabhūmi). For an English translation by Art Engle, see Asaṅga, Bodhisattva Path, 237–311.

f.d: gsum pa bzung nas ji ltar bslab pa'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3. Having taken these, how to train in the precepts
['di ]la gsum/ gang la bslab pa'i gzhi/ der bslab pa rnams 'du tshul/ de la ji ltar bslab pa'i rim pa'o/ /
This has three parts: the basis of the training, how the precepts are included in these, and the process by which to train in them.
dang po gang la bslab pa'i gzhi ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.1. The basis of the training

d.div: byang sems bslab bya mtha' dag phyin drug tu//[248]
All the precepts fall within the six perfections.

f.d: gnyis pa der bslab pa rnams 'du tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.2. How the precepts are included in these
['di ]la gnyis/ dngos kyi don grangs nges pa/ zhar la go rim nges pa'o/ /
This has two parts: certainty with respect to the number of actual topics and, in addition, certainty as to their sequence.
dang po dngos kyi don grangs nges pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.2.1. Certainty with respect to the number of actual topics

d.div: phyin drug grangs nges tshul ni rnam pa drug / mngon mtho la ltos don gnyis sgrub la ltos/ / gzhan don sgrub dang theg chen thams cad bsdu/ / thabs kyi rnam pa'i dbang du mdzad nas dang //[249]
bslab pa gsum la ltos pa'i grangs nges sogs/ / phun tshogs rten gyis rang gzhan don ji 'dra/ / theg gang la gnas thabs kyi rnam pa cis/ / bslab pa gang bsgrub phyin drug las mi 'da'//[250]

249 There are six ways to determine the six perfections’ number. The number is certain in terms of: high rebirth, accomplishing the two goals, fulfilling others’ goals, and encompassing the entire Great Vehicle. It is established in terms of including the different methods.

250 Their number is also certain in terms of the three trainings. With an excellent life basis, whatever the goal — yours or others — whatever vehicle you abide in, whatever methods you use, and whatever trainings you accomplish, they will fall within [the practice of] the six perfections.

f.d: gnyis pa zhar la go rim nges pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.2.2. In addition, certainty as to their sequence

d.div: phyin drug snga ma la brten phyi ma skye/ / phyi ma phyi ma mchog tu gnas phyir dang / / snga ma snga ma rags pas go rim nges//[251]

251 Among the six perfections, a subsequent perfection arises based on the one that precedes it. Since each is superior to the one preceding it, and the preceding one is coarser than the subsequent one, the sequence is certain.

f.d: gsum pa ngos zung nas ji ltar bslab pa'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3. The process by which to train in them[221]

d.div: [221] The Tibetan edition is in error here. The heading should be corrected to read gsum pa de la ji ltar bslab pa’i rim pa.

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ spyod pa spyi la bslab tshul/ khyad par du phar phyin tha ma gnyis la bslab tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: how to train in [bodhisattva] practice in general and how to train in the last two perfections in particular.
dang po spyod pa spyi la bslab tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1. How to train in [bodhisattva] practice in general
['di ]la gnyis/ rang gi sangs rgyas kyi chos smon par byed pa phar phyin/ gzhan rgyud smin par byed pa bsdu bzhi la bslab pa'o/ /
This has two parts: training in the perfections that develop into buddha qualities and training in the four means of gathering others to mature their minds.
dang po rang gi sangs rgyas kyi chos smin par byed pa phar phyin
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.1. Training in the perfections that develop into buddha qualities
['di ]la drug/ sbyin pa/ tshul khrims/ bzod pa/ brtson 'grus/ bsam gtan/ shes rab la bslab tshul lo/ /
This has six parts: the way to train in generosity, ethical discipline, forbearance, diligence, meditative absorption, and wisdom. [50]
dang po sbyin pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.1.1. The way to train in generosity
['di ]la gsum/ sbyin pa'i ngo bo/ /rab dbye/ rgyud la skye tshul lo/ /
This has three parts: the nature of generosity, its divisions, and the way to cultivate it in you.
dang po sbyin pa'i ngo bo ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.1.1.1. The nature of generosity

d.div: gtong sems dge dang dge des kun slangs dang / / lus ngag sbyin la 'jug dus kyi sems pa/ / sbyin pa'i ngo bo'o
252 The virtuous intention to give and what that virtue motivates — the intention in the mind when engaging in physical or verbal giving — constitute generosity’s actual nature.

f.d: gnyis pa rab dbye ni/

d.div: dbye na chos sbyin sogs//[252]
Its divisions are giving Dharma and so on.[222]
[222] The three divisions of generosity are giving Dharma, giving material things, and giving protection or freedom from fear.

f.d: gsum pa rgyud la skye tshul ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.1.1.3. The way to cultivate it in you

d.div: bdog pa thams cad gzhan la gtong ba yi/ / bsam pa snying nas skyes pa mchog yin gyi/ / ser sna bcom tsam sbyin pa'i phar phyin min/ / gtong sems mthar phyin sbyin pa'i mthar thug bzung / /[253]
lus dang longs spyod dge ba dus gsum skyes/[94] / sbyin tshe phar phyin drug ldan gyis zin na/ / gnas skabs mthar thug dgos pa mtha' dag 'grub/ /[254]

253 The best is to generate the heartfelt thought to give all your possessions to others. The perfection of generosity is not the simple rejection of miserliness. Understand that generosity is complete when the intention to give has been perfected.
254 When you give your body, possessions, and virtue produced in the three times, if you infuse it with all six perfections, you will fulfill all your immediate and long-term needs.
[94] gsum gyis/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa tshul khrims ni/

d.div: sdom pa'i tshul khrims gtso bo'i dbang byas nas/ / gzhan gnod gzhir bcas las ldog spong sems ni/ / tshul khrims ngo bo dbye na rnam pa gsum/ / byang sems rgyud kyi so thar sdom pa ni//[255]
de rgyud tshul khrims sdom yin byang sdom min/ / byang sems sdom pa'i tshul khrims nyams gyur na/ / de yis sdom pa thams cad nyams par gsungs/ / rang gis ji ltar khas blangs bslab pa'i gnas//[256]

phra mo rnams kyang g.yel med gtsang bar bsrung / / khrims gtsang skye rgu'i dbus na ri [95] ltar brjid/ / stobs kyis bsdigs [96] pa med par 'gro kun 'dud/ / skyon bral rgyan du 'gyur sogs phan yon mang //[257]

255 Referring mainly to the ethic of abstention, ethical discipline consists of the intention to give up and turn from harming others along with its bases;[223] it has three divisions.[224] The vow of individual liberation within a bodhisattva’s mind

256 is the vow of ethical discipline, not the bodhisattva vow.[225] If the bodhisattva vow of abstention degenerates, it is taught that all vows decline as a consequence. The precepts to which you have committed yourself,

257 even the subtlest, are to be kept pure without exception. Among sentient beings, those with pure ethical discipline are as majestic as mountains. Without duress or coercion, all beings pay them homage. They are faultless, adorned thereby, and so on — its benefits are numerous.
[95] lhun ltar/ rda sa shes dpar/
[96] sdig pa/ rda sa shes dpar/
[223] The three bases of harming others are the three mental nonvirtues: covetousness, ill will, and wrong views.
[224] On the three divisions of ethics, see pages 323–36.

[225] This is because their causes differ: when taking the vows of individual liberation, you vow to keep them for the duration of that life, whereas when taking bodhisattva vows, you vow to keep them until you attain buddhahood.

f.d: gsum pa bzod pa ni/

d.div: bzod pa'i ngo bo gnod byed sdug bsngal gyis/ / mi rdzi chos la mos pa'i sems pa'o/ / dbye na chos la nges sems la sogs gsum/ / gnod sems log ltas dge rtsa bcom pa dang //[258]
mi dge stobs bzhis sbyangs pa gnyis ka la/ / rkyen gzhan phrad kyang 'bras bu 'byin mi nus/ / de yang rnam smin bcom pa'i don yin gyis/ / rgyu mthun la ni nges pa med par gsungs//[259]

258 The nature of forbearance is not being affected by another’s harm or by suffering and having belief in the teaching. Its divisions are threefold — certainty regarding the Dharma and so forth.[226] Neither virtues destroyed by ill will and wrong views

259 nor nonvirtues neutralized by the four powers can produce their results, even when the conditions for them are met. This is what is meant by “destruction of the maturation effect.” It is taught that it is not necessarily the same for effects concordant with the cause.

[226] The three divisions are the patience dwelling in certainty about the Dharma, the patience of disregarding harm that others inflict on us, and the patience of accepting the suffering we experience.

log lta dam chos spong dang nga rgyal gyis/ / byang sems bla ma sogs la khyad gsod pa/ / rnam smin tshabs che dge rtsa 'joms pas na/ / khong khro lta bu 'di dag 'bad pas dgag / mdor na mi bzod pa dang bzod pa yi/ / phan yon nyes dmigs dran pa'i 'jug ldog gces//[260]

260 Because holding wrong views, abandoning the sacred teaching, scorning bodhisattvas or gurus out of pride, and so on produce very serious maturation effects and destroy virtues the same way anger does, you are to strive to put an end to them as well. [51] In brief, with respect to forbearance and non-forbearance, be mindful of their benefits and drawbacks, and prize adopting the one and rejecting the other.

f.d: bzhi pa brtson 'grus ni/

d.div: dge ba sdud dang sems can don byed la/ / spro bas rab phye'i sems pa brtson 'grus te/ / bskal pa grangs med bye ba 'bum 'gyur du/ / sems can gcig gi sdug bsngal bsal phyir yang //[261]
dmyal ba kho nar gnas kyang rdzogs byang la/ / spro bar cis mi 'gyur zhes go cha dang / / dge ba chos sdud sems can don byed gsum/ / sgyid lug bdag nyid brnyas dang ngan zhen spang //[97][262]

261 Diligence is mainly a mental state of delight in collecting virtue and helping sentient beings. For the sake of alleviating a single being’s suffering, abiding exclusively in the hells for billions and billions of countless eons

262 without allowing your zeal for complete enlightenment to wane is called “armor-like [diligence].” Adding to this the diligence for collecting virtue and for accomplishing sentient beings’ welfare, there are three. Reject sloth, self-deprecation, and attachment to negative activities.
[97] spangs/ rda sa shes dpar/
mthun rkyen mos brtan dga' dang dor ba'i stobs/ / dge la 'dun dang phar phyin drug ldan gyis/ / brtson 'grus la gnas gzhan yang tshul der 'god//[263]

263 Its conducive conditions are the powers of aspiration, constancy, joy, and suspension.[227] While associating it with the six perfections and aspiring to virtue, abide in diligence and nurture it in others as well.
[227] When you are becoming physically and mentally overtired, you are to suspend your practice of diligence and rest for a while before continuing.

f.d: lnga pa bsam gtan ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.1.5. Meditative absorption

d.div: bsam gtan ngo bo dge ba'i dmigs pa la/ / rtse gcig gnas pas rab phyi'i sems pa ste/ / ngo bo'i sgo nas 'jig rten de 'das gnyis/ / phyogs kyi sgo nas zhi lhag zung 'brel gsum//[264]

264 Meditative absorption is defined mainly as a mental state that focuses one-pointedly on a virtuous object. In terms of nature there are two kinds: mundane and supramundane. In terms of orientation there are three: tranquil abiding, insight, and both combined.
lus sems bder gnas yon tan mngon par bsgrub/[98] / sems can don byed byed las sgo nas dbye/ / gang la mnyam bzhag [99] lus sems shin sbyangs skye/ / mngon shes rnam thar zad par zil gnon sgrub//[265]
don bya bcu gcig ji ltar rigs sgrub rnams/ / byed las sgo nas phye ba gsum gyi don/ / phan yon nyes dmigs shes nas 'jug pa dang / / phar phyin drug ldan slob pa sngar dang 'dra//[266]

265 In terms of function, the divisions are: generating physical and mental bliss, achieving good qualities, and helping sentient beings. [The three functions are defined:] (1) whenever you enter a state of absorption, physical and mental pliancy arise, (2) you achieve the clairvoyances, liberations, totalities, and masteries,

266 and (3) you practice the eleven ways to assist others as needed.[228] These are the three divisions according to function. While aware of the benefits [of engaging] and the drawbacks [of not engaging], engage in it. As before, train in it while associating it with all six perfections.
[98] sgrub/ rda sa shes dpar/
[99] ma dper mnyam gzhag ces byung yang rda sa shes dpar ltar bcos/
[228] The details of these second and third functions are drawn from chapter 4 of Maitreya’s Ornament of Realization (Abhisamayālaṃkāra).

f.d: drug pa shes rab ni/

d.div: shes rab brtags pa'i dngos po la dmigs nas/ / chos rab rnam par 'byed pa'i sems pa ste/ / dbye na don dam kun rdzob rtogs pa dang / / sems can don byed shes rab gsum du gsungs//[267]

267 Wisdom observes an examined object and is a state of mind that analyzes phenomena thoroughly. Three divisions are taught: wisdom that realizes the ultimate, the conventional, and the welfare of sentient beings.
shes rab mthong dang ma mthong yon tan rtsa/ / srid zhi'i rgud pa mtha' dag drungs 'byin cing / / 'gal bar snang ba'ang 'di yis 'gal med sgrub/ / 'di bral lta ba tshul khrims dag mi 'gyur//[268]

268 Wisdom is the root of visible and invisible good qualities. It eradicates all the misfortunes of cyclic existence and of [personal] peace. It reconciles what appears to be incompatible. Without it, views and ethical discipline will be flawed.

thos bsam don la shes rab kyis dpyad na/ / sgom 'bras mchog gi shes rab myur du 'dren/ / chos brjed bcug nas sems 'dzin la re ba/ / nor dbyig bor nas rjes la zhen dang mtshungs/ / de phyir drug ldan shes rab nyams su blang //[269]

269 Using wisdom to analyze the topics of learning and reflection quickly leads to sublime wisdom, the fruit of meditation. Letting yourself forget the teaching and placing all your hopes in meditative absorption is like letting valuable cattle go and clinging to their hoofprints. [52] Therefore practice wisdom while associating it with all six perfections.

f.d: gnyis pa gzhan rgyud smin par byed pa bsdu bzhi la bslab pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.1.2. Training in the four means of gathering others to mature their minds

d.div: mkho ba sbyin pa srog la'ang mi phangs sogs/ / snyan smra phar phyin gdul bya la ston dang / / don spyod ji ltar bstan rnams len 'jug cing / / don mthun gzhan sbyar dang mthun rang gnas pas//[270]
gzhan rgyud smin pa'i gnad bzhi 'dir brtson bya/ / mkho ba sbyin pa dga' zhing tshig la nyan/ / de tshe snyan smras mi shes the tshom dor/ / don spyod bskul bas bsgrub par 'dod blo skye//[271]

270 “Giving necessities” [is giving] even your life and the rest without hesitation. “Pleasant speech” is teaching disciples the perfections. “Implementation of practice” is prompting them to implement what you have taught. “Consistency with practice” is doing what you have taught others to do.

271 Strive at these key elements to mature others’ minds. Giving necessities gladdens them, and they then heed you. Next, pleasant speech dispels their ignorance and doubts. Encouraging implementation of practice inspires them to accomplish it.

don mthun rang bsgrub gzhan gyi mthun dper 'dzin/ / phyin drug mnyam rjes gnyis su bskyang ba'i tshe/ / zhi lhag chos zab nges bzod mnyam bzhag [100] dang / / sbyin pa tshul khrims bzod pa'i phyogs gcig dang //[272]
bsam gtan shes rab phyogs gcig rjes thob bskyang / / 'jug sdom ma bzung gong du spyod pa la/ / spro ba shugs drag bsgrubs nas gdengs thob na/ / cho gas bzung tshe shin tu brtan par 'gyur//[273]

272 Consistency with practice is practicing yourself such that others take you as a model. Concerning cultivating the six perfections in meditative equipoise and post-equipoise, you cultivate tranquil abiding, insight, and the forbearance that is certainty regarding the profound Dharma in meditative equipoise and generosity, ethical discipline, part of forbearance,

273 and parts of meditative absorption and wisdom in post-equipoise.[229] If, before taking the vows of engagement, you have developed great enthusiasm for [bodhisattva] practice and become confident [that you can uphold them], they will be very firm when you take them in a ceremony.
[100] ma dper mnyam gzhag ces byung yang rda sa shes dpar ltar bcos/
[229] Although the author has not specified it, diligence is cultivated both in equipoise and post-equipoise.

f.d: smon sems sbyangs [101] pa dang rgyal sras kyi spyod pa spyi la slob pa'i sgo rnam par nges pa bshad zin to// //
This concludes the explanation of how to ascertain well the way to cultivate aspirational bodhicitta and train in bodhisattva practice in general.

d.div: [101] sbyong ba/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: khyad par du phar phyin tha ma gnyis la bslab pa/

b.i: Introduction to Tranquil abiding and Insight

f.d: gnyis pa khyad par du phar phyin tha ma gnyis la bslab pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2. How to train in the last two perfections in particular[230]

d.div: [230] Tranquil abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are, respectively, the very essence of the perfections of meditative absorption and wisdom.

f.d: ['di ]la drug /zhi lhag bsgom pa'i phan yon/ de gnyis ting 'dzin kun gyi sdud byed du bstan pa/ zhi lhag gi ngo bo/ gnyis ka bsgom dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan/ go rim nges tshul/ so so'i bslab tshul lo/ /

This has six parts: the benefits of cultivating tranquil abiding and insight, explaining how all states of concentration are included in the two, the nature of tranquil abiding and insight, why it is necessary to cultivate both, how the order is certain, and how to train in each.
dang po zhi lhag bsgom pa'i phan yon ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.1. The benefits of cultivating tranquil abiding and insight

d.div: dge la dmigs pa'i rtse gcig sems dang ni/ / so sor 'byed pa'i rnam dpyod phra mo yan/ / rim bzhin zhi lhag gnyis kyi phyogs 'du zhing / / sems kyi steng gi yul can phyin ci log/[274]

gong nas gong du bskyed pa'i bag chags dang / / bag chags de nyid gso bar byed pa yi/ / yul la log par zhen blo gang yin pa/ / gnas ngan len dang mtshan ma'i 'ching bar bsnyad/ / de dag lhag mthong zhi gnas sgom pas sel//[275]

274 All mental states of one-pointed focus on virtuous objects and all states of wisdom of discriminating analysis — be they initial or more — are included in the categories of tranquil abiding and insight, respectively. The latent predispositions that generate more and more

275 wrong perceptions in the mind, and the states of mind that by wrongly conceiving their objects activate these latent predispositions are known [respectively] as “dysfunctional tendencies” and “bondage to signs.” They are eliminated by cultivating tranquil abiding and insight.

f.d: gnyis pa de gnyis ting 'dzin kun gyi sdud byed du bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.2. Explaining how all states of concentration are included in the two

d.div: bsam gtan sher phyin yon tan gang yin pa/ / de kun zhi lhag yon tan yin pas na/ / ting 'dzin kun gyi sdud byed zhi lhag gnyis/ / nges par bstan pas gang de theg gsum gyi/ / yon tan rtsa ba bsgrub par rgyal bas gsungs//[276]

276 Since the good qualities, whatever they are, of the perfections of meditative absorption and wisdom [53] are qualities of tranquil abiding and insight, by thoroughly practicing both tranquil abiding and insight, which include all states of concentration, you accomplish the roots of the good qualities of the three vehicles that the Buddha taught.

f.d: gsum pa zhi lhag gi ngo bo ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.3. The nature of tranquil abiding and insight

d.div: phyi rol yul la g.yeng zhi dmigs pa la/ / rtse gcig ngang nas rnam par mi dpyod blo/ / shin sbyangs bde bas drangs gang zhi gnas te/ / zhi gnas rta la skyon pa'i dpyad sgom gyis/ / rang stobs shin sbyangs drangs tshe lhag mthong thob/ / de phyir khyad par mthong bas lhag mthong btags//[277]

277 Tranquil abiding is a nonanalytical mental state that, having quelled distraction to external objects, abides one-pointedly on its object and is induced by the bliss of pliancy. When analytical meditation, riding the mount of tranquil abiding, induces pliancy by its own power, special insight is attained. Since it perceives distinctly, it is called “special insight.”

f.d: bzhi pa gnyis ka bsgom dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.4. Why it is necessary to cultivate both [tranquil abiding and insight]

d.div: gang dag gsal cha'i ngar med zhi gnas dang / / de yod lhag mthong 'dod pa mi rigs te/ / khyad par de ni bying ba yod med yin/ / zhi gnas la yang bying ba sangs dgos shing //[278]
bying ba bral ba'i ting 'dzin thams cad la/ / sems kyi gsal cha nges par 'ong phyir ro/ / stong nyid la dmigs zhi lhag gang yin kyang / / stong nyid rtogs dgos mi rtog ting 'dzin la//[279]

stong nyid rtogs pa'i nges pa med pa'i phyir/ / stong nyid blo kha ma phyogs ting 'dzin dang / / stong nyid rtogs pa'i ting 'dzin gnyis ka la'ang / / bde gsal mi rtog 'byung bas mkhyen par mdzod//[280]

279 and all states of concentration free of laxity are guaranteed to have mental clarity. Whether it is tranquil abiding or insight that is observing emptiness, in either case emptiness must be understood; however, given that

280 not all nonconceptual states of concentration necessarily realize emptiness, you should keep in mind that both states of concentration not aimed at emptiness and states of concentration that understand emptiness can be blissful, clear, and nondiscursive.

zhi gnas grub nas yin lugs la dpyod pa'i/ / shes rab de yi g.yo ba'i skyon bzlog par/ / ma zad dpyad sgom dgos pa thams cad la/ / yul la ha cang g.yo ba'i skyon bsal nas/ / dge ba gang byed stobs dang ldan par gyur//[281]

281 With the achievement of tranquil abiding, not only does the wisdom analyzing the ultimate mode of being surmount the fault of instability, every topic requiring analytical meditation avoids the fault of excessive instability, and this strengthens any virtue that is accomplished.

f.d: lnga pa go rim nges tshul ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.5. How the order is certain

d.div: zhi lhag rim bskyed dgos pa'i lugs 'di la/ / sngon du bdag med go ba'i gang zag gis/ / stong nyid la dmigs zhi lhag dus gcig tu/ / bskyed na nyes pa ci yod ces 'dri na//[282]

282 As regards the present system in which tranquil abiding and insight must be produced in that order, one might ask, “What is wrong with a person with a preexisting understanding of selflessness achieving tranquil abiding and the insight into emptiness concurrently?”
yin lugs go dang myong ba skye tsam la/ / zhi gnas sngon 'gro dgos zhes mi smra yang / / stong nyid sgom byung ma thob gang zag gis/ / dpyad sgom sngon song med par stong nyid la//[283]
dmigs pa'i sgom byung dag gi lhag mthong ni/ / skye ba rnal 'byar blo _med la srid kyi/ / rgyud sde 'og ma gsum dang skabs 'dir ni/ / zhi gnas ma grub gong du bdag med pa'i//[284]
go ba btsal nas yang yang dpyad gyur kyang / / de tsam gyis ni zhi gnas 'grub mi srid/ /

283 [Answer:] We do not assert that having a simple understanding and experience of the ultimate mode of being requires achieving tranquil abiding first. For a person who does not yet have [a realization of] emptiness arisen-from-meditation, attaining special insight arisen-from-meditation with emptiness as its object

284 without prior analytical meditation is possible in highest yoga [tantra], but in the three lower classes of tantra and in this [sutra] context, although you may seek an understanding of selflessness
285 and analyze it repeatedly before you achieve tranquil abiding, that alone will not allow you to achieve tranquil abiding. [54]
gal te mi dpyod 'jog sgom nyid byed na/ / zhi gnas grub [102] kyang de la lhag mthong gi/[285]
skyong tshul med pas sngon du zhi gnas dang / / de rjes lhag mthong rim pa las ma 'das/ / lhag mthong bskyed tshul sor rtog shes rab kyis/ / dpyad nas shin sbyangs skyes pa nyid yin pas//[286]
ji lta ji snyed gang gi dbang byas kyang / / rim pa de ltar nges kyi gzhan du na/ / mdo dang mkhas grub du ma'i gzhung dang 'gal/ / rim pa de yang gsar skye'i tshe yin gyi//[287]
phyi nas lhag mthong sngon du bsgom pa dang / / nyer bsdogs kyis bsdus lhag mthong la brten nas/ / dngos gzhis bsdus pa'i zhi gnas sgrub pa'ang yod//[288]
If you practice nonanalytical placement meditation, you may achieve tranquil abiding, but since you lack
286 training in insight, you will achieve tranquil abiding first and insight only later, and thus the order remains the same. Insight is achieved by discerning wisdom’s analysis inducing pliancy.

287 Whether it is in relation to the way things are [ultimately] or in their diversity,[231] the order is certain; if it were otherwise, it would contradict the sutras and the treatises of numerous scholars and practitioners. This order concerns an initial attainment.

288 Afterward, you may meditate on insight first. Thanks to insight included in the preparatory stage [of the first absorption], some achieve the tranquil abiding that is included in the actual absorption.[232]
[102] 'grub/ rda sa shes dpar/
[231] These terms, “the way things are” (ji lta ba) and “things in their diversity” (ji snyed pa), refer respectively to the ultimate and conventional truths.

[232] The “preparatory” (nyer bsdogs) is the culmination of the nine stages of tranquil abiding and the initial stage of absorption of the first of the form realm’s four levels of meditative absorption (dhyāna) but not yet the “actual” (dngos gzhi) stage. When insight belonging to the preparatory stage gives rise to the actual stage of absorption, the sequence can be said to be reversed. See also note 247.

f.d: drug pa so so'i bslab tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6. How to train in each
['di ]la gsum/ zhi gnas la bslab tshul/ lhag mthong la bslab tshul/ de gnyis zung du 'brel tshul lo/ /
This has three parts: how to train in tranquil abiding, how to train in special insight, and how to unite the two.
dang po zhi gnas la bslab tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1. How to train in tranquil abiding
['di ]la gsum/ zhi gnas kyi tshogs bsten pa/ de la brten nas zhi gnas bsgom tshul/ bsgoms pas zhi gnas grub pa'i tshad do/ /
This has three parts: relying on the prerequisites for tranquil abiding, the way to cultivate tranquil abiding on their basis, and the measure of having achieved tranquil abiding by meditation.
dang po zhi gnas kyi tshogs bsten pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.1. Relying on the prerequisites for tranquil abiding

d.div: mthun yul yon tan lnga ldan gnas pa dang / / 'dod chung chog shes bya nyung tshul khrims dag / 'dod pa'i rnam rtog spangs pa zhi gnas tshogs//

289 The prerequisites for tranquil abiding are to reside in a harmonious place that has five good qualities,[233] have few desires, be content, have few activities, have pure ethical discipline, and reject thoughts of desire.

[233] The five aspects of a harmonious place are good access to necessities like food, no threat of violence, no conditions conducive to illness, virtuous companionship, and few distractions in the day and little noise at night.

f.d: gnyis pa de la brten nas zhi gnas sgom tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2. The way to cultivate tranquil abiding on their basis
['di ]la gnyis/ sbyor ba dang dngos gzhi'o/ /
This has two parts: the preliminary phase and the central phase.
dang po sbyor ba ni/

d.div: byang chub sems sogs sbyor ba'i chos bsgoms te//[289]
Meditate on the preliminary topics, the awakening mind, and so forth.

f.d: gnyis pa dngos gzhi
['di ]la gnyis/ lus kyi spyod lam ci 'dra bas bsgom pa/ sgom pa'i rim pa nyid bshad pa'o/ /
This has two parts: in what physical posture to meditate and an explanation of the meditative process.
dang po lus kyi spyod lam ci 'dra bas bsgom pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.1. In what physical posture to meditate

d.div: dngos gzhi lus kyi kun spyod brgyad ldan gyis//
290 In the central phase, sustain the physical posture having eight features.[234]
[234] See Tsongkhapa, Middle-Length Treatise (trans.), 289.

f.d: gnyis pa sgom pa'i rim pa nyid bshad pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2. An explanation of the meditative process
['di ]la gnyis/ ting 'dzin skyon med skyed pa'i tshul/ de la brten nas sems gnas skye ba'i rim pa'o/ /
This has two parts: how to generate faultless states of concentration and how to produce the mental states on that basis.
dang po ting 'dzin skyon med skyed pa'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1. How to generate faultless states of concentration
['di ]la gsum/ sems dmigs pa la gtad pa'i sngon du ji ltar bya ba/ dmigs pa la gtad pa'i dus su ji ltar bya ba/ dmigs pa la gtad pa'i 'og tu ji ltar bya ba'o/ /
This has three parts: what to do before focusing the mind on the object of meditation, what to do while focusing on the object, and what to do once focused on the object.
dang po sems dmigs pa la gtad pa'i sngon du ji ltar bya ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.1. What to do before focusing the mind on the object of meditation[235]

d.div: [235] This section describes the advantages of tranquil abiding that you are to contemplate before you start to cultivate it.
dga' bdes lus rgyas mthong chos bde bar gnas/ / shin sbyangs rnyed pas dge la bkol rung dang / / rang dbang med par phyin ci log yul la//[290]

g.yeng ba zhi bas nyes spyod mi 'byung zhing / / dge ba'i stobs che mngon shes rdzu 'phrul myur/ / zab mo'i lhag mthong rtogs skye 'khor bar ldog/ / gzhan yang gang zhig bsgoms na ting 'dzin gyi/ / yon tan mthong bas yid 'phrog dad pa skye//[291]
de las 'dun pa de las rtsol ba skye/ / de las shin sbyangs des ni ting 'dzin las/ / nyams par byed pa'i le lo rnam par 'gog/[292]

Possessing joy and bliss, you are physically satisfied and achieve happiness in this life. Since you have achieved pliancy, your mind is amenable to virtue. As uncontrolled distraction toward incorrect objects [55]

291 has been quelled, misbehavior is avoided. Your virtue is potent, and you soon attain clairvoyance and other supernormal powers. Realizing insight into the profound, you gain freedom from cyclic existence. Moreover, regardless of what you meditate on, you are enchanted 292 with the evident advantages of states of concentration and this enhances your faith.
Faith induces aspiration, which in turn inspires diligence. From it arises pliancy, which completely precludes the laziness that weakens states of concentration.

f.d: gnyis pa sems dmigs pa la gtad pa'i dus su ji ltar bya ba
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2. What to do while focusing on the object
['di ]la gnyis/ sems gang la 'jog pa'i gzhi dmigs pa ngos bzung ba/ de la sems ji ltar gtod pa'i tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: identifying the object, the basis on which the mind is placed, and how to focus the mind on it.
dang po sems gang la 'jog pa'i gzhi dmigs pa ngos bzung ba
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.1. Identifying the object, the basis upon which the mind is placed
['di ]la gnyis/ dmigs pa spyi'i rnam gzhag /skabs su bab pa'i dmigs pa ngos bzung ba'o/ /
This has two parts: objects of meditation in general and determining the objects relevant to the present context.
dang po dmigs pa spyi'i rnam gzhag
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.1.1. Objects of meditation in general
['di ]la gnyis/ dmigs pa dngos bstan pa/ gang zag gang gis gang la dmigs par bya bar bstan pa'o//
This has two parts: the actual objects and indicating the objects suited to specific persons.
dang po dmigs pa dngos bstan pa ni/

d.div: khyab 1dang dpyad 2pa rnam sbyong mkhas 3pa dang / / nyon mongs sbyong ba 4zhes pa'i spyi dmigs bzhi//
293 Universal objects, objects purifying behavior, objects of skill, and those purifying afflictions are the four kinds of general objects.[236]
[236] For an explanation of these four objects, see Tsongkhapa, Middle-Length Treatise (trans.), 291–92.

f.d: gnyis pa gang zag gang gis gang la dmigs par bya bar bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.1.1.2. Indicating the objects suited to specific persons

d.div: bye brag 'dod chags shas che mi sdug nas/ / rnam rtog shas che 'byung rngub dmigs pa dang //[293]
gzhan yang chags sogs yul ni rnam gsum la/ / chags sogs che 'bring chung ngu'i skye tshul brtag / de ni chags sogs spang gnyen shes phyir yin//[294]
Specifically, the object for those with strong attachment is ugliness; For those with much distraction, the movements of their breath.

294 Furthermore, to discern the remedies that reject attachment and so forth, examine how, in relation to objects of attachment and so on, attachment and the rest arise with great, average, or lesser intensity.

f.d: gnyis pa skabs su bab pa'i dmigs par ngos bzung ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.1.2. Determining the objects relevant to the present context

d.div: rnam rtog che na rlung nyid dmigs par bzang / / de bzhin gshegs sogs sku la dmigs gyur na/ / dgos pa mang phyir 'di nyid nyams su len/ / ston pa'i sku gzugs shin tu legs pa la//[295]
yang yang blta zhing mtshan ma yid la bzung / / de ni sangs rgyas don spyi 'char phyir yin/ / de nas yid ngor sangs rgyas dngos dmigs la/ / rang la 'char sla'i sku'i cha rags rim nas//[296]

295 In the case of great distraction, breathing is the appropriate object. As taking the body of the Tathāgata and so on[237] as an object serves many purposes, practice that. By repeatedly observing an excellent likeness of the Teacher,

296 memorize his physical features. This will allow an image of the Buddha to appear in your mind. Next, mentally picture it as the actual Buddha. To facilitate its appearance, first meditate on the physical features roughly.
[237] “And so on” refers to deities’ seed syllables, like hūṃ, and their attributes, like Mañjuśrī’s sword.
bsgoms nas brtan par gyur tshe phra sgom gyis/ / dmigs pa mang pos zhi gnas 'grub mi srid/ / de yang dbu dang phyag gnyis khog pa dang / / zhabs gnyis rim bzhin lan 'ga' gsal btab la//[297]

297 When these have become stable, meditate on the details. Having many different objects of meditation precludes achieving tranquil abiding. You visualize several times sequentially the head, the two arms, the torso, and the two legs; [56]
de'i mthar sku yi spyi de yid ngo nas/ / dbu zhabs bar gyi yan lag rags pa rnams/ / cha phyed tsam du dus gcig 'char thub na/ / 'od dang bcas pa'i gsal po ma byung yang //[298]
de tsam gyis chog dmigs rten rnyed pa yin/ / de las gsal 'dod yang yang gsal btab na/ / gsal du 'gro yang ting 'dzin gegs su 'gyur/ / cher mi gsal yang dmigs rten ma 'phyugs na//[299]
ting 'dzin myur rnyed gsal cha bde blag 'grub/ / de tshe dmigs rten kha dog dbyibs grangs dang / / che chung 'gyur na de rjes mi 'brang bar/ / sngar gyi de nyid 'phyugs med gnad du bzung //[300]

298 when you, in the end, have a general mental image of the entire body together and distinguish the features roughly from head to foot including the limbs, it may not be clear and include its radiance,

299 but you should content yourself with it, for you have “found the object.” If you keep repeating the sequential visualization in hopes of making it clearer, it may become sharper, but it will hinder your state of concentration. It may not be very well defined, but if you do not err concerning the object,

300 you will soon attain a state of concentration and easily achieve clarity. At this stage, if the color, shape, size, or number of the object of meditation changes, do not pursue it; unerringly maintain the original object — this is of great importance.
cis kyang lha yi rnam pa 'char dka' na/ / sngar bstan pa yi+i dmigs pa gang rung ngam/ / stong nyid nges pa'i lta thog bzhag nas bzung / / zhi gnas 'grub pa dgos gtso yin phyir ro//[301]

301 If it is difficult to get an image of the deity to appear no matter what you do, place your mind on one of the other objects mentioned above or on the view ascertaining emptiness and maintain it there, as achieving tranquil abiding is the priority.

f.d: gnyis pa de la sems ji ltar gtod pa'i tshul
['di ]la gsum/ skyon med pa'i lugs bzhag /skyon dang bcas pa'i lugs bsal ba/ thun gyi tshad bstan pa'o/ /
This has three parts: presenting the flawless method, rejecting flawed methods, and explaining the duration of sessions.
dang po skyon med pa'i lugs bzhag pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.2.1. Presenting the flawless method

d.div: ting 'dzin khyad chos gnyis ldan sems shin tu/ / gsal ba'i gsal cha'i ngar dang ldan pa dang / / gang dmigs de la rtse gcig gnas pa yi/ / mi rtog pa yi gnas cha yod pa'o//[302]
302 The two attributes that states of concentration require are the vigorous clarity that is a very clear mind and the nondiscursive stability that remains one-pointedly on the chosen object.
kha cig bde dwangs bsnan nas bzhir 'dod kyang / / dwangs pa 'dis 'grub bde ba 'dir mi dgos/ / de phyir sngar bshad khyad par gnyis ldan des/ / gsal bar thon la bying bas bar gcod cing //[303]
rgod pas rtse gcig mi rtog la gnod pas/ / 'gal rkyen bying rgod phra rags ngos zin nas/ / mthun rkyen dran dang shes bzhin bstan pa gces/ / sngar nas nges pa'i dmigs rten rnam pa shar//[304]
dmigs rten la sems btags zhes thu re dran/ / dmigs pa la sems gzhan du mi g.yeng ba'o/ / de ltar yul dang 'dzin stangs byed las kyi/ / khyad par gsum ldan skabs 'di'i dran pa'i khyad//[305]

303 Some assert four, adding bliss and limpidity. However, limpidity is already present, and bliss is not needed at this point. Therefore, as explained above, it definitely requires two features. Laxity hinders the achievement of vigorous clarity,

304 and excitation thwarts one-pointed nondiscursiveness. So, having identified the contrary conditions — coarse and subtle laxity and excitation — prize relying on the conducive conditions — mindfulness and meta-awareness. Once the previously ascertained object of meditation has appeared,

305 vigorous mindfulness is said to “tie the mind” to it and prevent the mind from being distracted by other objects. Thus, in the present context, mindfulness has three features: a specific object, a mode of apprehension, and a function.[238]

[238] According to Asaṅga’s definition of mindfulness in the Compendium of Abhidharma (Abhidharmasamuccaya), its specific object is one that is familiar (in that one has previously perceived it), its mode of apprehension is not forgetful, and its function is the complete prevention of distraction.
de yang sngar bshad dmigs rten rnyed mtshams nas/ / shes pas de bzung sems ni dmigs pa la/ / btags so snyam pa'i 'dzin stangs shugs drag la/ / 'phangs mtho skyed nas gsar du gang la yang //[306]
mi dpyod blo de'i shugs ni ma chad par/ / rgyun skyong ba ni dran pa bsten pa'i gnad/ / ting 'dzin sgrub pa'i gtso bo'i skyong tshul yang / / dran pa'i skyong tshul nyid yin dran pa ni//[307]
nges pa'i rnam can 'dzin stangs yin pas na/ / nges shes 'dzin stangs dam po med pa la/ / gsal cha 'ong yang ngar ldan gsal cha med/ / dmigs rten med pa'i sgom la mos rnams kyang //[308]
ma yengs pa yi sgom gcig 'dod dgos la/ / ma yengs pa yang dmigs rten ma brjed pa'i/ / dran pa'i skyong tshul nyid las ma 'das gsungs//[309]

306 Furthermore, as explained above, once the object of meditation is found, the mind maintains it and thinks that it is tied to the object. Once a heightened and firm mode of apprehension [57] is achieved, without thinking of anything else,

307 you unwaveringly sustain the force of that state. This is the key point of applying mindfulness. Moreover, cultivating states of concentration consists mainly of sustaining mindfulness; as for mindfulness,

308 as its mode of apprehension is one of ascertainment [of the object], if the ascertainment’s mode of apprehension is not tight, clarity may be achieved but not vigorous clarity. Even those who believe in objectless meditation[239]
309 must admit distraction-free meditation, in which case, as it is taught, the way to sustain mindfulness, free of distraction, without losing the focal object does not differ.
[239] Objectless meditation (dmigs rten med pa’i sgom) is meditation that does not take an object such as the body of a deity and instead simply sustains the thought “I will conceive no object.”

f.d: gnyis pa skyon dang bcas pa'i lugs bsal ba ni/

d.div: kha cig sngar bshad dran pa'i gnad de la/ / bying ba med kyang rgod shas che snyam nas/ / slod [103] rab sgom rab 'byung zhes smra ba mthong / / 'di ni bying skyes sgom du 'khrul ba yin//[310]
gsal cha yod [104] pas skyon ni med snyam na/ / de ni rmugs dang bying ba ma phyed skyon/ / de phyir grims lhod ran pa'i mtshams bshad kyi/ / shes ldan don gnyer rnams kyis srog ltar bzung //[311]
'di tsam sdod na rgod pa skye bar 'dug/ / snyam pa'i tshad de las ni lhod dgos shing / / 'di tsam bzhag na bying ba skye bar 'dug / snyam pa'i tshad de las ni 'phangs mtho ba'i//[312]

310 Some think that mindfulness — the key point explained above — may be free of laxity but that it runs a great risk of excitation, and I have seen them declare that good relaxation is good meditation; this is a case of mistaking laxity for meditation.

311 If you think there is no such fault since clarity is present, in this case the mistake lies in not distinguishing lethargy from laxity. Therefore, I will explain the right balance between tightness and looseness, which the wise and the serious should guard as they do their life.

312 When you sense that were you to heighten [your focus on the object], excitation would occur, you must slacken it a degree. When you sense that were you to leave it as is, laxity would arise, you are to heighten it a degree.
[103] glod/ rda sa shes dpar/
[104] yong bas/ rda sa shes dpar/
'jog tshul rang gi rigs pas brtags na shes/ / dran pa'i 'dzin stangs ma nyams ngang nyid nas/ / rtsa ba'i dmigs la gnas dang mi gnas dang / / bying rgod gang skyes lta ba tsam byed pa'i//[313]
shes bzhin bya ras zur nas lta ba'i tshe/ / snga ma'i blo shugs ma zad tsam la ni/ / ha cang ring thung min par bar bar du/ / bya ra byed cing de bzhin bar bar du//[314]

dmigs pa snga ma dran tsam dran tsam byas/ / bskyangs na dran pa stobs che bying rgod rig / dran pa'i gnad 'dis ma zin sgom yun ring / / shes rab brtul zhing brjed ngas che ba mang / / yid kyis dmigs pa yang yang brjod pa ni/ / dran pa mi brjed 'dzin pa'i don du bzung //[315]

313 You will know how to place your mind by observing it intelligently, without letting mindfulness’s focus decline. Meta-awareness just observes and watches from a corner of the mind, checking whether the root object is still present

314 and whether laxity or excitation has arisen. Before the vigor of the initial state of mind is depleted, from time to time, neither too seldom nor too often, monitor it and, similarly from time to time,

315 recall the original object of meditation. Meditating thus with strong mindfulness, you will be aware of laxity and excitation. If you meditate for long periods without comprehending the key point of mindfulness, your mental acuity will decline, and your forgetfulness increase greatly. Understand the phrase “the mind expresses the object again and again”[240] to mean that mindfulness sustains it and does not forget it.

[240] Here Gomchen is referring to a passage in Tsongkhapa’s Great Treatise (trans., 3:54) that explains the phrase “mentally express the instructions on stabilizing your mind” from Sthiramati’s commentary on Differentiation of the Middle and Extremes (Madhyāntavibāghaṭīkā). We find the following: “Hence, non-forgetfulness of the object of meditation — wherein forgetfulness is stopped — is when you ‘mentally express’ the object of meditation; you bring the object of meditation to mind again and again.”

4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.2.2.3. Explaining the duration of sessions

d.div: gang zhig yengs nas 'gro ba'i brjed nges dang / / bying rgod myur bor ngos ma zin pa yi/ / shes bzhin mthu chung ba yi skyon 'dug na/ / grangs mang yun thung skyong ba gnad yin la//[316]

skyon gnyis log na sgom thun cung ring bya/ / thun tshod chu tshod gcig gam thun phyed dam/ / thun gcig de bzhin ji srid nus bar du/ / rang gi blo yi nus pa dang sbyar te/ / u tshugs mi bya bar chad bsal nas sgom//[317]

316 While you still have the fault of weak meta-awareness that fails to quickly identify the forgetfulness that tends to distraction as well as laxity and excitation, the instruction is to conduct frequent but short meditation sessions.

317 Once you have overcome both faults, you may extend the sessions slightly. Setting an hour or two hours as the duration of [58] a meditation session, continue as long as you are able. Adapting [the duration] to your personal mental capacity, without forcing yourself, meditate even as you reject obstacles.

4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.1. Applying the antidote to failing to identify laxity and excitation
['di ]la gnyis/ bying rgod kyi mtshan nyid gtan la dbab pa/ sgom pa'i dus su de rtogs pa'i shes bzhin skyed pa'i tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: the definitions of laxity and excitation and the way to produce meta-awareness that is aware of them in meditation.
dang po bying rgod kyi mtshan nyid gtan la dbab pa la rgod pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.1.1. The definitions of laxity and excitation

d.div: rgod pa'i ngo bo 'dod chags cha shas te/ / dmigs pa sdug cing yid du 'ong ba la'o/ / 'dzin stangs rnam par ma zhi 'phro ba ste/ / yul la sred pa'i rnam pas 'jug pa'o//[318]
byed las khyad par sems ni dmigs pa la/ / gnas pa'i bar chad byed pa'i las can no/ / bying ba dge dang lung ma bstan gang rung / / dmigs pa'i 'dzin stangs dam par mi byed pas//[319]
dwangs cha yod kyang gsal ba'i ngar med pa/ / rmugs pa mi dge'i sgrib la lung ma bstan/ / bying ba'i rgyu yin gti mug cha shas te/ / lus sems lci zhing las su mi rung ba'o//[320]

318 By nature, excitation springs from attachment. Its object is pleasant and attractive. Its mode of apprehension [of its objects] is troubled and scattered. It attends to its object with the aspect of craving.
319 Its specific function and role is to prevent the mind from remaining focused on its object. Since laxity, which is either virtuous or ethically neutral, does not apprehend the object tightly,

320 limpidity is present, but the clarity lacks vigor. Lethargy is either nonvirtuous or an ethically neutral obstruction. It causes laxity and springs from ignorance. It is physical and mental heaviness and unserviceability.

f.d: gnyis pa sgom pa'i dus su de rtogs pa'i shes bzhin bskyed thabs ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.1.2. The way to produce meta-awareness that is aware of them in meditation

d.div: bying rgod skye grabs nyid nas rig pa yis/ / shes bzhin stobs ldan bsten pa med gyur na/ / bying rgod go ba chags tsam 'dir phan med/ / de ltar shes bzhin skyong thabs gnyis yin te//[321]
sngar bshad dran pa'i bsten tshul rgyun chags dang / / de yi ngang las sems ni dmigs pa las/ / gzhan du 'phro 'am mi 'phro brtag pa yi/ / zur nas bya ra thu res 'dzin pa ni//[322]
shes bzhin skyong ba'i gnas ni gnyis pa ste/ / dran pa stobs ldan shes bzhin rgyu yin ltar/ / zur nas yang yang rtog pa'ang de'i rgyu'i phyir//[323]

321 When you see that either laxity or excitation is on the verge of arising, if you do not apply strong meta-awareness, the simple knowledge of what laxity and excitation are will be useless. There are two ways to sustain meta-awareness:

322 as explained above, by maintaining mindfulness continually and, within that state, by standing guard from a corner of the mind and monitoring whether or not the mind has moved from its object toward another.
323 The latter is the second part of the key point for sustaining meta-awareness, for just as strong mindfulness is a cause of meta-awareness, so is repeated monitoring from a corner of the mind.

f.d: gnyis pa ngos zin kyang de spong ba'i phyir du mi rtsol ba'i gnyen po bstan pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.2. Applying the antidote to failing to make an effort to reject them once identified
['di ]la gnyis/ sems pa ngos bzung zhing bying rgod 'gog pa'i tshul/ gang la brten nas bying rgod skye ba'i rgyu ngos bzung ba'o/ /
This has two parts: identifying intention, the way to reject laxity and excitation, [59] and identifying the causes from which laxity and excitation arise.
dang po sems pa ngos bzung zhing bying rgod 'gog pa'i tshul ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.2.1. Identifying intention, the way to reject laxity and excitation

d.div: khab len dbang gis lcags ni g.yo ba ltar/ / lung ma bstan dge mi dge gang rung la/ / sems ni bskul ba'i sems byung sems pa yin/ / 'dir ni bying rgod byung na mi rtsol ba'i//[324]
gnyen po mngon par 'du byed sems pa bzung / / bying ba sems ni nang du bsdus drags nas/ / dmigs pa'i 'dzin stangs shor ba yin pas na/ / 'di ni dga' ba bsgoms bzlog skyo bas min//[325]

324 Just as the presence of a magnet makes a piece of metal move, the mental factor of intention turns the mind toward virtue, nonvirtue, or the ethically neutral. In this context, direct application — intention — is the antidote

325 to making no effort when laxity and excitation occur. Since laxity arises when the mind is turned too far inward, and its apprehension of the object has loosened, it is by cultivating joy, not sadness, that you overcome it.

gzhan yang lha sku snang ba'i mtshan ma dang / / gang 'dod yul la dpyad spro gzengs kyang bstod/ / dmigs pa rgya skyed 'dzin stangs bstod pa dang / / 'chag dang kha ton rjes dran drug sgom dang //[326]
gdong chus 'khru zhing gza' skar blta ba dang / / byang chub sems dang dal 'byor yon tan bsam/ / bying ba'i rgyu dgag dang bar gang 'gyur bsgom/ / rgod pa chags pa'i dbang gis yul rgyug pas//[327]
[241] The “six recollections” are the Three Jewels, ethical discipline, generosity, and deities.
'di la mi rtag yid 'byung skyo shas sogs/ / sgom pas rgod pa ngang gis zhi 'gyur gyi/ / 'phro shas che na 'phral 'gugs man ngag yin/ / rgod shas che na 'phral du 'gugs pa'ang rung //[328]

328 In this case, meditating on impermanence, renunciation, disillusionment, and so forth will automatically mitigate excitation. When mental scattering prevails, the instruction is to bring the mind back immediately. When excitation predominates, it is also appropriate to instantly recall the mind.[242]

[242] This verse discusses two obstacles to tranquil abiding: excitation, which is first referred to in verse 318, and mental scattering. According to Palmang’s Mirror Reflecting the Mind (25a2), the latter is not necessarily an affliction and can be virtuous, nonvirtuous, and ethically neutral. An example of virtuous mental scattering is thinking about Avalokiteśvara when you are meditating on Buddha Śākyamuni. Nonvirtuous scattering can be distraction, such as your mind drifting to an object of irritation when you are meditating. Neutral scattering is when the mind moves away from its object into a vague state with no clear object. Excitation derives from attachment and is necessarily drawn to attractive objects. Distraction is broader in that it can derive from any of the three mental poisons — attachment, aversion, and ignorance — and be drawn to any number of objects. When excitation is intense, and strong measures are needed, the instruction is to put aside the initial object of meditation and contemplate topics such as death, the flaws of cyclic existence and so on. When it is mild, simply bringing the mind back to the object will be sufficient.

f.d: gnyis pa gang la brten nas bying rgod skye ba'i rgyu ngos bzung ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.1.2.2. Identifying the causes from which laxity and excitation arise

d.div: dbang po ma bsrungs [105] zas kyi tshod ma zin/ / nyal dang [106] mi brtson shes bzhin mi gnas pa/ / bying rgod thun mong rgyu yin bying ba'i rgyu/ / gnyid che ha cang zhi gnas bsten drags dang //[329]
mun pa ltar 'dug dmigs rten 'dzin mi dga'/ / rgod pa'i rgyu ni skyo ba shas chung dang / / brtson 'grus ma goms ha cang 'dzin stangs dam/ / yul dang nye du sogs la g.yengs pa'o//[330]

329 Not guarding the senses, not eating the right amount, [untimely] sleeping, lacking diligence, and not exercising meta-awareness are causes common to both laxity and excitation; the causes of laxity are over-sleeping, practicing tranquil abiding excessively,

330 remaining in a fog, and not delighting in maintaining the focal object. The causes of excitation are a lack of disenchantment, unfamiliarity with diligence, an excessively tight focus, and distraction by thoughts of home, loved ones, and so on.
[105] ma bsrung / rda sa shes dpar/
[106] nyal bar/ rda sa shes dpar/
bying rgod skye grabs nyid nas bzlog bya yi/ / phra la brnyas na'ang ting 'dzin skyon can 'gyur/ / 'phro rgod skyes tshe nang du gnas cha btsal/ / gnas tshe bying zon bya zhing gsal ngar 'don//[331]
dwangs pa tsam gyis chog shes mi bya'o/ / 'di yi mnyam 'jug re zhig rnyed dka' yang / / goms na sla bar mi 'gyur yod ma yin//[332]

331 When laxity and excitation are about to arise, you must avert them. Ignoring them because they are minimal will mar your state of concentration. When mental scattering and excitation occur, seek stability within. When stable, if you suspect laxity, generate vigorous clarity
332 and do not content yourself with simple limpidity. At first it is difficult to find a balance between them, but through habit it will not fail to become easier.

f.d: gnyis pa bying rgod dang bral dus ji ltar bya ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.1.3.2. What to do when laxity and excitation are absent

d.div: thun tshad re tsam bying rgod mi 'ong ba'i/ / gdengs thob mtshams nas 'du byed btang snyoms kyi/ / rtsol ba glod sgom 'dzin stangs ngar gtong [107] min/ / des na sbyong [108] ba'i tshe na le lo dang //[333]
ting 'dzin brtson tshe gdam ngag brjed pa dang / / mnyam par bzhag pa la ni bying rgod dang / / bying rgod byung tshe mi rtsol bying rgod dang / / bral tshe sems la 'du byed nyes pa lnga//[334]

333 Once you feel confident that laxity and excitation will not occur for the duration of a session, meditate with the factor of equanimity [60] and ease your exertion, without reducing the vigor of your focus. At the preliminary stage, [the main fault] is laziness.

334 When striving to concentrate, it is forgetting the instruction.[243] When in meditative equipoise, it is laxity and excitation. When laxity and excitation occur, it is non-exertion. When free of laxity and excitation, it is application; these are the five faults.
[107] ngar gtod/ rda sa shes dpar/
[108] de nas sbyor bas/ rda sa shes dpar/
[243] “Forgetting the instruction” means failing to maintain the object in the mind by means of mindfulness.
dad dang 'dun pa rtsol dang shin sbyangs bzhis/ / le lo sel zhing dran dang shes bzhin dang / / 'du byed btang snyoms bzhi yis rim pa bzhin/ / brjed ngas bying rgod 'du mi 'du byed sel//[335]
de ltar nyes pa lnga spong 'du byed brgyad/ / rnal 'byor bla med la yang dgos par bzhed//[336]

335 The four that are faith, aspiration, exertion, and pliancy counteract laziness; the four that are mindfulness, meta-awareness, application, and equanimity, respectively, counteract forgetfulness, laxity and excitation, non-application, and application.
336 In this way, the eight applications oppose the five faults. Be aware that they are needed in highest yoga tantra as well.

4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.2.3. How the four attentions are involved in this

d.div: bsgrims te 'jug pa dang / / chad cing 'jug dang chad [111] pa med par 'jug / rtsol med 'jug la yid byed mthar sbyar bzhi/ / dang po gnyis la yid byed dang po dang //[339]
de nas lnga la yid byed gnyis pa dang / / brgyad pa la ni yid byed gsum pa dang / / dgu pa la ni yid byed bzhi pa ste/ / dgu la yid byed bzhi yi yod tshul lo//[340]
. . . There is tight focus, intermittent focus, uninterrupted focus, and effortless focus; adding “attention” to each gives the four. The first attention applies to the first two [mental states],
340 the second attention to the next five, the third attention to the eighth, and the fourth attention to the ninth. This is how the four attentions apply to the nine.
[111] bar chad/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gsum pa bsgoms pas zhi gnas grub pa'i tshad
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3. The measure of having achieved tranquil abiding by meditation
['di ]la gsum/ zhi gnas grub pa dang ma grub pa'i mtshams bstan pa/ zhi gnas la brten nas lam bgrod tshul spyir bstan pa/ khyad par du 'jig rten pa'i lam bgrod tshul bstan pa'o/ /

This has three parts: explaining the line between achieving and not achieving tranquil abiding, explaining how to travel the spiritual path in general based on tranquil abiding, and explaining how to travel the mundane path in particular. [61]
dang po zhi gnas grub pa dang ma grub pa'i mtshams bstan pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.1. Explaining the line between achieving and not achieving tranquil abiding
['di ]la gnyis/ dngos kyi don bstan pa/ yid byed dang ldan pa'i rtags dogs gcod dang bcas pa'o/ /
This has two parts: the actual meaning and, secondly, the signs of having attention[244] and the elimination of doubts.

d.div: [244] Here and in the following sections, the term attention (yid byed ) is generally used as an equivalent to tranquil abiding.

f.d: dang po dngos kyi don bstan pa
['di ]la gnyis/ shin sbyangs rdzogs pa thob ma thob kyi sgo nas zhi gnas thob ma thob tu bstan pa/ shin sbyangs rdzogs par thob nas zhi gnas 'grub lugs bstan pa'o/ /
This has two parts: how attaining tranquil abiding depends on attaining complete pliancy and how tranquil abiding is achieved once complete pliancy is attained.
dang po shin sbyangs rdzogs pa thob ma thob kyi sgo nas zhi gnas thob ma thob tu bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.1.1.1. How attaining tranquil abiding depends on attaining complete pliancy

d.div: bying rgod med kyang brgyad pa'i gnas skabs na/ / dran shes bar ma chad du bsten dgos pas/ / mngon par 'du byed pa'am rtsol byas zer/ / dgu par 'di mi dgos pas rtsol med btags/ / 'on kyang da dung shin sbyangs ma thob par/ / 'dod pa'i sas bsdus yin gyi yid byed min//[341]

341 Neither laxity nor excitation is present in the eighth mental state, but since mindfulness and meta-awareness must still be applied continually, it is called direct application or effort. Given that this is not necessary in the ninth state, it is called effortless. Nevertheless, as pliancy has not yet been attained, it is still part of the desire realm and is not attention.

f.d: gnyis pa shin sbyangs rdzogs par thob nas zhi gnas 'grub lugs bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.1.1.2. How tranquil abiding is achieved once complete pliancy is attained

d.div: lus sems dge la 'dod bzhin bkol mi rung / / lus sems gnas ngan len zhes ming du btags/ / de dang bral nas lus sems dge ba la/ / shing bal bzhin du shin tu bkol rung 'gyur//[ 342]

342 The inability to direct the mind and body toward virtue as you wish is called mental and physical dysfunction. Once freed of it, the body and mind become as [malleable as] cotton fluff — completely serviceable to virtue.
bkol rung de nyid goms mthar shin sbyangs dang / / rtse gcig pa yi zhi gnas 'gyur bar gsungs/ / shin sbyangs skye ba'i snga ltas sgrub pa po'i/ / slang [112] ba bde bar lci sogs byung ma thag/[343]
sems dang lus kyi shin sbyangs rim bzhin skye/ / dang po shes pa gnyis pa reg byar bzhed/ / lus kyi shin sbyangs thog mar skyes pa'i tshe/ / lus sems dga' bde'i nyams dang ldan mod kyang //[ 344]

da dung mtshan nyid rdzogs shing brtag sla ba'i/ / shin sbyangs ma thob de yi rjes thog tu/ / dga' bde rags pas sems g.yo log gyur te/ / dri [113] ma ltar srab mi g.yo'i ting 'dzin dang / / mthun pa'i shin sbyangs thob tshe zhi gnas dang / / mnyam gzhag [114] sas bsdus yid byed chung ngu thob//[345]

343 It is stated that when familiarization with serviceability is complete, it becomes tranquil abiding: a one-pointed [main mind] accompanied by pliancy. According to the five signs portending pliancy, as soon as the meditator’s brain feels pleasantly heavy and so on,

344 mental and physical pliancy arise in succession. The former is known as a perception and the latter as a tangible object. When physical pliancy first occurs, although it is associated with physical and mental feelings of bliss and well-being,

345 still the easily identifiable signs of complete pliancy are yet to be attained. Subsequently, when any coarse bliss and well-being that could unsettle the mind have subsided and a state of immovable concentration, as subtle as a shadow, along with its concordant pliancy are achieved, then tranquil abiding and equipoise — the lowest attention belonging to the [form] realm — are attained.
[112] glang pa/ rda sa shes dpar/
[113] grib ma/ rda sa shes dpar/
[114] mnyam bzhag_rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa yid byed dang ldan pa'i rtags dogs gcod dang bcas pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.1.2. The signs of having attention and the elimination of doubts
['di ]la gnyis/ yid byed dang ldan pa'i rtags dngos/ dogs gcod bshad pa'o/ /
This has two parts: the actual signs of having attention and the elimination of doubts.
dang po yid byed dang ldan pa'i rtags dngos ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.1.2.1. The actual signs of having attention

d.div: gang gi yid byed 'di thob mtshan [115] ma ni/ / nyon mongs sbyong la nus ldan mnyam gzhag tshe/ / myur ba myur bar shin sbyangs gnyis skye dang / / sgrib pa lnga po phal cher mi 'byung zhing //[346]
rjes thob tshe yang shin sbyangs 'ga' res ldan/ / de tshe zhi gnas dag dang shin sbyangs gnyis/ / phan tshun gcig gis gcig spel grogs su 'gyur/ / mnyam gzhag ngo na rags snang kun log nas//[347]

sems ni mkha' dang 'dres pa lta bu dang / / langs tshe rang lus glo bur rnyed 'dra 'byung / / nyon mongs shugs zhan 'phro yang mthud [116] mi nus/ / gnas cha mthug cing gsal nyams shin tu che/ / gnyid dang ting 'dzin bsre nus rmi lam dag/[348]
347 a measure of pliancy persists post-equipoise; [62] having reached this level, tranquil abiding and pliancy each enhance the other’s development; in equipoise all coarse appearances cease,
[115] tshad ma/ rda sa shes dpar/
[116] 'thud mi/ rda sa shes dpar/
[245] The five obstructions are (1) excitation and regret, (2) ill will, (3) lethargy and sleep, (4) attraction to sense objects, and (5) doubt.

f.d: gnyis pa dogs gcod bshad pa ni/

d.div: des na sngar bshad yid byed ting 'dzin 'dis/ / bdag med lta ba don spyi'i tshul rtogs na/[117] / so skye'i skabs kyi thar lam tsam du 'jog / byang chub sems kyis zin na theg chen lam//[349]

zin byed med na ting 'dzin rang ngo'o/[118] / phyi nang gnyis ka'i thun mong nyid du gnas/ / de phyir bde gsal mi rtog ting 'dzin la/ / yin lugs tshul bzhin rtogs pa'i sgom du ni/ / song dang ma song gnyis yod phyed par mdzod//[350]

349 Then, as explained above, if the state of concentration that is attention realizes the view of selflessness by means of a mental image, it is posited simply as a path to liberation of a non-ārya. When it is instilled with the awakening mind, it will be a Great Vehicle path.

350 If neither is present, then by nature it will be the state of concentration that is common to both Buddhists and non-Buddhists. Thus, among states of concentrations characterized by bliss, clarity, and nondiscursiveness, a distinction must be made between meditative states that correctly realize the ways things ultimately are and those that do not.
[117] rtogs nas/ rda sa shes dpar/
[118] rang ngo bo/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa zhi gnas la brten nas lam bgrod tshul spyir bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.2. Explaining how to travel the spiritual path in general based on tranquil abiding

d.div: de yang phyi nang gnyis dang nang pa yi/ / theg pa gsum gyi rnal 'byor pa kun gyis/ / nyon mongs mngon gyur sa bon gang spong ba'i/ / zhi rags rnam pa can dang khams bco brgyad//[ 351]
mtshan nyid rig dang bden rnam can la sogs/ / lhag mthong mtha' dag thog mar 'di brten nas/ / sgrub dgos de phyir sngar bshad zhi gnas 'di/ / nyer bsdogs mi lcogs med pa zhes byar bsnyad//[352]

351 Furthermore, both non-Buddhists and Buddhists and all yogis of the three Buddhist vehicles must first rely on tranquil abiding to achieve all the various kinds of special insight: those that eliminate manifest afflictions with the coarse and peaceful aspects[246]

352 and those that eliminate their seeds; or those that have the aspect of the eighteen elements, the discernment of characteristics, the truths, and so forth. Consequently, as explained above, tranquil abiding is called “the enabling preparatory phase of the first absorption.”[247]

[246] In insight meditation on the coarse and peaceful aspects, you begin by viewing the desire realm’s joys as coarse and those of the first absorption of the form realm as more refined (literally “peaceful”) and pursue the latter. The same process is followed for the subsequent levels of the form and formless realms.
