However as the afflictions are not opposed by the direct antidote to their root cause, grasping at self, these meditations do not culminate in liberation from cyclic existence and as such constitute a mundane path. Supramundane insight meditation views the sixteen aspects — impermanence and so forth — of the four noble truths, for example, in pursuit of the view of selflessness to eliminate the root cause of the afflictions and thereby achieve liberation from cyclic existence.

[247] The “enabling” (mi lcogs med ) preparatory phase, which, as its name implies, is achieved prior to the actual first absorption (dhyāna) of the form realm, is so called because its attainment enables the realization of insight. Of its seven divisions, the first two are called “novice at attention” and “novice at purification of afflictions.”

zhi rags rnam pa can gyi lhag mthong ni/ / sangs rgyas pa la'ang yod mod nges par min/ / phyi rol pa la bden sogs lhag mthong med/ / bla med pas kyang bskyed rim skabs su ni/ / zhi gnas bsgrub kyang de ni zhi rags kyi/ / rnam pa can gyi lhag mthong sgrub phyir min//[353]

353 Concerning insight with the coarse and peaceful aspects, some Buddhists practice it while others do not. Non-Buddhists do not have insight [with the sixteen aspects of the four] truths and so on. Practitioners of highest yoga tantra, when at the generation stage, may also achieve tranquil abiding but not for the purpose of achieving insight with the coarse and peaceful aspects.

f.d: gsum pa khyad par du 'jig rten pa'i lam bgrod tshul bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.1.3.3. Explaining how to travel the mundane path in particular

d.div: sems gnas dgu pa nas bzung yid byed par/ / yid la byed pa'i las dang po zhes bzhag / yid byed thob nas mtshan nyid so sor rig/ / bar 'dir nyon mongs rnam sbyong las dang por//[354]

nyan sar bshad phyir nyer bsdogs thog ma dang / / mtshan nyid so sor rig gnyis dus mnyam min/ / gal te de gnyis mnyam par rtogs na ni/ / 'jog sgom sngon du ma song zhi gnas dang / / nyer bsdogs sngon du'ang zhi gnas yod par 'gyur//[ 355]

354 The attention from the ninth mental state up to attention [tranquil abiding] is called “novice at attention.” The one from the attainment of attention up to [and including] discernment of characteristics is called “novice at purification of afflictions,”

355 as explained in the Śrāvaka Grounds. Thus, the first [of the seven divisions] of the preparatory phase and the discernment of characteristics are not concurrent. [63] If the two were considered concurrent, tranquil abiding without prior placement meditation would be possible, as would tranquil abiding prior to the preparatory phase.

f.d: bsam gtan phar phyin gyi ngo bo zhi gnas la 'jug pa'i sgo rnam par nges pa bshad zin to// //
This completes the explanation ascertaining well the gateway to tranquil abiding — the nature of the perfection of meditative absorption.
lhag mthong la bslab pa'i tshul/
gnyis pa lhag mthong la bslab pa'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2. How to train in special insight
['di ]la bzhi/ lhag mthong gi tshogs bstan pa/ lhag mthong gi rab dbye/ lhag mthong sgom pa'i tshul/ bsgoms pas lhag mthong grub pa'i tshad do/ /
This has four parts: relying on the prerequisites for insight, the divisions of insight, how to cultivate insight, and the measure of having achieved insight through meditating.
dang po lhag mthong gi tshogs bstan pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1. Relying on the prerequisites for insight
['di ]la gnyis/ lhag mthong gi tshogs bsten tshul spyir bstan/ khyad par du lta ba gtan la 'bebs tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: a general presentation of how to rely on the prerequisites for insight and how to establish the view in particular.
dang po lhag mthong gi tshogs bsten tshul spyir bstan ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.1. A general presentation of how to rely on the prerequisites for insight

d.div: klu sgrub 'phags pa lha sogs tshad ldan gyi/ / gzhung dang de dag dgongs 'grel rnam bshad rnams/ / nyan nas drang nges phyed pa'i rnam dpyod kyis/ / yang dag lta ba gtan la 'bebs pa ni//[356]

rnam par nges pa'i lhag mthong rgyu tshogs te/ / de phyir sangs rgyas bskyangs dang zla ba'i gzhung / / gzhir bzhag gzhan yang zab mo'i gzhung mchog ni/ / mtha' dag brjod bya'i zab khyad 'di longs shig/[357]

356 Studying the authoritative works of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva and the commentaries that expound their intentions and establishing the excellent view with the intellect that distinguishes the definitive meaning from the provisional

357 are the vital prerequisites for special insight. Consequently, rely primarily on the works of Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti, and relate to them the deep and distinctive contents of all other excellent treatises on the profound.

f.d: gnyis pa khyad par du lta ba gtan la 'beb tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2. How to establish the view in particular
['di ]la gsum/ nyon mongs can gyi ma rig pa ngos bzung ba/ de 'khor bar 'khor ba'i rtsa bar bstan pa/ bdag 'dzin de spong bar 'dod pas bdag med kyi lta ba btsal ba'o/ /

This has three parts: identifying the affliction ignorance, demonstrating that it is the root of turning in cyclic existence, and seeking the view of selflessness out of a wish to eliminate grasping at self.
dang po nyon mongs can gyi ma rig pa ngos bzung ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.1. Identifying the affliction ignorance

d.div: thog ma med nas rtog pa'i dbang gis ni/ / bzhag pa min par rang gi ngo bo yi/ / sgo nas yul steng du grub 'dzin pa ni/ / dgag bya bden par 'dzin pa'i tshul yin pas//[358]
de [119] gzhan yul la bdag gam rang bzhin zer/ / de nyid khyad gzhi gang zag chos steng du/ / med pa gnyis ni bdag med gnyis yin pas/ / de nyid khyad gzhi de nyid kyi steng du//[359]
yod par zhen blo gnyis kyang bdag 'dzin gnyis/ / dbu sems kha cig gang zag bdag 'dzin gyi/ / dmigs par nga tsam 'dzin pa bzhed mod kyang / / nga tsam de yi mtshan gzhi dris pa'i tshe//[ 360]
kun gzhi dang ni yid kyi rnam shes sogs/ / yin tshul so sor smra yang lugs 'dir ni/ / nga'o snyam pa tsam zhig skye ba yi/ / dmigs pa'i nga tsam de yi dmigs par bzhed//[361]
358 The object of negation, true existence, is grasped not conceptually but as established by way of its own nature, from the side of the object, since beginningless time.

359 This conceived object is known as “self” or “nature.” In relation to their bases — persons and phenomena — the two absences [of this object] constitute the two forms of selflessness; as such, the two thoughts conceiving this mode of existence

360 in relation to the two bases constitute the two kinds of grasping at self. Some proponents of Madhyamaka and Cittamātra tenets maintain that the object of grasping at the self of persons is the mere “I,” yet when asked for the referent of that mere “I,” [64]

361 for some it is the storehouse consciousness, for others mental consciousness, and so on. The answers vary, but according to the present system,[248] the mere “I” that is the object giving rise to the simple thought “I am” is asserted to be the object [of grasping at the self of persons],
[119] de'i/ rda sa shes dpar/
[248] In the verses on insight, “the present system” is always to be understood as the Prāsaṅgika system of tenets.
de yi mtshan gzhir phung po yud tsam yang / / mi 'dzin pa ni lugs 'di'i khyad chos yin/ / de bzhin nga yi'o snyam blo lhan skyes kyi/ / dmigs pa'ang nga yi ba ni nyid yin gyi//[362]
rang gi mig rna sogs la mi bzung gsungs/ / 'jig lta lhan skyes dmigs pa yin na ni/ / nga 'am nga yi'o snyam pa'i blo ngang gis/ / skyes pa dgos phyir gang zag lhas byin gyis//[ 363]

mchod sbyin rang bzhin gyis grub 'dzin pa'i blo/ / 'jig lta min zhing bdag 'dzin lhan skyes yin/ / chos kyi bdag 'dzin lhan skyes dmigs pa ni/ / gzugs phung mig rna snod kyi 'jig rten sogs/ / rnam pa chos dang gang zag bdag 'dzin ni/ / gnyis ka'ang rang bzhin gyis grub 'dzin stangs can//[364]

362 and the aggregates are not considered to be its referents, even for a second; this is a unique feature of this system. Similarly, the object of the innate thought “This is mine” is just “mine” as well,

363 and it is taught that your eyes, ears, and so on are not to be considered “mine.” If something is the object of the innate view of personal identity, it must spontaneously give rise to the thought “I” or “mine”; therefore Devadatta’s

364 perception apprehending Kratu[249] as established by way of his own nature is not a view of personal identity but a case of innate grasping at a self. The objects of innate grasping at the self of phenomena are the form aggregate — eyes, ears, the world as a container, and so on. The aspect [mode of perception] of grasping at both the self of persons and the self of phenomena is the apprehension of them as established intrinsically.
[249] Or if you prefer, John’s perception apprehending George.

f.d: gnyis pa de 'khor bar 'khor ba'i rtsa bar bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.2. Demonstrating that it is the root of turning in cyclic existence

d.div: de'i phyir 'di gnyis grub mthas kun btags pa'i/ / rtag gcig rang dbang can du 'dzin pa dang / / gzung 'dzin rdzas gzhan sgro 'dogs tsam min gyi/ / grub mtha'i skyon gyis bslad la ma bltos bar//[365]
dud 'gror bskal mang bskyal la'ang 'di yod phyir/ / lhan skyes kyis ni bdag 'dzin zhes byar bsnyad/ / gal te 'jig lta 'khor ba'i rtsa ba na/ / phung po bden 'dzin 'khor rtsa nyid yin pas//[366]
'khor rtsa ris mi mthun gnyis 'gyur zhe na/ / phyi ma rgyu dang snga ma 'bras bu dang / / dmigs yul 'gal yang 'dzin stangs mthun pas na/ / ji skad smras pa'i skyon de nged la med//[ 367]

365 For that reason, neither of these is the mere postulation through tenets of a permanent, unitary, and independent [self] or of the perceived and the perceiver as having distinct substances. Because they do not rely on conditioning by faulty tenets —

366 those born as animals over many eons also have them — they are known as “innate grasping at self.” If the root of samsara is the personal identity view, since grasping at the aggregates’ true existence is [also] the root of samsara,

367 you may wonder “does that not make two distinct roots of samsara?” In fact, the latter is the cause, and the former is its result, and although their objects are different, they share the same mode of apprehension. Thus the objection that you raise does not concern me.

dper na ma rig rigs 'dra snga phyi gnyis/ / khyod kyi lugs la'ang 'khor rtsar 'dod pa bzhin/ / 'jig lta bden 'dzin can gyi ma rig pa/ / 'dod pa'i phyir yang skyon de 'byung ba med/ / gti mug gis ni yul rnams bden bzung tshe/ / yul de rang gi yid dang mi mthun na//[368]
de la dmigs nas khong khro skye 'gyur zhing / / yid dang mthun na chags skye bar ma la'ang / / gzhan gnyis min yang gti mug rigs 'dra skye/ / lhag ma'i skye tshul skyes bu 'bring du bshad//[369]

368 They are like, for example, two successive similar moments of ignorance that your system also recognizes as roots of samsara. Since the personal identity view is considered to be the ignorance that apprehends true existence, your objection is not relevant.[250] When, through ignorance, an object is held to exist truly and the object in question does not match with your way of thinking,

369 anger flares toward it. When it matches with your way of thinking, attachment ensues; when it is neutral, neither of these occurs, but another similar moment of ignorance arises. The way the rest follows is explained in the intermediate person’s path.[251]

[250] In verses 367–68 the author refutes the objection that there would be two distinct roots of samsara if both the personal identity view and grasping at the true existence of the aggregates (i.e., phenomena) are considered to be roots of samsara by pointing out that since the personal identity view also grasps at true existence, they share the same mode of apprehension of their objects and as such are not distinct.
[251] See verses 176–81 on the origins of suffering.

f.d: gsum pa bdag 'dzin de spong bar 'dod pas bdag med kyi lta ba btsal ba
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3. Seeking the view of selflessness out of a wish to eliminate grasping at self
['di ]la gnyis/ ma rig pa de spong 'dod na bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba 'tshol dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan/ bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba bskyed pa'i tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: why seeking the view realizing selflessness is necessary if you want to reject ignorance, and how to generate the view realizing selflessness. [65]
dang po ma rig pa de spong 'dod na bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba 'tshol dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.1. Why seeking the view realizing selflessness is necessary if you want to reject ignorance

d.div: yul la bdag med mthong na srid pa yi/ / sa bon bzlog par gsungs phyir bdag 'dzin gyis/ / ji ltar bzung ba'i yul de legs khegs na/ / shing rtsa chad pa'i yal 'dab ji bzhin du//[370]
nyon mongs skyon rnams ma lus bzlog par 'gyur/ / de phyir 'khor rtsa bdag 'dzin lhan skyes dang / / 'dzin stangs 'gal ba'i lam bor lam gzhan gyis/ / bdag lta'i sa bon 'byin par mi nus te//[371]

370 Since it is stated[252] that perceiving the object’s selflessness neutralizes the seeds of cyclic existence, by correctly refuting the object as it is perceived by grasping at self, you avert all faults — the afflictions —

like the branches and leaves of a tree whose root has been cut. 371 Therefore, if you forego the path that opposes the mode of apprehension of samsara’s root, innate grasping at self, you will find no other path able to eradicate the seed of the view of self.
[252] Āryadeva, Four Hundred Stanzas, 14.25cd, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 16a5.
blo gang bdag med gnyis la ma zhugs pas/ / bdag med rtogs par 'jog mi nus phyir dang / / 'tsher ma 'don bzhin spong ba'ang min phyir ro/ / mdor na bden med shes bsgoms bden 'dzin bzlog/[ 372]

de tshe tshul min yid byed rnam rtog bzlog/ / de log 'jig lta'i rtsa can chags sogs bzlog / de tshe de yis kun bslang las bzlog cing / / las med dbang med 'khor bar skye mi 'gyur/ / de tshe thar pa thob la nges brtan bya//[373]

372 Without a mind engaging the two kinds of selflessness, realizing selflessness is inconceivable, as rejecting [grasping at self] is not like extracting a thorn. In sum, it is identification of and meditation on the lack of true existence that averts grasping at true existence;

f.d: gnyis pa bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba skye ba'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2. How to generate the view realizing selflessness
['di ]la gsum/ bdag med kyi lta ba gnyis bskyed pa'i rim pa dang / lta ba gnyis rim can du skye ba dngos/ kun rdzob dang don dam gyi bden pa rnam par bzhag pa'o/ /

This has three parts: the order in which the two views of selflessness are cultivated, the actual process of successively cultivating the two views, and a presentation of the conventional and ultimate truths.
dang po bdag med kyi lta ba gnyis bskyed pa'i rim pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.1. The order in which the two views of selflessness are generated

d.div: ji ltar chos kyi bdag med gzugs brnyan gyi/ / steng du nges sla ji bzhin gzhan steng min/ / de bzhin rang bzhin gyis med gang zag gi_| steng du nges sla ji bzhin chos steng min//[374]

'di yang dpe bzhin khyad gzhi'i dbang gis yin/ / de phyir sla ba'i rim pa'i dbang byas nas/ / ji ltar khyod kyis bdag gi 'du shes ni/ / shes pa de bzhin kun la blos sbyar bya/ / zhes sogs gsungs [120] pas sgom pa'i go rim nges//[375]

374 Ascertaining the selflessness of objects based on a mirror image is easy; based on other objects it is not. Similarly, realizing the lack of intrinsic existence in relation to the person is easier; in relation to other phenomena it is not.

375 As in the case of similes, it depends on the base. For this reason, the order is established according to what is easier: “Just as you have discerned it in relation to your own self, extend this mentally to all [phenomena].”[253] As this explains, the order of meditation is certain.
[120] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 12_shog_44_na2
[253] King of Meditations Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), chap. 44, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 44a2.

f.d: gnyis pa lta ba gnyis rim can du skye ba dngos
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2. The actual process of successively cultivating the two views
['di ]la gnyis/ gang zag gi bdag med gtan la dbab pa dang / chos kyi bdag med gtan la dbab pa'o/ /
This has two parts: establishing the selflessness of persons and establishing the selflessness of phenomena.
dang po gang zag gi bdag med gtan la dbab pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1. Establishing the selflessness of persons
['di ]la gnyis/ gang zag ngos bzung ba dang / de rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa'o/ /
This has two parts: identifying the person and establishing its lack of intrinsic nature. [66]
dang po gang zag ngos bzung ba ni/

d.div: skye 'phags gang zag thams cad phung po la/ / brten nas btags pa'i nga tsam nyid du zad/ / de phyir phung po gdags gzhi gang zag ni/ / btags chos yin par mdo las gsal bar gsungs//[376]
'di yi gdags gzhi btags chos ma yin phyir/ / phung por lta ba'ang gang zag bdag lta min/ / bdag lta phung por lta ba yin gsungs pas/ / phung las rdzas gzhan bdag 'gog la dgongs so//[377]

376 Be they ordinary beings or āryas, every being exists solely as a mere “I” designated on the basis of the aggregates. For that reason, the aggregates are the bases of designation, and the person is what is designated, as the sutras clearly explain.

377 As a basis of designation is not the thing designated, the view of the aggregates is not the view of the self of persons. When it is stated[254] that the view of the self perceives the aggregates, this is to refute a self that is a substance distinct from the aggregates.
[254] In many sutras and in Candrakīrti’s Entering the Middle Way.

f.d: gnyis pa de rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2. Establishing its lack of intrinsic nature
['di ]la gsum/ nga rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa dang / nga yi ba rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa dang / de la brten nas gang zag sgyu ma lta bur 'char tshul bstan pa'o/ /
This has three parts: establishing the lack of intrinsic nature of the “I,” establishing the lack of intrinsic nature of “mine,” and explaining how the person appears as an illusion on that basis.
dang po nga rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.1. Establishing the lack of intrinsic nature of the “I”

d.div: bdag lta'i 'dzin stangs shes pa dgag bya'i gnad/ / bden pa'i phung gsum khegs pa khyab pa'i gnad/ / grub tshul gnyis la gnod mthong phyogs chos gnad/ / nges pa rang shugs kyis 'dren sgrub bya'i gnad//[378]
gnad bzhi 'di tshang lta ba rnam dag skye/ / gcig gam tha dad min par grub med pas/ / bden par grub la'ang 'di yi de mi 'dod/ / zla bcas zla med min pa'i tshul med phyir//[379]
ltos med tshugs thub dgag bya'i snang tshul te/ / snang tshul de ltar grub na bden grub 'gyur/ / gzhan yang bdag phung rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i/ / ngo bo gcig na tha dad gtan med 'gyur//[380]

378 The key point of the object of negation is to identify the mode of apprehension of the view of self, the key point of the entailment is to refute a third possibility regarding true existence, the key point of the property of the subject is to see the error of each mode of existence, the key point of what is to be established is that this naturally leads to ascertaining [the lack of true existence],[255]

379 and when all four key points are present, a perfect view will emerge. Since [an existent] can only be established as either one or distinct [from its parts], what exists truly must also be established as either [one or distinct]. Since all [phenomena] possess parts and since partless [phenomena] do not exist,

380 the object of negation appears to be self-sufficient and stand on its own. If things existed in this way, as they appear to, then they would have to exist truly. Furthermore, if an intrinsically existing self and aggregates shared the same nature, they would be entirely indistinct.

[255] Gomchen’s listing of the third and the fourth key points differ from the standard version, as formalized in Tsongkhapa’s Middle-Length Treatise (trans., 353–54), where the third and the fourth pertain, respectively, to the absence of identity and the absence of difference. Gomchen is using a slightly different listing of the four key points, based on Gyaltsab Jé’s Jewel Garland: A Guide to the Profound View (190), which is based on Tsongkhapa’s guide to the view.
'dod na bdag la phung po'i 'dor len med/ / phung po'i grangs bzhin bdag kyang de rnyed 'gyur/ / khyod la phung po 'jig tshe bdag 'jig na/ / 'di yi las gsog phyi ma'i myong ba po//[381]
rang bzhin gyis gzhan de phyir 'brel med 'gyur/ / 'dod na bdag ni 'di lta bur gyur zhes/ / skye dran mi 'gyur rgyud cig khegs phyir ro/ / bdag phung rang bzhin gyis gcig 'jig 'dod na//[382]
skye ba snga phyi'i rgyud cig mi srid 'gyur/ / 'dod na ma byas pa dang phrad pa dang / / las byas chud za nyid du cis mi 'gyur/ / gal te bdag phung ngo bos grub gzhan na//[383]
de ni dmigs rung tshad mas ma dmigs phyir/ / phung po'i mtshan nyid skye 'jig gnas pa sogs/ / bdag la med phyir bdag de rtags sogs 'gyur//[384]

f.d:
381 If you agree with this, then the self could not take up and discard aggregates; there would have to be as many selves as there are aggregates; when your aggregates disintegrate, the self too would have to disintegrate, in which case, the karma accumulator and the one experiencing [its results] in the future,
382 being intrinsically other, would be unrelated. If you agree with this, then you could not recall your past lives and say who you were, for sharing a single continuum has been refuted. If you assert the disintegration of a self and aggregates that were intrinsically one,
383 then a single continuum of past and future lives becomes impossible. Agreeing with this would mean experiencing [results of] karmas you have not accomplished and the karma you accomplished being depleted. If an intrinsically established self and aggregates were distinct,
384 valid cognitions should discern it, but none does. The aggregates are characterized by production, maintenance, disintegration, and so on, and since the self would have none of these, it would be permanent and so forth. [67]
gnyis pa nga yi ba rang bzhin med par gtan la dbab pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.2. Establishing the lack of intrinsic nature of “Mine”

d.div: de ltar dpyad tshe bdag phung rang bzhin gyis/ / gcig dang tha dad gang du'ang ma rnyed pas/ / bdag la'ang rang bzhin gcig gam tha dad med/ / de med nyid phyir bdag de rang bzhin med//[385]

385 When you analyze the matter in this way, since you cannot find that the self and the aggregates are intrinsically one nor that they are intrinsically distinct, the self as well is neither intrinsically one nor distinct, and as such the self lacks intrinsic existence.

mo gsham bu med de'i mig mi skye bzhin/ / bdag med tshul des bdag gi'ang rang bzhin med/ / rang gi gdags gzhi btags chos rang bzhin gyis// gcig dang tha dad btags pa'i rigs pa 'dis/ / shes bya kun la dpyad pa su 'jug pa/ / de dag bden pa gnyis shes ngo mtshar skye//[386]

386 Just as the nonexistent child of a barren women cannot develop eyes, the self’s lack of intrinsic existence applies to “mine.” With the reasoning that examines whether the phenomena ascribed to their bases of designation are intrinsically one or distinct, anyone analyzing knowable entities can realize the two truths — how marvelous!

f.d: gsum pa de la brten nas sgyu ma lta bur 'char tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.3. Explaining how the person appears as an illusion on that basis
['di ]la gnyis/ sgyu ma lta bur gsungs pa'i don bstan pa/ thabs gang la brten nas sgyu ma lta bur 'char tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: explaining the meaning of the expression “to be like an illusion” and the method through which illusion-like appearances occur.
dang po sgyu ma lta bur gsungs pa'i don bstan pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.3.1. Explaining the meaning of the expression “to be like an illusion”
['di ]la gnyis/ sgyu ma bzhin du 'char tshul phyin ci ma log pa dang / sgyu ma bzhin du 'char tshul ltar snang bstan pa'o/ /
This has two parts: the correct way illusion-like appearances occur and the incorrect way illusion-like appearances occur.
dang po sgyu ma bzhin du 'char tshul phyin ci ma log pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.3.1.1. The correct way illusion-like appearances occur

d.div: rang 'dzin mngon gsum shes ngor bslu med cing / / yod kyang bden grub khegs pa'i dbang byas te/ / mya ngan 'das pa'ang sgyu ma lta bur gsungs/ / de bzhin shes ngo der snang snang ba ltar//[387]

rang bzhin med pa'i gang zag gzugs sgra sogs/ / snang stong tshogs phyir snang ba sgyu mar gsungs/ / stong yang bya byed 'thad phyir chad stong min/ / chos rnams gdod ma nyid nas rang bzhin gyis//[388]
med la de ngo shes phyir blos byas min/ / tshul 'di shes bya kun khyab nyi tshe min/ / blos gtan phebs phyir blo yul mi rung min/ / rig shes kyis rnyed phyir na rig rgyu'ang yod//[389]

387 Although nirvana exists from the perspective of a direct nondeceptive perception apprehending it, it is taught that nirvana too is like an illusion from the perspective of refuting true existence. Similarly, although [in post-equipoise] things appear to this perception [as truly existent], they do not exist intrinsically

388 as they appear to; that is, in the perception of persons, forms, sounds, and so on, appearance [as truly existent] is combined with [awareness of] emptiness, and so it is taught that their appearance is like an illusion. Emptiness is not nihilistic, since agents and actions, although empty, do exist. As phenomena fundamentally lack intrinsic existence,

389 and this is known, it is not a mental contrivance.[256] As this [lack of intrinsic existence] applies to all knowable entities, it is not partial. As it is established by mind, it is not an unsuitable object of perception. As it is discoverable by a mind understanding emptiness, it is knowable as well.

[256] This is a reference to the view that since emptiness of intrinsic existence cannot be “found” and is not identifiable, it is artificial to assert it, and it is best is therefore to remain in a state lacking any thought (tsom ’jog).
'on kyang bden khegs sgyu ma lta bur gsungs/ / gal te gzugs brnyan rmi lam sgyu ma sogs/ / snang ba ltar med mngon sum gyis grub pas/ / so so skye bo 'phags par 'gyur snyam nas[121] //[390]

390 Yet, as true existence has been negated, it is said to be like an illusion. [Question:] Since ordinary beings’ direct perceptions can establish that reflections, dreams, magical illusions, and so forth do not exist as they appear, does that fact not make them āryas?
[121] snyam na/ rda sa shes dpar/
gzugs brnyan byad bzhin sgyu ma rta glang dang / / rmi lam snang ba'i khang khyim khang pa dngos/ / min sogs grub pas stong nyid grub pa min/ / 'on kyang mthun dper 'gro tshul sngar bshad zin//[391]
'di dag steng gi stong nyid phra mo ni/ / snang tshul ltar med rags pa de tsam yang / / bden grub tshul la 'gal ba bsam pas 'grub/ / rdzun par grags dpe rang bzhin med rtogs rjes//[392]
rdzun par ma grags chos rnams der rtogs pas/ / dpe don rtogs tshul rim nges chos gcig gi / lta po kun gyi lta por gsungs pa'i don/ / rtogs pa'i dus 'dir blo kha phyogs tsam gyis//[393]

rtogs nus don yin mngon sum tshul la ni/ / cig car rtogs pa kho nar dgongs par snang / / gzugs brnyan byad bzhin sgyu ma rta glang dang / / rmi lam snang ba khang khyim min shes pas/ / de dag rang bzhin med par shes pa yi/ / cha tsam bskrun par nus pa ma yin no//[394]

391 [Answer:] Establishing that a face’s reflection, magical horses and elephants, and houses that appear in dreams are not actual houses and so on does not mean that you have established their emptiness. Nevertheless, as previously explained, these are used as concordant examples.

392 The subtle emptiness relative to these phenomena is the fact that they do not exist in the way they appear; these coarse appearances exclude their being truly established, a fact that can be established by contemplation. [68] After realizing the lack of intrinsic existence using these familiar examples of falseness,

393 you then realize it in relation to phenomena not known to be false. Thus the order of realization is certain — first the examples and then the meaning. “The realizer of one thing’s [emptiness] realizes all [things’ emptiness];”[257] the meaning of this statement is that when [the emptiness of the example] is first realized [inferentially], by simply changing the mind’s orientation [to the person],

394 it can be realized in relation to it. As for the way a direct realization [occurs], [the example and the meaning] are realized concurrently; this is the [sutra’s] intent. Simply knowing that reflections, magical horses and elephants, and houses that appear in dreams are not real cannot produce even a partial awareness of their lack of intrinsic existence.
[257] Āryadeva, Four Hundred Stanzas (Catuḥśataka), 8.16, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 9b6.

f.d: gnyis pa sgyu ma bzhin du 'char tshul ltar snang bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.3.1.2. The incorrect way illusion-like appearances occur

d.div: sngar bshad dgag bya'i tshad ngos ma zin par/ / yul rnams rigs pas gsal tshe ma rnyed pas/ / dpyod mkhan blo yang 'di dang 'dra'o zhes/ / med par nges mkhan nyid kyang gtan med dgos//[395]
'di yin 'di min nges pa med bzhin du/ / snang ba ban bun sna tshogs 'char ba yang / / rten 'brel bshig pa'i chad lta'i mnyam rjes yin/ / dgag bya khegs pa'i gnad sgom ma bskyangs par//[396]
ci yang yid la mi byed yun ring du/ / bskyangs pa'i rjes su du ba 'ja' tshon ltar/ / snyi zhing srab la skrag med 'char ba yang / / thogs bcas rags pa bkag tsam mnyam rjes yin//[397]

395 By failing to identify the limits of the object of negation as explained above, some affirm that since the objects, once excluded [one by one] by reasoning, are not found, the same is true of the mind of the analyzer: the person ascertaining this nonexistence must also not exist in the least;

396 just as [in equipoise, they say,] there is nothing to be ascertained as either existing or not existing, [in post-equipoise] various hazy appearances arise. These are nihilistic states of equipoise and post-equipoise that demolish interdependence. Instead of meditating on the key point of refuting the object of negation,

397 they merely sustain non-mentation for long periods,[258] following which things appear like smoke or rainbows — flimsy, insubstantial, and vague — but these states of equipoise and post-equipoise do no more than negate things’ coarse obstructive property.
[258] See note 216.
rang bzhin gyis grub 'ga' yang med pa dang / / rgyu 'bras skyon med 'jog thub gnyis tshogs 'di/ / gang gi tshad mas grub des [122] zab lam rnyed//[398]

398. Whoever by valid cognition succeeds in faultlessly establishing both the utter absence of intrinsic existence and [the reality of] cause and effect, along with the relationship between them, has discovered the profound path.
[122] grub tshe/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa thabs gang la brten nas sgyu ma lta bur 'char tshul ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.1.2.3.2. The method through which illusion-like appearances occur

d.div: de phyir mnyam par bzhag tshe mtshan 'dzin gyi/ / dmigs gtad khegs la [123] nam mkha' lta bu yi/ / stong pa sgom pa gnad du song ba na/ / de las langs nas yul snang ltas pa'i tshe//[ 399]
rjes thob sgyu ma lta bur ngang gis 'char/ / de bzhin stong phyogs dpyad sgom shugs drag gis/ / nges drangs rjes su'ang sngar bzhin sgyu ma ltar/ / 'char phyir sgyu ma ltar sgom zur na med//[400]

399 Therefore, once you have negated the reference point of apprehension of signs in meditative equipoise and have effectively accomplished space-like meditation on emptiness, when, having risen from that state, you observe objects’ appearance,

400 the illusion-like post-equipoise state naturally emerges.[259] Similarly, after intense analytical meditation on emptiness has induced an ascertainment, as stated previously, illusion-like perception occurs; there is no specific meditation for illusion-like perception.
[123] khegs pa/ rda sa shes dpar/

[259] It is illusion-like because of the apparent contradiction between the way things appear to you — as existing intrinsically — and the way you know that they exist — free of the slightest intrinsic existence.
mdor na rang gi rgyud kyi ma rig pas/ / ji ltar sgro btags dgag bya'i spyi shar nas/ / rang bzhin de 'dra yod na tha dad dang / / yang na gcig las mi 'da' gnyis ka la'ang //[401]
gnod byed yod lugs legs par dmigs phyed pa'i/ / nges pa drangs mthar gang zag rang bzhin gyis/ / grub pa cung zad tsam yang med do zhes/ / sngar gyi rigs pa'i stobs kyis thag chod 'byung //[402]

401 In brief, once the mental image of the object of negation has appeared, conceived by the ignorance within your mind, [the person and its aggregates] would have to be distinct or one if intrinsic existence were to exist as such, [69]

402 but you clearly see that each has arguments to disprove it, and this induces an ascertainment. Then, by the power of the prior reasoning, the conclusion dawns that the person has not the slightest degree of intrinsic existence.
stong phyogs la ni de 'dra mang du sbyangs/ / de nas gang zag tha snyad bsnyon med rnams/ / 'char du bcug nas rang bzhin med pa la/ / rten 'brel 'thad lugs rnams la nges rnyed bya//[403]

403 Train again and again in meditating on emptiness in this manner. Then [post equipoise] let persons and [other] conventional things appear to your mind and reflect on how dependent arisings are tenable despite their lack intrinsic existence until you are certain of it.

de yi mthun dper gzugs brnyan byad bzhin gyis/ / stong yang byad dang mi long rkyen las skye/ / de bzhin gang zag ngo bos ma grub kyang / / las nyon sogs las skye zhing myong ba por/ / 'thad pa'i tshul rnams yang yang dran par bya//[404]

404 The concordant example is that a reflection of a face is devoid of being a face yet it arises from the conditions mirror and face. Similarly, although persons are not intrinsically established, they result from karma, afflictions, and so forth and are the experiencers [of their results]. Reflect again and again on how this is tenable.

f.d: gnyis pa chos kyi bdag med gtan la dbab pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.2. Establishing the selflessness of phenomena
['di ]la gnyis/ sngar bshad pa'i rigs pa kha spos nas 'gog pa dang / sngar ma bshad pa'i rigs pa gzhan gyis dgag pa'o/ /
This has two parts: negation by application of the previously explained reasoning and negation by another reasoning not previously explained.
dang po sngar bshad pa'i rigs pa kha spos nas 'gog pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.2.1. Negation by application of the previously explained reasoning

d.div: de nas chos kyi bdag med bsgoms pa ni/ / sngar bshad rigs pa spos pas nges par 'grub//
405 Next, meditation of the selflessness of phenomena is fully accomplished by applying the reasoning explained above.

f.d: gnyis pa sngar ma bshad pa'i rigs pa gzhan gyis dgag pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.2.2. Negation by another reasoning not previously explained
['di ]la gnyis/ rten 'byung gi gtan tshigs bstan pa/ de dang rigs pa snga mas 'dus ma byas kyang bden med du 'grub tshul lo/ /
This has two parts: the reasoning of dependent origination and the way to establish the lack of intrinsic existence of noncomposite phenomena as well by means of this and the former reasoning.
dang po rten 'byung gi gtan tshigs bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.2.2.1. The reasoning of dependent origination

d.div: gzhan yang brten nas ma skyes [124] 'bras bu dang / / rang gi cha la ma ltos cha can med//[405]
de phyir brten nas skyes dang brten nas btags/ / gang la brten pa de dang rang bzhin gyis/ / gcig dang tha dad brtags nas bden grub dgag/[406]
Additionally, these do not exist: results occurring not in dependence [on their causes] and things having parts not being dependent on their parts.

406 As such, by analyzing how things that arise dependently and are designated dependently are either intrinsically one with or distinct from what they depend on, you are to refute their true existence.
[124] ma skyed/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa de dang rigs pa snga mas 'dus ma byas kyang bden med du 'grub tshul ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.2.2.2.2. The way to establish the lack of intrinsic existence of noncomposite phenomena as well by means of this and the former reasoning

d.div: des na 'gog pa nam mkha' myang 'das sogs/ / thob bya gzhal bya de bzhin skyabs gnas su/ / 'jog pa rang bzhin grub la mi 'thad phyir/ / tha snyad dbang gis mtshan mtshon rnam dbye 'thad//[407]

gzhan du 'brel med thams cad mtshan mtshon 'gyur/ / gal te 'brel ba 'dod na bden grub nyams/ / gcig dang tha dad brtags pa'i rigs pas kyang / / 'dus ma byas kyi cha dang cha can gnyis/ / rang bzhin gcig dang tha dad brtag bya ste/ / 'dis kyang rang bzhin med par bde blag 'grub//[408]

Therefore cessation, space, nirvana, and such are posited [respectively] as what is to be attained, known, and taken as a refuge. If they were established intrinsically, this would not be tenable. However, conventionally the distinction between definition and definiendum for each is tenable,

408 otherwise all unrelated things could be others’ definitions and definienda. If you assert that they are related, that nullifies their true existence. [70] With the reasoning called “one with or distinct from” too, the parts of noncomposite things and the possessors of those parts are to be analyzed as either intrinsically one or distinct. This reasoning also easily establishes their lack of intrinsic existence.

f.d: gsum pa kun rdzob dang don dam gyi bden pa rnam par bzhag pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3. A presentation of the conventional and ultimate truths
['di ]la gsum/ bden gnyis gang la 'byed pa'i gzhi dang ji ltar du phye ba'i grangs/ de ltar du phye ba'i don/ phye ba so so'i don bshad pa'o/ /
This has three parts: the bases and number of the two truths, the significance of these divisions, and an explanation of each division.
dang po bden gnyis gang la 'byed pa'i gzhi dang ji ltar du phye ba'i grangs ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.1. The bases and number of the two truths

d.div: shes bya tsam la bden pa gnyis su phye//
409 Only knowable entities are classified into the two truths.

f.d: gnyis pa de ltar du phye ba'i don ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.2. The significance of these divisions

d.div: bden gnyis ngo bo gcig kyang ldog pas dbye//
Although the two truths share the same nature, their conceptual and nominal identities are distinct.[260]

[260] Ldog pa tha dad: the two are mentally conceived and designated differently. In the Middle-Length Treatise (Tib., 380), Tsongkhapa explains, “If a sprout, for instance, were a different entity from its own ultimate nature, it would also be a different entity from its emptiness of true existence, so the sprout would be truly established. Since it is not a different entity, it is one entity.”

f.d: gsum pa phye ba so so'i don bshad pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3. The explanation of each division
['di ]la gsum/ kun rdzob bden pa dang / don dam bden pa dang / bden gnyis kyi grangs nges bstan pa'o/ /
This has three parts: conventional truths, ultimate truths, and why it is certain the truths are two in number.
dang po kun rdzob bden pa
['di ]la gsum/ kun rdzob dang bden pa'i sgra don bshad pa/ kun rdzob bden pa'i mtshan nyid/ kun rdzob kyi dbye ba'o/ /
This has three parts: the literal meanings of “conventional” and “truth,” the definition of conventional truth, and the divisions of the conventional.
dang po kun rdzob dang bden pa'i sgra don bshad pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.1.1. The literal meaning of “conventional” and “truth”

d.div: gzugs sogs dngos rnams kun rdzob tsam du ni/ / ma rig spangs pa'i gang zag rnams kyis gzigs//[409]
gang zag bden 'dzin can de'i bden 'dzin ngor/ / bden pas dngos rnams kun rdzob bden zhes bsnyad/ / kun rdzob bden pa bden 'dzin gyis ma grub/ / bden 'dzin ngor ni bden pa tsam gyis kyang //[410]
kun rdzob bden pa yin par 'jog pa min/ / bden 'dzin spangs pa'i gang zag rnams kyi ngor/ / kun rdzob ya gyal bden pa bzhag tu med/ / 'on kyang de'i ngor kun rdzob bden pa 'jog/[411]
Persons who have abandoned ignorance perceive things — forms and so on — as mere conventional phenomena.

410 Since things exist truly from the perspective of the apprehension of true existence in those who apprehend it, they are called conventional truths.[261] However, conventional truths are not established by the apprehension of true existence. That is, it is not just because something exists truly from the perspective of the apprehension of true existence

411 that it is established as a conventional truth. From the perspective of those who have eliminated the apprehension of true existence, only conventional is posited [in the pair conventional and truth], not true existence. Nevertheless, conventional truth can be posited from their perspective.

[261] What is translated here as “conventional truth” (kun rdzob bden pa) could also be rendered “obscuring truth,” or “truth for an obscured perception,” for the standard etymology of saṃvṛti, the Sanskrit for “conventional,” is “veil,” and conventional truths veil or obscure the perception of ultimate truth.

f.d: gnyis pa kun rdzob bden pa'i mtshan nyid ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.1.2. The definition of conventional truth

d.div: gang la tha snyad tshad ma tha snyad pa'i/ / tshad mar song ba'i tshul gyis rnyed pa'i don/ / kun rdzob bden pa'i mtshan nyid skyon med yin//[412]

412 The flawless definition of a conventional truth is this: any phenomenon that is perceived by a conventional valid cognition and in relation to which phenomenon such a cognition is valid on the conventional level.

f.d: gsum pa kun rdzob kyi dbye ba ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.1.3. The divisions of the conventional

d.div: shes pa rang mtshan 'dod pa'i rang rgyud pa/ / yul can yang log mi 'dod yul la smra/ / lugs 'dir 'jig rten tha snyad tshad ma yi/[125] / yang log dbye ba 'byed pa bzhad gad gnas//[413]

de phyir 'jig rten lhan skyes blo 'ga'i ngor/ / yang log dbye ba gsungs kyang rgyu mtshan des/ / lugs 'dir kun rdzob yang log yod mi 'grub/ / snang tshul gnas tshul mthun pa'i kun rdzob ni/ / mi srid de phyir log pa nyid du zad//[414]

413 Svātantrikas, who assert a consciousness that exists through its own characteristics, deny the distinction between true and false for subjects but admit it for objects. Those who make a distinction between true and false in the present system on the basis of worldly conventional valid cognition are laughable.

414 For that reason, although a distinction between true and false conventional realities is made from the perspective of some ordinary perceptions, [71] in our system that does not justify establishing true and false conventional realities. Given that it is impossible for there to be conventional realities wherein the way things appear matches the way they [ultimately] exist, they can only be false.
[125] tshad ma yis/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa don dam bden pa bstan pa
['di ]la gsum/ don dam dang bden pa'i don bshad pa/ don dam bden pa'i mtshan nyid bshad pa/ don dam pa'i dbye ba bshad pa'o/ /
This has three parts: the meaning of “ultimate object” and “truth,” the definition of ultimate truth, and the divisions of ultimate truths.
dang po don dam dang bden pa'i don bshad pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.2.1. The meaning of “ultimate object” and “truth”

d.div: don yin dam pa'ang yin pas don dam dang / / de nyid bslu ba med phyir bden par bshad//
415 Since it is the “object” and also “ultimate,” it is ultimate object, and since it is nondeceptive, it is said to be a truth.[262]

[262] The “object” in question here is one that is perceived by a rational cognition — in other words, a cognition of emptiness. The term usually translated by “ultimate truth” translates literally as “ultimate object truth.”

f.d: gnyis pa don dam bden pa'i mtshan nyid bshad pa
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.2.2. The definition of Ultimate Truth
['di ]la gnyis/ dngos kyi don dang / rtsod pa spang ba'o/ /
This has two parts: the actual meaning and a refutation of objections.
dang po dngos kyi don ni/

d.div: gang la rigs shes tshad ma rigs shes kyis/ / tshad mar song ba'i tshul gyis rnyed pa'i don//[415]

don dam bden pa'i mtshan nyid dpyad bzod med/ / yod kun tha snyad dbang gis yod 'jog kyang / / tha snyad dbang gis gang gzhag yod ma khyab/ / lugs 'dir 'gog bden myang 'das don dam bzhed/ / 'on kyang de yod tha snyad dbang gis 'jog/[416]
The irrefutable definition of an ultimate truth is this: a phenomenon that is perceived by a valid rational cognition[263]

416 in relation to which phenomenon such a cognition is valid on the ultimate level. Although anything that exists is posited as existing from the perspective of conventional minds, not everything posited by conventional minds exists. In the present system, the truth of cessation and nirvana are asserted to be ultimate truths, yet their existence is posited from the perspective of conventional minds.
[263] See verse 419.

f.d: gnyis pa rtsod pa spang ba ni/

d.div: sangs rgyas ji lta mkhyen pa'i ye shes la/ / snang gzigs gnyis phye gzigs ngor gnyis snang log/ / kha cig myang 'das shes bya min pa dang / / sangs rgyas sa na shes rgyud med par 'dod//[417]
ma rig bde thob brtson pa don med 'gyur/ / sems kyi rgyu [126] ba'ang rnam rtog la dgongs phyir/ / yul rnams bden snang sangs rgyas rang snang gi / dbang byas min yang gzhan la snang ba snang //[418]
de kun rnam mkhyen mnga' ba'i gnas [127] kyis so/ / ji lta ji snyed mkhyen pa'i sangs rgyas kyi/ / ye shes de dag ngo bo gcig yin kyang / / snga ma rigs shes phyi ma tha snyad par//[419]
'jog pa yul gyi rnyed tshul dbang gis yin/ / de phyir mkhyen gnyis yul gnyis mi 'gal yang / / yul can gnyis ni 'gal ba kho nar bzhed//[420]

417 Within the superior wisdom of a buddha knowing the way things are ultimately, appearance and perception are distinguished, and in that perception, duality has ceased.[264] Some assert that nirvana is not a knowable entity and that in buddhahood there is no consciousness either,

418 in which case all the effort made to attain the equivalent of a state of ignorance would be pointless. The mention of “the mind’s turnings [having ceased]” refers to [the ceasing of] conceptual thoughts.[265] Truly existing phenomena do not appear to buddhas’ own perceptions, but what appears to others does appear to them;

419 all these [appear to buddhas] because they possess omniscience. Although the buddhas’ superior wisdom that knows both how things are ultimately and how they are in their diversity is of one nature, the former is known as “rational cognition” and the latter as “conventional cognition”

420 according to the way the object is perceived. Therefore, although the two objects of the two kinds of perception are not mutually exclusive, it is maintained that the two subjects are entirely mutually exclusive.
[126] rgyud pa'ang / rda sa shes dpar/
[127] gnad/ rda sa shes dpar/
[264] “Duality” in the present context refers to true existence.

[265] The reference here is to a passage in Candrakīrti’s Entering the Middle Way Autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Toh 3862 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 255a4), where he writes, “As for the buddhas, given that they have thoroughly comprehended and realized the nature of all phenomena, we maintain that all turnings of mind and mental factors have come to cease permanently.” For Jé Tsongkhapa’s position on this debate on the presence or absence of mental continuum in buddhahood, which Gomchen is presenting here, see Illuminating the Intent (trans.), 245–47 and 541–42.

f.d: gsum pa don dam pa'i dbye ba bshad pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.2.3. The divisions of ultimate truths

d.div: don dam bden la phye na bcu drug ste/ / bsdu na bdag med rnam pa gnyis su nges/ / dngos dang mthun pa'i don dam tha snyad ni/ / rang rgyud smra ba chen po rnams kyis bzhed//[421]

421 Ultimate truths can be classed into sixteen varieties;[266] [72] if condensed, it is certain that there are the two kinds of selflessness. As for the terms actual ultimate and concordant ultimate, these are asserted by the great proponents of Svātantrika tenets.[267]

[266] The sixteen types of emptiness, derived from the Perfection of Wisdom literature, are enumerated by Candrakīrti in Entering the Middle Way 6.181–218. See Tsongkhapa, Illuminating the Intent (trans.), 487–513.
[267] Mainly by Bhāviveka in his Blaze of Reasoning (Tarkajvālā).
'di la rnam grangs yin min tha snyad ni/ / bod kyis btags kyang snga ma'i dgongs pa ni/ / rtog med rtog bcas rigs shes yul bcas pa/ / snga ma gnyis dngos phyi ma gnyis mthun pa'i//[422]
don [128] de nyid du 'jog pa dgongs par snang / / de yang bden spros gnyis snang spros pa gnyis/ / snga ma'i ngor med phyi mar gnyis snang yod/ / de bzhin yul gyi chos nyid gnyis la yang //[423]
snga ma'i yul can ngo der spros gnyis bral/ / phyi mar bden tsam log pa'i dbang gis bzhag/ /

422 Tibetans use the terms approximate and non-approximate but the intent of former masters in reference to nonconceptual and conceptual rational cognitions along with their objects is that the first two [nonconceptual rational cognition and their objects] are actual ultimates and the latter two [conceptual rational cognition and their objects] are concordant ultimates.[268]

423 This appears to be the understanding [of that Svātantrika view]. Furthermore, of the two elaborations — that of true existence and that of [subject-object] duality — neither is found in the former perception; duality however is found in the latter. Similarly, there are two kinds of emptiness that are objects.[269]
424 From the perspective of the former subject,[270] both kinds of elaborations are absent. The latter is posited [as an approximate ultimate] simply in terms of the lack of true existence.[271]
[128] don dam/ rda sa shes dpar/
[268] The first two refer to direct valid cognition of emptiness and the emptiness that is its object, while the latter two refer to inferential valid cognition and the emptiness that is its object.

[269] The distinction is made in relation to the subject that perceives emptiness: the object of direct valid cognition is emptiness itself whereas the emptiness that is the object of inference is in fact a mental image of emptiness
[270] The direct realization of emptiness.

[271] Inferential valid cognition of emptiness is free of the elaboration that is the perception of true existence, but it maintains the second kind of elaboration — perception of subject-object duality — in the sense that although true existence appears to the inferential cognition, it is not grasped by it.

f.d: [bden gnyis kyi grangs nges bstan pa ]
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.1.2.3.2.3.3.3. Why it is certain the truths are two in number[272]

d.div: [272] This section heading, announced following verse 409, is missing in the Tibetan text but has been added here.
bslu dang mi bslu'i phung gsum mi srid phyir/ / shes bya 'di la bden pa gnyis grangs nges//[424]
Since something is either deceptive or nondeceptive and there is no third possibility, there are, for knowable entities, definitely only two truths.

f.d: gnyis pa lhag mthong gi rab dbye ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.2. The divisions of insight

d.div: rnam par 'byed dang rab tu rnam 'byed la/ / rtog dpyod gnyis gnyis phye bas ngo bo bzhi/ / so sor rtog dang yongs su tshol ba dang / / mtshan ma las byung sgo gsum lhag mthong 'dod//[425]
don dang dngos po mtshan nyid phyogs dang dus/ / rigs pa yongs su tshol rnam[129] tshol ba drug / mdor na de ltar tshol lugs drug byas pas/ / ngo bo nyid bzhi'i lhag mthong 'grub pa'o//[426]
bsgrims te 'jug pa la sogs yid byed bzhi/ / lhag mthong la yang yod par nyan sar gsungs//[130] [427]

425 There is differentiation and complete differentiation, each dividing into two: inspection and analysis; these are the four from the angle of nature. Analytical discrimination, thorough searching, and arising from signs are asserted to be the categories of insight from the angle of three doors.

426 The six [bases] sought by thorough searching are meanings, things, characteristics, categories, times, and reasonings. In brief, the four kinds of insight in terms of nature are attained by the six kinds of searching.
427 It is taught in the Śrāvaka Grounds that the four kinds of attention — tight focus and so on — relate to insight as well.[273]
[129] rnams/ rda sa shes dpar/
[130] sde dge_4036_bstan/ sems tsam/ dzi_'phags pa thogs med/ rnal 'byor spyod pa'i sa las nyan sa/ shog_149_na1
[273] Asaṅga, Śrāvakabhūmi, Toh 4036 Tengyur, sems tsam, dzi, 149a1. These four were given in verse 339.

f.d: gsum pa lhag mthong sgom pa'i tshul
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.3. How to cultivate insight

['di ]la gsum/ zhi gnas la brten nas lhag mthong sgom par gsungs pa'i don bstan pa/ lugs de theg pa che chung gang gi lam gang gi dbang du byas pa/ zhi gnas la brten nas lhag mthong sgom tshul dngos bstan pa'o/ /

This has three parts: what it means to cultivate insight based on tranquil abiding; which path in that system belongs to which vehicle, great or lesser; and how to actually cultivate insight based on tranquil abiding.
dang po zhi gnas la brten nas lhag mthong sgom par gsungs pa'i don bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.3.1. What it means to cultivate insight based on tranquil abiding

d.div: zhi lhag dmigs pas mi 'byed bden pa gnyis/ / re re la dmigs zhi lhag gnyis gnyis yod//
428 Tranquil abiding and insight are not distinguished by their focal objects, since each of the two truths can be objects of both tranquil abiding and insight.

f.d: gnyis pa lugs de theg pa che chung gang gi lam gang gi dbang du byas pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.3.2. Which path in that system belongs to which vehicle, great or lesser

d.div: rnal 'byor bla med rdzogs rim mnyam gzhag tshe/ / lhag mthong dpyad sgom gzhung gzhan ltar mi dgos/ / 'on kyang rtse gcig lta thog 'jog par bzhed//[428]

When in meditative equipoise at the completion stage of highest yoga tantra, special insight is not necessarily analytical meditation, as in the other systems.[274] Instead, one-pointed placement on the view is asserted. [73]
[274] “The other system” refers to sutra and the other three classes of tantra.

f.d: gsum pa zhi gnas la brten nas lhag mthong sgom tshul dngos bstan pa ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.3.3. How to actually cultivate insight based on tranquil abiding

d.div: dpyad sgom 'jog sgom gnyis kyi skyong tshul la/ / zhi lhag blo cha mnyam par bsgrub pa'i thabs/ / zhi gnas rta la skyon pa'i dpyad sgom dang / / bar bar du ni 'jog sgom spel mar bya//[429]

429 Regarding the way to sustain both analytical and placement meditations, the means to achieve a balance between tranquil abiding and insight is to make analytical meditation ride the mount of tranquil abiding and occasionally practice placement meditation: you are to alternate the two.
kha cig rtog pa ji tsam goms na yang / / de las mi rtog ye shes mi 'byung zer/ / zag bcas zag med 'jig rten 'jig rten 'das/ / so skye las ni 'phags pa la sogs pa//[430]
snga ma rnams las phyi ma mi 'byung 'gyur/ / rgyu 'bras rigs mi 'dra bar mtshungs phyir ro/ / kha cig chos nyid blo las 'das gyur pas/ / blo gang gis kyang de sgom mi nus so//[431]
bsam mi khyab dang blo 'das la sogs pa/ / thos bsam tsam gyis shes rlom dgag phyir yin/ / zab don bden 'dzin dgag phyir yin par gsungs/ / gzhan du lung rigs du mas gnod phyir ro//[432]

430 Some say that no matter how much you familiarize yourself with conceptual thought, nonconceptual superior wisdom cannot arise from it. This would suggest that that the latter cannot result from the former in the cases of noncontamination from contamination, the supramundane from the mundane,

431 āryas from ordinary beings, and so on since they too are causes and effects of different categories. Some maintain that thusness is beyond the realm of cognition and that no mind, whatever it may be, can meditate on it,

432 but it is explained that the purpose of expressions like “inconceivable” and “beyond the realm of cognition” is to counteract the conceit of understanding [emptiness] by learning and reflection alone and to oppose apprehending the profound as truly existent; otherwise, they would contradict many scriptures and reasonings.

f.d: [bsgoms pas lhag mthong grub pa'i tshad ]
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.1.3.3.2.6.2.4. [The measure of having achieved insight through meditation]

d.div: sbyor ba'i chos drug thun dang thun rjes mtshams/ / bying rgod sel la dran shes bskul ba sogs/ / gnad kyis zin pa'i gnas cha'i ngang nyid nas/ / so sor rtog pa'i shes rab kyis dpyad pas//[434]
sngar bshad shin sbyangs rdzogs pa de drangs tshe/ / lhag mthong thob cing zung 'brel nyid kyang thob/ /

433 During the six preliminaries practices, in sessions, and in between, by recalling the key points for rejecting laxity and excitation impelled by mindfulness, meta-awareness, and so on and sustaining stability, you analyze with discerning wisdom.
434 When this induces complete pliancy, as explained before, insight is achieved and union of the two is attained as well.

f.d: [de gnyis zung du 'brel tshul ]

d.div: de la zhi lhag gnyis ni zung yin la/ / 'brel ba phan tshun bcings nas 'jug pa'i don//[435]
dpyad stobs kyis drangs zhi gnas thob pa'i tshe/ / chos rab 'byed dang rtse gcig zhi gnas gnyis/ / mtshungs ldan 'dres te cha mnyam 'jug pa'o/ / tshul 'di ji lta ji snyed gang la'ang 'dra//[436]
de ltar bshes gnyen nas bzung zhi lhag bar/ / mkhas pa'i nyams len rnam par nges pa'i sgo/ / go sla'i tshigs su bcad pas rab mngar [131] bar/ / rang nyid lam 'di skal bzang bya phyir yin//[437]
The “two” are tranquil abiding and insight; “union” means that the two mutually bind and imbue one another.

435 When, by the force of analysis, tranquil abiding [pliancy] is attained, both “full differentiation of phenomena” [insight] and one-pointed tranquil abiding mix and combine in equal balance. The process is the same for both [objects]: the way things are ultimately and in their diversity.

436 In this way, as a means to ascertain the sages’ practice, from relying on spiritual teachers up to tranquil abiding and insight, [I have composed] this sweet nectar in intelligible verse so that I may have the good fortune to meet this path.
[131] dngar ba/ rda sa shes dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa [khyad par rdo rje theg pa la bslab tshul ]ni/
4.2.2.2.3.3.3.2. [How to train in the mantrayāna in particular]

d.div: 'di na thun mong lam sbyangs shes ldan dag/ / zab mo rdo rje theg pa'i dga' ston la/ / 'jug pa'i blo gros khur chen 'degs bzod na/ / bya spyod rnam 'byor lam gyi tshul shes nas//[438]

smin byed dbang bzhi'i chu bo nges 'thungs la/ / grol byar rim gnyis lam la bde bar rol/ / 'dir 'bad dge ba nyin mo'i 'od zer des/ / skye dgu'i blo yi mun pa rab bsal nas/ / rgyal ba dgyes pa'i lam bzang yongs rdzogs kyi/ / 'bras bu'i go 'phang mchog tu nges 'byor shog/[ 439]

437 Provided they have the intelligence and courage to bear the great responsibility of joining the festival of the profound Vajrayāna, the wise, who have trained in the common path, having learned the paths of action, performance, and yoga [tantras],

438 will drink the river of the four initiations that mature them and joyfully partake of the liberating path’s two stages. May the sunrays of this effort’s virtue completely dispel the darkness in all beings’ minds, [74] and may they be certain to reach the supreme state — the fruit of completing the good path that delights the buddhas!

f.d: ces byang chub lam gyi rim pa nas 'byung ba'i nyams len gyi sgo rnam par nges pa legs gsungs kun gyi nying khu zhes bya ba 'di ni/ sgom chen ngag gi dbang po gzhan la phan pa'i sde zhes bya bas/ ze gdong dkar po nyi shar du sbyar ba 'dis kyang rgyal ba'i bstan pa yun ring du gnas la dar zhing rgyas par gyur cig/ // sarba mang+ga laM/

This work, entitled the Essence of all Excellent Discourses Well Ascertaining the Way to Practice Taught in the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment, was composed by the one known as Master of Altruism Gomchen Ngaki Wangpo at White Sunrise in Sedong. May it ensure the preservation, spread, and growth of the Buddha’s teaching for a long, long time! May all that is auspicious prevail! [77]
lam rim dmar khrid bde lam/ @#/ /byang chub lam gyi rim pa'i dmar khrid thams cad mkhyen par bgrod pa'i bde lam zhes bya ba bzhugs so//

b.i: A Direct Guide to the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment

f.d: paN chen blo bzang chos kyi chos rgyal mtshan/
Panchen Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen
@#/ /rje btsun bla ma dam pa thub dbang rdo rje 'chang dang dbyer ma mchis pa'i zhabs la dus thams cad du phyag 'tshal lo/ / brtse ba chen pos rjes su gzung du gsol/
I pay homage at all times at your feet, my most holy and sublime guru, who is indivisible from Munīndra Vajradhara.[275] Pray sustain me with your great compassion.

d.div: [275] Munīndra, “the able sovereign,” is an epithet of the historical Buddha Śākyamuni. Vajradhara is the form assumed by the Buddha in the Vajrayāna scriptures, wherein he is depicted as a deity, clad in nonmonastic garments and adorned with jewel ornaments. This compound Munīndra Vajradhara refers to your root guru, a combination of these two aspects of the Buddha. The guru to whom Panchen Lama is paying homage here at the outset of his text is Khedrup Sangyé Yeshé (1525–91).

f.d: 'dir skal ldan gyi skyes bu sangs rgyas kyi sar bgrod par byed pa'i thabs zab mo byang chub lam gyi rim pa'i khrid la gnyis/ lam gyi rtsa ba bshes gnyen bsten pa'i tshul dang / bsten nas blo ji ltar sbyang ba'i rim pa'o/ /

I present here a guide to the stages of the path to enlightenment, a profound way for fortunate ones to travel to buddhahood. This has two parts: the way to rely on a spiritual teacher and the stages of training the mind having thus relied.
lam gyi rtsa ba bshes gnyen bsten pa'i tshul/
1. The way to rely on a spiritual teacher
dang po la gnyis/ thun gyi ngo bo la ji ltar bya ba dang / thun mtshams su ji ltar bya ba'i tshul lo/ /
The first has two sections: how to practice during the actual session and how to practice between sessions.
thun gyi ngo bo la ji ltar bya ba las sbyor ba/
1.1. How to practice during the actual session
dang po la/ sbyor dngos mjug gsum las/
The first is threefold: the preliminaries, the main part of the session, and the concluding practice.
dang po sbyor ba ni/
1.1.1. The preliminaries

yid mthun gyi gnas su bde ba'i stan la lus 'dug lugs brgyad dam spyod lam gang bder gnas nas/ rang rgyud la legs par brtags te/ dge sems khyad par can gyi ngang nas/ rang gi mdun gyi thad drang gi nam mkha'i gnas su seng ge chen po brgyad kyis bteg pa'i rin po che'i khri mtho zhing yangs pa'i steng khar/ sna tshogs pad zla nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor gyi gdan la/ ngo bo rang gi drin can rtsa ba'i bla ma yin pa la/ rnam pa rgyal ba shAkya thub pa sku mdog gser btso ma lta bu/ dbu gtsug tor dang ldan pa/ zhal gcig phyag gnyis kyi g.yas sa gnon dang / g.yon mnyam gzhag gi steng na bdud rtsis gang ba'i lhung bzed bsnams pa/ sku la chos gos ngur smrig mdog can gsum mdzes par gsol ba/ mtshan dpes brgyan pa'i dwangs gsal 'od kyi rang bzhin can/ sku las skyes pa'i 'od kyi phung po'i dkyil na zhabs gnyis rdo rje skyil krung gis bzhugs pa/ de nyid kyi mtha' skor du dngos dang brgyud pa'i bla ma yi dam sangs rgyas byang sems/ dpa' bo dpa' mo bstan bsrung ye shes pa'i tshogs rnams kyis bskor nas bzhugs pa/ de dag rang rang gi mdun na gdan khri phun tshogs la rang rang gis gsungs pa'i lung gi chos rnams 'od kyi rang bzhin can gyi pu ti'i rnam par yod pa/ tshogs zhing rnams kyang rang nyid la dgyes pa'i tshul dang / rang nyid kyang tshogs zhing rnams kyi yon tan dang thugs rje dran pa'i dad pa chen po'i ngang nas 'di ltar bsam ste/

Seat yourself on a comfortable cushion in a space conducive to practice, adopting an eight-featured posture or whatever posture is most amenable.[276] Then, carefully examining your mindstream, cultivate an excellent virtuous state of mind, and while in that state, visualize the following: In the space in front of you is a high and spacious jeweled throne hoisted by eight great lions. Seated on this throne, on a cushion of multicolored lotus and discs of moon and sun, is your kind root guru in the form of Buddha Śākyamuni. His body is the color of refined gold, and he is adorned with a crown protrusion. He has one face and two arms; with his right hand he performs the gesture of touching the earth, while his left hand, in the gesture of meditation, holds an alms bowl filled with nectar. Perfectly clad in the three robes of saffron color,[277] [78] he is endowed with the major and minor noble marks. His body has the nature of light, clear and radiant. He is seated cross-legged amid the mass of light radiating from his body. Around him, in circles, are assembled your direct and indirect gurus, meditation deities, buddhas, bodhisattvas, heroes, heroines, and wisdom Dharma protectors.[278] In front of each of them, on a perfect throne, are the scriptural teachings they have given appearing as texts made of light. Imagine that the figures in this merit field are pleased with you. For your part, contemplating their enlightened qualities and their kindness, you generate great devotion toward them all. Having established this, contemplate the following:[279]

d.div: [276] The eight-featured posture for meditation relates to the position of your (1) legs, (2) hands, (3) back, (4) shoulders, (5) head, (6) eyes, (7) mouth and teeth, and (8) tongue. For a description of these eight features, see pages 461–63 below. Often the list includes just the first seven, a posture known as “the sevenfold posture of Vairocana” (lus rnam snang gi chos bdun).
[277] The “three robes of saffron color” are the upper garment (bla gos, uttarāsaṃga), the lower garment (mthang gos, antarvāṣa), and the ceremonial shawl (snam sbyar, saṃghāṭi).
[278] The Dharma protectors visualized in the merit field include supramundane protectors such as Mahākāla and Kālarūpa as opposed to worldly protectors.

[279] Although they are not explicitly set off in the original Tibetan text, I have indented the specific meditation instructions when these function as guided meditations, largely rendered here in the first person.

f.d: bdag dang ma sems can thams cad kyis thog ma med pa nas da lta'i bar du/ spyir 'khor ba dang khyad par ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal sna tshogs shig myong 'dug tu zin kyang / da dung sngug bsngal gyi gting dang mtha' mngon par dka' bar 'dug/ des na da res rnyed par dka' zhing rnyed na don che ba'i mi lus khyad par can thob pa'i dus 'dir/ 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal thams cad spangs pa'i thar pa mchog bla ma sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang zhig da lta nyid du thob par ma byas na/ slar yang spyir 'khor ba dang khyad par ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal ci rigs pa zhig myong dgos pa 'dug/ des na sdug bsngal de dag las skyob pa'i nus pa mdun na bzhugs pa'i bla ma dkon mchog gsum la yod pas/ bdag gis ma sems can thams cad kyi don du yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che ci nas kyang thob par bya/ de'i phyir du bla ma dkon mchog gsum la snying thag pa nas skyabs su 'gro bar bya'o snyam du bsams la/

From beginningless time until now, I and all mother sentient beings have been experiencing the suffering of cyclic existence. In particular, we have endured the myriad sufferings of the three lower realms. Still it remains difficult to fathom the depths and extent of our suffering. So today, at this juncture, when I have obtained this excellent human existence that is so hard to find but once found has great value, if I do not ensure the attainment of supreme liberation, the state of a guru buddha — that is, the total elimination of all sufferings — I will once again have to undergo the suffering of cyclic existence in general and all manner of diverse sufferings in the three lower realms in particular. Since the power to save me from these sufferings lies in you, my guru and the Three Jewels seated before me, I pledge, for the sake of all mother sentient beings, to secure the precious state of a perfect and fully awakened buddha. To this end, I go for refuge to you, my guru and the Three Jewels, from the depths of my heart.

skyabs 'gro sems bskyed tshad med bzhi bsgom pa sngon du btang nas/
khyad par ma sems can thams cad kyi don du myur ba myur bar yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che ci nas kyang thob par bya/ de'i phyir du lam zab mo bla ma lha'i rnal 'byor gyi sgo nas byang chub lam gyi rim pa'i khrid bsgom pa la 'jug par bgyi'o snyam pa bdun nam nyer gcig sogs bya'o/ /

In this way, go for refuge and generate the awakening mind and the four immeasurable thoughts. Then recite the following seven, twenty-one, or more times:
In particular, for the sake of all mother sentient beings, I seek to achieve, swiftly, swiftly, the precious state of a perfect and fully awakened buddha. To this end, I now embark on the profound path of meditation on the stages of the path to enlightenment on a basis of guru-deity yoga. [81]

de nas rang gi mdun gyi thad drang gi nam mkha'i gnas su seng ge chen po brgyad kyis bteg pa'i rin po che'i khri mtho zhing yangs pa'i steng khar/ sna tshogs pad zla nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor gyi gdan la ngo bo rang gi drin can rtsa ba'i bla ma yin pa la/ rnam pa rgyal ba shA_kya thub pa sku mdog gser btso ma lta bu/ dbu gtsug tor dang ldan pa/ zhal gcig phyag gnyis kyi g.yas sa gnon dang / g.yon mnyam gzhag gi steng na bdud rtsis gang ba'i lhung bzed bsnams pa/ sku la chos gos ngur smrig mdog can gsum mdzes par gsol ba/ mtshan dpes brgyan pa'i dwangs gsal 'od kyi rang bzhin can/ sku las skyes pa'i 'od kyi phung po'i dkyil na zhabs gnyis rdo rje skyil krung gis bzhugs pa/

Now visualize in space in front of you a high and spacious jeweled throne hoisted by eight great lions. Seated on this throne, on a cushion of multicolored lotus and discs of moon and sun, is your kind root guru in the form of Buddha Śākyamuni. His body is the color of refined gold, and he is adorned with a crown protrusion. He has one face and two arms; with his right hand he performs the gesture of touching the earth, while his left hand, in the gesture of meditation, holds an alms bowl filled with nectar. Perfectly clad in the three robes of saffron color, he is endowed with the major and minor noble marks. His body has the nature of light, clear and radiant. He is seated cross-legged amid the mass of light that radiates from his body.

de nyid kyi steng gi rgyab la phyogs par sna tshogs pad zla nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor gyi gdan la/ rgyal ba rdo rje 'chang la nyams len byin rlabs brgyud pa'i bla ma rnams kyis bskor nas bzhugs pa/ g.yas phyogs su rje btsun byams pa la rgya chen spyod brgyud kyi bla ma rnams kyis bskor nas bzhugs pa/ g.yon phyogs su rje btsun 'jam dbyangs la zab mo lta brgyud kyi bla ma rnams kyi bskor nas bzhugs pa/ mdun du drin can rtsa ba'i bla ma la chos 'brel yod pa'i bla ma rnams kyis bskor nas bzhugs pa/ de dag gi mtha' skor du yi dam sangs rgyas byang sems dpa' bo dpa' mo bstan bsrung ye shes pa'i tshogs rnams kyis bskor nas bzhugs pa/ de dag rang rang gi mdun na gdan khri phun tshogs la rang rang gis gsungs pa'i lung gi chos rnams 'od kyi rang bzhin can gyi pu ti'i rnam par yod pa/ de dag gi phyi rol tu gang la gang 'dul gyi sprul pa'i bkod pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa phyogs bcur 'phro ba'i gtso 'khor thams cad kyi spyi bor oM dkar po/ mgrin par AHdmar po/ thugs kar hUM sngon po/ lte bar sA ser po/ gsang bar hA ljang khu 'od zer lnga 'phro ba/ bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i thugs ka'i hUM las 'od zer phyogs bcur 'phros pas/ rang bzhin gyi gnas nas bsgoms pa dang 'dra ba'i ye shes pa spyan drangs/ dam tshig pa so so la thim pas skyabs gnas kun 'dus pa'i bdag nyid du mos nas/ yan lag bdun pa maN+Dal dang bcas pa phul te/ gsol ba 'debs pa man ngag bzhin rgyud dang 'dres nges par bya'o//

Above and behind him, seated on a cushion of multicolored lotus and discs of moon and sun, is the conqueror Vajradhara surrounded by the masters of the lineage of blessing and practice.[280] On his right is Maitreya, who is surrounded by the masters of the lineage of vast practice, while on the left is Mañjuśrī, who is surrounded by the masters of the lineage of the profound view. In front is your own kind root guru surrounded by the masters from whom you have received teachings directly. Around these [four clusters] are meditation deities, buddhas, bodhisattvas, heroes, heroines, and wisdom Dharma protectors. In front of each of them, on a perfect throne, are the scriptural teachings they have given appearing as texts made of light. Beyond all of these assemblies, radiating in all ten directions, is an inconceivable number of enlightened emanations manifesting in all manner of forms in harmony with and appropriate to the needs of spiritual trainees. All the figures — the principals as well as their retinues — have at their crown a white oṃ, at their throat a red āḥ, at the heart a blue hūṃ, at the navel a yellow svā, and at their secret place a green hā. From these syllables radiates light of five colors. As beams of light radiate from the syllable hūṃ at the heart of Guru Munīndra throughout the ten directions, they invite, from their natural abodes, wisdom beings identical in appearance to those you have visualized. As they dissolve into their corresponding commitment beings, think that they have now transformed into embodiments of all the sources of refuge. With this backdrop, perform the rite of seven limbs and offer a mandala.[281] Recite the supplicatory prayers too in accord with the oral tradition so that they definitely penetrate your mental continuum. [80]

d.div: [280] Nyams len byin rlabs brgyud. I am reading nyams len byin rlabs in conjunctive form as “practice” (nyams len) and “blessing” (byin rlabs). This lineage, beginning with Vajradhara, is essentially a lineage of mahāsiddhas through whom have emerged more esoteric (visionary) and tantric instructions, in which the guru’s blessing is an essential element in one’s practice.

[281] The seven limbs are (1) prostrating, (2) making offerings, (3) confessing negative karma, (4) rejoicing in good deeds, (5) requesting to turn the wheel of Dharma, (6) appealing not to enter nirvana, and (7) dedicating. Two well-known sources for the rite of seven limbs are the Vows of Good Conduct (Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna, a part of the Flower Garland Scripture) and chapters 2 and 3 of Śāntideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva Way (Bodhicaryāvatāra). “Offering a mandala” refers to the chanting of a specific prayer while imaginatively offering the entire universe to the objects of worship.

f.d: de nas bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i thugs ka'i hUM las 'od zer 'phros pa/ mtha' skor na bzhugs pa'i zhi khro rab 'byams thams cad la phog pas/ de rnams 'od kyi rnam par bsdus nas thub pa'i dbang po la thim zhing / thub pa'i dbang po yang rang gi spyi bo'i rtsa ba'i bla ma la thim/ de nyid yongs su gyur pa las rang gi spyi bor seng khri pad zla nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor gyi gdan la/ ngo bo rang gi drin can rtsa ba'i bla ma yin pa la/ rnam pa rgyal ba shAkya thub pa dbu gtsug tor dang ldan pa/ zhal gcig phyag gnyis kyi g.yas sa gnon dang / g.yon mnyam gzhag gi steng na bdud rtsis gang ba'i lhung bzed bsnams pa/ sku la chos gos ngur smrig mdog can gsum mdzes par gsol ba/ mtshan dpes brgyan pa'i dwangs gsal 'od kyi rang bzhin can/ sku las skyes pa'i 'od kyi phung po'i dkyil na zhabs gnyis rdo rje skyil krung gis bzhugs pa la dmigs nas/ yan lag bdun pa maN+Dal dang bcas pa mdor bsdus phul ba'i rjes su/ rang dang rang gi mtha' skor na gnas pa'i ma sems can thams cad kyis mgrin gcig tu gsol ba 'debs par bsams la/

Then, beams of light emanate from the hūṃ syllable at the heart of Guru Munīndra. The light rays touch all the assembled figures, both peaceful and wrathful, and melting into light, they dissolve into the heart of Guru Munīndra. Guru Munīndra then dissolves into your own root guru, who remains seated on your crown. From this total transformation emerges on your crown your own kind root guru in the form of Buddha Śākyamuni. He is seated on a lion throne with a cushion of lotus, moon, and sun. He has one face and two arms; his right hand performs the gesture of touching the earth, while his left hand, in the gesture of meditation, holds an alms bowl filled with nectar. Perfectly clad in the three robes of saffron color, he is endowed with the major and minor noble marks. His body has the nature of light, clear and radiant. He is seated cross-legged amid the mass of light that radiates from his body. Visualizing this, briefly perform the rite of seven limbs and offer a mandala. Then imagine yourself and all sentient beings around you chanting, as if in one voice, the following supplications:

d.div: sku bzhi'i bdag nyid bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
sgrib bral chos sku'i bdag nyid bla ma lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
Guru deity, embodiment of four buddha bodies, to you, O Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
Guru deity, embodiment of dharmakāya, the absence of obscurations, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
bde chen longs sku'i bdag nyid bla ma lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
sna tshogs sprul sku'i bdag nyid bla ma lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
Guru deity, embodiment of saṃbhogakāya, the great bliss, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
Guru deity, embodiment of nirmāṇakāya, the diversity of forms, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
bla ma kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
yi dam kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
Guru deity, embodiment of all the gurus, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
Guru deity, embodiment of all meditation deities, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
sangs rgyas kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
dam chos kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
Guru deity, embodiment of all buddhas, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
Guru deity, embodiment of all sublime teachings, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
dge 'dun kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
mkha' 'gro kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ /
Guru deity, embodiment of all spiritual communities, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
Guru deity, embodiment of all ḍākinīs, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.

f.d:
chos skyong kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs/ khyad par/
skyabs gnas kun 'dus bla ma lhag pa'i lha/ / thub dbang rdo rje 'chang la gsol ba 'debs//

Guru deity, embodiment of all Dharma protectors, to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.” In particular,
Guru deity, embodiment of all sources of refuge, [81] to you, Munīndra Vajradhara, I supplicate.
