The attitudes in relation to them are liking the first in each pair and disliking the second. They are said to be black, white, or two-toned according to various criteria.

f.d: gnyis pa snying po ji ltar len pa'i tshul
2.2. The way to take full advantage [of leisure and opportunity]

['di ]la skyes bu chung ngu dang thun mong ba'i lam gyi rim pa la blo sbyang ba/ skyes bu 'bring dang thun mong ba'i lam gyi rim pa la blo sbyang ba/ skyes bu chen po'i lam gyi rim pa la blo sbyang ba dang gsum/

This has three parts: training the mind on the stages of the path shared with persons of lesser capacity, training the mind on the stages of the path shared with persons of intermediate capacity, and training the mind on the stages of the path of persons of great capacity.
dang po [skyes bu chung ngu dang thun mong ba'i lam gyi rim pa la blo sbyang ba ]ni
2.2.1. The path shared with persons of lesser capacity

lam sgron las/
gang zhig thabs ni gang dag gis/ / 'khor ba'i bde ba tsam dag la/ / rang nyid don du gnyer byed pa/ / de ni skyes bu tha mar shes/[61] / zhes skyes bu chung ngu phal pa tshe 'di'i bde ba don du gnyer zhing sdug bsngal spong ba tsam lhur len pa dud 'gro dang rigs mthun pa lta bu rnams ni skabs 'dir ngos 'dzin pa'i skyes bu chung ngu ma yin la/ 'dir bstan skyes bu chung ngu khyad par can tshe 'di don du mi gnyer bar phyi ma'i bde ba tsam lhur len pa zhig dgos na'ang / skabs 'dir sa bcad du thun mong ba'i lam zhes gsungs pa'i tshig gi nus pas 'khor ba mtha' dag la yid 'byung ba'i sngon du ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal la yid 'byung ba zhig dgos pas 'di la 'jig rten phyi ma don gnyer gyi blo bskyed pa/ 'jig rten phyi mar bde ba'i thabs bstan pa gnyis/

[On training the mind on the stages of the path shared with persons of lesser capacity,] Lamp on the Path to Enlightenment states:
Those who, by whatever means, take personal interest in the pleasures of cyclic existence alone are known as persons of lesser capacity.[407] [153] Ordinary persons of lesser capacity, who are interested only in the happiness of this life and strive to overcome its sufferings as do animals, do not qualify as persons of lesser capacity in the present context. According to [Atiśa’s] exposition, superior persons of lesser capacity must not be concerned with this life and should instead strive only for happiness in the next. In the present outline, the expression “the path shared [with person of lesser capacity]” implies that prior to renunciation of samsara in its entirety, it is necessary to develop renunciation of the sufferings of three unfortunate realms. For this there are two topics: cultivating concern for future lives and relying on the methods for happiness in future lives.

d.div: [61] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_jo bo rje dpal ldan a ti sha_byang chub lam gyi sgron ma/ shog_238_ba1
[407] Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa, verse 3, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 238b1.

f.d: dang po ['jig rten phyi ma don gnyer gyi blo bskyed pa/]
2.2.1.1. Cultivating concern for future lives
['di ]la 'chi ba mi rtag pa bsam pa dang / ngan 'gro'i sdug bsngal bsam pa gnyis/
has two parts: contemplating impermanence in the form of death and contemplating the suffering of unfortunate rebirths.
dang po ['chi ba mi rtag pa bsam pa ]ni/
2.2.1.1.1. Contemplating impermanence in the form of death

blun rmongs la la 'chi ba 'ong mi 'ong gi rtog dpyod tsam yang mi byed la/ phal cher ni nam zhig 'chi ba zhig 'ong snyam pa yod kyang ma rgas kyi bar dang lo zla zhag grangs re re bzhin nas mi 'chi snyam pa'i dbang gis 'chi nad kyis thebs pa'am lo brgya phrag lon kyang re zhig gson du re ba'i bsam pa mngon gyur des dper na phyogs gzhan du mi 'gro ba bsdod pa'i blo yod na 'gro grabs ye mi byed par mkhar rtsig pa dang so nam sogs kyi gshom ra byed pa bzhin tshe 'di'i 'dun ma 'ba' zhig gi dbang du 'gro la/ bsam pa de las log ste sang tsam yang mi 'chi ba'i nges pa med/ zla ba rting ma'i brgyags grabs byas kyang de'i dus su rang nyid lus rten 'di dang dbyibs mi 'dra ba rwa co zing nge ba zhig tu mi skye ba'i nges pa ci yod snyam pa'i blo zhig dur re ba yod tshe/ dper na yul gzhan du mgyogs par 'gro ba'i 'dun pa can de gzhis su sdod pa'i grabs mi byed par khal rta sogs byes kyi sta gon lhur len pa ltar myur du 'chi snyam pa'i blo des 'di snang gi bya ba la mi brtson par tshe phyi mar phan pa'i thabs ngam ngam shugs kyis byed pa chos nyid yin pa'i phyir/ chos 'di don du gnyer ba rnams ni 'chi ba mi rtag pa'i chos skor la blo sbyong ba gal che bas 'di la gsum/ nges par 'chi ba bsam pa/ nam 'chi nges med bsam pa/ 'chi ba'i tshe chos ma gtogs pa gzhan gang gis kyang mi phan par bsam pa'o//

Except for some foolish and ignorant people who do not ask whether they will die, most people think that they will die one day but not until they are old. Every year, month, and day they continue to imagine that they will not die, and so even when they are struck with a mortal illness or have reached the age of a hundred, they plainly expect to go on living. As a result, just as, when you have no travel plans and intend to stay home, you do absolutely nothing to prepare for a departure and instead arrange to do things like build a house or plant fields, you are driven only by this life’s concerns. To reverse this attitude, think: There is no guarantee that I will not die tomorrow. I may gather supplies for next month, but it is not at all sure that by that time I will not have been reborn with a body very different from the one I have now, with horns sticking out! Once this thought is firmly anchored in you, just as someone who is planning to leave soon for another place makes no arrangements for staying at home but works hard to prepare for the trip, getting packhorses ready and so on, the thought of dying soon naturally prevents you from working hard for this life’s goals and automatically prompts you to accomplish what will be useful for your future lives. It is very important that those of you who are interested in this teaching train your mind in the topic of death and impermanence. It has three parts: contemplating death’s certainty, contemplating the uncertainty of the time [of death], and contemplating that at the time of [154] death nothing but the Dharma will be of any use.
dang po [nges par 'chi ba bsam pa ]ni
2.2.1.1.1.1. Regarding the contemplation of death’s certainty,

mi rtag pa'i tshoms las/
gang yang sangs rgyas rang sangs rgyas/ / sangs rgyas rnams kyi nyan thos kyang / / sku lus 'di ni spong mdzad na/ / skye bo phal pa smos ci dgos/[62] / zhes dang / tshoms las/
gang du gnas na'ang 'chi bas mi tshugs pa'i/ / sa phyogs de ni yod pa ma yin te/ / bar snang la med rgya mtsho'i nang na'ang med/ / ri bo rnams kyi gseb tu zhugs na'ang min/[63] / zhes rang cag rnams nges par 'chi ste sngon byon pa'i yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas skye 'chi la dbang thob pa rnams kyang gdul bya rtag 'dzin can rnams bskul ba'i don du mya ngan las 'das/ de bzhin du rgya bod kyi paN grub rgyal blon byang chub sems dpa' sogs gang zag mchog dman grangs med pa byon pa chos 'byung deb ther gtam rgyud sogs las bshad pa mtha' dag ma brtags pa'i gnas skabs su da lta yod yod 'dra ba zhig 'ong na'ang / legs par dpyad na byung ba'i gtam tsam ma gtogs yul dus gnas skabs gang na bzhugs med par mya ngan las 'das pa'i tshul bstan zin/

the Collection of Aphorisms says:
If even buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and the buddhas’ śrāvakas must give up their physical bodies, what need be said of ordinary beings?[408] The Collection of Aphorisms further states:
Wherever you may reside, there is no place where death will not find you: not in the sky, nor in the depths of the sea, not even if you dwell in the heart of a mountain.[409] We are sure to die because the fully accomplished buddhas who appeared in the past, despite having gained mastery over birth and death, passed into nirvana to prompt those disciples holding the view of eternalism to practice. The same is true of countless superior, average, and lesser people — Indian and Tibetan scholars and saints, kings, ministers, bodhisattvas, and so on, whose lives are narrated in religious histories and annals, in oral traditions, and elsewhere. When you do not think about it, you may have the impression that they are still alive today, but when you examine the matter more closely, except in accounts of past events, none of them remain in any time, place, or circumstance — all have demonstrated passing into nirvana.

d.div: [62] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ mi rtag pa'i tshoms/ shog_210_na1
[63] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ mi rtag pa'i tshoms/ shog_210_na1
[408] Udānavarga, “Chapter on Impermanence,” 1.25, Toh 376 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 210a1.

f.d:
rang gi mngon sum gyi spyod yul can mkhan slob pha ma mched grogs mdza' bshes sogs dgra gnyen bar ma'i 'gro ba mtha' yas pa zhig 'jig rten pha rol tu song / da lta khrom chen po khri phrag mang po tshogs pa'i tshe na'ang der 'khod pa mtha' dag dus tshod 'di nas bzung ste lo brgya tshun gyi nang du 'chi bar nges/ sngar byung ba'i mi 'di zhes bya ba ma shi bar tshe thar zhes pa med na bdag gcig pu la dmigs kyis bsal te 'chi mi dgos pa ga la 'ong / tshe tshad drug cu kha ral du bshad pa bzhin thub na'ang dbugs 'byung rngub nyi khri chig stong gi zhag re 'dzad/ zhag sum cus zla ba 'dzad/ zla ba bcu gnyis kyis lo 'dzad/ lo de 'dra bcu gnyis la lo skor du ming btags pa lnga tsam song ba na tshe'i tshad la yang gtugs pas rgya cher rol pa las/
srid gsum mi rtag ston ka'i sprin dang 'dra/ / 'gro ba'i skye 'chi gar la blta dang mtshungs/ / 'gro ba'i tshe 'gro nam mkha'i glog 'dra ste/ / ri gzar 'bab chu bzhin du myur mgyogs 'gro[64] / zhes tshe skad cig kyang mi sdod la/

Think: Among the people that I have known personally — preceptors, teachers, parents, friends, relatives, and so on — so many of them have gone on to their next life: friends, enemies, and neutral people alike. Although a large crowd of many thousands of people may gather today, between now and a hundred years from now, everyone in it is sure to die. Given I cannot point out a single person who in the past has not died, who has avoided it somehow, how could I possibly be the sole exception to the rule and escape death? Even if I manage to have an average life span of sixty years, each day is eaten up by twenty-one thousand breaths, each month by thirty days, and each year by twelve months. Twelve of those years constitute a cycle of years, and once five of them have passed, I will have reached the end of my life. The Play in Full Sutra says:
The impermanence of the three worlds is like autumn clouds, [observing] beings’ birth and death is like watching scenes in a play, lives pass like flashes of lightning in the sky and are swiftly spent like water down a steep mountainside.[410] Not for a single moment does a life remain still. [155]

d.div: [64] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde/ kha_rgya cher rol pa'i mdo/ shog_88_na2
[410] Lalitavistarasūtra, Toh 95 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 88a2.

f.d:
zas nor lta bu sngon ma rnams rim gyis zad kyang slar gsar pa bsnan du yod pa lta bu ma yin par tshe zad pa la gsar du bsnan rgyu med pas spyod 'jug las/
nyin mtshan sdod pa yod med par/ / tshe 'di rtag tu god 'gyur zhing / / snon pa'ang gud nas 'ong med na/ / bdag lta 'chi bar cis mi 'gyur/[65] / zhes sogs dpe dang gtan tshigs kyi sgo nas legs par bsams te nges par 'chi ba 'ong ba thag ma chod kyi bar bsgom mo//

Unlike food and wealth, which can be replenished as they are gradually depleted, you cannot add to a spent life span. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way states:
Pausing neither day nor night, this life shortens constantly. If it can never be prolonged, how could someone like me not die?[411] Reflecting thoroughly on the question in this way, referring to examples and reasonings, you meditate until you reach the conclusion that you will definitely die.

d.div: [65] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 2_sh+loka_39_shog_5_ba2
[411] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 2.39, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 5b2.

f.d: gnyis pa [nam 'chi nges med bsam pa ]ni/
2.2.1.1.1.2. The second step is the contemplation of the uncertainty of the time of death.

de ltar bsgoms pas mthar 'chi ba las ma 'das mod re zhig dgra 'dul gnyen skyong gi bya ba dang chos sgrub pa'i mthun rkyen sogs rtsol ba byas te mthar chos shig bya'o snyam na/ khams gsum gyi sems can rnams la tshe'i tshad re bshad kyang de ring mtha' la bshad pa bshad pa bzhin du thub pa'i nges pa ni sgra mi snyan pa ma gtogs pa la med la/ khyad par du 'dzam bu gling pa rnams ni mdzod las/
'di na ma nges tha mar ni/ / lo bcu dang po dpag tu med/[66] / ces nges pa shin tu chung bar bshad cing / bshad pa ltar rang gis dngos su mthong ba sngon chad rang las gzhon pa shin tu mang ba zhig shi song zhing da lta rang las rgan pa mang po zhig 'dug pas de dag gi sngon du bdag mi 'chi ba'i nges pa ga la yod de/

With the above meditation, you come to understand that in the end there is no escaping death. You might imagine however that once you have spent some time working on subduing your enemies, caring for your friends, creating conditions conducive to religious practice and so on, you will then be able to practice the Dharma. Although a specific life span for beings in each of the three realms is taught, only the inhabitants of [the northern continent] Kuru are sure to have the long life announced. Specifically, regarding the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa, the Treasury of Abhidharma states:
For them [life span] is uncertain; at the end it is ten years long, to start it is immeasurable.[412] As such, it is explained that life span is very uncertain, and this is directly verifiable for until now, many people younger than you have died, and many older than you are still alive. Given this there is no guarantee that you will not die before them.

d.div: [66] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuslob dpon dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_79_shog_9_ba7
[412] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa, 3.79, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 9b7.

f.d:
tshoms las/
sang dang 'jig rten phyi ma gnyis/ / sngon du gang 'ong gtol med pas/ / sang gi tshes la mi 'bad par/ / phyi ma'i don la 'bad par rigs/[67] / zhes sang gi tshes grangs dang 'jig rten phyi ma'i bar srid gnyis sngon la gang 'grub kha tshon mi chod/

The Collection says:
Of the two, tomorrow and the next life, it is unknown which will occur first. So instead of striving for tomorrow’s sake, it would be better to strive for the sake of future lives.[413] Of the two, tomorrow or the intermediate state of your next life, you cannot be sure which will occur first.

d.div: [67] sang dang 'jig rten phyi ma gnyis/ /zhes sogs tshoms kyi lung 'di 'tshol zhib zhus kyang brnyed son ma byung /
[413] This verse was not found in the Udānavarga.

f.d:
la la dag zas bcos sman dpyad sogs thabs mang po'i sgo nas gson pa'i rkyen mang ngo snyam na/ rin chen 'phreng ba las/
'chi ba'i rkyen ni mang ba ste/ / gson pa yi ni cung zad cig / de dag rnams kyang 'chi ba'i yang / / de bas rtag tu chos mdzod cig[68] / ces zas ma 'phrod pa/ sman log pa/ gnas khang rdib pa/ gru bshan zhig pa/ mdza' bos bslus pa sogs gson rkyen 'chi rkyen du 'gyur ba shin tu mang / mar me la sdong bu dang mar khu la sogs pa ring du gnas pa'i rkyen du ma yod kyang rlung lta bus bskyod de glo bur du 'chi ba bzhin/ tshe'i 'phen pa ma zad kyang 'byung ba 'khrugs pa/ bar du gcod pa'i bgegs phan gnod res 'jog tu byed pa'i gdon sogs nyer 'tshe shin tu mang bas bshes spring las/
tshe ni gnod mang rlung gis btab pa yi/ / chu yi chu bur bas kyang mi rtag na/ / dbugs rngub dbugs 'byung gnyid kyis log pa las/ / sad khom gang lags de ni ngo mtshar che/[69] / zhes gang la bsams kyang nam 'chi cha med par myong ba thon nges kyi bar bsgoms pas rang la dgra ma rung ba zhig 'ong bar nges shing dus gang la 'ong ma nges na nyin re zhing zon byed pa dang 'dra bas gnad che'o//

Some people imagine that because of the many available means like diet and medical treatment, factors that sustain life abound. However, as the Precious Garland states:
The conditions for death are many, those sustaining life are few. As these too may become causes for death, always practice the Dharma.[414] Think: Food may disagree with me. I may react badly to medicine. As houses may collapse, boats sink, friends deceive me, and so on, the factors sustaining life often become instruments of death. Several elements ensure that a butter lamp continues to burn for a good while — a wick, clarified butter, and so on — but when something like a gust of wind strikes it, it immediately goes out. In the same way, even if my life span is not yet depleted, very many things can affect it — an imbalance of my body’s elements, obstructive spirits, spirits who are alternately helpful and harmful, and so forth. As it says in the Friendly Letter: [156]
Many things harm this life, and as it is more impermanent than a water bubble struck by a gust of wind, it is extraordinary that one has the chance to inhale after exhaling and to rise having gone to sleep.[415] Meditate on this until you truly ascertain that in all cases, your time of death is uncertain. It is crucial that you be on your guard every day, for this terrible enemy is sure to come, and it is uncertain when it will.

d.div: [68] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 3_sh+loka_79_shog_117_ba1
[69] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / shog_43_na6
[414] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī, 3.78, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 9b7.
[415] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha, verse 55, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig nge, 43a6.

f.d: gsum pa ['chi ba'i tshe chos ma gtogs pa gzhan gang gis kyang mi phan par bsam pa ]ni
2.2.1.1.1.3. The third part is to contemplate that at the time of death, nothing but the Dharma is of any use,

spyod 'jug las/
gshin rje'i pho nyas zin pa la/ / gnyen gyis ci phan bshes ci phan/ / de tshe bsod nams gcig skyabs na/ / de yang bdag gis ma bsten to/[70] / zhes 'chi ba mi rtag par grags pa'i lam po che ri gzar gyi rbab 'dra ba de nges par 'ong ba'i dus la bab pa'i tshe rdzas sngags ting 'dzin dang dpa' bo'i mtshon gyis mi bzlogs/ phyug po'i nor gyis bslu ba dang smra mkhas gtam gyis 'drid du med cing / gnyen bshes mang pos mtha' nas bskor/ stobs dang longs spyod 'khor los sgyur rgyal la 'gran du bzod pa rnams kyang 'khrid pa dang 'khyer ba'i dbang lta ci smos/ ma'i mngal nas lhan cig tu 'grogs pa'i lus 'di yang cam gyi bzhag ste rnam par shes pa gcig pu dbang med du 'gro ba'i tshe rjes su 'brang zhing phan thogs pa ni sngon bsags kyi dge ba sogs dam pa'i chos kho na las mi 'dug snyam du myong ba thon par bsgom mo/ /

regarding which Guide to the Bodhisattva Way states:
When I am seized by Yama’s[416] messengers, what use are relatives? What use are friends? At the time only merit could protect me, but that I have failed to acquire.[417] Think: When the time inevitably comes to take the great route known as death and impermanence that comes down like a rockslide on a steep mountainside, then no potions, mantras, states of concentration, or hero’s weapons can avert it. The wealth of the affluent cannot bribe it; the words of the eloquent cannot fool it. And it goes without saying that I will not have the right to bring with me the many friends and relatives who surround me, nor any power and riches, even if they rivaled a universal sovereign’s. I will even have to abandon completely the very body that will have been my constant companion since my mother’s womb. Powerless, my consciousness alone will move on, like a hair extracted from a slab of butter. Then the only thing of any use that will follow me is the virtue I will have previously acquired — in other words, the perfect Dharma, nothing else. Meditate on this persistently until you gain an experience of it.

d.div: [70] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 2_sh+loka_41_shog_5_ba3
[416] Yama, the Lord of Death, is death personified.
[417] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 2.41, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 5b3.

f.d: blun po la la 'chi ba'i tshe chos kyis phan pa de 'chi mi dgos pa zhig la go bar snang mod/ 'di pa'i lugs la mi 'chi ba ma yin par [71] 'chi lugs mi gcig ste/ chos pa rab 'chi ba la brod/ 'bring mi mtsher/ tha ma mi 'gyod bya ba bka' gdams gong ma'i gsung 'phros las byung ba yin no// //

Some silly people interpret the statement that nothing but the Dharma is of any use when you die to mean that you do not have to die. In our tradition, it is not a matter of not dying but of the way you die. As past Kadam masters used to say, the best practitioners die happily, average ones do not shirk it, and lesser ones die with no regrets.

d.div: [71] yang / rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/

f.d:
smras pa/
las nyon dbang gis 'phangs pa'i skye srid 'di/ / grub tsam nyid nas mi rtag 'chi ba'i drung / / cung zad ngal gso med par 'gro bzhin du/ / gtan du sdod grabs byed las blun pa su/ /
lo zla tshes kyi ma nges dus min du/ / rgan gzhon go rim med par 'chi ba dag / mthong bzhin nam 'chi'i cha la dus 'debs pa'i/ / chu bur mig ldan khyod nyid cer re long / /
nam yang mi 'bral dkar po dge ba'i grogs/ / spangs nas khrel chung mdza' bshes 'khor g.yog nor/ / rtag tu phan par sems khyod bar do yi/ / bgrod dka'i 'phrang der gcig pur phyin gyi dogs/ / zhes bya ba ni bar skabs kyi tshigs su bcad pa'o// //

d.div: Once this rebirth impelled by karma and afflictions has been attained, you proceed toward death and impermanence without pause. What fool would prepare to remain indefinitely?

The year, month, and day are uncertain; there is no fixed time and no precedence between the old and young. You observe death and yet allot yourself time and so are like a blind person who only seems to see.

As you neglect pure virtues, your ever-faithful companions, and continue to imagine that your unfaithful loved ones, entourage, and wealth will always serve you, you may have to travel the intermediate state’s difficult passage empty-handed.

f.d: Unfortunate realm suffering
gnyis pa ngan 'gro'i sdug bsngal bsam pa
2.2.1.1.2. The second part [of cultivating concern for future lives] is contemplating the suffering of unfortunate rebirths.
['di ]la dmyal ba/ dud 'gro /yi dwags kyi sdug bsngal bsam pa dang gsum/
It has three parts: [157] reflecting on the sufferings of hell beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
dang po [dmyal ba'i sdug bsngal bsam pa ]
2.2.1.1.2.1. The first, reflecting on hell beings’ sufferings,
['di ]la tsha dmyal dang / grang dmyal gnyis/
has two parts: the hot hells and the cold hells.
dang po [tsha dmyal ]ni/
2.2.1.1.2.1.1. Regarding the first, the hot hells,

de yang gong du 'chi ba mi rtag pa'i chos skor sgom pa'i rgyu mtshan/ de ltar shi ba'i 'og tu mar me shi ba'am rtsa phung mes bsregs pa ltar rigs 'dra phyi ma rgyun chad pa zhig ni mi 'ong / nges par skye ba zhig len pa las 'os med/ skye ba de yang bde 'gro dang ngan 'gro gang rung zhig tu skye ba las ma 'das pas bde 'gror skye ba'i rgyu dge ba ni sngon chad rang nyid kyi blo bde sing nge ba bsags pa zhig ni mi dran zhing tshe rabs sngon ma rnams su bsags ma bsags kyang cha med/ mi dge ba'i las ni rgyal po'i gan mdzod bzhin du gang la bltas bltas nas gsog 'dug/ / de'i 'bras bu ngan song gi sdug bsngal zhig myong dgos byung na lus 'di ga la byung ba dang lus gzhan du 'phos nas byung bar khyad med/ da lta ma brtags pa'i gnas skabs su rma 'bras kyi nad byung ba lta bu de ga'i thad kyi sha rus kyi thog tu myong ba 'dra zhig 'dug na'ang don du myong byed ni sems yin te/ min na shi ba'i 'og tu ro la mtshon bsnun pa la yang na tsha 'byung dgos pa la mi 'byung bar nges pas de ring lha mi'i dpal 'byor myong bzhin pa'i sems 'di'i thog tu sang nas mnar med kyi sdug bsngal mi 'byung ba'i nges pa ci yod/

[first reflect on] the purpose of meditating on the previous topic, death and impermanence: The moment following death, a person does not just cease to exist the way a butter lamp goes out or a pile of straw is consumed by fire. It is certain that there is no choice but to be reborn, and there are only two possible kinds of rebirth, in a fortunate realm or an unfortunate realm. As for the cause of rebirth in a fortunate realm — virtue — I do not recall having produced enough of it in the past to feel completely comfortable. Nor can I know what virtue I may or may not have accomplished in my previous lives. My nonvirtuous karma, on the other hand, is the size of a royal treasury — wherever I look, I have created it. If I have to experience its results, unfortunate realms’ sufferings, it would be the same regardless of it happening with my present body or after having moved into another body. When I do not think about it, I have the impression that it is my flesh and bones that feels the pain of a wound for example, but in fact it is my mind that experiences it. Otherwise stabbing a corpse would necessarily cause pain, which it certainly does not. With my present kind of mind, today I enjoy human and divine resources, but when it is suddenly gone, there is no guarantee that I will not be subjected to the agony of the relentless hell.

de dag gi tshul la yid 'byung skye ba la mgon po klu sgrub kyis/ rab tu tsha zhing grang ba yi/ /dmyal ba nyi ma gcig bzhin dran/[72] /zhes gsungs pa ltar dmyal ba'i sdug bsngal de bsam dgos te/ bsam tshul da lta phal cher lung dang de'i tshigs bcad yam me ba zhig ngag tu brjod nas kha phyir bltas kyi shes pas gzhan gyi sdug bsngal la blta ba lta bu byed pa de rgyud thog tu ye mi khel te/ dper na rgyal po'i khrims rar nag can zhig chad las kyis nan tur sna tshogs byed pa mthong ba na/ sems dge ba rnams de la brten pa'i nges 'byung dang snying rje skye ba 'ong na'ang phal che ba ni ltad mo dang nyams dga' ba'i snang ba skye mod/ snang ba de ga skye bzhin pa'i mi de khrims rar khrid nas yan lag lcags kyis bcing ba sogs byas byung tshe sngar gyi bde sems de skad cig kyang mi bzod pa'i sdug bsngal gyi sems su gyur nas 'di las thar na ci ma rung snyam pa ma gtogs blo gzhan mngon gyur mi skye ba dang 'dra bas/ skabs 'dis mtshon pa'i 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal sgom pa'i skor phal cher la rang nyid 'gro ba rigs drug gang yin pa der skyes nas sdug bsngal de rang thog la byung ba'i tshul gyis blo nang du bkug nas sgom dgos pa'i phyir na/ zhe sdang gi mthus bsags pa'i mi dge ba'i 'bras bu dmyal ba'i bar srid grub pa'i tshe lus la bsil ba'i snang ba shar te tsha ba don du gnyer ba na bar srid 'gags nas tsha dmyal du skye bar bshad pas/

In this way, to inspire renunciation in you, as the protector Nāgārjuna says, “Every day recall the hells, extremely hot and extremely cold.”[418] Accordingly, it is necessary to contemplate hell beings’ sufferings. As for the way to do it, these days most often people just rattle off quotations and verses. Broaching the matter externally, they observe others’ suffering like a show and fail to relate it to themselves. [158] It is like people watching a court of justice where criminals are punished and tormented in various ways. Although kind people in this situation feel renunciation and compassion, for most it is just a kind of entertainment to be relished. However, if the same people who see it that way were to find themselves in court with their limbs bound in fetters and the rest, their former feeling of pleasure would soon become so painful they could hardly bear it for a moment, and they would be able to think only of how to escape their torment and nothing else. Similarly, when meditating on the sufferings of prison-like samsara, you are in most cases meant to visualize yourself born in one of the six realms and personally experiencing its sufferings. You are to meditate on them subjectively. It is taught that once you have produced the intermediate state for a hell rebirth as a consequence of a nonvirtue created by hatred, you will have the impression that your body is cold. By longing for warmth, the intermediate state ceases, and you are born in a hot hell.

d.div: [72] sde dge_4330_bstan/ thun mong ba lugs kyi bstan bcos/ ngo _mgon po klu sgrub/ skye bo gso ba'i thigs pa/ shog_115_na6
[418] Nāgārjuna, A Drop to Rejuvenate the Person (Jantupoṣaṇabindu), Toh 4330 Tengyur, lugs kyi bstan bcos, ngo, 115a6.

f.d: spyi khyab tu 'og thams cad lcags bsregs kyi sa gzhi/ khor yug lcags sregs kyi ra ba/ steng 'og me lce kun tu 'bar zhing 'khrug pa'i nang du/ yang sos ni/ bshad ma thag pa'i gnas de 'dra ba zhig tu rang nyid mngon sum du skyes 'dug snyam du 'bad nas bsgoms pas lus rtsed yam yam pa/ sems 'jigs zhum zhum pa 'ong ngo / / de lta bu byung ba na der skyes pa'i sems can mang po tshogs te zhe sdang gi dbang gis phan tshun gcig gis gcig la mtshon cha sna tshogs rdeg par bsam/ de la brten nas rang gi lus tshal pa brgya stong du song ba dang brgyal thabs su 'gyel ba sogs kyi rnam pa dngos su myong rgyu yod pa lta bu ma byung gi bar gsal gdab/ de nas nam mkha' las/ khyod rnams yang sos par gyur cig pa'i sgra byung ba dang gsos te sngar ltar mtshon bsnun pa sogs kyis sdug bsngal khor mo yug tu bsgom/ de ltar nyams len rdo rus thug pa byas pas zas skom gyi dang kha 'gags pa snyam byed pa dang / bre mo'i gtam dang 'du 'dzi'i g.yeng ba la mi spro zhing / spyod lam mtha' dag tu 'bad pa med par sdig spong dge sgrub la ngang gis 'jug pa zhig 'ong / sngar gyi sems dang spyod tshul so na 'dug tshe chos dang gang zag tha dad du song ba yin no//

Generally, in a hot hell environment, the ground below is burning iron, and the periphery burning iron walls. The space above and below is filled with flames. To meditate on the hell called Revival, diligently imagine that you are actually born in a place like the one just described. This should make your hair stand on end and your mind shrink in fear. Once you feel this, think that the vast number of beings born there congregate and, impelled by anger, strike one another with a variety of weapons. As a result, your body is chopped into a hundred or a thousand pieces, you collapse in a faint, and so forth. Continue until you have the impression that you are truly experiencing these. Next, when you hear a voice from the sky cry out, “All of you, revive!” you immediately recover and are once again stabbed with weapons and the like. This is the way to meditate on continuous suffering. Practicing it well will make you lose your appetite and your interest in idle talk and distracting conversations; you will naturally and effortlessly devote all your energy to rejecting sin and accomplishing virtue. If your thoughts and behavior remain unchanged, it means that you are not relating the practice to yourself. [159]

thig nag ni/ dmyal srung rnams kyis lus la thig brgyad btab ste mtshon chas gsheg par byed do/ / bsdus 'joms ni/ dmyal ba brgyad kar rim pa bzhin skye dgos pa min yang 'dir 'khrid rim ltar sgom pa'i dbang du byas te sngar gyi sdug bsngal de las 'bros pa'i snang ba shar te phyin pa na ri ra lug glang seng lta bu'i gdong pa can gyi bar du chud de btsir ba na sgo thams cad nas khrag gi rgyun 'bab bo/ / ngu 'bod ni/ yang bros pas lcags kyi khang pa'i nang du sleb pa na sgo dbyer med du 'grig ste phyogs kun nas me 'bar te bsregs pas da 'bros sa yang mi 'dug snyam nas ngu 'bod lhang lhang ba byed do/ / ngu 'bod chen po ni/ lcags khang de ga la lcags khang gcig gis bskor te bsgom par bshad kyang / bla ma'i bzhed pa lcags khang de nas thon te bros pa na lcags khang nyis rim du chud de sdug bsngal sngon ma las nyis 'gyur gyis che ba ni bsam pa'i khyad par lcags khang nang ma nas thon srid kyang phyi ma las mi thon snyam pa ste/ dper na btson khang la gyang nyis rim du yod na gyang nang ma brtol thub kyang phyi ma brtol ma thub dogs pas sdug bsngal ba bzhin no//

In the Black Lines hell, guardians sear eight lines on your flesh and then chop you to pieces with sharp weapons. Rebirths in the eight hells do not necessarily occur in this order, but when meditating, you follow the sequence found in the commentaries. In Crushing, which comes next, you have the impression of having escaped the former suffering, but when you move on, you find yourself forced between mountains shaped like the faces of goats, sheep, oxen, or lions and are crushed between them until blood streams from all your orifices. In Screams, having escaped once more, you find yourself inside an iron building. The doors slam shut behind you, and as fire blazes from every direction, you are roasted. Conscious that there is no escape, you erupt in piercing screams. For Great Screams, it is taught that you are to meditate that the same iron house is enclosed in a second one. However, according to my guru’s explanation, when you leave the [first] iron house and run away, you find yourself forced into a double iron house. As a result, the suffering is twice as great as before. The difference is emotional, for you think, “Although I may escape the inner iron building, I will never manage to escape the outer one!” For example, if you are in a prison with two sets of walls, although you might manage to pierce the first one, doubting your ability to pierce a second one, you agonize.

tsha ba ni/ lcags kyi gsal shing me 'bar bas 'phongs dang spyi bo'i bar tal mar phug ste dbang po'i sgo thams cad nas me lce 'bar ba dang / lus ril bu khro chu'i nang du 'tshod pa'o/ / rab tu tsha ba ni/ gsal shing rtse gsum gyi dbus ma spyi bo dang g.yas g.yon phrag pa nas thon pa dang / lcags bsregs leb mo lus la snam bu ltar dkri ba dang / khro chu'i nang du 'tshod pa na sha khrag rnams zhig ste keng rus ltar 'gro ba'o/ / mnar med ni/ phyogs mtshams kun nas me 'bar bas lus dang me dbyer med pa lta bu'i tshul gyis ngu ba'i skad thos pa tsam mo/ / sdug bsngal de dag kyang yun thung ngu tsam zhig gis mi chog ste/ chos mngon pa las/ mi'i lo lnga bcu la 'dod lha'i nyin zhag gcig tu byed pa [73] sogs cung zad go dka' zhing mi gsal bas/ dmyal ba brgyad po'i nang gi tshe thung shos yang gsos [74] pa'i tshe tshad mi lo khrag khrig gcig [75] ther 'bum chen po drug ther 'bum gnyis yin pas/ gzhan rnams rim gyis log por 'phar tshul bsams na snying 'gas par thug pa las 'os ci yod/

In Heat, you are impaled straight from your anus to your crown on a blazing iron spear, and flames shoot out from all your orifices, or else your entire body is cooked in a cauldron of molten bronze. In Extreme Heat, you are impaled on tridents; the central point pierces your crown, the lateral ones your shoulders. Your body is wrapped in a sheet of red-hot metal like a roll of woolen cloth. When boiled in molten bronze, your flesh and blood dissolve, and you are reduced to a skeleton. In the Relentless hell, as fire blazes from all cardinal and intermediary directions, your body is indistinguishable from the flames; only your cries are heard. You don’t endure these sufferings for just a short period of time. The Treasury of Abhidharma says, “When you calculate fifty human years as a day for desire-realm gods. . .”[419] which is unclear and somewhat difficult to work out. Among the eight hells, Revival has the shortest life span. It lasts 1.62 trillion human years. The life span of each successive hell doubles. When you contemplate this, you cannot help but feel that your heart is about to explode. [160]

d.div: [73] sde dge_4090_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuslob dpon dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod kyi bshad pa/ gnas/ 3_shog_153_na4
[74] sos pa'i/ rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/
[75] gcig dang / rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/
[419] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Toh 4090 Tengyur, mngon pa ku, 153a4.

f.d:
bshes spring du/
ji srid mi dge de zad ma gyur pa/ / de srid srog dang 'bral bar mi 'gyur ro/[76] / zhes pa ltar na da lta'i rang cag rnams kyi spyod tshul dang bcas te de las yun ring ba zhig mi 'ong ba'i nges pa ci yod snyam du yid 'khul nges shes pa'i bar du bsgom mo/ /

The Friendly Letter says:
As long as your nonvirtue is not spent, your life will not come to an end.[420] Thinking, “Given this and given my present behavior, what is there to stop my lives in the hells from lasting even longer?” meditate until you are truly shaken.

d.div: [76] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / shog_44_ba5
[420] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha, verse 87, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44a5.

f.d: gnyis pa [grang dmyal ]ni/
2.2.1.1.2.1.2. For the second part, the cold hells,

dmyal ba'i bar srid pa de'i lus la tsha ba'i rnam pa shar bas grang ba la dga' ba'i bsam pas rkyen byas te bar srid 'gags nas mtha' thams cad gangs ri'i phreng bas bskor ba 'og kha ba'i thang dang 'khyag rom gyi gcong rong zab mo/ steng kha ba bu yug 'tshubs pa/ mun pas gtibs shing rlung drag pos btab pa'i gnas dang der skye tshul sogs ni tsha grang gi khyad par ma gtogs sngar ltar la/ bye brag tu chu bur can ni/ kha ba'i bu yug chen po rlung gis phyogs bzhi nas btab ste lus la phog pas chu bur byung zhing 'khums pa'o/ / chu bur rdol ba ni/ de las rnag khrag 'dzag pa'o/ / a chu zer ba ni/ sdug bsngal cher song bas skad kyi gdangs drag por 'don pa'o/ / kyi hud zer ba ni/ sdug bsngal de bas cher song bas skad kyi gdangs chag ste rkan gyi phug nas 'don pa'o/ / so tham tham pa ni/ sdug bsngal sngar las kyang je cher 'phel bas skad 'don ma nus par so tham tham byed pa'o/ / ut+pal ltar gas pa ni/ rlung chen pos btab pas kha dog sngo zhing ser chung phra mo kha drug tu gas pa'o/ / pad+ma ltar gas pa ni pags pa sngon po rnams zhus te sha'u dmar hu re ba tshal pa bcur gas pa'o/ / pad+ma ltar cher gas pa ni/ mdog sngon ma ltar la ser kha brgya'am de bas kyang mang ba ste/

it is taught that while in the intermediate state prior to a rebirth in this kind of hell, you have a sensation of heat and long to be cool. As a result, your intermediate state ends, and you are born in a place surrounded by ranges of frozen peaks. Below are snowy expanses and glaciers with deep crevices; above, snow and sleet storms rage. The place is thick with darkness, and you are struck by piercing winds. Otherwise, the place, the way you are born there, and so on, except for the difference in temperature, are as explained above. As for the particular hells, in Blisters blizzards blow in from the four directions and strike your body, making you hunch and develop blisters. In Burst Blisters, blood and pus ooze from the blisters. In Achoo, as suffering increases, you cry out loudly. In Kyihoo,[421] as suffering amplifies, your voice cracks, and you emit squeaking sounds from the back of your throat. In Chattering Teeth, suffering intensifies further; you are unable to emit a single sound, and your teeth chatter. In Split Like an Utpala Flower, your body is stung by strong winds; it turns blue and splits into six small cracks. In Split Like a Lotus, your blue skin peels, exposing bright red flesh, which divides into ten cracks. In Greatly Split Like a Lotus, the color is as before, but a hundred cracks or more form.

d.div: [421] Achoo is a Tibetan interjection used when one feels cold, and kyihoo is an interjection equivalent to “Woe is me!”

f.d:
skyes rabs las/
med par lta ba tshe rabs phyi ma la/ / gnas pa de na mun nag rlung grang ldang / / de ni rus pa'ang 'jig pa'i nad slong na/ / bdag la phan 'dod su zhig de ru 'jug[77] / ces so// sdug bsngal de yang ma ga ng+ha'i bre bo che'i khal brgyad cu 'gro ba'i til gyi bang ba nas lo brgya brgya na til re phyung bas de zad pa'i tshe chu bur can gyi tshe tshad du bshad pa sogs la lus 'dar ba dang yid skyo shas kyi snang ba drag tu bskyed do/ / de ltar dmyal ba tsha grang gi sdug bsngal bcu drug po 'di rgyud thog tu khel nges shes pa'i sdug bsngal la yid 'byung skyes na nye 'khor dang nyi tshe ba'i dmyal ba sogs rgyas bshad rnams la shugs kyis yid 'byung gi myong ba thon 'ong bas/ ha cang rgyas par mi spro na 'di tsam gyis chog gsung / zla ba gnyis tsam gyi long yod na nye 'khor nyi tshe'i sdug bsngal gyi dmigs skor spros te mdzad pa yi ge'i tshegs kyis 'jigs te ma bkod pas gzhan las shes par bya'o//

The Garland of Birth Stories says:
By holding nihilistic views, I will find myself in my future lives in a place of deep darkness where cold winds blow. When I am tormented by the pain of my bones’ disintegration, who will venture there in the wish to relieve me?[422] It is taught that the duration of a life in Blisters and its suffering is measured by the time it takes to empty a large storage bin filled with eighty khal[423] of sesame seeds — each khal being composed of [twenty] large Magadhan dré — by removing a single sesame seed every hundred years. The thought of this should make you tremble and induce a strong feeling of revulsion. If you can generate a feeling of disgust with suffering by understanding the sixteen hells’ torments of heat and cold in relation to yourself, an extensive explanation of the adjacent and intermittent hells should naturally prompt a similar experience of renunciation. [161] For this reason, it is taught that it is not strictly necessary to expand on the latter and that the former meditation is sufficient. If you have about two months available, you could extend the meditation topic to include the sufferings of the adjacent and intermittent hells, but for fear of being longwinded, I will not explain them here. You can refer to other works.

d.div: [77] sde dge_4150_bstan/ skyes rabs/ huslob dpon dpa' bo/ skyes pa'i rabs kyi rgyud/ shog_111_ba4
[422] Āryaśūra, Jātakamālā, Toh 4150 Tengyur, skyes rab, hu, 111b4.

[423] A khal is a Tibetan unit of both volume and weight, composed of twenty dré (bre). Dré is the name for both a square container and a unit of volume that approximates a quart. Three khal make up the load that a yak can carry.

f.d: gnyis pa dud 'gro'i sdug bsngal bsam pa ni
2.2.1.1.2.2. For the second part, contemplating the suffering of an animal,

bshes spring las/
dud 'gro'i skye gnas na yang gsod pa dang / / bcing dang rdeg sogs sdug bsngal sna tshogs pa/ / zhi gyur dge ba spangs pa rnams la ni/ / gcig la gcig za shin tu mi bzad pa/[78] / zhes dud 'gro la byings dang kha 'thor ba gnyis su sa sde las bshad pa'i byings na gnas pa ni ri rab kyi chu mtshams man chad kyi khongs su yod de lus kyi che chung sogs ma nges pa sna tshogs 'bru'i phung po ltar spungs pa rnams ni che bas chung ba khyur mid dang / chung bas che ba'i lus 'bugs pa dang / gzhan dag mun pa shin tu gnag pas lag pa brkyangs bskums tsam yang mi mthong ba dang / rgya mtshor gnas pa'i chu srin sogs ni gnas dang bza' btung dang grogs la nges pa med pa'o/ / kha 'thor ba'i ri dwags rnams ni lings pa dang khyi dang gcan gzan sogs kyis dbang med du 'dod pa/ bdag tu bzung ba rnams ni gsod rdeg bkol ba/ gzhan yang klu'i rigs rnams ni bye tshan dang mkha' lding gi 'jigs pa/ srog chags phra mo rnams ni rkyen cung zad tsam gyis 'chi ba sogs dang / mtha' dag kyang blang dor mi shes pa'i rang bzhin can te/ rang nyid bshad ma thag pa'i dud 'gro de dag ci rigs par skyes pa dang sdug bsngal gyi myong tshul sogs kyi nyams len myong ba skye nges su bsgom/ tshe'i tshad ni ring ba rnams bskal pa tsam nas/ thung ba nyin zhag kyang yod pas mtha' gcig tu ma nges so//

the Friendly Letter says:
In an animal rebirth, there are a variety sufferings: those of being killed, bound, beaten, and so forth. People who forsake virtue, the cause of liberation, must eat others and be horribly eaten.[424] Of the two categories of animals, aquatic and terrestrial, that are explained in [Asaṅga’s Five] Sections on Grounds,[425] those living at the bottom of the sea are found in the depths below the shores of Mount Meru’s oceans. Their size and so on are indefinite and diverse. Among those piled up like heaps of grain, the larger swallow the smaller, and the smaller bore into the bodies of the larger. Moreover, it is so dark that they cannot even see their own limbs when they extend and retract them. The habitat, food, drink, and companions of those like crocodiles who live in the ocean are unpredictable. As for the animals scattered on the land, they are pursued by hunters, dogs, and predators against their wishes. Domestic animals are beaten, exploited, and slaughtered. Furthermore, those of the serpent class fear hot sands and [birds of prey like] garuḍas. As for tiny organisms, the slightest change in conditions brings about their death. None of them have the slightest idea of what should be adopted and what should be rejected. Be sure to meditate that you are born as one of the animals just mentioned until you gain a meditative experience of their suffering and so on. Their life span may be as long as an eon or as short as a day; nothing about them is definite.

d.div: [78] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / shog_44_ba6
[424] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha, verse 90, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44b6.
[425] The Five Sections on Grounds (Sa sde nga) here refers to the Yogācāra Grounds (Yogācārabhūmi) Toh 4035.

f.d: gsum pa yi dwags kyi sdug bsngal ni
2.2.1.1.2.3. For the third part, contemplating the suffering of hungry ghosts,

bshes spring las/
yi dwags na yang 'dod pas phongs pa yis/ / bskyed pa'i sdug bsngal rgyun chags mi 'chos pa/ / bkres skom grang dro ngal dang 'jigs pa yis/ / bskyed pa shin tu mi bzad bsten 'tshal lo/[79] / zhes yi dwags la rigs gsum du yod par bshad pa'i phyi'i sgrib pa can ni ljon pa'i 'bras bu dang chu klung sogs mthong ste longs spyod par phyin pa na mtshon cha thogs pas bsrung ba'am rnag khrag sogs su mthong ba'o/ /

the Friendly Letter says: [162]
Hungry ghosts are continuously subjected to the suffering of never seeing their desires fulfilled and must undergo the unbearable [torments] of hunger and thirst, heat and cold, and fatigue and fear.[426] Among the three categories of hungry ghosts taught, those with outer obstacles see fruit trees and rivers, but when they go to help themselves to them, they perceive guards brandishing weapons, or pus and blood, in their stead.

d.div: [79] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / shog_45_na1
[426] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha, verse 91, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 45a1.

f.d: nang gi sgrib pa can ni grong khyer ser skya zhes bya ba chu dang rtsi shing sogs 'dod pa'i dngos po ci yang med pa der zas skom mi rnyed pa dang / cung zad rnyed kyang kha khab mig mgrin pa rta rnga lto ba ri rab yan lag 'jag ma lta bur gyur pa'i dbang gis zas khar mi shong / nyung zad song ba rnams mgrin pa nas mi thar/ thar kyang lto ba ma khengs pas sdug bsngal ba'o/ / zas skom gyi sgrib pa can ni zas skom rnams kyang me 'bar nas lus 'tshig pa dang / bshang gci dang rang sha za bas nyam thag pa'o/ / gzhan yang so ga zla ba'i reg bya tsha zhing dgun nyi ma grang ba/ bltas pa tsam gyis chu klung bskams te ngam grog tu 'char ba sogs bkres skom gyi sdug bsngal sna tshogs myong ba de dag tu bshad ma thag pa'i yi dwags de 'dra'i gzugs su rang nyid skyes par bsams te rgyud thog tu khel nges shes pa zhig bsgom mo/ / sdug bsngal de yang yun thung ngu tsam ma yin par mi lo chig khri lnga stong myong dgos par bshad pa sogs la rjes su dpags te bsams na nges 'byung bcos min skye bar snang /

Those with inner obstacles are found in a town called Kapila that lacks everything desirable — water, fruit trees, and so on — and where they find nothing to eat or drink. If they happen to find a little, given that their mouths are the size of the eye of a needle, their throats as narrow as a horsehair, their stomachs as large as Mount Meru, and their limbs as thin as blades of grass, the food does not fit into their mouths, or if some does, it cannot descend their throats, or when it does, it does not fill their stomach. As a result, they suffer. The food and drink of those with obstacles regarding food and drink catches fire and burns their body, or they eat excrement, urine, and their own flesh — such are their hardships. Furthermore, the moonlight in summer feels hot to them, the sunlight in winter, cold; merely glancing at a river is enough to dry it up and make it appear as a deep ravine. In meditation, you are to truly relate these to yourself: you think that you are born with the body of a hungry ghost and experience the various sufferings of hunger and thirst described. These lives do not last just a short time. It is taught that they must be experienced for 15,000 human years. Continue to reflect, getting the measure of it all, until uncontrived renunciation arises in you.

don hril gyi dril na da lta rang re rnams ja phor pa gang 'thung yun tsam zhig lag pa me dong du 'jug pa/ dgun grang bsgang la zhag gcig tsam gcer bu byed pa/ zhag gsum bzhi tsam bza' btung ye med pa/ sa rdo mang po spungs pa'i 'og tu 'gul skyod mi nus par gnas dgos pa lta bu byung na bzod bsran mi thub pa mngon sum gyis grub pa de ltar na ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal bzod ga la nus pas mgon po klu sgrub kyis/
thob dka' 'dzam gling mi yi lus/ / de thob dus su ngan song rgyu/ / rab tu bsgrims te bcad par bya/[80] / zhes da res mi dang dud 'gro'i khyad par 'byed pa'i dus 'dir snying rus bskyed dgos snyam pa'i rang la yang yang lcag gis brab par bya'o// //

To sum up fully the significance of the above, if we were forced to hold our hand in a flame for the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, to remain naked in the depths of winter for about a day, to go without food and drink for three or four days, or to remain under a pile of stones and earth unable to move, clearly we would find it unbearable. Given that, how could we possibly bear the torments of the three unfortunate realms? The protector Nāgārjuna says:
A human rebirth in Jambudvīpa is difficult to acquire. Having attained one, channel all your efforts into ending the causes of the unfortunate realms.[427] Thinking, “As a human, now is the time to distinguish myself from an animal. I must pluck up my courage,” spur yourself on again and again. [163]

d.div: [80] sde dge_4330_bstan/ thun mong ba lugs kyi bstan bcos/ ngo _mgon po klu sgrub/ skye bo gso ba'i thigs pa/ shog_115_na7
[427] Nāgārjuna, A Drop to Rejuvenate the Person (Jantupoṣaṇabindu), Toh 4330 Tengyur, lugs kyi bstan bcos, ngo, 115a7.

f.d:
smras pa/ tsha sreg rab 'bar lcags kyi khang pa'i nang / / bcad gtubs btsir ba'i khrag gi chu klung 'bab/ / dbang po'i sgo nas lhab lhab me 'bar ba'i/ / tshul 'dir mi 'jigs snying la gdon gyis brlams/ /
mun nag gangs ri'i sbubs kyi 'thor rlung khrod/ / grang reg rnon po'i mtshon gyis nyam chung lus/ / brgya stong mang por gas kyang mi 'chi ba'i/ / byed po mi dge'i dgra 'dis rtag tu mnar/ /
rma 'bras nad kyi zug gzer chung ngu yang / / mi bzod bzhin du sha rus pags pa'i ched/ / gsod cing za ba'i sdug bsngal mtha' med la/ / snying rtsa mi 'dar sems med bem po'am ci/ /
da lta'i tshe thung 'di yi zas skom don/ / ngal bar nus na mi lo khri lnga stong / / mi bzad bkres skom gdung ba sel slad du/ / lus srog 'dor nus snying rus bskyed kyang chubs/ /
bzod dka' ngan 'gro'i g.yang la ba spu'i rtse/ / 'gul ba tsam gyi ya nga ma mchis kyang / / dgra 'dul gnyen skyong 'di snang chos brgyad la/ / spyang grung khur 'dzin khyod las blun pa su/ / zhes bya ba ni bar skabs kyi tshigs su bcad pa'o// //

d.div: In a blazing iron house that is scorching hot, you are cut, chopped, and squeezed until your blood flows. From the doors of your senses, flames shoot forth. The heart of those who do not fear these must be under a demon’s sway.

Amid fierce winds, surrounded by dark snowy mountains, although the sharp weapon of bitter cold has cracked your feeble body into thousands of pieces, still you do not die. It is the foe nonvirtue that causes such constant torment.

When you cannot bear the minor pain of a small wound, you must be mindless matter if you do not tremble at the prospect of the endless torment of being killed to eat your flesh or for your bones and skin.

You are capable of toiling for the sake of the food and drink of this short life, but to overcome the horrific torments of hunger and thirst lasting fifteen thousand human years, even exertion so intense that you risk your very life will not suffice.

Your fear of the unbearable abyss of the three unfortunate realms is insufficient even to give you gooseflesh, yet you think yourself very clever in adopting this life’s eight concerns — overcoming enemies and caring for friends. Where is there a greater fool than you?

f.d: bstan pa la 'jug pa'i sgo skyabs su 'gro ba/
gnyis pa 'jig rten phyi mar bde ba'i thabs bsten pa la bstan pa
2.2.1.2. The second part, relying on the methods for happiness in future lives,
['di ]la 'jug pa'i sgo skyabs su 'gro ba/ bde legs thams cad kyi rtsa ba las 'bras sgom pa gnyis/
has two parts: taking refuge, the gateway to the Dharma, and contemplating karma and its effects — the source of all goodness and happiness.
dang po ['jug pa'i sgo skyabs su 'gro ba ]
2.2.1.2.1. The first, [refuge]
['di ]la dngos dang / bslab bya gnyis/
has two parts: the main topic — taking refuge, the gateway to the Dharma — and its precepts.
dang po [dngos dang /]ni
2.2.1.2.1.1. On the main topic,

spyod 'jug las/
ji ltar mtshan mo mun nag sprin rum na/ / glog 'gyu skad cig rab snang ston pa ltar/ / de bzhin sangs rgyas mthu yis brgya lam na/ / 'jig rten bsod nams blo gros thang 'ga' 'byung / /
de ltas dge ba nyam chung nyid la rtag/ / sdig pa stobs chen shin tu mi bzad pa/[81] / zhes nyes dmigs la 'jigs pa/ yon tan la dad pa/ rang 'dra'i 'gro ba la snying rje gsum gyi sgo nas bsam pa la dam pa'i chos kyi sgra tsam mi thos pa'i mun bskal ni mtshan mo sprin nag 'khrigs pa'i smag rum lta bu nas chos dang mjal rgyu yod pa'i sgron bskal ni mun rum de na glog 'khyug pa bzhin du dkon pas sngon chad sdig pa rgya mtsho chen po tsam nas dge ba ku sha'i rtses chu thigs blangs pa ltar stobs shin tu chung ba'i steng du tshe 'dir yang chos pa'i ming gzugs kyi blo 'drid kyis gzhan mgo bskor ba las gsung rab dang rang sems spyod tshul rnams zhus dag btang na mi dge ba'i phyogs ches mang bar gda'/ de yang rang la dgra ma rung ba zhig yod dogs pa las myur du 'ong ba'i gtam dang dgra de'i dpa' nus tshur lus srog longs spyod la ji ltar gnod sogs kyi rgyu mtshan yang ma nges na de la 'jigs pa dang zon byed pa mi 'ong la/ dgra de byung na rmeg med du 'joms pa dang / dus kyang lo gcig tshun la 'ong nges shing de'i bar la nam 'ong cha med par shes na dal bar sdod pa skad cig mi nus par/ pha rol gyi dgra las stobs mnga' thang che nges kyi dpon zhig 'tshol zhing grogs su sbron nam/ mkhar btsan po bzo'am/ des mi sleb pa'i thag ring du 'gro ba sogs sta gon gang rung byed pa ltar dgra ngan song gi sdug bsngal zer ba de lo brgya tshun la 'ong par nges shing / zla ba rting ma dang mnar med kyi dmyal ba gnyis gang snga mi shes pas 'chi ba mi rtag pa dang ngan 'gro'i ngang tshul la gong du myong bas thon pa'i dbang gis skyabs gnas shig 'tshol ba las 'os mi 'dug/

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way states:
Just as the night, swathed in clouds and darkness, is momentarily illuminated by flashes of lightning, likewise, by Buddha’s power, in beings a virtuous thought occasionally dawns.
Thereby comprehend that while virtue remains feeble, powerful sins are not in the least depleted.[428] With the three — fear of misdeeds, faith in good qualities, and compassion for beings like you — first think that dark eons in which one can never hear the words of the perfect Dharma are like nights swathed in darkness and laden with black clouds. The rarity of an eon of light in which you can meet the Dharma is like a flash of lightning in that dark night. [164] Compared to the ocean of your past sins, your virtues are as feeble as the few drops that a blade of kuśa grass dipped in water picks up. Moreover, in this life, having become accustomed to the title and appearance of a Dharma practitioner, you have in this way misled others, for when you check your thoughts and behavior against the Buddha’s words, almost all of them tend toward nonvirtue. Suppose you suspect a fierce enemy might come, and you hear he will be arriving soon. If you are not aware of how his great strength could kill you, mutilate you, destroy your belongings, and so on, you will neither fear him nor take any precautions. However, if you know that on his arrival, he will destroy you completely, and that he is sure to come within the year, although you do not know exactly when, you cannot possibly feel easy even in passing. To prepare yourself, you might seek out a leader much stronger than the enemy and send for him, perhaps build a sturdy fort or escape to a distant land where he cannot reach you. In the same way, your prior familiarization with impermanence and the unfortunate realms within meditation makes you certain that (1) within the next hundred years you are to meet the enemy, unfortunate realm suffering, and of the two — next month or the Relentless hell — you do not know which will come first, and (2) nothing is more important than for you to seek protection from that suffering.

d.div: [81] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u+o/ 1_sh+loka_5_shog_2_na1
[428] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 1.5–6, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 2a1.

f.d:
skyabs yul yang slob dpon phyogs glang gis/
gting mtha' med pa'i 'khor ba ni/ / rgya mtsho'i nang na rnam par gnas/ / 'dod chags la sogs mi bzad pa'i/ / chu srin gyis ni lus zos pas/ / de ring gang la skyabs su mchi/[82] / zhes 'khor ba 'di rgya mtsho ltar gting zab cing / 'dod chags la sogs pa mi dge ba'i chu srin gdug pa can gyis gtses par chud pa'i rang re skye rgu rnams gang la skyabs su 'gro zhes dri ba'i tshul du gsungs pa la lan gyi tshul du bstod pa brgya lnga bcu pa las/
gang zhig la ni nyes pa kun/ / gtan nas yong ye mi mnga' zhing / / gang la rnam pa thams cad du/ / yon tan thams cad gnas gyur pa/ / gal te sems shig yod na ni/ / de nyid la ni skyabs 'gro zhing / / de bstod de ni bkur ba dang / / de yi bstan la gnas par rigs/[83] / zhes dgra zla las stobs dang kha drag chung ba zhig gis rang pha rol gyi dgra de'i 'jigs pa las skyob mi nus pa bzhin tshangs pa dang khyab 'jug dang dbang phyug sogs lha mi mthu bo che la brten kyang khong rang rnams 'khor ba las ma thar bar 'khor ba'i nyes pas mnar bzhin pa yin pas gtan gyi skyabs su mi 'os/ gang 'os na/

Concerning the objects of refuge, Master Dignāga states:
While abiding in the ocean that is samsara, both boundless and deep, as I am devoured by the countless sea monsters of attachment and the rest, today in whom am I to take refuge?[429] While plunged in samsara, which is as deep as the ocean, and maimed by the hideous sea monsters of nonvirtue — attachment and the like — the author asks the question: who should sentient beings seek out for refuge? The Praise in Hundred and Fifty Verses provides the answer:
Whoever is utterly free of all faults, whoever completely possesses all good qualities, if you have any sense at all, take refuge in such a being. It is only fitting to praise this being, serve him, and dwell in his teaching.[430] [165] Someone less powerful and mighty than your enemy cannot protect you from the fear of him. You might count on powerful gods like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara and the rest, but as they are not free of samsara themselves and continue to be subject to its torments, they are not definitive objects of refuge. Who are?

f.d:
skyabs 'gro bdun cu par/
sangs rgyas chos dang dge 'dun ni/ / thar pa 'dod pa rnams kyi skyabs/[84] / zhes dkon mchog gsum gtan gyi skyabs su gsungs pa ni bshad ma thag pa'i skyon dang bral zhing yon tan dang ldan pas bslu ba med par nges pa rnyed nas skyabs su 'gro ba la/ 'gro tshul gyi dmigs skor mang yang 'dra bcos rgyas bkab gyis rang bzo med pa'i chos 'di ga'i lugs srol gyi bzhed pa/

Seventy Verses on Going for Refuge explains:
The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are the refuges of those desiring liberation.[431] The Three Jewels are said to be the definitive objects of refuge. Once you have ascertained that they are infallible, being free of all the aforementioned faults and endowed with all good qualities, you are to take refuge in them. This can be achieved using many different visualizations. I will explain how to take refuge according to the [lamrim] teaching tradition, which is free of the personal fabrication of making up something similar or taking something from another source.

d.div: [84] sde dge_3971_bstan/ dbu ma/ gi_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ skyabs 'gro bdun cu pa/ shog_251_na1
[431] Candrakīrti, Triśaraṇagamanasaptati, Toh 3971 Tengyur, dbu ma, gi, 251a1.

f.d:
dpe la bstod pa las/
khyod sku mtshan gyis spras gyur pa/ / mdzes gyur mig gi bdud rtsi ni/ / sprin med ston gyi nam mkha' la/ / skar ma'i tshogs kyis spras pa 'dra/[85] / zhes pa ltar bsam dgos pas sangs rgyas kyi sku sgom tshul yang gsang sngags kyi skabs su sgom pa'i/ mdun du dam tshig pa bskyed pa lta bu'i ched du gsal btab pa de 'dra ma yin par/ dper na khrom dang tshong 'dus chen por phyin pa na dro shon la sogs pa'i ltad mo sna tshogs dang rgyan cha lugs dang 'khor g.yog gi mdzes pa sogs gang zag mchog dman rang blo 'jug pa'i rigs mthong ba na/ slar gnas de ma yin pa'i gzhan du sleb pa'i dus dran shes kyis gsos btab pa'i tshe de rnams kyi byad dbyibs rgyan cha lugs spyod lam sogs mig gis mthong rgyu yod pa lta bur bkra lam gyi 'char ba yin gyi/ de rnams mdun gyi thang lta bur ched gnyer sgom pa'i snang ba mi 'char ba bzhin du 'dir yang de bzhin gshegs pa'i bris 'bur gyi sku gzugs la yang yang bltas shing / sems kyis de bzhin gshegs pa de sku mdog gser btso ma lta bu na bza' chos gos gsum dang ldan pa mtshan dang dpe byad kyis spras pa lta bas chog mi shes pa zhig yod pa 'dug go snyam du gsos btab pa na sngar mig shes kyi yul du gyur pa des rkyen byas nas gsal laM laM pa 'char bas de'i tshe mthong na mi mthun pa med cing mthong ba tsam gyis don dang ldan par byed nus pa de lta bu byang chub sems dpa' man chad la med pa'i sangs rgyas kyi sku'i yon tan phul du byung bar 'dug snyam pa'i dad pa lhang lhang ba dang / dngos su mjal rgyu byung na snyam pa'i gdung ba dang / sangs rgyas rjes su dran pa 'di lta bu bsod nams che snyam pa'i spro ba rnams shug drag po ma byung gi bar du bsgom/

The Praise with Similes says:
Your body adorned with the marks is beautiful — ambrosia for the eyes, like a cloudless autumn sky adorned with clusters of stars.[432] You should reflect accordingly. You are not to meditate on the Buddha’s form as in tantra — doing [an elaborate] visualization in which you picture the commitment beings and so forth before you.[433] It is more like when you visit a large marketplace or festival, and you see all sorts of performances that you enjoy — dances and so on — and the [performers’] beautiful jewelry, trappings, entourage, and so on and all the grand and ordinary people. After leaving and going elsewhere, you can bring them to mind once more through your faculty of recollection. There is no need to make a special point of meditating on them for the jewelry, trappings, performances, and so on to appear to you again as clearly as if you were seeing them with your very own eyes. In the same way, at this point begin by repeatedly examining a painting or statue of the Tathāgata’s physical form. Then picture it in your mind, thinking: Here is the Tathāgata, his body the color of refined gold. He wears the three monastic garments and is adorned with the marks and signs. One never tires of seeing him. Thanks to having first perceived this through visual consciousness, it will appear to you distinctly. Then you reflect, thinking, “It is never displeasing to view, and just seeing it has a beneficial effect.[434] The Buddha’s body has extraordinary qualities that are lacking in all those who are bodhisattvas and below,” until you are filled with intense faith, longing to meet him directly, and great joy at the thought of your good fortune in having the opportunity just to picture the Buddha in your mind. [166]

d.div: [85] sde dge_1138_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon ma ti tsi tra/ bsngags 'os bsngags bstod/ le'u/ 13 shog_99_ba4
[432] Mātṛceṭa, Praise to the One Beyond All Praise (Varṇārhavarṇestotra), Toh 1138 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 99b4.

[433] In tantra you visualize the objects of refuge or members of the merit field, called commitment beings, and then you invite the actual buddhas and so on, called wisdom beings, to come from their abodes and dissolve into the beings you have visualized.
[434] Just seeing it purifies you of wrongdoing, for example.

f.d:
de bzhin du gsung gi yon tan ni bden pa po'i le'u las/
'di ltar sems can kun gyis nges pa'i tshig/ / mang po dag gis dus gcig zhu zhus na/ / sems kyi skad cig gcig la thugs chud nas/ / gsung dbyangs gcig gis so sor lan yang 'debs/ /
de lta bas na 'dren pa 'jig rten na/ / tshangs pa'i sgra dbyangs gsung sgrog mkhyen par mdzod/ / de ni lha mi'i sdug bsngal mthar 'byin pa'i/ / chos kyi 'khor lo rab tu skor bar mdzad/[86] / ces pa ltar bsam dgos kyang sangs rgyas kyi gsung dang 'dra ba'am de'i dper 'os pa zhig dngos su thos pa'i skal ba phra bas/ da lta pi wang lta bu rang gi blo 'gro ba'i sgra snyan pa zhig las rjes su dpags te/ gong gi sku shin tu mdzes pa'i sangs rgyas de'i mgur las 'ongs pa'i gsung gi sgra snyan pa yan lag drug cu rtsa bzhi'i dbyangs can/ khams gsum gyi sems can thams cad kyis dus gcig tu dri ba zhus na/ legs sbyar gyi skad lta bu gcig gi sgo nas bstan pa'i dri lan de 'gro ba so so'i skad du shar te the tshom cig car du sel ba sogs sngar bzhin dad gdung spro gsum gyi sgo nas nyams su myong bar bya/

On his qualities of speech, the Satyaka Chapter states:
It is like this: if all sentient beings simultaneously asked him a great variety of questions, he would understand them in an instant, and with a single utterance answer each.
Therefore, know that in the world, the Guide voices Brahmā’s pleasing melody and turns the wheel of the Dharma that eradicates the sufferings of gods and humans.[435] You should reflect in this manner, but since the likelihood of hearing anything resembling the Buddha’s speech or finding anything that could qualify as an illustration of it is so small, you are to imagine it by drawing on the sweet sound of, for example, a lute that you find melodious. Think how the pleasing tone of the speech that issues from the throat of the Buddha, with the magnificent physical form described above, has sixty-four harmonious traits, and how if each being of the three realms of existence were to ask him a question simultaneously, the answer he would give in a single language like Sanskrit would be heard in each being’s language and would immediately dispel all their doubts. As before, ensure that you gain a meditative experience of this that involves faith, longing, and joy.

d.div: [86] sde dge_146_bka'/ mdo sde/ pa_byang chub sems dpa'i spyod yul gyi thabs kyi yul la rnam par 'phrul ba bstan pa/(bden pa po'i le'u/) le'u/ 9_shog_121_na7

f.d:
thugs kyi yon tan ni bsngags 'os bsngags bstod las/
khyod 'ba' zhig gi ye shes kyis/ / shes bya mtha' dag khyab lags kyi/ / khyod las gzhan pa thams cad kyi/ / shes bya kho na lhag pa lags/[87] / zhes mkhyen pa'i yon tan chos mtha' dag la lkog tu ma gyur bas rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa'i ye shes kyis gdul bya'i dbang po dang 'tsham par rjes su 'dzin pa la mkhas/

As for his mental qualities, Praise to the One Beyond All Praise states:
Only your sublime wisdom comprehends all objects of knowledge. For everyone other than you, there remain objects to be known.[436] His quality of knowledge is such that to him no existents are unknown to it. Thanks to his superior wisdom of omniscience, he is skilled in caring for his followers according to their capacities.
