[184] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_1_shog_23_na7
[185] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_16_shog_10_ba6
[564] Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra, chap. 3, Toh 106 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 9b2.

[565] Dysfunctional tendencies are defined in Tsongkhapa’s Great Treatise (Tib.), 422, as a mind’s predispositions that can generate more and more afflictions; signs are defined as the habitual manifest cravings for wrong objects that activate these predispositions.
[566] Here “grasping at signs” is mainly grasping at the wrong object that is intrinsic existence.
[567] Candrapradīpasūtra (a.k.a. King of Meditations Sutra, Samādhirājasūtra), chap. 7, Toh 127, Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 20b6.
[568] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 8.1 Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma la, 23a7.
[569] Ibid. 5.16, 10b6. The Knower of Suchness here is the Buddha.

f.d:
de yang zhi ba lhas/
zhi gnas rab tu ldan pa'i lhag mthong gis/ / nyon mongs rnam par 'joms par shes byas te/ / thog mar zhi gnas btsal bya/[186] / zhes bdag 'dzin gyi rtsa ba chod par byed pa la bdag med rtogs pa'i shes rab sgom dgos/

Śāntideva also states:
Knowing that insight fully combined with tranquil abiding completely conquers the afflictions, first seek tranquil abiding.[570] To cut the root of grasping at self, you must cultivate the wisdom understanding selflessness.

d.div: [186] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_4_shog_23_ba1

f.d:
de'i sngon du zhi gnas sgom pa la/ mdo sde rgyan las/
blo ldan gang du bsgrub pa'i yul/ / legs par rnyed dang gnas bzang dang / / sa bzang ba dang grogs bzang dang / / rnal 'byor bde ba'i yo byad ldan/[187] / zhes zas gos sogs chos sgrub pa'i mthun rkyen rnyed sla zhing / gcan gzan dang chom rkun dgra gdon gyi 'tshe ba med pa/ nad mi bskyed pa'i sa bzang ba/ chos ldan gyi grogs dang ldan pa/ don med kyi g.yeng ba'i 'du 'dzi mtha' dag gis dben pa ni chos 'di nyams su len pa'i gnas kyi khyad par yin la/ gnas de dang ldan yang gang zag rang ngos nas rnam g.yeng gi rgyu bsgrubs na thabs shes ya bral du 'gro bas zas gos bzang po dang mang ba la dga' ba spangs te 'dod pa chung ba/ zas bsod snyoms dang gos phyag dar khrod pas chog shes pa/ tshong khe spogs sman dpyad dang skar rtsis sogs bya ba mang po la mi 'jug cing tshul khrims dag pa/ 'dod pa'i nyes dmigs dang mi rtag pa'i ngang tshul legs par bsam pa'i chos drug la brten nas nyams su blang bar bya ba yin no//

Prior to that you are to develop tranquil abiding, regarding which the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
The place where the intelligent practice is one with ready supplies, in a safe and healthy location, and with good companions and the requirements for a meditator’s success.[571] Supplies like food and clothing needed for spiritual practice should be readily available. The place should be free of harmful elements like dangerous animals, thieves, enemies, and evil spirits. It should be healthy, not one where you fall sick, and include practitioner companions. It should be free of all kinds of diversions that are pointless distractions. Such is the ideal place for applying this instruction. [237] Those who, despite having such a place available to them, create sources of distraction have failed to link method and wisdom. You should (1) have few desires and (2) not delight in large quantities of good food and clothing; (3) be content with begging for food and with clothes made from rags from the refuse heap; (4) avoid involvement in numerous activities like business, medicine, astrology, and so on; (5) uphold pure ethical discipline; and (6) reflect well on the drawbacks of attachment[572] and on impermanence. Your practice should be grounded in these six conditions.

d.div: [187] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 14_sh+loka_12_shog_17_ba7
[571] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, 14.7, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 17b7.

[572] In the context of the six favorable conditions for cultivating tranquil abiding, “attachment” refers to eight thoughts of desire to reject, which are enumerated in Asaṅga’s Śrāvaka Grounds: desire, ill will, physical violence, thoughts concerning your circle of family and friends, thoughts concerning compatriots, thoughts of not dying, scorn for others, and thoughts concerning worldly wealth and so on.

f.d: [dmigs pa gtad par bya ba'i yul ]
a. [Objects of meditation]

de'i tshul la/ dmigs pa gtad par bya ba'i yul de bzhin gshegs pas rnal 'byor ba'i dmigs pa bzhi gsungs pa'i 'dod chags kyi gnyen por mi sdug pa dang / zhe sdang gi gnyen por byams pa dang / gti mug gi gnyen por rten 'brel dang / 'byung ba lnga dang rnam shes kyi cha rnams so sor dmigs pa dang / dbugs phyi nang du 'gro ba bgrang ba lta bu rnams spyad pa rnam sbyong gi dmigs pa/ gzugs la sogs pa'i phung po lnga dang mig la sogs pa'i khams bco brgyad dang / skye mched bcu gnyis dang / rten 'brel yan lag bcu gnyis dang / dge mi dge'i las 'bras kyi rgyu rkyen la dmigs pa lta bu rnams mkhas pa'i dmigs pa/ 'dod pa'i sa nas ci yang med pa'i skye mched kyi bar gyi gong ma la zhi ba dang 'og ma la rags pa'i zhi rags kyi rnam pa can du blta ba lta bu nyon mongs rnam sbyong gi dmigs pa/ khyab pa'i dmigs pa de thams cad kyi khongs su 'du ba yin la/

As for the way to practice, the Tathāgata taught four kinds of objects of meditation. The objects for purifying behavior are ugliness as the antidote to attachment, love as the antidote to aversion, interdependence as the antidote to ignorance, the five elements and the aspects of consciousness visualized individually [as the antidote to pride], and counting the movements of your breath [as the antidote to distraction]. Objects of expertise are, for example, the five aggregates — form and so on — the eighteen elements, the eyes and so on, the twelves spheres, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the causes and conditions of virtuous and nonvirtuous karmas and their effects. Affliction-purifying objects are, for example, the view of peaceful and coarse aspects — the relative peacefulness of higher realms compared to the coarseness of lower ones — and so on, from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness. Universal objects include all the above.

de yang / nam grus zhus pa nyan sar drangs pa las/
nam gru gal te dge slong rnal 'byor pa rnal 'byor spyod pa de 'dod chags spyod pa kho na zhig yin na ni dmigs pa mi sdug pa la sems nye bar gtod par byed do/ / zhe sdang spyod pa zhig yin na ni byams pa la'o/ / gti mug spyod pa zhig yin na ni rkyen 'di nyid rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba la'o/ / nga rgyal spyod pa zhig yin na ni khams kyi rab tu dbye ba la sems nye bar gtod par byed de/[188] zhes skye ba sngon ma nas chags sogs nyon mongs pa la shas cher goms pas yul chung ngu la yang dug gsum che zhing yun ring du skye ba rnams kyi gnyen por 'dod chags sogs nyon mongs pa gang shas che ba de nyid 'joms par byed dgos pa yin zhing / tshe sngon ma nas goms 'dris chung ba dang / tshe 'dir nyon mongs cha mnyam du spyod pa rnams la rang nyid gang 'dod pa'i dmigs pa zhig las dmigs kyis dkar [189] mi dgos pa/ dper na rlung nad dang ma 'dres pa'i tshad pas na bar tsha ba'i bcos kho nas chog la tshad rlung 'dres ma yin na tsha ba'i sman steng du rlung gi sman gyi kha tshar bsnan dgos pa bzhin no//

Śrāvaka Grounds quotes the following from Questions of Revata:
Revata, if a monk-meditator engaged in meditation is exclusively affected by attachment, he should focus his mind on the object ugliness; if he is affected by anger, on love; if he is affected by ignorance, on the links of dependent origination; if he is affected by pride, on the classifications of the elements.[573] Due to strong habituation to afflictions like attachment over past lives, the three poisons may arise at the slightest pretext and persist a long time. [238] To remedy this, you need to counteract your strongest affliction, such as attachment. If you did not become particularly habituated to afflictions in past lives, and if in this life you are involved in a number of them in equal measure, you may choose whatever object you like; there is no need to favor one. When, for example, you have a fever but no wind illness is associated to it, a treatment for fever alone will be sufficient, but for a combination of fever and wind illnesses, you will need to complement the fever medicine with a wind medicine.

d.div: [188] sde dge_4036_bstan/ sems tsam/ dzi_'phags pa thogs med/ nyan thos kyi sa/ rnal 'byor gyi gnas gnyis pa/ shog_77_na5
[189] bkar mi/ rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/
[573] Asaṅga, Śrāvakabhūmi, chap. 2 Toh 4036 Tengyur, sems tsam, dzi, 77a5 ā.

f.d:
la la dag mdo las ting nge 'dzin gyi dmigs pa bzhir gsungs pas na dmigs pa de dag thams cad sgom dgos so snyam pa'i log rtog skye srid mod/ de ltar byas na sems gnas pa'i grogs su mi 'gyur bar ma zad g.yeng ba'i rgyu byed pas dpal ldan dpa' bos/
dmigs pa gcig la brtan tshul du/ / yid kyi bsam pa brtan par bya/ / dmigs pa mang po brgyud pa las/ / yid ni nyon mongs 'khrug par 'gyur/[190] / zhes gsungs pa ltar yin pas gnad du 'gro ba'i dmigs pa slob dpon byang chub bzang pos/
lus kha T+wAM gar sgom pa dang lus la brten pa'i thig le la dmigs pa lta bu kha nang bltas kyi zhi gnas dang / sku dang gsung la dmigs pa kha phyir bltas kyi zhi gnas [191] zhes gsungs pa'i phyag len phyi ma nyid gtso che bar gnang mod/ sku gzugs mdun du bzhag pa la mig gis bltas pa'i har sgom byed par mi rigs par slob dpon ye shes sdes bkag pa'i shugs la/ rten can rde'u shing bu zhes sogs sgom chen pa mtha' dag gi ngag las rlung ltar grags pa kun shugs kyis khegs 'gro bas/ lugs 'di la ting nge 'dzin yid shes la sgrub pa nyid thog ma nas byed dgos mod/

Since the sutras teach four kinds of objects of states of concentration, some people wrongly imagine that all four are to be meditated on, but this will not only fail to further mental stability, it will in fact cause distraction. As Āryaśūra states:
Maintaining a single focal object, stabilize your mental reflections. By changing focal objects often, your mind will be disturbed by afflictions.[574] It is as taught. Regarding the most relevant objects, the master Bodhibhadra says:
There is “inward-turned tranquil abiding,” such as meditating on the body as a khaṭvāṇga staff and observing drops in relation to the body, and “outward-turned tranquil abiding” that focuses on a [deity’s] body and speech.[575] The latter is the principal tradition, but it is not suitable to place the image of a deity in front of you and just stare at it. Master Yeshé Dé’s[576] refutation of this indirectly challenges many “great meditators” who take the likes of pebbles and small fruits as objects of meditation and whose words are as widespread as the wind. According to the present tradition, from the start, states of concentration must be cultivated based on mental consciousness.

d.div: [190] sde dge_3944_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_slob dpon dpa' bo/ phar phyin bsdus pa/ bsam gtan phar phyin gyi le'u/ shog_229_na4
[191] sde dge_3924_bstan/ dbu ma/ ki_slob dpon byang chub bzang po/ ting nge 'dzin tshogs kyi le'ur/ shog_90_na5
[574] Condensed Presentation of the Perfections (Pāramitāsamāsa), Toh 3944 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 229a4.
[575] Chapter on the Conditions for Meditative Concentration (Samādhisambhāraparivarta), Toh 3924 Tengyur, dbu ma, ki, 90a5.

f.d: [nyes pa lnga spong ba'i 'du byed brgyad ]
b. [The five faults and the eight applications]

de yang nyes pa lnga spong ba'i 'du byed brgyad kyi sgo nas zhi gnas sgrub par gong ma mtha' dag bzhed cing / lam rim che chung rnams su rgyas par gsungs pas/ dbus mtha' las/
der gnas las su rung ba nyid/ / don rnams thams cad 'byor bar 'gyur/ / nyes pa lnga spong 'du byed brgyad/ / bsten pa'i rgyu las byung ba 'o/ /
le lo dang ni gdams ngag rnams/ / brjed dang bying dang rgod pa dang / / 'du mi byed dang 'du byed de/ / 'di dag nyes pa lngar 'dod do/[192] / zhes zhi gnas sgom pa la mi spro zhing de'i mi mthun phyogs la dga' ba ni le lo/ gang dmigs par bya ba'i yul mi gsal par dmigs pa stor ba ni brjed pa/ dmigs pa ma brjed kyang bying rgod gang rung gi dbang du shor ba/ de'i dbang du shor ba ngos zin kyang de spong ba'i gnyen po 'du mi byed pa/ bying rgod dang bral ba'i tshe dmigs pa gnad du mi bsnun par bying rgod kyi gnyen po ha cang 'du byed pa ste nyes pa lnga po 'di bcar gyis ngos zin pa byas nas de'i gnyen po ni dbus mtha' las/
gnas dang de la gnas pa dang / / rgyu dang 'bras bu nyid du 'o/ / dmigs pa brjed par ma gyur dang / / bying dang rgod pa rtogs pa dang / / de spong mngon par 'du byed dang / / zhi tshe rnal du 'jug pa'o//[193] zhes pa ting nge 'dzin la brtson 'grus rgyun ldan du rtsom nus pa ni gnas pa po yin la de gang la gnas na/ ting nge 'dzin la don gnyer gyi 'dun pa las byung zhing gnas/ 'dun pa de ting nge 'dzin gyi yon tan mthong bas yid phrogs pa'i dad pa las byung / brtson 'grus brtsams pa'i 'bras bu shin sbyangs bzhis ni le lo 'joms par byed/

All past masters agree, however, that tranquil abiding is achieved by rejecting the five faults using the eight applications. This is explained at great length in the Great and Middle-Length treatises. Differentiation of the Middle and Extremes states:
By maintaining [diligence], serviceability is achieved, by which all goals are attained; it results from reliance on the eight applications that reject the five faults.
Laziness, forgetting the instruction, laxity and excitation, nonapplication, and application are viewed as the five faults.[577] [239] The five faults are laziness that is the absence of delight in meditation and being drawn to its opposing factors; forgetfulness that is the lack of clarity of the chosen object of meditation or the loss of it; being affected by either laxity or excitation, even if the object is not lost; not applying the antidotes that reject these despite you knowing they are affecting you; and excessive application of the antidotes to laxity and excitation when they are absent instead of focusing primarily on the object. These are to be identified promptly. Regarding their antidotes, Differentiation of the Middle and Extremes continues:
The base [aspiration] and what is based on it [diligence], the cause [of aspiration, faith] and its effect [pliancy], not forgetting the focal object, identifying laxity and excitation, application to reject them, and remaining serene once they have been quelled.[578] The ability to diligently persist in cultivating states of concentration is what has a base; what it is based on and arises from is the aspiration that seeks states of concentration; once its benefits have been seen, then it is faith captivated by states of concentration that prompts aspiration; striving diligently results in pliancy. These four exclude laziness.

d.div: [192] sde dge_4021_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ dbus mtha' rnam 'byed/ le'u/ 4_sh+loka_3_shog_43_na3
[193] sde dge_4021_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ dbus mtha' rnam 'byed/ le'u4_sh+loka_5_shog_43_na4
[577] Maitreya, Madhyāntavibhāga, 4.3, Toh 4021 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 43a3.

f.d:
brjed pa'i gnyen po ni kun las btus las/
dran pa gang zhe na/ 'dris pa'i dngos po la sems kyi brjed pa med pa ste rnam par mi g.yeng ba'i las can no/[194] / zhes sngar nas yang yang 'dris par byas pa'i dmigs pa'i yul gang yin pa de ma dor bar thu re dran pa ni ma brjed pa yin la/ dmigs pa de las sems gzhan du mi 'phro ba'i khyad chos gsum ldan gyi dran pas ni brjed pa 'joms par byed do/ /

With regard to the antidote to forgetting, the Compendium of Abhidharma says:
What is mindfulness? In relation to a familiar object, it is mental nonforgetfulness; its function is to prevent distraction completely.[579] Nonforgetfulness is continual mindfulness that does not abandon any focal object with which you have repeatedly familiarized yourself in the past. Since mindfulness with its three traits prevents the mind from wandering from its object, it quells forgetting.

d.div: [194] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_'phags pa thogs med/ chos mngon pa kun las btus pa/ shog_5_ba3
[579] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 4b3.

f.d:
bying rgod kyi gnyen po ni dbu ma snying po las/
yid kyi glang po log 'gro ba/ / dmigs pa'i ka ba brtan po la/ / dran pa'i thag pas nges bcings nas/ / shes rab lcags kyus rim dbang bya/[195] / zhes dran pas sems dmigs pa la gnas pa de bying rgod kyi dbang du song na glang po che ma dul ba lcags kyus 'dul ba bzhin shes bzhin gyis bying rgod kyi bya ra byas nas de'i dbang du mi gtong ba spyod 'jug las/
lus dang sems kyi gnas skabs la/ / yang dang yang du brtag bya ba/ / de de kho na mdor na ni/ / shes bzhin bsrung ba'i mtshan nyid do/[196] / zhes sems bzung ste dmigs pa'i rgyun bskyangs pas bying ba dang rgod pa sel/

Regarding the antidotes to laxity and excitation, Essence of the Middle Way says:
Tie this wandering elephant of mind, firmly to a sturdy post, its object, with the rope of mindfulness, and gradually tame it with the hook of meta-awareness.[580] If laxity or excitation occur while mindfulness is maintaining the mind on its object, just as a wild elephant is tamed with an iron hook, meta-awareness monitors laxity and excitation and prevents them from taking over. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way states:
Examining over and over again the state of your mind and body, this in brief is all that characterizes guarding yourself with meta-awareness.[581] You eliminate laxity and excitation by focusing the mind on the focal object and maintaining it there continually.

d.div: [195] sde dge_3855_bstan/ dbu ma/ dza_slob dpon legs ldan 'byed/ dbu ma snying po/ shog_4_na6
[196] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_108 shog_14_ba1
[580] Bhāviveka, Madhyamakahṛdaya, Toh 3855 Tengyur, dbu ma, dza, 4a6.
[581] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 5.108, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 14b1.

f.d:
de lta bu'i bying rgod sel ba la/ da lta bying rgod ces sgom chen kun gyi ngag las rlung ltar grags na'ang / phal cher ni ming tsam las ngos 'dzin rgyu med cing / ngos zin pa'i lugs su byas pa rnams bying rmugs kyi dbye ba ma phyed par gcig tu byas te bying ba mtha' dag ting nge 'dzin rnal mar ngos bzung nas ri sul du mi tshe stong par 'dzad pa ches mang ngo / / ji ltar na/ kun las btus las/
rgod pa gang zhe na/ sdug pa'i mtshan ma'i rjes su 'jug pa'i 'dod chags kyi char gtogs pa'i sems rnam par ma zhi ba ste zhi gnas kyi bar du gcod pa'i las can no/[197] / zhes yul yid du 'ong ba la 'dod chags kyis sems ma zhi ba zhig la bshad pas zhe sdang ba'i dbang gis dgra la rnam rtog 'phro ba rnams ni rgod pa ma yin yang / zhi gnas la bar du gcod pa'i sems gzhan du 'phro ba'i rnam rtog mtha' dag zhi gnas kyi gegs su byas te dgag dgos so/ /

As for rejecting laxity and excitation, nowadays the terms laxity and excitation are on the lips of all great meditators, who have rendered them as widespread as the wind. [240] Nevertheless most only know the terms and are not capable of identifying them. Those who attempt to detect them fail to distinguish laxity from lethargy and confuse the two. As they take all instances of laxity for genuine states of concentration, the majority spend their entire life in the mountains in vain. The Compendium of Abhidharma says:
What is excitation? It is mental agitation that derives from attachment and draws one toward attractive objects. Its function is to hinder tranquil abiding.[582] It is described as a mental state that is agitated by desire for pleasant things. Thoughts influenced by anger that direct the mind toward enemies are not instances of excitation. Nevertheless, all thoughts that turn the mind to other objects and impede concentration must be halted since they hinder tranquil abiding.

d.div: [197] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_slob dpon thogs med/ chos mngon pa kun las btus pa/ shog_8_na5
[582] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 8a5.

f.d:
de bzhin du sgom rim bar pa las/
gang gi tshe dmus long lta bu'am mi mun par zhugs pa lta bu'am/ mig btsums pa lta bur sems kyis dmigs pa gsal bar mi mthong ba de'i tshe bying bar gyur par rig par bya'o/[198] / zhes dmigs pa gang la gtad pa de la dwangs cha tsam yod kyang dmigs pa'i 'dzin stangs kyi ngar cha dam sbring nge ba med na mi gsal zhing 'dzin stangs dma' ru song ba'i shes pa zhig la bying bar ngos 'dzin/

Moreover, the second Stages of Meditation states:
You should know that when a mind does not perceive its object clearly and resembles a person blind from birth, someone sitting in the dark, or someone with their eyes closed, then laxity is present.[583] While observing any object, if only the limpidity aspect is present and vigor is lacking in the apprehension of the object, this mental state that lacks clarity and is slack in its mode of apprehension is to be identified as laxity.

d.div: [198] sde dge_3916_bstan/ dbu ma/ ki_slob dpon ka ma la shi la/ sgom rim bar pa/ shog_47_ba7
[583] Kamalaśīla, Bhāvanākrama II, Toh 3916 Tengyur, dbu ma, ki, 47b7.

f.d:
rmugs pa ni gti mug gi cha shas lus sems lci zhing las su mi rung ba'i rnam pa can gyi shes pa [199] mi dge ba zhig yin pas rmugs pa la dge ba med la bying ba la dge ba yang yod de/ bying rgod byung tshe spong ba'i gnyen po 'du mi byed pa'i ldog phyogs su kun las btus las/
sems pa gang zhe na/ sems mngon par 'du byed pa yid kyi las te dge ba dang mi dge ba dang lung du ma bstan pa rnams la sems 'jug par byed pa'i las can no/[200] / zhes sems dge mi dge lung ma bstan gang rung la skul ba'i sems byung de sems pa yin pas skabs 'dir shes bzhin gyis bying rgod ngos zin na dbu ma snying po las/
zhum pa dmigs pa rgya chen dag/ / bsgoms pas yangs pa nyid du bya/[201] / zhes sems nang du bsdus drags pa'i skyon yin pas na dmigs pa cung zad spros bas bzlog /

Lethargy, on the other hand, is a mental state that derives from ignorance, whose aspect is mental and physical heaviness and unserviceability. As it is either an obstructive indeterminate[584] or nonvirtuous, lethargy is never virtuous, while laxity can be. Concerning the opposite of not applying the antidotes that counter laxity and excitation when they occur, the Compendium of Abhidharma says:
What is intention? It fully brings together the mind [and its object] and is mental karma. Its function is to cause the mind to engage in virtue, nonvirtue, and the ethically neutral.[585] Intention is the mental factor that engages the mind in virtue, nonvirtue, or the ethically neutral. In the present context, when with meta-awareness you have identified laxity and excitation, as Essence of the Middle Way indicates:
When slack,[586] lighten [your mind] by meditating on vast objects.[587] Because laxity occurs when the mind is turned too far inward, you combat it by expanding your object slightly.[588]

d.div: [199] sgrib lung ma bstan nam/ rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/
[200] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_slob dpon thogs med/ chos mngon pa kun las btus pa/ shog_5_na7
[201] sde dge_3855_bstan/ dbu ma/ dza_slob dpon legs ldan 'byed/ dbu ma snying po/ shog_4_na7

[584] The reference to an “obstructive indeterminate” (bsgribs lung ma bstan) is missing in the critical version on which the present translation is based but is found in the blockprint version known as Drepung Parma printed at Miruk Phuntsok Ling Monastery in Lhasa at the request of the seventieth Ganden Throneholder Ngawang Chöphel (1760–1839) and in the version printed by the Sera Jé Library (Bylakuppe) in 2003. The Great Treatise (Tib., 463) also describes lethargy as either nonvirtuous or an obstructive indeterminate.
[585] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 5a7.
[586] The term translated as “slack” (zhum pa) here translates literally as “discouraged.”
[587] Bhāviveka, Madhyamakahṛdaya, Toh 3855 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 4a7.
[588] When focusing on the Buddha’s form, you could increase the size of the figure for example.

f.d:
des kyang ma sel bar bying ba shugs cher song na re zhig dmigs pa glod nas dkon mchog gsum dang gtong ba tshul khrims lha rjes su dran pa drug dang / dal 'byor thob pa'i phan yon sogs bsam pa/ spyod lam 'chag pa/ snang ba'i mtshan ma yid la byed pa/ gdong chus 'khru ba/ bsil sar gnas pa sogs kyi sgo nas bzlog pa dang / dbu ma snying po las/
rgod pa mi rtag la sogs pa/ / yid la byed pas zhi bar bya/[202] / zhes 'dod chags kyi yul la rgod pa ni mi rtag pa dang sdug bsngal sogs skyo shas drag po bsgoms pas bzlog pa yin no/ /

If that is insufficient to eliminate laxity and it persists, check it by abandoning your meditation topic momentarily and reflecting on the six [objects of] mindfulness — the Three Jewels, generosity, ethical discipline, and deities — and on the advantages of attaining a life with leisure and opportunity. Alternatively, you could go for a walk, visualize light, wash your face, sit in a cool place, and so forth. [241] [On excitation,] Essence of the Middle Way says:
Quell excitation by recalling impermanence and so forth.[589] When excited by objects of attachment, counter it by cultivating intense disenchantment with [reflection on] impermanence, suffering, and so on.

d.div: [202] sde dge_3855_bstan/ dbu ma/ dza_slob dpon legs ldan 'byed/ dbu ma snying po/ shog_4_na6

f.d: des mtshon pa'i zhe sdang sogs rtog pa sna tshogs gang 'phro ba de ga'i gnyen po sgom pa gnad du che/ mdor na dbang po'i sgo mi srung ba/ zas kyi tshod mi rig pa/ nam gyi cha stod cha smad la nyal ba/ gnyid rmugs dang 'dod pa'i yul ha cang bsten drags pa sogs thun mong gi rgyu rnams kyang spang ba'o//

Following this example, it is vital to contemplate the antidotes to any factor, like anger, that scatters your thoughts. In brief, you are to reject the causes common [to both laxity and excitation]: not guarding the doors of the senses, not eating in moderation, sleeping at the beginning and the end of the night, sleep, lethargy, indulging excessively in sense objects, and so on.

bying rgod kyi gnyen po ha cang 'du byed pa sel ba ni/ sgom rim phyi ma gnyis las/ gal te sems mnyam par zhugs pa la rtsol ba byas na de'i tshe sems rnam par g.yeng bar 'gyur ro/[203] /zhes sems gnas brgyad pa'i mthar bying ba dang rgod pa gang rung gi dbang du mi 'gro ba'i sems mnyam pa'i dus yin pas de'i tshe sems gzengs bstod pa dang nang du 'gugs pa sogs bying rgod kyi zon chen po 'du byed pa'i rtsol ba ches na ting nge 'dzin gyi skyon yin pas glod shes pa'i 'du byed btang snyoms byed pa ni bying rgod kyi gnyen po bsten drags pa de'i gnyen po yin la/ glod zer ba'i ming tsam rna bar thos pas glod rab la sgom rab ces smra mod/ de ni bying ba'i dbang du song ba'i sems kyi dwangs cha tsam la sgom rnal mar ngos bzung ba'i rang mtshang ste/ skabs 'dir glod shes pa ni rtsol ba glod pa yin gyi/ 'dzin stangs kyi ngar gtong ba ni min zhing / dus kyang sgom chen phal cher nyams myong cung zad skyes pa na glod la/ rang re'i lugs bying rgod kyi dpal gzhom pa zhes sems gnas dgu pa'i dus yin pas mi 'dra'o// de ltar nyes pa lnga dang / de'i gnyen po spong ba'i 'du byed brgyad kyis nyams su len tshul rnams nyams 'og tu legs par tshud par byas nas nyams su len dgos pas/ len tshul bshad ma thag pa'i tshig ris de 'dra zhig blo la byang bar byas pas chog gi snyam na/ don de dag thos par byas pa'i sgo nas nyams len sems thog tu 'dril ma shes na kha phyir bltas kyi bshad yam gyis chos dang gang zag so sor song ba mang zhing / blun po la man ngag gi snying po zhig gis chog mod sngar bshad pa'i gzhung chen po nas bshad pe da dag ngal ba tsam gyi 'bras bur zad do snyam du sems pa ni/ dper na yul thag ring po zhig tu 'gro na 'gro ba'i lam gyi gnas tshul mtha' dag rang stobs sam gzhan la brten pa gang rung gis rgyus yod pa zhig nges par dgos kyi/ tham thom du phyin pas don mi 'grub pa ltar/ sgom gyi skyon sel bogs 'don gyi gnad mi shes par lus gnad bsrangs pa dang mig btsums nas sdod pa'i snying rus la grub pa'i dbang phyug chen por re ba mtha' dag sdom gsum du/
blun pos phyag rgya che bsgoms pa/ / phal cher dud 'gro'i rgyu ru gsungs/[204] / zhes pa'i don thog tu bab par snang mod/ deng dus ni rang gzhan kun la ngang tshul 'di dag gis dbyar gyi srin bu'i grangs bzhin khyab cing 'phel ba'i phyir thams cad mkhyen pa bus/
bdag gis chos min smra ru chos dang 'gal/ / chos bzhin smras na bod rnams dgra ru ldang /[205] / zhes sgros gleng mang ba rang nyid bya rog lus dkar sgrub par zad do//

Concerning countering excessive application of laxity and excitation’s antidotes, the latter two Stages of Meditation say: “If you exert yourself when the mind is in equipoise, it will be distracted.”[590] At the end of the eighth mental state, as the mind is free of any influence of laxity and distraction, it is balanced. At that point, being overly wary of laxity and excitation and making excessive effort to apply [their antidotes] — heightening the mind, drawing it inward, and so on — will only impair your state of concentration. The application of equanimity, which knows to relax, is the remedy to excessive use of the antidotes to laxity and excitation. On simply hearing the term “relax,” some assert that good relaxation is good meditation. They let their mind come under the sway of laxity and wrongly take this state of simple clarity for true meditation. At this point, knowing to relax means relaxing your effort, not loosening the vigor of your mode of apprehension. As for the timing, most great meditators relax once they have achieved a little experience [of meditation]. In our system it is different: the time for it is when the intensity of laxity and excitation has declined, which is to say at the ninth mental state. You are to practice once you have properly understood how to adopt the eight applications that reject the five faults. For this, do not imagine that it is enough to have learned the terms just explained. If you do not know how to use what you have learned in your practice, learning will remain a purely intellectual exercise, and like many people, you will fail to relate the teaching to yourself. [242] Some fools imagine that a core instruction is sufficient and that all that comes of the aforementioned explanations by the great treatises is fatigue. But before traveling to a distant land, for example, you certainly need to learn all about the situation on the route, either on your own or from someone else. If you depart uninformed, the undertaking will fail. In the same vein, concerning all those who claim to be great meditators but have no idea how to progress by solving the problems that arise in meditation, just sitting determinedly with their body straight and their eyes closed, [Sakya Paṇḍita] says in his Clear Differentiation of the Three Vows:
It is said that the mahāmudrā meditations of ignorant people in most cases lead to animal rebirths.[591] I believe this passage applies perfectly here. Nowadays, this tendency is increasingly prevalent in us and in others. It is as common as insects in summer, which is why the omniscient Butön stated:
Were I to speak nonvirtuously, it would contravene the Dharma. Were I to speak according to the Dharma, the Tibetan people would rise against me.[592] If I dwell on this too much, I will stick out like a white crow.[593]

d.div: [203] sde dge_3916_bstan/ dbu ma/ ki_slob dpon ka ma la shi la/ sgom rim phyi ma/ shog_50_ba5
[204] sa skya paN+Di ta kun dga' rgyal mtshan gyi gsung 'bum/ na_sdom pa gsum gyi rab tu dbye ba'i bstan bcos/ shog_25_ba2_sa skya bka' 'bum pod/ 5_shog_25_ba2
[205] bu ston rin chen grub kyi gsung 'bum/ dza_shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa grub pa'i rab tu byed pa lta ba ngan sel zhes bya ba/ shog_31_na2
[590] Kamalaśīla, Bhāvanākrama II, Toh 3916 Tengyur, dbu ma, ki, 50b4.
[591] Sakya Paṇḍita, Clear Differentiation, 24b2.
[592] Butön, Dispelling Bad Views, 31a2.
[593] The literal expression is “turn myself into a white crow” (bya rog lus dkar sgrub pa).

f.d: c. How to focus on one object

sngar bshad pa de dag nges par byas nas dmigs pa gcig la sgril tshul/ lam sgron las/
dmigs pa gang rung gcig dag la/ /yid ni dge la bzhag par bya/[206] / zhes skabs su bab cing rang nyid dmigs pa gcig la gtod pa'i yul ni spyir btang la sku gzugs lta bu 'os shing / de'i nang nas/ ting 'dzin rgyal po las/
gser gyi kha dog lta bu'i sku lus kyi/ / 'jig rten mgon po kun tu mdzes pa ste/ / dmigs pa de la gang gi sems 'jug pa/ / byang chub sems dpa' de mnyam gzhag ces bya/[207] / zhes de bzhin gshegs pa'i sku gzugs la dmigs pas zhar byung du sangs rgyas rjes dran gyi bsod nams rgya cher gsog pa/ dper na zung rdo gcig gis rtsig pa gnyis kyi go chod pa dang / mi gcig gis tshong lta bu'i don gcod pa'i zhor la brel ba gzhan chod 'gro ba dang mtshungs pas/ thog mar sku gzugs bris 'bur sogs la blta ba dang bsam pa mang du byas pas gtsug tor zhal khyim spyan phyag zhabs na bza' sogs kyi dbyibs dang / spyan gyi dkar nag gis mtha' rten pa tshun gyi kha dog kyang ma 'dres pa so sor bsam/ bzhugs pa la bzhengs pa'i rnam pa dang sngon po la dkar por 'char ba lta bu ldog phyogs sna tshogs kyi rjes su mi 'brang zhing / thog ma nyid nas sangs rgyas dngos kyi rnam pa dang spyan gyi dkar nag tshun ma 'dres par mi 'byung yang / dang po sku gzugs mthong ba'i dbyibs dang sku'i rnam pa rags pa tsam 'char ba la rgyun bskyangs nas bsgoms pas mthar ji ltar bshad pa ltar 'byung gi /nyams len byas tsam nas ji lta ba 'byung du re ba'i sha thang thang byas na sgom gyi gegs su 'gro bas mtshams zin par byas te/ stan 'jam zhing bde ba la rkang pa skyil krung ngam phyed skyil/ mig 'byed 'dzum ran par sna rtser phab/ lus drang por bsrangs/ lag pa mnyam gzhag mgo thad kar sna rtse dang lte ba drang por byas/ so dang mchu rang babs/ lce rtse rkan la reg pa/ dbugs dal bus rgyu ba ste lus kyi spyod lam brgyad dang ldan pa'i sgo nas rlung gi 'gro 'ong nyer gcig bgrang ba sogs bya ba ni phyi rol tu g.yeng ba bzlog pa'i thabs yin gsung /

Having ascertained the above, Lamp on the Path to Enlightenment says,
“Place your mind in a virtuous state on any one of the given objects.”[594] In the present context, concerning the single object on which to focus, generally the Buddha’s form is appropriate. Among the reasons for this, the King of Meditations Sutra says:
With a physical form the color of gold, the Protector of the World is forever splendid. A bodhisattva whose mind is absorbed on such an object is said to be a meditator.[595] As visualizing the Tathāgata’s body coincidently produces the great merit that recollecting the Buddha brings, it is analogous to a cornerstone that supports two walls, or a person who, while resolving something like a commercial concern, settles another matter at the same time. Begin by looking at a two or three-dimensional image of the Buddha’s form and then visualize it repeatedly. You are to picture each of the following — the shape of the crown protuberance, the face, eyes, arms, legs, clothes, and so on, and the color of each as well, from the whites of the eyes, pupils, and so on — individually without confusing any of them. [243] Do not succumb to various changes that may occur, like a seated position turning into a standing one or a blue color changing into white. You may not succeed immediately in clearly perceiving the Buddha’s actual form with the whites of the eyes, the pupils, and so on, but by consistently meditating on the general shape and appearance of the Buddha’s form, you will eventually come to see it as described. Since your meditation will be hindered by persevering in the hope of soon seeing the form as it is, keep your expectations reasonable. You are to sit in the eightfold posture on a soft and comfortable seat with your legs in full or half-lotus position, your half-closed eyes lowered toward the tip of your nose, your body straight, your hands in the equipoise mudrā, your head straight so that the tip of your nose and your navel are aligned, your teeth and lips in their natural position, the tip of your tongue touching the palate, and your breathing calm. Counting your inhalations and exhalations twenty-one times, for example, is taught as the means to overcome distraction toward the exterior.

d.div: [206] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_jo bo rje dpal ldan a ti sha_byang chub lam gyi sgron me/ shog_240_na1
[207] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_13_ba5
[594] Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 240a1.
[595] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 4, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 13b5.

f.d:
de nas ting nge 'dzin gyi yon tan la dad pas drangs pa'i 'dun pa shugs drag po'i sgo nas dge sbyor la spro sing nge ba'i brtson 'grus dang bcas te sngar goms 'dris su byas pa'i sangs rgyas kyi sku gzugs de nyid sangs rgyas dngos kyi rnam par smin mtshams kyi thad kyi nam mkhar che chung blo dang 'tsham pa zhig gsal btab/ dmigs yul de nyid ma brjed par dran pa'i sems dmigs pa la thu rer gnas pa'i gsal cha'i ngar dang ldan zhing / gzhan du mi 'phro ba'i gnas cha brtan po gnyis zung ldan gyi sgo nas stod du hags pa sogs kyi skyon mi 'byung tsam gyi ngos bsgrims te bsgom/ de la cung zad gnas pa snyam byed pa na dmigs pa dran pas ma brjed pa'i mu nas shes bzhin gyis bya ra byas pas dmigs pa'i gsal cha dang 'dzin stangs kyi ngar cha'i shugs dam sbring sbring ba de cung zad zhan du song ba mthong tshe bying ba phra mo byung snyam ste bkag /gsal cha'i ngar cha had kyi shor nas dwangs cha tsam las mi 'dug na bying ba rags par ngo shes par byed/ 'dod pa'i yul yid du 'ong ba'i rnam pa 'char la khad byung ba na rgod pa phra mo dang 'dod chags kyi rnam pa had kyi skyes pa rgod pa rags par rtogs nas de dag gi gnyen po'i sgo nas bying rgod bcad de rtsa ba'i dmigs pa'i steng du sal le hrig ger thun tshad chu tshod gcig gi ring 'jog gang thub byed dgos kyang bsgrims drags na rgod shas dang / glod drag pa na bying shas skye ba'i phyir grims lhod ran pa'i mtshams shin tu dka' bas mkhas pa tsan dra go mis/
brtson pa bsten na rgod pa 'byung 'gyur zhing / / de spangs na ni zhum pa skye bar 'gyur/ / 'di yis rigs par mnyam 'jug rnyed dka' na/ / bdag gis sems dkrugs pas ni ci zhig bgyi/[208] / zhes

Then, with intense aspiration induced by faith in the benefits of states of concentration, and diligence that wholeheartedly delights in the practice of virtue, visualize in the space before you, at the level of the point between your eyebrows, the buddha form that you have previously familiarized yourself with in the size that suits you. Without forgetting the object and constantly mindful of it, and combining both vigorous clarity and firm stability that does let the mind scatter elsewhere, meditate in a fully focused manner free of faults like excessive tension. When you think that you have achieved some mental stability, do not lose the object but sustain it with mindfulness and guard yourself with meta-awareness. When clarity is present but you observe a slight decrease in the level of vigor in the mode of apprehension, note that subtle laxity has arisen and check it. If the clarity suddenly loses its vigor, and only limpidity[596] remains, then be aware that coarse laxity is present. When a pleasant object of desire is on the verge of appearing, recognize it as subtle excitation, and when an object of attachment suddenly emerges, recognize it as coarse excitation. [244] Quell laxity and excitation with their antidotes, and do your best to maintain your mind on the very clear object for an hour. As too tight a focus leads to an increase in excitation and excessive looseness to an increase in laxity, it is difficult to achieve the right degree of vigor. As the wise Candragomin says:
When effort is applied excitation arises; when it is neglected slackness occurs. When between them it is hard to find a proper balance, what am I to do with my perturbed mind?[597]

d.div: [208] sde dge_1159_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon tsan dra go mi/ bshags bstod/ shog_205_ba5

[596] In the case of coarse laxity, the loss of clarity implies that the object is no longer present in the mind. Here limpidity refers to one of the mind’s fundamental features, the ability to reflect or take on the aspect of the objects it perceives.
[597] Praise in the Form of a Confession (Deśanāstava), Toh 1159 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 205b5.

f.d: [sems gnas dgu dang yid byed bzhi ]
d. [The nine mental states and four attentions]

las dang po pa la nyes pa lnga spong 'du byed brgyad ldan gyi nyams len gnad du dril ba de nyid sgra ji bzhin pa mi skye na'ang / sems gnas dgu'i nang tshan sems 'jog pa'i dmigs pa zhes dmigs rten la yun du mi gnas kyang nyams dang sbyar te bsgrims nas sgom pa la tshul ji ltar bya na/ sems gnas dang po'i tshe dmigs pa kho na la sems kyi gnas cha mi sdod par rnam rtog ri gzar gyi 'bab chu lta bur 'ong bas/ da nyams len byas pas rtog pa mang du song snyam pa 'byung mod/ de ni sngar nyams len gyi gnad med pa'i dus dper na lam chen zhig la 'grul pa rgyun mi 'chad du 'gro yang de la ched du blta ba'i 'dun pa med pa'i dbang gis mang nyung gi rtog dpyod mi 'byung la/ 'bad pas bltas na mi khal sogs mang po 'di 'dra byung snyam pa/ sngon chad rtog pa 'og 'gyu'i 'khor lo bskor yang ngos ma zin pa la skabs 'dir sems kyi nyams len byas pa la brten nas rnam rtog ngos zin gyi nyams shig 'ong bas mgon po byams pas mdo sde rgyan du sems gnas pa'i thabs dgu po de stobs drug gis 'grub lugs yid la byed pa bzhir bshad pa'i skabs kyi stobs drug gi nang tshan thos pa'i stobs kyis 'grub pa'i sems gnas dang po sems 'jog pa zhes bya ba dmigs pa'i gdams pa thos pa tsam gyi rjes su 'brangs nas dmigs pa la sems gtad pa tsam gyi skabs yin no/ /

A beginner may not perfectly master how to practice all eight applications that reject the five faults. Be that as it may, among the nine mental states, in the [first] one called mental placement, the mind may not remain on the object for long, but you meditate with effort that is consistent with your capacity. In the first mental state, your mind does not remain focused on the object. Other thoughts ensue the way water flows down a steep mountainside, and you have the impression that since you began to practice, your discursive thoughts have increased. What then are you to do? In the past, before you received the instructions for this practice, your situation was comparable to finding yourself on a thoroughfare with a continuous stream of travelers: when you have no interest in watching them, you do not notice how many there are, but when you make an effort to observe them, you can estimate the number of caravans and so on. In the past you were unaware of the constant flow of your underlying thoughts. Now, thanks to the work on your mind that you have undertaken, you begin to be conscious of your thoughts. In his Ornament of Mahayana Sutras, the protector Maitreya explains the four attentions and how to achieve the nine mental states by means of the six forces. Accordingly, among the six, it is with the force of hearing that you achieve the first mental state, mental placement. At this point you simply focus your mind on the object following the instructions on how to meditate that you have only heard [and have yet to apply].

de nas rim gyis bsgoms pa na gcong rong dog mo'i 'bab chu ltar res rnam rtog zhi zhing res tho ler skye ba'i rnam rtog ngal gso ba'i nyams shig 'ong / de'i tshe stobs gnyis pa bsam pas 'grub pa'i sems gnyis pa rgyun du 'jog pa zhes bya ba dmigs pa la rgyun cung zad mthud nus pa yin/ sems gnas 'di gnyis la bying rgod ches mang zhing ting 'dzin nyung ngu las mi 'ong bas yid byed bzhi'i nang gi dang po bsgrims te 'jug pa'i skabs so/ /

Gradually as you meditate, like the irregular rate at which water flows through a gorge, at times your thoughts calm down, at others they suddenly increase, and you have the impression that your thoughts are abating. At this point, through the force of reflection, you achieve the second mental state of continuous placement, in which you can maintain the object for a short while. [245] During these two states, laxity and excitation are frequent, a state of concentration infrequent, and among the four attentions, tight focus is present.

de nas cung zad goms pa na lung pa phu gsum gyi rdzing chu lta bu 'gal rkyen gyis ma dkrugs pa'i tshe sems gnas pa snyam byed la/ rkyen byung tshe mi gnas pa'i rnam rtog thang chad pa'i nyams shig 'ong / de'i tshe stobs gsum pa dran pas grub pa'i sems gnas gsum pa glan te 'jog pa zhes bya ba sems g.yeng ba myur du rtogs nas slar dmigs pa la glon pa dang / sems gnas bzhi pa nye bar 'jog pa zhes bya ba rgya chen po las bsdus te phra bar byed pa dang / stobs bzhi pa shes bzhin gyis 'grub pa'i sems gnas lnga pa dul bar byed pa zhes bya ba ting nge 'dzin gyi yon tan la dga' ba dang / sems gnas drug pa zhi bar byed pa zhes bya ba rnam g.yeng gi nyes dmigs rig nas 'gog pa dang / stobs lnga pa brtson 'grus kyis 'grub pa'i sems gnas la bdun pa dang brgyad pa gnyis yod pa'i bdun pa rnam par zhi bar byed pa zhes bya ba chags sems nyon mongs rtsol bas spangs te zhi bar byed/ sems gnas gsum pa nas bdun pa'i bar gyi lnga po 'di la bying rgod kyis bar du gcod pas yid byed bzhi'i nang gi gnyis pa skabs su chad cing 'jug pa'i dus so//

Next, after further familiarization, like a pool of water fed by three distant sources, you find your mind stable when it is not disturbed by any opposing conditions and unstable when they occur. You have the impression that your discursive thoughts are wearing out. At the time, by the third force, mindfulness, you accomplish the third mental state called renewed placement, in which you become quickly aware when you are distracted and refocus your mind on the object. In the fourth mental state, called close placement, you reduce the size of your originally larger object. The fifth mental state called subjugation is achieved by the force of meta-awareness; it delights in the virtues of states of concentration. In the sixth mental state called pacification, you become aware of the drawbacks of distraction and stop it. Both the seventh and eighth mental states are achieved by the fifth force, diligence. The seventh state, called complete pacification, with effort rejects afflictions such as attachment and quells them. As these five mental states, from the third to the seventh, are interrupted by laxity and excitation, among the four attentions, this is the time of the second, intermittent focus.

de nas rim gyis bsgoms pas rgya mtsho rlabs dang bcas pa lta bu rnam rtog ci byung yang gnyen po dran 'dzin cung zad bsten pas rang mal du zhi 'gro bas rnam rtog 'du byed pa zhes bya ba'i nyams 'ong / de'i tshe sngar bshad pa'i stobs lnga pas 'grub pa'i sems gnas brgyad pa rtse gcig tu byed pa zhes bya ba ting nge 'dzin rgyun chags su 'grub pa yin no/ / sems gnas brgyad pa la bying rgod kyis bar du mi gcod par yid byed bzhi'i nang gi gsum pa skabs su chad pa med par 'jug pa'i dus so/ /

Next, as you gradually pursue meditation, like an ocean with waves, whatever discursive thoughts arise are dispelled on the spot by mild application of the antidotes; given this, the impression you have is called thought application.[598] At that point, by the above-mentioned fifth force, you attain the eighth mental state called one-pointed attention and achieve a continuous state of concentration. Since the eighth mental state is not interrupted by laxity and excitation, among the four attentions, this is the time of the third, uninterrupted focus.

d.div: [598] In the context of cultivating tranquil abiding, thought application (rnam rtog ’du byed pa) and non-thought application (rnam rtog ’du mi byed pa) refer, respectively, to the seventh and eighth of the eight applications (’du byed brgyas) that are antidotes to the five faults. Of the nine mental states covered in the process, in the eighth state, although neither laxity nor excitation are present, mindfulness — which is what “thought” in the expression “thought application” refers to — must still be employed to keep them at bay. In the ninth state, as they are no longer a threat, their antidotes are not needed, and it is a mistake to employ them. As such, the appropriate action is “non-thought application,” often called nonapplication or equanimity.

f.d: de nas rim gyis bsgoms pas rgya mtsho rlabs dang bral ba lta bu yul rkyen ci byung yang gnyen po dran 'dzin gyi 'bad rtsol la ma bltos par ting 'dzin rang babs su 'char bas rnam rtog mngon par 'du mi byed pa'i nyams kyi mnyam gzhag 'ong / de'i tshe stobs drug pa yongs su 'dris pa las 'grub pa'i sems gnas dgu pa mnyam par 'jog pa zhes bya ba rtsol med du dmigs pa la 'jog pas yid byed bzhi'i nang gi bzhi pa lhun gyis grub par 'jug pa'i dus so/ / 'di'i skabs su bying rgod 'gog pa'i rtsol ba skyon du 'gyur bar dgongs nas gong ma rnams glod rab ces gsung pa ma go bar 'dzin stangs kyi ngar cha glod par go ba'i skyon 'byung bas gnad 'gag 'di dag legs par shes dgos kyi/ pus 'khyud sgom zhwa dra phad tsam yod pas sgom rgyud la skye ba ni min no//

Steadily continuing to meditate, like a waveless ocean, a state of concentration occurs naturally in all circumstances, independent of any effort to sustain it with the antidote, mindfulness. In this way an equipoise arises in which you have the impression [called] non-thought application. Through the force of thorough familiarization, you then achieve the ninth mental state called balanced placement. [246] As you focus on the object effortlessly, among the four attentions this is the time of the fourth, spontaneous focus. Thinking that it would be wrong at this stage to make an effort to stop laxity and excitation, some past masters have stated that relaxation is excellent, which has been misunderstood and misconstrued to mean that the vigor of the mode of apprehension should be reduced. This important point must be understood, for it is not just because a person owns a meditator’s special knee strap, hat, and bag that he is successfully meditating!

de ltar sems gnas dgu la yid byed bzhir bshad pa'i dang po gnyis la bsgrims te 'jug pa dang bar pa lnga la chad cing 'jug pa'i tha snyad byas na dang po gnyis la'ang chad cing 'jug pa dang bar pa lnga la yang bsgrims te 'jug pa dgos pas mi rigs so snyam pa'i log rtog skyes na skyon med de/ bar pa lnga la bsgrims pa dang chad pa'i 'jug tshul gnyis ka yod kyang dang po gnyis la chad pa'i tha snyad byar med de/ bying rgod shin tu mang ba'i bar bar la gnas pa cung zad las mi skye la/ bar pa lnga'i skabs ting nge 'dzin shas cher sgom pa'i bar bar la bying rgod kyis yang yang gcod pa'i phyir/ dper na mi gsum gyi dang po la sha /bar pa la thud dang sha gnyis ka /tha ma la de'i steng du mar khu dang bcas gsum drangs na dang po la sha byin pa'i tha snyad dang / bar pa la sha yod kyang sha byin mi zer bar nyis spel gyi tha snyad 'dogs shing / gsum pa la nyis spel tshang yang sum spel yod pa'i dbang gis nyis spel byin zhes byar mi rung ba lta bu yin no/ /

For the nine mental states, among the four attentions explained above, the attention that corresponds to the first two states is called tight focus and the one for the next five is called intermittent focus. Perhaps you think this must be an error, that it should be intermittent focus for the first two and tight focus for the following five, but it is not actually a problem. The middle group of five involves both tight and intermittent focus, but the focus for first two cannot be called “intermittent” because both laxity and excitation are prevalent and a state of concentration only occurs from time to time. On the other hand, the middle five for the most part consist of placement meditation that is occasionally (but repeatedly) interrupted by laxity and excitation. It is like the following example: of three people present, the first is given some meat, the second both meat and tü,[599] and the third, in addition to these two foods, is given clarified butter. The first person will be called “the one who was given meat.” The second, although he was given meat, will not be called “the one who was given meat” but “the one who was given both.” The third has both of these, but calling him “the one who got both” would not be right, as he received all three foods.

d.div: [599] Thud, a delicacy made of clarified butter and dried cheese.

f.d: [zhi gnas ]
e. [Attainment of tranquil abiding]

de ltar sems gnas dgu pa bying rgod phra mo dang bral bar yun ring du skyong nus pa'i rtsol med kyi ting nge 'dzin skyes pa de zhi gnas yin nam snyam na/ mdo sde rgyan las/
de goms pa las 'du mi byed/ / de nas de yi lus dang sems/ / shin tu sbyangs pa che thob nas/ / yid la byed dang bcas zhes bya/[209] / zhes skabs 'di nas bzung ste yid la byed pa zhes bshad pa'i zhi gnas rjes mthun pa yin te/ zhi gnas mtshan nyid pa 'thob pa la lus sems shin sbyangs kyi dga' bde khyad par can thob dgos so//

When the ninth mental state arises in this way, where the state of the concentration is free of subtle laxity and excitation and is effortlessly sustained for long periods, you might wonder whether this is tranquil abiding. Ornament of Mahayana Sutras states:
Through familiarization, no application [is needed]; then when strong mental and physical pliancy are attained, it is called mental contemplation.[600] From this point onward, what is known as mental contemplation is an approximation of tranquil abiding. To attain actual tranquil abiding, it is necessary to achieve the superior bliss of physical and mental pliancy.

d.div: [209] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 15_sh+loka_14_shog_19_na7
[600] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, 15.14, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 19a7.

f.d: de ltar na sems gnas dgu pa'i ting nge 'dzin thog mar skyes pa'i dus shin sbyangs med par dogs na/ shin sbyangs phra mo skyes pa chung bas rig dka' yang / 'di dag gi skabs zhi gnas rjes mthun pa'i yid byed du 'chad pa'i rgyu mtshan/ dper na tshes bco lnga'i zla ba'i cha shas yongs su rdzogs pa la tshes gnyis nas rim gyis cha shas gsog dgos na'ang / tshes gnyis kyi zla ba'i cha phra mo de zla ba yin yang bco lnga'i zla ba min pa ltar/ shin sbyangs kyi cha phra mo de gong du 'phel ba las mthar nyon mongs pa'i phyogs su gyur pa dge ba la gang 'dod du bkol mi rung ba'i gnas ngan len zhi nas sems kyi shin sbyangs skye/ de'i mthus las rung gi rlung lus la rgyu bas lus kyi gnas ngan len dang bral nas bal ltar yang ba'i lus kyi shin sbyangs skye/ de la brten nas lus la bde ba'i nyams chen po skye/ de'i mthus yid bde nyams kyi sems shin sbyangs kyi bde ba skye/ de yang lus shin sbyangs skyes ma thag tu sems dga' yal yal ba byung ba de'i tshe zhi gnas cung zad ma thob la/ dga' yal ba de chung du song nas sems dmigs pa la lhan ne sdod pa'i ting nge 'dzin dang rjes su mthun pa'i shin sbyangs mi g.yo ba thob pa dang dus mnyam du zhi gnas 'grub pas da lta'i grub chen du rlom pa rnams kyis gzhung chen po 'di dag dang bstun na gar yang ma phyin par snang ngo / / 'on kyang dga' yal ba de chung du song bas shin sbyangs zad pa ma yin te/ dper na gtam snyan thos ma thag tu sems dga' g.yeng nge ba de yun zhig song ba na zhi 'gro yang / gtam snyan mi bden pa ma yin pa dang 'dra gsung /

That said, you may wonder whether pliancy is entirely absent when the state of concentration of the ninth mental state first arises. [247] Actually, although subtle pliancy is in fact present, it is difficult to discern because it is faint, which is why the state is qualified as “mental contemplation that is concordant with tranquil abiding.” For example, the full moon of the fifteenth day of the month can only be achieved by the gradual increase of portions of moon from the second day onward. Although the small slice of the moon of the second day is a moon, it is not the moon of the fifteenth day. Similarly, mental pliancy arises once subtle pliancy has developed to the point that it quells the dysfunctional tendencies that depend on afflictions and prevent you from generating virtue at will. Thanks to it, serviceable winds circulate in the body, freeing it of all physical dysfunctional tendencies and generating physical pliancy with which the body feels as light as cotton fluff. From it dawns an intense feeling of physical bliss, which in turn generates a feeling of mental pleasure that is the bliss of mental pliancy. When you attain physical pliancy and immediately experience very intense mental bliss, you have yet to achieve tranquil abiding. You realize it as soon as the strong pleasure subsides slightly and you attain immoveable pliancy concordant with the mind’s stable concentration on the object. (Given this, when those who now pride themselves on being great meditators are measured against the great treatises, I have the impression that they have in fact achieved nothing.) The decline in the strong pleasure does not, however, imply that pliancy has ceased. It is taught that it is like the case of the agitating delight you feel on hearing good news subsiding after some time, which does not change the fact that you heard good news.

lus sems shin sbyangs kyi bde ba khyad par can gyi zhi gnas de mngon du byas pa dang bsam gtan dang po'i nyer bsdogs thob pa yin yang / 'di ga tsam gyis nyon mongs pa mngon gyur yang mgo gnon mi nus mod/ 'o na sngar lhag pa ting nge 'dzin gyi bslab pa dang zhi gnas kyis nyon mongs pa mngon gyur mgo gnon par bshad pa dang 'gal lam snyam na de ni zhi rags kyi rnam pa can gyi lhag mthong sogs kyang zhi gnas su bsdus pa la dgongs pa yin gsung / des na da dung lam la slob dgos/ slob tshul 'jig rten pa'i lam zhi rags kyi rnam pa can gyi lhag mthong bsgoms pas 'dod pa na spyod pa'i bsgoms pas spang bar bya ba'i nyon mongs phal cher nub/ dga' bde dang bcas pa'i bsam gtan dang po'i dngos gzhi 'thob/ mngon shes rdzu 'phrul kyang mtshan nyid pa 'byung / rim gyis bsgoms pas ci yang med man chad kyi nyon mongs pa mngon gyur thams cad spangs te srid rtse'i sems 'thob pa yin la/ bsam gtan dang po'i nyer bsdogs thob pa'i steng nas bdag med gnyis kyi don la dpyod pa'i lhag mthong bsgoms pas nyan thos kyi mthong lam lta bu thob na zhi rags kyi rnam pa can gyi bsam gtan dang po'i dngos gzhi yan chad dngos su ma bsgoms kyang de dag gi yon tan shugs kyis 'thob cing / theg pa gsum po gang rung gi sgom lam bar chad med lam gyis nyon mongs pa'i gnyen po byas te rtsa ba nas spong ba lags so// //

The attainment of tranquil abiding with its superior bliss of physical and mental pliancy coincides with the attainment of the preparatory phase of the first absorption [of the form realm], but it does not enable you to control manifestations of the afflictions. If you wonder whether this conflicts with what was said about the higher training of concentration — that tranquil abiding checks manifestations of the afflictions — in fact that statement referred to insight having the aspect of peacefulness and coarseness and so on, which is included in the category of tranquil abiding. For this reason, further training on the path is required. By following the training that consists in meditating on the mundane path — insight with the aspect of peacefulness and coarseness — most desire-realm afflictions to be abandoned by the path of meditation decline, and you attain the actual first absorption along with joy and bliss, various kinds of clairvoyance, and genuine supernormal powers. [248] By meditating gradually, you abandon all manifestations of afflictions up to the nothingness level and attain the mind of the peak of existence. If, after reaching the preparatory phase of the first absorption, you instead meditate on the insight that analyzes the two kinds of selflessness, you can realize the śrāvaka path of seeing, for example, and in the process attain the advantages of the actual first absorption with the aspect of peacefulness and coarseness and above without having to meditate on them. It is however the uninterrupted paths of the path of meditation[601] of any of the three vehicles that serve as the antidote to the afflictions and eradicate them.

d.div: [601] “Uninterrupted paths of the path of meditation” (sgom lam bar chad med lam) are direct realizations of emptiness in a state of meditative equipoise in which the innate afflictive obscurations and obscurations to knowledge are eliminated in succession.

f.d:
smras pa/
le lo la sogs nyes pa'i rang mtshang rig / dad sogs 'du byed brgyad kyi phan yon mthong / / sems gnas dgu pas nyer drangs shin sbyangs kyi/ / bde gsal mi rtog zhi gnas ting 'dzin mtshar/ /
sngon chad cung zad bsgoms blo'i nyams len gyis/ / nyon mongs dug gsum ma brid bag la zha/ / bder gnas chos pa'i bzang brdzu rkyen ngan gyi/ / phra mo'i gnod pas tha mal rang mtshang ston/ /
mu stegs byed dang thun mong sems gnas la/ / ma dul yid 'di cung zad mi gnas kyang / / srid zhi'i mtha' las 'das pa'i sangs rgyas su/ / zhal gyis 'ches rnams mdzub mo nang du khug/ /
dka' gnad 'di 'dras mngon shes rdzu 'phrul sogs/ / 'grub par gsung rab dgongs 'grel las bshad na/ / lto 'grangs nyi mas dros pa'i 'gying bag la/ / grub rtags brag las chu bo rdol ba bzhin/ /
kye ma sngon chad blo ྄brid rnam g.yeng gis/ / don med stong pa'i ngang du mi tshe zad/ / da ni 'du 'dzis dben pa'i gnas mchog tu/ / tshul 'di nyams su len la rnam par spro/ /
sems dang lus la khyab pa'i bde ba yis/ / ci byas dge ba'i phyogs su bkol nus pa'i/ / sa phyod [210] 'di lta'i gnad 'gag shes gyur na/ / grags can sangs rgyas de yang mi ring nye/ / zhes bya ba ni bar skabs kyi tshigs su bcad pa'o// //

d.div: Having understood the drawbacks of the faults of laziness and the rest and seen the advantages of the eight applications, faith and so on, [you attain] the marvelous state of concentration — conception-free[602] tranquil abiding with the clarity and bliss of pliancy that the ninth mental state induces.

Having practiced little meditation in the past, the three mental poisons — the afflictions — are not reduced, only hidden; those who then take their ease and profess to be good practitioners are then destabilized by small obstacles, which exposes their flaw of mediocrity.

Though their minds are completely unstable, being untrained in the [nine] mental states shared with tīrthikas, they boast of having attained buddhahood beyond samsara and personal peace. They need to think again!

If, as it is said, the various clairvoyances, supernormal powers, and so on are attained thanks to the difficult points taught in the sutras and commentaries, the signs of attainments of those who proudly sit in the sun on a full stomach will be [nonexistent] like water extracted from rock.
Alas, over time with delusions and distractions, I have wasted my life in meaningless pursuits. Now in an excellent place free of diversions, I will delight in practicing in this way.
With bliss that pervades mind and body, if I understand the important techniques that ensure the easy transformation of all I do into virtue, illustrious buddhahood should not be far off!
[210] sa chod/ rme ru phun tshogs gling gi dpar ma/
[602] In this context, the conceptions (rtog pa) referred to are laxity and excitation.

f.d: drug pa shes rab kyi phar phyin ni/
2.2.3.2.1.6. The perfection of wisdom

de kho na nyid kyi don 'jal ba don dam rtogs pa'i shes rab/ rig pa'i gnas lnga la mkhas pa kun rdzob rtogs pa'i shes rab/ sems can gyi 'di phyi'i don kha na ma tho ba med pa sgrub tshul shes pa'i shes rab rnams kyi sems kyi goms pa mthar phyin pa na shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa yongs su rdzogs pa yin no/ / shes rab brgya pa las/
mthong dang ma mthong yon tan 'di/ / kun gyi rtsa ba shes rab yin/ / de ltar gnyis ka bsgrub pa'i phyir/ / shes rab yongs su bzung bar bya/[211] / zhes rang gi sha byin yang sman gyi sdong po las blangs pa ltar nga rgyal dang zhum pa med pa'i sbyin pa sogs phar phyin dang po lnga rnam par dag pa dang / 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po byang chub sems dpa' 'dod yon gyi dbang du mi 'gro ba yang shes rab la rag lus shing mdor na 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i yon tan mtha' dag shes rab la brten nas 'byung ba'i phyir na 'di nyid don du gnyer dgos la/ gnyer bya'i shes rab de la rigs mang du yod pa'i nang nas nyon mongs pa phra rags zhi bar byed pa'i lhag mthong sgom pa gal che zhing / de yang nyon mongs pa mngon gyur mgo gnon pa'i 'jig rten pa'i zhi rags kyi lhag mthong don du gnyer bya yin nam snyam na/

The perfection of wisdom is fully accomplished once the mind’s familiarization with the wisdom realizing the ultimate that understands suchness, the wisdom realizing the conventional — skill in the five sciences — and the wisdom knowing how to faultlessly accomplish sentient beings’ present and future welfare is complete. [249] [Nāgārjuna’s] Hundred Verses of Wisdom says:
Wisdom is the root of all visible and invisible good qualities. For this reason, to accomplish both, thoroughly train in wisdom.[603] The purity of the first five perfections, generosity and so on — such as giving away your flesh as if it were no more than an extract from a medicinal plant, free of pride and discouragement — and the way bodhisattva universal sovereigns are not drawn to sense objects depend on wisdom. In brief, wisdom is to be pursued because all good qualities, mundane and supramundane, arise in dependence on it. Among the many possible kinds of wisdom to seek, it is crucial you cultivate the special insight that eradicates both coarse and subtle afflictions. You may wonder whether you should cultivate special insight into the worlds’ peacefulness and coarseness, which prevents the afflictions from manifesting.

d.div: [211] sde dge_4328_bstan/ sna tshogs/ ngo _mgon po klu sgrub/ shes rab brgya pa/ shog_99_ba6
[603] Nāgārjuna, Prajñāśataka, Toh 4328 Tengyur, bzo rig pa / thun mong ba, ngo, 99b6.

f.d:
bsngags 'os bsngags bstod las/
khyod kyi chos la mi phyogs pa'i/ / skye bo gti mug gis ldongs pa/ / srid rtse'i bar du song nas kyang / / sdug bsngal yang 'byung srid pa bsgrub/[212] / ces phyi rol pa sogs ci yang med man chad kyi nyon mongs pa mngon gyur thams cad spangs te srid rtse'i sems thob kyang 'khor ba las mi grol bas ting 'dzin rgyal po las/
ting nge 'dzin de sgom par byed mod kyi/ / des ni bdag tu 'du shes 'jig mi byed/ / de yis nyon mongs phyir zhing rab 'khrug ste/ / lhag spyod 'di na ting 'dzin sgom pa bzhin/[213] / zhes bdag 'dzin ma spangs pa'i mthus mu stegs lhag spyod bzhin nyon mongs 'khrugs te/ slar yang gnas 'og ma'i sems su ltung bas na skyes bu chen po'i gdul bya rnams kyi don du gnyer bya ga la yin/

Concerning this, Praise to the One Beyond All Praise states:
Although the people not following your teaching, who are blinded by ignorance, may go as far as the peak of existence, they will fall again into the world and be subjected to suffering.[604] Although tīrthikas and so on reject all manifest afflictions up to nothingness and attain the mental state of the peak of existence, they are not free of samsara. The King of Meditations Sutra says:
Although you cultivate mundane concentrations, as they do not destroy the notion of self, the afflictions arise again, as when Udraka cultivated these concentrations.[605] Because they had not rejected grasping at self, beings like the tīrthika Udraka Rāmaputra were troubled by the afflictions and regressed to lower mental states. Given this, in no case are followers of the Great Vehicle to pursue these states of concentration.

d.div: [212] sde dge_1138_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon ma ti tsi tra/ bsngags 'os bsngags bstod/ le'u/ 9_shog_96_na3
[213] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 9_shog_27_na7
[604] Mātṛceṭa, Varṇārhavarṇestotra, Toh 1138 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 96a3.
[605] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 9, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 27a7.

f.d:
'o na sngar 'bad pas bsgoms pa'i zhi gnas de la don med dam snyam na/
khyod kyi bstan pa'i rjes 'gro ba/ / bsam gtan dngos gzhi ma thob kyang / / bdud kyi mig ras btsa' bzhin du/ / srid pa dag ni bzlog par bgyid/[214] / ces bsam gtan dang po'i nyer bsdogs thob pa'i rjes su bsam gtan dang po'i dngos gzhi sgrub pa sogs kyi rtsol ba bzhag nas 'jig rten las 'das pa'i lhag mthong bdag med pa'i don bsgoms pas 'khor ba las grol ba'i thar pa thob par 'gyur ro/ /

If you then question the purpose of the tranquil abiding that you have striven in the past to meditate on, [Praise to the One Beyond All Praise] says: [250]
Although the followers of your teaching do not attain the actual [first] absorption, they are able to overcome cyclic existence, even with the demons glaring at them.[606] Once you have attained the preparatory stage of the first absorption, put aside pursuing the actual first absorption and the rest and then, by meditating on supramundane insight into selflessness, attain a state of liberation that is freedom from cyclic existence.

d.div: [214] sde dge_1138_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon ma ti tsi tra/ bsngags 'os bsngags bstod/ le'u/ 9_shog_96_na4
[606] Mātṛceṭa, Varṇārhavarṇestotra, Toh 1138 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 96a4.

f.d:
de ltar na phar phyin tha ma'i nyams len 'dis thams cad mkhyen pa thob par mi 'gyur na skyes bu 'bring las lhag pa'i lhag chos gang yang ma byung bar dogs tshe/ de ltar log rtog shar ba ni g.yag zhar ba'i rtswa ltar phyogs re'i mig can du song ba'i nyes pas nongs pas skyes bu 'bring dang mi 'dra ba'i khyad par gong du byang chub kyi sems dang rgyal sras kyi spyod par slob tshul rgyas par song yang / rje bla mas/
gnas lugs rtogs pa'i shes rab mi ldan na/ / nges 'byung byang chub sems la goms byas kyang / / srid pa'i rtsa ba gcod par mi nus pas/ / de phyir rten 'brel rtogs pa'i thabs la 'bad/[215] / ces byang chub kyi sems yod par ma zad de dang zung du 'brel ba'i lam lhag pa shes rab kyi bslab pa'i lam sgom pa yin gyi skyes bu 'bring man chad ltar phyogs re ba'i lam min no//

Since in this case you are not achieving omniscience through the practice of the final perfection, you might doubt that this path is in any way superior to the path of persons of intermediate capacity. Your limited vision, like the way a one-eyed yak eats grass, is to blame for entertaining such a mistaken notion. I have already explained at length the way to train in the awakening mind and bodhisattva deeds, which are quite distinct from the path of persons of intermediate capacity. Furthermore, the Great Lord [Tsongkhapa] says:
Without the wisdom realizing the ultimate nature, though you gain familiarity with renunciation and the awakening mind, you will be unable to cut the root of cyclic existence. So strive in the methods for realizing dependent origination.[607] [As persons of great capacity] not only have the awakening mind but in conjunction with it meditate on the path that is the higher training in wisdom, their path is complete, unlike the paths of persons of lesser and intermediate capacity.

d.div: [215] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ kha_gsung thor bu/ lam gyi gtso bo rnam gsum/ shog_194_na6
[607] Three Principal Elements of the Path, verse 9. See page 52 above.

f.d:
'o na zhi lhag gnyis skyes bu 'bring gi skabs kyi ting 'dzin dang shes rab kyi bslab pa'i nyams len du gtogs tshe rgyal sras kyi spyod pa rnams dang zung du 'brel dgos pa ci yin snyam na/ rigs pa drug cu pa las/
dge ba 'di yis skye bo kun/ / bsod nams ye shes tshogs rdzogs shing / / bsod nams ye shes las byung ba/ / dam pa gnyis ni thob par shog[216] / ces sangs rgyas 'grub pa la gzugs kyi sku dang chos kyi sku gnyis thob dgos la/ de gang la brten nas bsgrub na/

Since tranquil abiding and insight are included in the practice of training in meditative concentration and wisdom within the path of persons of intermediate capacity, you may wonder what need there is to join them to the bodhisattva deeds. [Nāgārjuna’s] Sixty Verses of Reasoning states:
By this virtue, may all beings complete the collections of merit and wisdom and attain the two excellent [bodies of a buddha] that result from merit and wisdom.[608] To achieve buddhahood you need to attain both a form body and a truth body. On what basis are they achieved?

d.div: [216] sde dge_3825_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rigs pa drug pa/ sh+loka tha ma/ shog_22_ba4
[608] Nāgārjuna, Yuktiṣaṣṭikā, verse 60, Toh 3825 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 22b4.

f.d:
dpal ldan zla bas/
tha snyad bden pa thabs su gyur pa dang / / don dam bden pa thabs byung gyur pa ste/ / de gnyis rnam dbye gang gis mi shes pa/ / de ni rnam rtog log pa'i lam ngan zhugs/[217] / zhes pa'i shugs la/
de gnyis rnam dbye gang gis legs shes pa/ / de ni phyin ci ma log lam bzang zhugs/ / zhes gzhi'i lta ba kun rdzob bden pa snang ba'i cha chos thams cad tha snyad du grub cing rgyu 'bras ma 'chol bar 'byung ba'i rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba dang / don dam bden pa stong pa'i cha chos thams cad rang gi ngo bos grub pa cung zad tsam yang med pa gnyis phyin ci ma log par shes na lam gyi gnas skabs su sbyin sogs kyi spyod pa rlabs po ches tshogs gsog pa dang stong pa nyid kyi lta ba zab mo zung 'brel du nyams su blangs pa la brten nas 'bras bu gzugs kyi sku dang chos kyi sku gnyis thob par 'gyur bas skyes bu chen po pa rnams kyi thob bya mthar thug pa yin pas/

The glorious Candrakīrti explains:
Conventional truths are the methods; ultimate truths result from the methods. Whoever does not know how to distinguish the two enters the bad path of mistaken conceptions.[609] This implies the following:
Whoever knows well how to distinguish the two enters the good and unmistaken path.[610] [251] The view at base level is the correct understanding of conventional truths, the appearance aspect — which is that all existents are established conventionally and arise interdependently without error between cause and effect — and the correct understanding of ultimate truths, the emptiness aspect — which is that no existent is even slightly established by way of its own nature. On the path you practice a vast accumulation of merit, with bodhisattva deeds such as generosity, and concurrently you practice the profound view of emptiness. In this way you attain the two results, a form body and a truth body, which are the ultimate objectives of persons of great capacity.

d.div: [217] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_80_shog_208_na2
[609] Entering the Middle Way (Madhyamakāvatāra) 6.80, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 208a2.
[610] Here the author is suggesting the conclusion to be drawn based on Candrakīrti’s words.

f.d: [The stages of training in wisdom]

thob byed kyi thabs bsod nams kyi tshogs gsog tshul gyi nyams 'khrid sngon du song zin nas/ ye shes kyi tshogs gsog pa'i nyams len gyi rim pa la spyir 'phags pa'i yul du grub mtha' smra ba bzhi so sor yod pa nas lta ba mi mthun yang gtso bo ni dbu sems gnyis kyi lugs 'di grags che zhing /

As for the methods to attain them, I have already given an experiential explanation on how to achieve the collection of merit. Regarding the stages of practice for accomplishing the collection of wisdom, generally, in the Land of Āryas[611] there were four distinct schools of tenets with varying views. However, two major traditions, Madhyamaka and Cittamātra, are preeminent.

d.div: [611] An epithet for India.

f.d:
de yang rin chen phreng ba las/
chos 'di zab phyir skye bo yis/ / shes par dka' ba thugs chud de/ / des na thub pa sangs rgyas nas/ / chos bstan pa las log par gyur/[218] / ces las 'bras dang stong nyid kyi rnam gzhag mi 'gal bar 'jog shes pa'i gnad 'di gzhan gyis rtogs dka' bas sangs rgyas kyis chos kyi 'khor lo bskor bar zhal gyis bzhes pa dka' dka' ltar mdzad la/ dka' ba'i gnad de 'khrul pa med par ston pa po ni rgyal bas lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo las lung bstan pa'i dpal mgon 'phags pa klu sgrub yin zhing / de nyid kyi rjes su 'brang bar khas 'che ba mang na yang chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis grub par khas len pa'i lta ba tsam gyis thar pa'ang 'thob pa'i skabs med pas dpal ldan zla bas/
slob dpon klu sgrub zhabs kyi lam las ni/ / phyi rol gyur la zhi ba'i thabs med do/ / de dag kun rdzob de nyid bden las nyams/ / de las nyams pas thar pa 'grub yod min/[219] / zhes gsungs pa'i phyir na mgon po klu sgrub kyi dgongs pa 'khrul pa med par rtogs dgos pas de 'grel byed gang gi rjes su 'brang na/

Furthermore, Precious Garland says:
As this teaching is profound, he knew it would be difficult for beings to understand, which is why, after attaining buddhahood, the Sage declined to teach the Dharma.[612] Knowing it would be hard for others to realize the key point of establishing the absence of incompatibility between emptiness and the system of karma and effects, the Buddha acted as if it would be difficult for him to agree to turn the wheel of the Dharma. The glorious protector Nāgārjuna, whose advent the Buddha prophesized in the Descent into Laṅkā Sutra,[613] correctly explained this difficult system. Although many people claim to be his followers, liberation cannot be attained with just the view [held by Svātantrikas, for example] that asserts that all existents are established by way of their own nature. The glorious Candrakīrti states:
Those outside the path of the worthy teacher Nāgārjuna do not possess the means to attain peace. They deviate from conventional and ultimate truths and, because of this divergence, fail to achieve liberation.[614] As the protector Nāgārjuna’s intent must be correctly established, which of his commentators should be followed?

d.div: [218] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 2_sh+loka_18_shog_111_na6

[613] Laṅkāvatārasūtra, Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 165b5.
[614] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra, 6.79, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 208a1.

f.d:
jo bo chen pos/
stong nyid gang gis rtogs zhe na/ / de bzhin gshegs pas lung bstan cing / / chos nyid bden pa gzigs pa yi/ / klu sgrub slob ma zla grags yin/ / de las brgyud pa'i man ngag gis/ / chos nyid bden pa rtogs par 'gyur/[220] / zhes dpal ldan zla ba grags pas bkral ba'i rjes su 'brangs te nyams su len pa la bzhi brgya pa'i 'grel pa las/
de la bdag ces bya ba ni gang zhig dngos po rnams kyi gzhan la rag ma las pa'i ngo bo rang bzhin te de med pa ni bdag med pa'o/ / de ni chos dang gang zag gi dbye bas gnyis su rtogs te/ chos kyi bdag med pa dang gang zag gi bdag med pa'o/[221] / zhes bdag med pa'i tshul gnyis po go rim ji lta bu snyam na/
bsod nams min pa dang por bzlog / bar du bdag ni bzlog pa dang / / tha mar lta zhig kun bzlog pa/ / gang gis shes de mkhas pa yin/[222] / zhes las rgyu 'bras med par blta ba'i lta ngan sogs ni sngar skyes bu chung 'bring gi skabs nas bzlog zin pas/
re zhig nyes kun 'byung ba'i gnas/ / med nyid rnam par bzlog zin gyi/[223] / zhes gsungs nas/

[In Entering the Two Truths] the great Atiśa writes:
If you ask, “Who realized emptiness?” Nāgārjuna, whose coming the Tathāgata prophesized, and his disciple Candrakīrti, who saw the truth of ultimate nature. Only with the instruction stemming from them do you realize the truth of ultimate nature.[615] [252] You should practice according to the commentaries of the glorious Candrakīrti. His Extensive Commentary on Four Hundred Verses states:
Here self is any thing’s nature, or character of nondependence on others. Its nonexistence is selflessness. Know that it is twofold, as it is distinguished in relation to phenomena and persons: the selflessness of phenomena and the selflessness of persons.[616] What is the order between the two kinds of selflessness? [Four Hundred Verses states:]
First non-merit is to be overcome, in the middle the self is to be overcome, in the end all views are to be overcome. Whoever knows this is wise.[617] Bad views such as the repudiation of karmic cause and effect have been rejected previously in the context of the paths of persons of lesser and intermediate capacity, as [Nāgārjuna] says:
First, the source of all faults, nihilism, was completely rejected.[618]

[617] Āryadeva, Catuḥśataka, 8.14, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 7b2.
[618] Sixty Verses of Reasoning (Yuktiṣaṣṭikā) verse 3, Toh 3825 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 20a2.
