de yang bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba 'ba' zhig bdag 'dzin de'i dngos kyi gnod byed du 'gyur ba las gzhan byams snying rje sogs dge ba rlabs po che gang gis kyang de spong mi nus pas bdag med rtogs pa'i lta ba la myong ba phul byung skye ba zhig cis kyang bya'o/ / de la yang ting nge 'dzin rnam par dag pa zhig dgos la bslab pa de gnyis kyi gzhi dang rten lta bu yang tshul khrims kyi bslab pa nyid yin la/ mdor na mngon mtho nges legs mchog thun mong gi dngos grub sogs gang sgrub par 'dod kyang khas blangs pa'i tshul khrims tshul bzhin du bsrung ba la rag las pa dang / bsrung na phan yon che zhing ma bsrung na nyes dmigs kyang shin tu che bar bcom ldan 'das kyi bka' yang dag pa las grub pa des na/ khas blangs pa'i tshul khrims tshul bzhin du bsrung ba 'di la ma 'bad na thabs gzhan ji 'drar zhugs kyang mngon mtho nges legs 'grub pa'i gzhi rtsa chad 'gro ba las 'os mi 'dug pas/ khas blangs pa'i tshul khrims 'di la sdig ltung gis gtan nas ma gos pa'am/ gos kyang de ma thag tu sdig ltung sbyong ba'i thabs shig la skyes bu'i rtsal ci yod kyis 'bad par bya'o//

The only antidote to this ignorance is the view realizing selflessness. No other powerful virtuous states of mind, including loving kindness and compassion, can eliminate it. I will therefore strive my best to gain excellent experience of this view of selflessness. For this, I need to attain perfect concentration, and the sole foundation for these two trainings [of wisdom and concentration] is the training in morality. In brief, whatever spiritual aspirations I have, whether aimed at birth in the higher realms or at the definite goodness of nirvana, whether for common or for supreme siddhis, all of them are contingent on observing moral discipline based on the precepts I have vowed to uphold. Moral precepts, established through the perfect words of the Blessed Buddha, lead to great benefits if one observes them and lead to grave negative consequences if one fails to observe them. So if I do not strive in guarding the precepts I have taken, it makes no difference what other methods I pursue; I will inescapably cut short the life thread of birth in the higher realms and attainment of liberation. Therefore, with all my effort, I will strive to ensure that the precepts I have taken remain unblemished, and when the stains of transgressions do come about, I will strive in the means to purify them. [355]

de ltar khams gsum 'khor ba thams cad sdug bsngal gyi rang bzhin du mthong nas de las thar 'dod kyi bsam pa shugs drag pos rgyud bskul te/ lam bslab pa rin po che gsum la tshul bzhin du bslabs pas khams gsum 'khor ba 'di las gtan du thar pa'i thar pa zhig thob kyang / de tsam gyis ni rang don yongs su ma rdzogs pas gzhan don yang nyi tshe ba tsam las mi yong ba red/ der ma zad sems can 'di dag thams cad ni bdag la cir mi yong zhing 'brel med lta bu zhig gtan nas min par/ sngon thog ma med pa nas 'khor ba 'dir res res bdag gi ma ma byas pa gcig kyang med pa dang / byas pa yang grangs dang mtha' med pa dang / ma nam byas res shing bdag srog las gces shing nor gyi snying po yid bzhin gyi nor bu las kyang phangs par byas nas bdag gi don du lus srog khyad du bsad pa'i dka' spyad bya dgos byung ba yang grangs dang mtha' med pa dang / bdag gi don du sdig pa mi dge ba bsags nas ngan song gsum du ltung dgos byung ba yang grangs dang mtha' med pa dang / sdig sdug gtam ngan lus srog longs spyod gang yang khyad du bsad nas sha thang thang gis bsgrubs pa'i zas nor thams cad bdag la phangs pa med par btang ba tsam bsags na 'jig rten gyi khams 'dir yang shong sa med pa dang / brtse ba'i sems kyis khar nu zho bsnun pa tsam bsags na'ang chu bo bzhi 'dus pa'i rgya mtsho las kyang mang bar dri ma med pa'i lung rigs kyis grub pa des na/ sems can de rnams kyis sngon thog ma med pa nas bdag srog las gces shing nor gyi snying po yid bzhin gyi nor bu las kyang phangs par byas tshar pa dang mnyam du sdig sdug gtam ngan lus srog longs spyod gang la'ang ltos pa med par bdag 'ba' zhig brtse zhing byams pa'i bsam sbyor gyis kun nas bskyangs bskyangs pa de'i sku drin dang thugs rje de la ngas ji 'dra bgyi na 'jal thabs yod/

Now, seeing the entire samsaric world of the three realms as characterized by suffering and thus being motivated by a strong desire for liberation, even if I engage correctly in the path of the threefold training and, as a result, attain permanent freedom from this cycle of existence, even my own aims would not be fulfilled, and as for others’ welfare, such attainment can lead to only partial fulfillment. Furthermore, all these sentient beings are not random beings with no connection to me whatsoever. Every last one of them has been my mother in this beginningless cycle of existence. Not only that, each has been my mother countless times beyond measure. And each time they were my mother, they cared for me like I was the most precious thing imaginable, more important than even their own life. There is no counting the times they endured pain and hardship for my sake, sacrificing their own body and life. Countless times they were plunged into the lower realms because of negative acts they committed in their devotion to me. And if one were to gather up all the material resources, food, clothing, and possessions that they had to accumulate with such efforts through committing negative acts, gaining ill repute, and sacrificing their body, life, and resources for my benefit, there wouldn’t be enough space on this earth! The milk they have fed me would be greater than an ocean! This is established by authoritative scriptures and logic. So, when I look at the number of times these sentient beings cared for me as if I were more precious than a wish-granting jewel, the number of times they showered me with kindness through loving hearts and actions, heedlessly committing negative acts, enduring pain, attracting ill repute, and sacrificing their body, life, and material resources in the process, how could I ever repay their kindness?

der ma zad da dung yang nged kyis sems can de rnams kyi bur skye ba grangs dang mtha' med pa zhig blang dgos yong / de dag gis kyang bdag bur nam skyes res shing srog las gces shing nor gyi snying po yid bzhin gyi nor bu las kyang phangs par byas tshar ba dang mnyam du/ yang sdig sdug gtam ngan lus srog longs spyod gang yang khyad du bsad nas bdag 'ba' zhig brtse zhing byams pa'i bsam sbyor gyis rang dbang med par skyong dgos pa yang grangs dang mtha' med pa/ des na skye ba nas tshe rabs thams cad du sems can de rnams ma yin na bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs sus sgrub/ gnod pa dang sdug bsngal sus sel su la brten nas kyang bdag gis bde ba myong / des na sems can 'di dag thams cad ni skye ba nas tshe rabs thams cad du bdag la med du mi rung ba'i bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs sgrub pa'i mdza' bshes gtso bo ma rgan sha stag red/ de ltar na'ang da lta kho rang tsho la skyid sdug legs nyes gang byung yang de la cir yang mi sems par bdag 'ba' zhig bde zhing skyid pa'i thabs 'ba' zhig la sems sems pa 'di ni ma rabs khrel med dud 'gro rnams dang khyad par med pa red/

Not only that, but I will also be reborn as their child countless times beyond measure in the future. And every time I am born as their child, they will hold me as more precious than a wish-granting jewel. [356] They will care for me countless times with loving hearts and actions, making sacrifices in negative karma, pain, ill repute, body, life, and material resources for my sake. Were it not for these sentient beings who care so much for me, who else would ensure my well-being? Who else would relieve my harm and suffering? Who else could I depend on for my happiness? Therefore, these sentient beings are all truly my dear mothers, my closest loved ones, who have been and will be crucial to my well-being, who safeguard my welfare. Thus, were I to remain oblivious to their situation, whether they are well or not, and instead attend to my own welfare alone, this would be thoughtless indeed; I would be no different from an animal.

der ma zad rang gces par 'dzin pa de ni rgud pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba yin te/ mi dang mi min gyi gnod 'tshe/ sems med dug mtshon sogs kyi 'jigs pa/ sems ldan gcan gzan khro bo sogs kyi 'jigs pa/ mdor na 'khor ba spyi dang bye brag ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal ji snyed yod pa thams cad ni rgyu dang rkyen gang la bltas kyang gtso bor rang gces 'dzin gyi mthu kho na las byung ba yin pas/ ya gi srid pa'i rtse mo nas ma gi mnar med kyi bar khams gsum gang du phyin kyang rjes su 'brang ba'i dgra bo/ sdig sdug gtam ngan sogs mi 'dod bzhin du 'khrid yong ba'i 'gong po/ mtho ris dang thar pa'i srog rtsa gcod pa'i gshed ma/ rmi lam gyi gnas skabs tshun chad bde ru mi ster ba'i nang gi khong skran lta bu rang gces 'dzin 'di'i dbang du skad cig kyang mi gtong bar gzhan gces par 'dzin pa'i bsam sbyor 'di la skyes bu'i rtsal ji yod kyis 'bad par bya dgos te/

Furthermore, the root of all misfortune is self-cherishing. Whether the harm caused by humans or nonhumans, threats from such inanimate objects as poison or weapons, the menace of predatory animals, and so on — in brief, all the sufferings of samsara in general and of each specific realm — whatever the causes and conditions that underlie them, they come about primarily through the power of self-cherishing alone. From the peak of existence to the depths of the Relentless hell, self-cherishing is the enemy that never fails to prey on me; it is the demon that draws forth negative karma, suffering, and ill repute against my will; it is the butcher that cuts short the life vein of fortunate rebirth and of attainment of liberation; it is the malignant tumor that prevents me from experiencing happiness even in my dreams. So I must never let myself be under the sway of this self-cherishing, even for a moment, but strive instead with all my strength to cultivate the thought that cherishes others’ welfare.

de yang tshe 'di'i bde skyid snyan gsum/ phyi ma'i lha mi'i go 'phang / de la mkho ba'i bde 'byor phun tshogs/ thar pa dang thams cad mkhyen pa sogs gang sgrub par 'dod kyang sems can la brten nas bsgrub dgos shing sems can la brten na bde blag tu 'grub pa dang / mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa'i tshe sangs rgyas kyi mdzad pa 'phrin las thams cad kyang sems can la brten nas sgrub pa ma gtogs/ sems can la ma brten par sangs rgyas kyi mdzad pa 'phrin las kyi ming tsam yang 'byung sa med pas/ gcig tu na sems can 'di rnams ni skye ba nas tshe rabs thams cad du bdag la med du mi rung ba'i bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs sgrub pa'i mdza' bshes/ gnyis su gzhi dang lam dang 'bras bu gang gi gnas skabs na yang bdag la med du mi rung ba'i bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs bde blag tu ster ba'i yid bzhin gyi nor bu rin po che dang bla ma dang lhag pa'i lha rnams dang khyad par cung zad kyang med pas/ sems can 'di rnams ni srog las kyang gces shing / nor gyi snying po yid bzhin gyi nor bu las kyang phangs par byas tshar ba dang mnyam du 'di dag mgu bar bya zhing mnyes par byed pa'i don du ni lus dang srog kyang gtong ba'i dka' spyad la'ang cis kyang 'jug par bya dgos pa 'dug/

Whether it is this life’s happiness, joy, and fame or whether it is birth as a god or a human and the prosperity and happiness that they desire, or even the attainment of liberation and a buddha’s omniscience, we can only attain them in dependence on the sentient beings. And when we do rely on sentient beings, we can achieve these goals more easily. At the moment of attaining buddhahood too, all the enlightened activities of the buddha [357] are accomplished in dependence on sentient beings. Without depending on sentient beings, not even the words “a buddha’s enlightened deeds” could exist. So, on the one hand, these sentient beings are indispensable friends who seek my welfare; on the other hand, they are indispensable during the stages of my path [to enlightenment] and the resultant state [of buddhahood]. So, like a wish-granting jewel securing my welfare and happiness, there is no difference at all between them and my guru and meditation deities. I must therefore hold these sentient beings as dearer than my own life and view them as more precious than a wish-granting jewel. And on this basis, I will undergo whatever hardships I must for their sake to make them happy, including even sacrificing my body and life.

'on kyang da lta sems can 'di rnams kyis ni bde ba gcig rang 'dod mod kyi bde ba khyad par du gyur pa lta ci smos/ tha na zag bcas kyi bde ba phra mo re dang phrad pa'ang nyin mo'i skar ma dang 'dra/ bde ba phra mo re byung yang de ma thag sdug bsngal du 'gyur ba las bde ba'i rang bzhin du gnas pa med/ sdug bsngal ni tha na rmi lam gyi gnas skabs tshun chad du yang mi 'dod bzhin du 'khor ba spyi dang bye brag gi sdug bsngal brgya phrag du mas rtag tu gzir/ sdug bsngal mi 'dod bzhin du de'i rgyu las ngan mi bzad pa gsog pa la ni khyis khrag mthong ba lta bur ngam ngam shugs kyis 'jug/ /

Although sentient beings wish for happiness, even just meeting the ordinary joys of contaminated character is rare, like a star in day light, to say nothing of extraordinary levels of happiness. Even when they do encounter some minor happiness, it immediately acquires the character of suffering; nothing endures as genuine happiness. As for suffering, they do not wish for this even in a dream, and yet they remain tormented constantly by the general and specific sufferings of samsara. They do not wish for suffering, but they instinctively chase the causes of suffering like a dog attracted by the sight of blood.

las ngan de'i 'bras bur tshe 'dir lus sems gdung ba'i nad dang gnod pa sogs mthong chos kyi bkra mi shis pa rnams char bzhin du 'bab/ phyi mar ngan song du ltung nas tsha grang gi sdug bsngal sogs rnam smin gyi 'bras bu dang / gal te de las thar nas kyang tshe thung ba nad mang ba sogs dang kha zas dang sman la sogs pa rnams 'ju dka' zhing nad skyed pa sogs myong ba rgyu mthun dang bdag 'bras gnyis kyis gzir/ khyad par las ngan de'i byed pa rgyu mthun gyis rang dbang med par bskul te las ngan gsog tu 'jug nas slar yang las des ngan song gsum du 'jug cing 'khrid par byed pa las 'os mi 'dug pas/ sems can 'di rnams 'di ltar las dang nyon mongs pa dang sdug bsngal gsum gyi gzhan dbang du gyur nas 'di 'dra 'phral phugs kun tu brlag par 'gyur ba snying re rje snying re rje/

As a result of such negative karma, they face all sorts of adversities in their present lives, illnesses and harms and such that assail the body and mind like rain falling from the sky. In future lives too, they will fall to the lower realms and experience the fruitional effects[840] [of karma] in the sufferings of both heat and cold. Even if they avoid such a fate [of rebirth in a lower realm], they will meet with the concordant experiential effects and environmental effects, such as lives that are short and fraught with numerous illnesses, difficulty digesting food and medicine, and so on. In particular, as the effect concordant with such karma, they will be uncontrollably led to further commit the same type of acts, thus casting them to the three lower realms. Such will be their fate. Under the sway of karma and the afflictions, [358] these sentient beings are doomed, both immediately and long term. This is sad! How tragic, indeed!

[840] Classical Buddhist texts differentiate three types of karmic effects: (1) the fruitional effect, the primary result in the form of a specific rebirth; (2) a causally concordant effect, an effect correlated to a specific karma; and (3) environmental effects, qualities of the physical environment where one is born and lives. The second is further differentiated further into (a) concordant experiential effects — having a short life, for example, for the karma of killing — and effects concordant with the act, which manifest as an attraction to pursuing similar behaviors.

'di ltar gyur pa'i sems can 'di rnams kyang sdig sdug gtam ngan lus srog longs spyod gang la yang mi lta bar bdag 'ba' zhig brtse zhing byams pa'i bsam sbyor gyis legs par bskyangs shing skyong bar 'gyur ba'i drin can gyi ma rgan/ bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs bde blag tu ster ba'i yid bzhin gyi nor bu dang bla ma dang lhag pa'i lha rnams dang khyad par med pa sha stag yin pa la/ da lta'i gnas skabs 'di 'dra'i nyam thag pa'i gnas su gyur pa'i ngang tshul shes shing dran bzhin du ci'i phyir yal bar 'dor/ des na sems can 'di rnams sdug bsngal dang sdug bsngal gyi rgyu kun dang bral zhing / bde ba dang bde ba'i rgyu phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan pa zhig bdag gis bya'o/ /

All these sentient beings are truly my dear mothers, my closest loved ones, who have cared for me and will care for me with loving hearts and actions without regard to their own negative karma, suffering, ill repute, or costs in body, life, and material resources. When it comes to granting my welfare and happiness, they are no different at all from a wish-granting jewel, my guru, and my meditation deities. So, knowing at this moment how desperate their situation is, how could I abandon them? Therefore I will ensure that they are free from suffering and all its causes and that they find happiness and all its causes.

khyad par sems can 'di rnams kho rang tsho'i ngos nas nyon mongs pa'i gdon drag pos rgyud dkrug ste dran pa la rang dbang ma thob par smyo/ mngon mtho dang nges legs kyi lam la lta ba'i blo gros kyi mig ni ldongs/ yang dag pa'i dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi long khrid dang ni bral/ mnog chung la nyes dmigs shin tu che ba'i rnyed bkur gyis dbyen spyos shing sgo gsum gyi nyes spyod drag po'i gom pa re re rdeg cing 'cha' nas/ spyir 'khor ba dang sgos ngan song gsum gyi 'jigs su rung ba'i g.yang kha mi bzad par rab tu 'grims pa'i nyam thag pa'i gnas su gyur pa las 'os mi 'dug pas/ ma rgan de rnams kyang bu bdag la mi re na su la re/ bdag kyang ma rgan de rnams 'di 'dra 'phral thes phugs thes su song zhing mgon med skyabs med du gyur pa'i ngang tshul 'di ltar shes shing dran bzhin du ci'i phyir yal bar 'dor/ des na sems can 'di rnams sdug bsngal kun dang bral zhing bde ba phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan par sgrub pa'i don du lus dang srog la'ang ltos pa med pa'i dka' spyad dang rlabs po che'i brtson 'grus kyis da lta nyid du 'jug par bya'o//

On their part, given that their minds are possessed by the powerful demon of affliction, they have no control over their mind; they are mad. Their eyes of intellect to see the path to the higher birth and liberation have been blinded. They are bereft of the guidance of a perfect spiritual teacher. They remain beguiled by the pursuit of mundane pleasures and honor, which are seemingly innocent yet so fraught with problems. With every step and stride of their negative actions of body, speech, and mind, they venture toward the cliff of unimaginable suffering of samsara in general and of the three lower realms in particular. Their fate is thus likely to remain nothing but desperate. Now, if these mother sentient beings do not place their hopes in me, their child, who else can they place their hopes in? On my part too, how could I abandon them, especially when I am aware of their desperate situation, both presently and long term, and the way they remain bereft of protector and refuge? Therefore I will strive with diligence from this moment, with no concern for even my body and life, in pursuit of their freedom from all suffering and their perfect happiness.

f.d: de yang sems can 'di rnams kyi rgyud la nyon mongs pa brgyad khri bzhi stong dang des nye bar bsags pa'i las ngan mi bzad pa rnams dang / de'i 'bras bu tshe 'dir lus sems gdung ba'i nad dang gnod pa sogs mthong chos kyi bkra mi shis pa rnams dang / phyi mar ngan song du ltung ba'i rnam smin gyi 'bras bu/ myong ba rgyu mthun dang bdag 'bras/ khyad par byed pa rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu dang bcas pa da lta nyid du bdag gi rgyud steng 'dir blangs nas/ ji srid 'khor ba ma stongs kyi bar du khams gsum gyi sems can thams cad kyi rgud pa'i tshogs thams cad nged gcig pus nyams su myong ste/ sems can de rnams kyis sdug bsngal ming tsam yang go rgyu med pa dang / bdag gi lus longs spyod dus gsum dge ba'i dngos po thams cad da lta nyid du sems can 'di rnams la btang nas gnas skabs dang mthar thug gi phan bde'i legs tshogs rnams dang rmi lam du'ang 'bral ba med pa zhig bdag gis bya'o/ / de ltar byed nus pa bla ma lhas byin gyis brlab tu gsol/

I take upon my mindstream this very moment, from all these sentient beings, their eighty-four thousand afflictions together with the most grave karmic acts they have created and their effects — [359] their effects in the present lives, such as all the adversities of illness and harm that assail the body and mind, the fruitional effects of being plunged to the lower realms, their concordant experiential effects and environmental effects, and, in particular, the effects concordant with the act. By taking these from them, I shall ensure that I alone experience all the misfortune of sentient beings until samsara comes to an end, such that these sentient beings will not know suffering, not even its name. I will send them, this very moment, my body, resources, and virtues of all the three times and ensure that they never remain divorced of immediate and long-term welfare, even in their dreams. Bless me, O guru deity, that I may be able to do this.

d.div: sems can 'di rnams sdug bsngal kun las grol zhing bde ba phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan par sgrub pa'i khur de bdag la bab 'dug kyang / da lta'i gnas skabs 'di 'dras ni sems can thams cad lta ci smos/ sems can gcig gi sdug bsngal mtha' dag sel zhing bde ba mtha' dag sgrub pa'i nus pa yang med/ nged phar zhog nyan rang dgra bcom pa rnams la'ang sems can gcig gi don mthar phyin pa yang sgrub pa'i nus pa med/ sems can thams cad sdug bsngal kun las grol zhing bde ba phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan par sgrub pa'i nus pa ni yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas nyag gcig la yod de/

f.d:
[Again contemplate:]
Now, although the responsibility to free these sentient beings from all suffering and grant them perfect happiness falls upon me, my own current state is such that, let alone all sentient beings, I cannot remove all the suffering and ensure the happiness of a single sentient being. Not just me, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot accomplish the complete welfare of a single sentient being. Only a fully enlightened buddha can eliminate the suffering of all sentient beings and enable them to achieve all happiness.

d.div: sku'i yon tan mtshan dpe gsal rdzogs kyis spras pa/ mthong na mi mthun pa med pa/ mthong thos dran reg tsam gyis 'gro ba kun gyi phan bde'i gsos su gyur pa/ sku'i ba spu bu ga re re nas 'phro ba'i 'od zer dang sprul pa re res kyang sems can dpag tu med pa smin grol gyi lam la 'god nus pa/

The enlightened attributes of the body of a buddha is his adornment with the major and minor noble marks; nothing in his appearance is unappealing to the eyes; he is a source of help and benefit to all beings even through mere sight, hearing, and thought; and each and every light ray and emanation emitted from his body has the ability to lead countless beings to the paths of maturation and freedom.

gsung gi yon tan yan lag drug cu'i dbyangs dang ldan pas gsung dbyangs skad re res kyang sems can rnams kyi rang rang gi skal ba dang 'tshams pa'i zab rgyas kyi chos rgyas 'bring bsdus pa rnams rang rang gi skad du dus gcig tu go bar byas nas smin grol gyi lam bzang po 'god nus pa/

As for the enlightened attributes of his speech, it is endowed with sixty melodies, and the utterance in even a single language has the ability to reveal at once the teachings, both brief and extensive, pertaining to both the profound and the vast aspects of the path, appropriate to the fortunes of sentient beings in their own languages. And through this, his speech can lead beings to the excellent paths of maturation and freedom.

thugs kyi yon tan shes bya ji lta ba dang ji snyed pa thams cad dang / sems can thams cad kyi khams dang bsam pa dang bag la nyal thams cad mngon sum du gzigs shing ma bu gcig pa la brtse ba ltar thugs rje chen po kun la nye ring med par 'jug pas 'dul ba'i dus las skad cig kyang g.yel ba med pa dang /

Regarding the enlightened attributes of his mind, he knows in a direct manner the entire field of knowledge, the way things truly are and things in their diversity, as well as the natural inclinations, mental dispositions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings. [360] Given that his great compassion extends to all sentient beings, without any discrimination, holding them most dear as a loving mother holds her only child, he never wavers even a moment from the right time to help beings tame themselves.

'dul ba'i mdzad pa 'phrin las thams cad kyang 'bad med lhun gyis 'grub cing rgyun mi 'chad du 'jug pas skad cig ma re re yang sems can dpag tu med pa zhig gi don mdzad pa'i nus mthu thogs med du 'jug pas gzhan don mthar phyin pa yang da gzod de nas 'byung ba red/ rang gis kyang ji srid go 'phang dam pa de thob par ma gyur pa de srid du rang don yang yongs su ma rdzogs pas/ rang gzhan thams cad kyi don gnyis mthar phyin pa rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che de ci nas kyang thob par bya/ de'i phyir du lam zab mo bla ma lha'i rnal 'byor gyi sgo nas phyag rgya chen po'i khrid bsgom pa la 'jug par bya'o//

As for his enlightened activities aimed at taming beings, these all come about spontaneously, without effort and without interruption. Thus the buddha’s enlightened activities have the capacity to engage, in each and every moment, with the welfare of infinite beings without hindrance. Thus buddhas have fully realized the ability to secure the perfect welfare of other beings. On my part too, until and as long as I have not actualized this state of buddhahood, I will fail to fully realize even my own ultimate welfare. Therefore I will strive my best to attain the precious state of buddhahood, the complete fulfillment of the twin welfare of self and others. To this end, I will engage in the meditative practice of mahāmudrā on the basis of the profound path of guru yoga.

de yang rang gces par 'dzin pa ni rgud pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba dang / gzhan gces par 'dzin pa ni phan bde'i legs tshogs thams cad kyi 'byung gnas yin par dri ma med pa'i lung rigs kyis grub pa/ des na rang nyid gcig pu'i ched du ni sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang lta bu la'ang rmi lam du yang 'dod pa bskyed par mi rigs kyang / gzhan gyi don du ni sems can re re'i sdug bsngal bsal zhing bde ba sgrub pa'i don du rang nyid sa chen po'i rdul gyi grangs dang mnyam pa'i bskal pa'i bar du dmyal ba mnar med du gnas nas/ de lta bu'i tshul gyis sems can thams cad kyi sdug bsngal rim gyis bsal zhing bde ba rim gyis bsgrub dgos byung yang dbul pos gter rnyed pa lta bu dga' bzhin spro bzhin du 'jug par rigs na'ang / sems can de rnams yun ring po de tsam sdug bsngal rim gyis bsal zhing bde ba rim gyis sgrub pa la ltos dgos byung na sus kyang bzod glags mi 'dug pas/ da ni ma sems can thams cad kyi don du myur ba kho nar rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che mngon du byas nas skad cig ma re rer yang sems can grangs dang mtha' med pa zhig gi don byed pa'i nus mthu thogs pa med par 'jug pa zhig ngas bya'o/ /

Flawless scripture and logical reasoning have established that self-cherishing is the root of all misfortune and that the thought cherishing others’ welfare is the source of all benefit, happiness, and good fortune. It is inappropriate, therefore, even in a dream to desire the attainment of buddhahood for my own sake alone. If it is for the benefit of others, however — even remaining in the hells for eons equal to the number of particles on this great earth to help bring about the welfare of a single sentient being — it would be appropriate to plunge into a task with the joy and zeal of a poor person who has just unearthed a treasure. This said, it should be unbearable if sentient beings have to wait so long to have their suffering removed and their happiness achieved via such an incremental approach. I shall thus actualize the precious state of complete buddhahood so I can secure the welfare of countless and immeasurable sentient beings in each and every single moment.

f.d: de'i phyir du snyigs dus kyi tshe thung gcig la 'ja' lus rdo rje'i sku 'grub pa'i myur lam zab mo rje bla ma'i snyan brgyud kyi gdams pa 'di rnams nyams su blang bar bya'o snyam pa'i byang chub kyi sems snga phyi gnyis shugs drag tu bskyed pa 'di ni dngos gzhi'i nyams len rnams thams cad mkhyen pa'i lam du gtong ba'i thabs mkhas kyi 'phrul yin par yid 'gyur nges kyi myong ba re 'don dgos la/ khyad par byang chub kyi sems phyi ma 'di ni rnal 'byor bla med kyi thun mong min pa'i 'jug sgo yin par bla ma grub pa'i dbang phyug blo bzang rnam rgyal gyi gsung gi babs las 'byung bar bla ma yongs 'dzin rin po ches gsungs zhes bdag gi dpal ldan bla ma de nyid kyis gsungs so//[50]

To this end I will engage in the meditative practice of Master Tsongkhapa’s oral teachings, which constitute a profound and swift path that will bring about the realization of rainbow vajra body within a single lifetime of this age of degeneration. [361] In these ways, you should forcefully generate the two forms of awakening mind, the former and the latter.[841] This is the magical method to ensure that your practices of the main part of the session are transformed into the path to a buddha’s omniscience. It is essential that you cultivate them [the two forms of awakening mind] until they make a deep impression in your mind. In particular, the second form of awakening is the gateway to enter the practice of this unique guru yoga. My precious teacher said that Yongzin Yeshé Gyaltsen stated that this important point emerges in the oral teachings of Drupwang Losang Namgyal.[842]

d.div: [50] 'dir bya bral bas rang gi bla ma'i zhal shes kyi man ngag bkod pa las gzhung la zhal 'phangs mdzad par mi snang /

[841] By “two forms of awakening mind,” the author is referring to the two forms of aspiration presented in sequence toward the end of the long series of contemplation. The first one involves aspiring to attain “the state of buddhahood, which constitutes the perfect fulfillment of the twin aims,” buddhahood as defined generally in Mahayana texts, while the second involves aspiring to attain “the vajra rainbow body,” buddhahood defined uniquely in highest yoga tantra.

[842] Drupwang Losang Namgyal (1671–1741) was a famed Geluk yogi and master who devoted most of his time to solitary meditation as a hermit, hence the epithet drupwang (grub dbang), literally a “lord among siddhas.” His disciples include many noted Geluk teachers of eighteenth century, especially Yongzin Yeshé Gyaltsen, who composed the master’s biography.

f.d: dge sbyor gang la 'jug kyang kun slong 'chos pa'i tshul 'di nyid gnad kyi don por gzung dgos pa ni skyes bu gsum gyi chos gang zhig nyams su blangs kyang de rnams gnad du 'gro mi 'gro ni gong du bsnyad pa ltar skyes bu gsum gyi lam la rim bzhin blo sbyong bas myong ba skyes pa yod med kyi rjes su 'gro ldog byed par rje btsun 'jam dpal gyis rje thams cad mkhyen par gsungs shing /

The reason setting your intention is of utmost importance, whatever virtuous activity you are engaged in, is this. Whether or not any practice of the paths of three capacities meets with success depends on whether you have gained genuine experience through training your mind sequentially in the paths of the three capacities. This is what Mañjuśrī told the omniscient Jé Tsongkhapa.

gzhan yang mnyam med jo bo chen po dang dge bshes 'brom gnyis kyi gsung sgros sogs las 'byung zhing /[51] de dag gi rgyab rten yang 'dul ba lung las/
chos rnams sngon du yid 'gro yid gtso ste/ / yid mgyogs rab tu dang ba'i sems kyis ni/ / byas sam smras na 'bras bu myong ba ni/ / shing gi grib mas de ni btang ma gyur/ /
chos rnams sngon du yid 'gro yid gtso ste/ / yid mgyogs rab tu sdang ba'i sems kyis ni/ / byas sam smras na 'bras bu myong ba ni/ / shing rta 'phyan pas de yi mgo bo gcod/[52] / ces rgyal rigs dang dmangs rigs kyi sprang po gnyis kyi mthong chos kyi las las brtsam ste/ lus ngag gi las thams cad kyi rtsa ba sems yin par gsungs pa dang /

The same point emerges also in the sayings of the peerless Atiśa and the spiritual mentor Dromtönpa. As a background support, we also find the following in the Vinaya scripture, where it says:
The mind precedes phenomena and mind is primary; the mind is swift; accordingly, when someone has acted or uttered words with a pure mind, their effects follow him, just as the shadow of a tree never abandons him [the prince].
The mind precedes phenomena and mind is primary; the mind is swift; accordingly, when someone has acted or uttered words with a hateful mind, their effects follow him, just as the cart driver’s head was severed by the cart.[843] The scripture here explains, on the basis of stories connected with the observable effects of the karma of a prince and a poor person of the śūdra caste,[844] how the mind lies at the root of all karmic acts of body and speech.

d.div: [51] 'dir gsung sgros gsungs pa gtso bo pha chos kyi dngos gzhi zhus lan nor bu'i phreng ba la go dgos/ gzhung 'di cha tshang bod kyi gtsug lag gces btus pod gnyis pa/ bka' gdams glegs bam las btus pa'i chos skor shog grangs _25_nas _232_bar bzhugs/
[52] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ kha_lung gzhi/ bam po/ 33_shog_95_na5
[843] Vinayavastu, Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, kha, respectively, 94a7 and 93a5; the same verses are found also in the Collection of Aphorisms (31.24–25). A variation on them opens the Dhammapada.

[844] In the story in the Chapters on Vinaya, as well as in Prajñāvarman’s commentary on the Collection of Aphorisms (Udānavargavivaraṇa, Toh 4100, Tengyur, mngon pa, thu, 161a1), the story is about a prince and a poor brahman boy, not one of the śūdra caste.

f.d:
mgon po klu sgrub kyis bshes pa'i spring yig/
snyems dang bral la mang du gsol ci 'tshal/ / mchog tu phan pa'i don po 'di lags te/ / khyod kyi thugs dul mdzod cig bcom ldan gyis/ / sems ni chos kyi rtsa ba lags par gsungs/[53] / zhes dang / AR+ya de was/
sems ma gtogs par 'gro sogs la/ / gang phyir bsod nams la sogs pa/ / ma mthong de phyir las kun la/ / yid ni don por brjod par bya/[54] / zhes so/ /

Also, in his Friendly Letter, the guardian Nāgārjuna says:
Be free of hubris; what more is there to say. This alone is the most beneficial point: Discipline your mind, for the Blessed Buddha said, “The mind is the root of Dharma.”[845] [362] Āryadeva says:
I have not seen merit and so forth in sentient beings separate from the mind; so I declare that in relation to all deeds, the mind is most important.[846]

d.div: [53] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _slob dpon klu sgrub kyi bshes pa'i spring yig_shog_46_na4_ma dper 'di'i khungs rin chen phreng bar gsungs kyang bshes spring yin pas 'dir de bzhin du bcos/
[54] sde dge_3846_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsha_slob dpon 'phags pa lha'i bzhi brgya pa/ rab byed/ 5_sh+loka_4_shog_6_na5
[845] Suhṛllekha, verse 117, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 47a4.
[846] Four Hundred Stanzas (Catuḥśataka), 5.4, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 6a5.

f.d: slob dpon yon tan 'od kyis/ 'dul ba'i dgag sgrub gnang gsum gyi bcas mtshams phra rags gang la 'jug ldog byed pa thams cad kyang / nges 'byung gi bsam pas zin na thar pa'i rgyur 'gro ba la dgongs nas 'dul ba'i mdor dang po nyid du/ nges par 'byung ba'i tshul khrims kyi dbang du byas te/[55] zhes gsungs pas tshul 'di la nges pa gting nas skyes na nyams len gyi gnad la mkhas par 'gyur ro//

[In addition] understanding that if all of one’s Vinaya practice — the omissions, commissions, and exceptions — are sustained by the attitude of true renunciation, they would then become the cause for attaining liberation, master Guṇaprabha writes, “With morality of true renunciation as the foundation . . .”[847] In light of these statements, if you generate conviction from the depth of your heart on this point [about setting your intention], you will become skilled in the essential points of practice.

d.div: [55] sde dge_4117_bstan/ 'dul ba/ wuslob dpon yon tan 'od/ 'dul ba'i mdo/ shog_1_ba1
[847] Vinayasūtra, Toh 4117 Tengyur, ’dul ba, wu, 1b1.x

f.d: gzhan yang lus gnad kyi skor 'di la/ gtum mo gru gsum drug 'bar 'cha lugs ni/ sgom thag gam pus 'khyud ces pa zheng mtheb gang ba'i snam bu sogs chur nyis lteb byas te/ rnal 'byor pa rang gi mgor 'khor bar bcings pa'i mdun ngos kyi sne mor lag pa'i khu tshur gnyis phred du gshibs te bzung ba'i tshad kyi mthar bcad nas phan tshun gyi bcad 'phro mthud de bcom pas gor mor 'gyur zhing phan tshun gnyis kyang mthud de btsem pas sbubs can du gyur pa des/ rgyab tu rked stod tsam dang mdun du pus mo'i mgor bcings pas rkang pa gnyis tsog pu dang 'phongs mgo stan gyi steng du btsug ste/ byin pa gnyis snol rkang bol gyi phyi glo gnyis gdan du bzhag ste rkang pa gnyis gzar/ lag pa gnyis glo g.yas g.yon gyi sgom thag gi 'og tu bcug ste lte 'og sor bzhir mnyam gzhag gi phyag rgya bca' ba ste/ byin pa gnyis bsnol ba'i steng 'og tu gru gsum gnyis/ pus mo gnyis kyi mgor pus 'khyud kyis bcad de gsum phrag gi bar gru gsum gcig/ / pus mo'i rtse gnyis nas rtsib 'gram g.yas g.yon du sgom thag gis bcad de dpyi mgo gnyis kyi bar du gru gsum re re ste gru gsum lnga/ lte 'og mnyam gzhag gi phyag rgya gru gsum gyi rtse mo nang gi gtum mo'i thad du babs pa ste/ phyi'i gru gsum drug gi gnad kyis nang gi gtum mo 'bar ba'i rten 'brel yod pas na gtum mo gru gsum drug 'bar zhes bya ba rje btsun mi las bsngags pa cher mdzad pa'i lus gnad yin gsungs/

Once again, regarding the key points of posture, there is also the tradition of adopting the “six blazing triangles of tumo.”[848] To do this use a meditation belt known as a “knee wrap.” You can make this by folding a long woolen fabric in half, then measuring its length by wrapping it around your head with your two hands formed into fists extended touching each other in front of you. Cut the fabric to this length and sew the two ends to form a looped sash. You wear this just above your waist and wrap it around just below your two knees, thus forming the following sitting posture: your buttocks are on the cushion, with your two knees slightly raised and your legs crossing each other with the outsides of your feet touching the ground and your hands placed around and under the sides of the sash wrapped around from your back, your palms in the gesture of meditative equipoise about four fingerwidths below the navel. On top and below where the two legs are crossed are two triangles; the belt wrapped around the two knees form one triangle; on both sides of the body is a triangle where each knee is tied to your back with the belt; and below the navel, your hands in the gesture of meditative equipoise form a triangle where the tumo inner heat resides. Forming of these six outer triangles lays the auspicious basis for the blazing of the inner tumo. This posture, the six blazing triangles of tumo, is the posture highly praised by Jetsun Milarepa, the teacher said. [363]

d.div: [848] Gtum mo gru gsum drug ’bar. This paragraph, as indicated by its opening phrase “Once again” (gzan yang), seems to be an addition from Gyalrong as an afterthought concerning a topic he had already addressed above: the appropriate posture for prolonged meditation, which began on page 461.

f.d: e. Going for refuge and generating the awakening mind

de ltar dge sems khyad par can gyi ngang nas skyabs 'gro sogs bya ba la thog mar skyabs yul gsal 'debs lugs la khrom tshogs dang / kun 'dus nor bu'i lugs gnyis las/ dang por deng sang yongs grags kyi khrom tshogs dang / gzhan yang mdun gyi nam mkhar seng ge'i khri mtho zhing yangs pa'i steng du rgyab phyogs su cung zad nye bar seng khri chung ngu zhig gi steng du rtsa ba'i bla ma dang dbyer med pa'i thub dbang / seng khri chung ngu'i g.yas g.yon gyi mdun ngos nas mar zla ba tshes pa'i dbyibs lta bu'i gral sgrig pa'i pad zla'i gdan rnams kyi steng du/ g.yas su rje btsun byams pa sogs rgya chen spyod brgyud kyi bla ma rnams dang / g.yon du rje btsun 'jam dpal sogs zab mo lta brgyud kyi bla ma rnams bzhugs pa/ rgyal sras zhi ba lha'i man ngag bdag gzhan mnyam brje'i tshogs zhing ltar na/ g.yas g.yon gnyis su rje btsun 'jam dpal re re bzhugs pa'i g.yas kyi gral gnyis par rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ de nas e la ng+ha ri dang dpa' bo rdo rje sogs rlabs chen spyod brgyud kyi bla ma rnams dang / g.yon gyi gral gnyis par klu sgrub/ de nas zla grags sogs zab mo lta brgyud kyi bla ma rnams bzhugs pa/ bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i seng khri'i mdun du sa stong cung zad yangs tsam bzhag nas/ de nas yang seng khri chung ngu zhig gi steng du/ skyong rgyu'i khrid phog pa'i rtsa ba'i bla ma sku'i dbyibs dang kha dog spyod tshul rnams mjal dus kyi rnam par bzhugs pa/ seng khri de'i g.yas g.yon nas phan tshun du gral rim drang po dang / rgyab nas gral gor mor sgrig pa'i pad zla'i gdan rnams zla gam gyi dbyibs ltar sgrig pa rnams kyi steng chos 'brel dngos thob kyi bla ma ji yod yar thub dbang la zhal bstan nas bzhugs pa/

Thusly, in an especially virtuous state of mind, go for refuge [in the Three Jewels]. When it comes to visualizing the objects you are seeking refuge in, there are two traditions: visualizing the field in the manner of gathering at a marketplace and visualizing it in the manner of an all-embodying jewel. The first approach is actually two methods — one that is popular today and the following variant. Here, you visualize a tall and spacious lion throne in the space above. On this throne, slightly to the back, visualize a somewhat smaller lion throne on which sits Buddha Śākyamuni inseparable from your root guru. On the two sides of this smaller throne and slightly in front, imagine rows of figures all seated on lotuses in an arc. On the right are the lineage masters of the vast practice such as Maitreya, and on the left are the lineage masters of the profound view such as Mañjuśrī. If you visualize the merit-field tree according to Śāntideva’s instruction on equalizing and exchanging self and others, then imagine a Mañjuśrī on each side [of the Buddha], followed in the second row of the right side by Śāntideva, then Eladhari, Viravajra, and so on, who form the lineage masters of the expansive practice.[849] On the left, in the second row imagine Nāgārjuna, then Candrakīrti, and so on, who constitute the lineage masters of the profound view.

d.div: [849] Rlabs chen spyod brgyud. This should not be confused with “vast practice” (rgya chen spyod brgyud ), the lineage stemming from Maitreya through Asaṅga and so on pertaining primarily to the vast aspect of the path as opposed to the profound aspect, which is represented by the lineage of “profound view” (zab mo lta brgyud ) stemming from Mañjuśrī through to Nāgārjuna and so on. When the lineage of Śāntideva’s unique bodhicitta instruction of equalizing and exchanging of self and others is identified distinctly, it is referred to as “expansive practice.”

f.d: bla ma thub dbang gi steng gi nam mkhar rgyab la cung zad phyir phyogs pa'i sar/ seng khri chung ngu zhig gi steng du rgyal ba rdo rje 'chang / de'i 'og nas g.yas g.yon dang 'og rnams su te lo/ nA ro/ DoM b+hi pa/ a ti sha/ rje tsong kha pa sogs nyams len byin rlabs brgyud kyi bla ma rnams bzhugs pa/ thub dbang gi rgyab tu nye bar rang rang gi gdan gyi steng du bla med kyi lha tshogs/ de'i phyi rol rnal 'byor rgyud kyi lha tshogs/ de'i phyi rol spyod rgyud kyi lha tshogs/ de'i phyi rol bya rgyud kyi lha tshogs te rgyud sde bzhi'i lha tshogs rnams thub dbang dang zhal gzigs phyogs gcig par bzhugs/ g.yas g.yon gyi rgya chen spyod brgyud dang / zab mo lta brgyud kyi bla ma rnams kyi rgyab nas mar bskal bzang sangs rgyas rnams dang sangs rgyasasu ma cu so lnga sogs sangs rgyas rnams bzhugs/ de rnams kyi rgyab nas 'jam dpal/ phyag na rdo rje/ spyan ras gzigs/ sa snying sogs byang chub sems dpa' rnams dang / de rnams kyi rgyab nas 'phags pa rang rgyal rnams dang / 'phags pa gnas brtan bcu drug gis gtsos pa'i nyan thos rnams bzhugs/ de rnams kyi rgyab nas dpa' bo dpa' mo rnams dang / de rnams kyi rgyab nas chos skyong srung ma rnams bzhugs par gsal gdab pa'i khrom tshogs dang /

Facing Buddha Śākyamuni, leaving a small interval space, is another small lion throne. On this, visualize your own root guru from whom you have received transmission of the instruction, with his physical appearance and skin color as in his normal everyday form. To his right and left, as well as behind this lion throne [of your root guru], forming a semicircle, are seated on lotuses the teachers from whom you personally have received teachings, all facing Buddha Śākyamuni. In the space above and slightly behind Buddha Śākyamuni is a small lion throne on which is seated Vajradhara. Below him, on the right and left, are Tilopa, Nāropa, Ḍombīpa, Atiśa, Tsongkhapa, and so on, who are the lineage masters of blessing and practice.[850] Behind Buddha Śākyamuni, close to him, are the meditation deities of highest yoga tantra each seated on their appropriate cushions. Outside them are the meditation deities of yoga tantra, outside whom are the deities of performance tantra, outside whom are the deities of action tantra. In this way, the deities of the four classes of tantra are all facing Buddha Śākyamuni. [364] Behind the lineage masters of vast practice and the profound view on the two sides [of Buddha Śākyamuni] are buddhas such as the buddhas of the fortunate eons and the thirty-five buddhas of confession. Behind them are the bodhisattvas like Mañjuśrī, Vajrapāṇi, Avalokiteśvara, and Kṣitigarbha. Behind them are the ārya pratyekabuddhas and the śrāvakas, including the sixteen arhats. Behind them are the heroes and heroines, and behind them are the Dharma protectors. This then is a way of visualizing [the objects of refuge] like a gathering at a marketplace.

d.div: [850] Nyams len byin rlabs brgyud. See note 280.

f.d: yang gzhan thams cad sngar dang 'dra ba la/ bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i thugs ka nas mar g.yas g.yon du 'od zer kha dog sna lnga pa dbang gzhu lta bu 'phros pa/ seng khri chen po'i steng du nye bar g.yas g.yon nas dbang gzhu'i dbyibs lta bu gor mo phyed kyi tshul du lding ba'i steng du pad zla'i gdan la rgya chen spyod brgyud dang zab mo lta brgyud kyi bla ma rnams bzhugs pa'i rgyab phyogs g.yas g.yon gnyis su seng khri chen po'i steng du reg par sangs rgyas byang sems sogs sngar bzhin bzhugs pa gsal gdab pa'i khrom tshogs dang / bla ma mchod pa'i tshogs zhing lta bu'i khrom tshogs sogs mang du yod kyang / deng sang yongs su grags pa re re tsam las mi 'dug gsungs/ kun 'dus nor bu'i lugs ni lha brgya ma'i tshogs zhing dang gcod kyi tshogs zhing lta bu rnams la zer gsungs/ de dag ni skyabs yul gyi zhal shes so//

Alternatively, there is the approach where everything is as just described with one difference: you visualize rainbow-colored beams emanating from the heart of Buddha Śākyamuni to the right and left. From these emit crescent rainbows, and above the large lion throne [of the Buddha] and on the two sides are, seated on lotuses and moon discs, the lineage masters of vast practice and the profound view. Behind them, touching the large lion throne, are the buddhas, bodhisattvas, and so on, as described above. This is a variant on the marketplace format. The teacher said that there are numerous variations of this gathering at a marketplace format, such as the merit field of Offering to the Guru, but these days only one or two formats seem to be known widely. As for the “all-embodying jewel” format, this is the merit field in the Hundreds of Gods of Tuṣita guru yoga[851] and in Cutting Off practice, the teacher said. These then are the oral teachings connected with the practice of going for refuge.

d.div: [851] On the visualization of the merit field of this specific guru-yoga practice, see 477.

f.d:
de ltar skyabs yul gsal btab zin pa na/ skyabs 'gro'i rgyu dang des drangs pa'i skyabs 'gro'i ngo bo yid la bya tshul ni/
ga na bdag sogs sems can phal cher gyi sgo gsum gyi spyod pa 'di thams cad sdig pa mi dge ba'i phyogs su 'gro ba la ni bkag kyang khegs sa med par ngam ngam shugs kyis 'jug /dge ba'i phyogs su gtong dgos byung na chu klung gyen du 'dren pa las ches shin tu dka' ba mngon sum du grub pa 'di ni sngon thog ma med pa nas sdig pa mi dge ba la goms shugs shin tu che zhing dge ba sgrub pa la goms shugs shin tu chung ba'i 'bras bu'i rtags yang dag yin/ tshe 'dir yang bcas rang gi nyes ltung sngar med gsar du 'byung ba ni char 'bab pa lta bu yin/ sngar yod gong 'phel du 'gro ba ni rgya mtsho chen po la chu bo bzhi 'dus pa bzhin du ngang gis 'phel yong ba red/ sdig pa'i phung po mi bzad pa de tsam mi dgos sdig pa skad cig ma re res kyang thogs pa med par ngan song du ltung bar 'gyur ba bcom ldan 'das thugs rje can de nyid kyis bdag cag rnams la thugs brtse ba chen pos ma bzod nas rdzun g.yo dang sbas gsang med par rnam grangs du mar lung bstan pa des na/ da sdig pa'i phung po mi bzad pa de lta bu dang bcas bzhin par dbugs 'di chad song na dbugs chad long ma nyid du thogs pa med par ngan song du ltung ba las 'os mi 'dug/

Once you have established the merit field depicting the objects to whom you go for refuge, you cultivate the causes for seeking refuge and engage in the actual practice of going for refuge by contemplating the following:
Alas! As for the activities of the three doors of myself and most other sentient beings, when it comes to negative karmic deeds, we find it difficult to prevent negative karma even when trying to, and we instinctively gravitate toward them. [365] But when it comes to positive karma,[852] however, I find it difficult to prevent negative karma even when I make an effort; I am instead drawn to it instinctively. And when it comes to positive karma, I find it as hard as trying to make a stream flow uphill. This is because my habituation to negative karma in the past was strong while my habituation to positive karma was weak. This clearly demonstrates the kind of causes that preceded. Even in this life, I accumulate new karma and infractions of precepts, both natural and prescribed, like the falling of rain. And the karma I already possess tends to expand on its own, just as the great ocean absorbs the four great rivers. Leaving aside the power of such a great heap of negative karma, even a single moment of negative karma can lead to birth in one of the three lower realms. This is something the great compassionate one, the Blessed Buddha, declared repeatedly for our sake out of his concern for our fate, without holding anything back or engaging in lies or deception. If this breath of mine were to be cut short while I am still fraught with such an immense heap of negative karma, I will no doubt fly to the lower realms with nothing to prevent it.

d.div: [852] From this point on until the phrase “I would be truly insane” appeared verbatim above (pp. 466–67). The only variation is the inclusion of the two new sentences: “In any case, there is no guarantee that I will stay alive this night and will not die. What if I were to end up in such place of terror, how would I bear this?”

ngan song du ltung song na dmyal bar bsreg cing 'tshed pa/ brdung zhing dmyal ba/ gsheg cing gtubs pa/ sha dang rus pa rnams kyang 'gas shing zhigs pa lta bu'i tsha grang gi sdug bsngal/ yi dwags la bkres skom/ grang dro ngal zhing 'jigs pa sogs kyi sdug bsngal/ dud 'gro la glen zhing gti mug pa/ gcig gis gcig za ba/ bkol ba spyod pa gsod pa sogs kyi khrims gcod drag po de 'dra lus sems kyi steng nas dngos su myong ba lta ci smos/ de dag gi gtam thos pa dang gzugs su bgyis pa mig gis mthong ba tsam gyis kyang snying yang 'gas 'gro ba'i tshod tsam du 'dug na/ ngas de 'dra'i sdug bsngal de lus sems kyi steng nas dngos su myong dgos byung tsa na ci 'dra bgyi na bzod glags yod/ 'on kyang mi myong ba'i rang dbang ni med de sdug bsngal de myong ba'i rgyu tshogs thams cad spungs pa bzhin du bsags zin/ myong bar yang ring po mi thogs te 'jigs rung gi gnas mi bzad pa de dang da lta'i lus rten 'di gnyis kyi bar du dbugs phyi nang du rgyu ba 'di tsam gyi chod pa las 'os mi 'dug /dbugs kyi rgyu ba 'di ni da lta phyi nang du rgyu ba'i bar 'dir yang sbud de mi 'gro ba'i nges pa med/ ji ltar na yang nyi ma da dgung tshun chad shi ba las sdod pa'i gdeng drod gtan nas mi 'dug pas/ da lta rang 'jigs rung gi gnas mi bzad pa der slebs song na ngas ci 'dra bgyi na bzod glags yod/

Now, if I were to be reborn in the three lower realms, the hell realm has the following sufferings of heat and cold — being burned and cooked, being beaten up and tormented, being cut and sliced open, and having my body splintering into a hundred or a thousand pieces. In the hungry ghost realm, there are the pains of hunger and thirst, of hardship and terror. In the animal realm are the pains of ignorance and delusion, one kind eating another, being abused for labor, being slaughtered, being tied up, and being beaten. Let alone actually experiencing sufferings like this with my body and mind, even hearing about them and seeing them in person could bring on a heart attack. How could I bear it if and when I must undergo these sufferings myself with my own body and mind? Yet I have no power to spare myself from such suffering, for I have already gathered the causes to undergo such suffering; in fact, I indulged in gathering their causes with joy and delight! The time when I must experience such suffering is not in a distant future. In fact, the gap between such unbearable suffering and the present is only this current movement of my breath! And there is no guarantee that this flow of air, moving in and out, will not suddenly cease. In any case, there is no guarantee that I will stay alive this night and will not die. [366] What if I were to end up in such place of terror, how would I bear this?

de'i tshe thabs gang gis kyang de las thar ba'i thabs med/ de las skyob pa'i skyabs 'tshol yang mi rnyed/ skye ba nas tshe rabs mang por mtho ris dang thar pa'i srog rtsa chad pa'i 'go ni da gzod de nas brtsams zin pas phyis tshar ba yin/ des na da res 'jigs rung gi gnas mi bzad pa der mi 'gro ba'i thabs shig e sgrub mi sgrub rang la rang dbang yod pa'i skabs 'dir yang 'jigs rung gi gnas mi bzad pa der mi 'gro ba'i thabs shig la mi 'bad par/ gnas der 'gro ba'i rgyu sdig pa mi dge ba sgrub pa la khyis khrag mthong ba ltar dga' bzhin 'jug pa 'di ni nges par smyos pa red/

At that point, nothing will save me from my fate. Even if I were to seek out a refuge to protect me, I would have already initiated the process of turning myself into fuel for the suffering of the three lower realms, having already cut the thread of life for birth in the higher realms and the attainment of liberation. It would be too late. Therefore, today, when I have in my own hands still the opportunity to move toward or away from the unbearable suffering of the terrifying realms, if I fail to strive in the means to avert such suffering and instead, like a dog attracted to the sight of blood, willfully indulge in negative and nonvirtuous karmic acts, I would be truly insane.

da nas bdag sogs nam mkha'i mtha' dang mnyam pa'i sems can thams cad 'jigs rung gi gnas mi zad pa der mi 'gro ba'i thabs shig ci nas kyang 'tshol dgos la/ de yang mi shes pa'am rmongs pas bstan pa'i thabs la ji tsam 'bad kyang ngal ba 'ba' zhig gi rgyur 'gro ba las 'os mi 'dug pas/ thabs de phyin ci ma log pa shes pa'i shes ldan 'ba' zhig 'tshol nas des gsungs pa'i thabs la nan tan snying po bya dgos pa'i phyir ro// de yang blang dor gyi gnas mtha' dag rang gis mngon sum du gzigs shing nyid kyis gzigs pa ltar gzhan la rang dbang du gsal bar mdzad pa'i tshad ma'i skyes bu zhig dgos kyi/ gzhan du mngon shes rdzu 'phrul sogs thun mong ba'i yon tan ni ji 'dra ji snyed cig ldan yang de tsam gyis 'jigs pa mtha' dag las sgrol ba'i thabs bstan pa la bslu ba med par mi 'grub pa'i phyir ro/ /

So I must search from now on for the means to help free myself and all other sentient beings equaling the expanse of space from such a place of terror. But as long as I continue to seek those means with ignorance and delusion, my efforts will only create more problems. So I will exclusively seek out wise guides who know the undistorted means to freedom and strive in the means they teach. What we need is a truly authoritative teacher who can reveal to others independently and clearly, on the basis of their own direct vision, what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected. There may be teachers with mundane attainments such as clairvoyance, miraculous powers, and so on, but this alone does not make them infallible as to the means for gaining freedom from all fear.

de yang sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das nyag gcig de 'dra'i tshad ma'i skyes bu yin gyi/ gzhan tshangs pa brgya byin sogs su la'ang de lta bu'i yon tan gyi phyogs dang cha tsam yang ma mchis pas/ 'jig rten 'di na sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das la skyabs su 'gro mi 'gro lha mi'i 'gro ba su yin kyang rung / 'jigs pa mtha' dag las sgrol ba'i thabs shig 'dod na thabs de ston pa po ni sangs rgyas nyag gcig dang / thabs de yang des gsungs pa'i dam pa'i chos 'ba' zhig dang / de sgrub pa'i grogs kyang 'phags pa'i dge 'dun kho nar nges kyi/ de las gzhan pa'i skyabs su 'os pa dang skyabs su 'gyur ba ni sa steng gang na'ang mi rnyed pa red/

It is the Blessed Buddha alone who is such a truly authoritative teacher; others like Brahmā and Indra do not possess even a portion of the qualifications necessary [to be a truly authoritative teacher]. Whether one is a human or a deva god, if one wishes to find the method to gain freedom from all fears, it is the Buddha alone who reveals such a method; [367] the Dharma is that revealed method; and the ārya Sangha are the companions for engaging that method. Apart from these three [Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha], no refuge can be found anywhere.

'on kyang bdag cag 'jigs pa mtha' dag las sgrol zhing skyob pa la'ang phyi nang gi yan lag gnyis tshang dgos la/ de yang phyi'i yan lag ma tshang ba med pa ston pa thugs rje can de nyid kyis bskal pa grangs med pa'i snga rol nas dka' ba brgya phrag gi sgo nas bsgrubs zin te/ bdag cag rnams kyi mgon skyabs dpung gnyen gyi tshul du dus skad cig kyang g.yel ba med par bzhugs bzhin pa zhig yin na'ang / nang gi yan lag de la blo 'gel nas skyabs su 'gro ba dang blang dor gyi gnas la 'jug ldog tshul bzhin du byas pa 'di ma byung ba kho nas khams gsum 'khor bar rang dbang med par 'khyams shing mgon med skyabs med du gyur pa 'di bzhin byung ba red/ des na skyabs bslu ba med pa dkon mchog rin po che rnam pa gsum la snying nas skyabs su 'gro zhing dkar nag gi las rnams la 'jug ldog tshul bzhin du byed na 'jigs rung gi gnas mi bzad pa de las sgrol mi sgrol dang skyob mi skyob la the tshom cung zad kyang mi 'dug pas/ da ni bdag sogs nam mkha'i mtha' dang mnyam pa'i sems can thams cad skyabs bslu ba med pa dkon mchog rin po che khyed rnams la skyabs su 'gro bar bya'o/ /

This said, for us to be freed and saved from all fear, both external and internal conditions need to converge. With respect to complete external conditions not lacking in anything, there is the presence of our compassionate Teacher, who attained his state through hundredfold endeavors across innumerable eons. He remains our protector, our refuge, and our ally without wavering in his task even for an instant. This is the case, but because we have failed to manifest the inner condition on our part — namely, placing our trust in him and going to him for refuge and, on that basis, conducting ourselves according to what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected — we have wandered uncontrollably in the cyclic existence of the three realms and have remained bereft of a protector and refuge. Therefore, were I to seek refuge in the Three Precious Jewels, the infallible refuge, from the depths of my heart and conduct myself in accord with what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected, they would without doubt free me and save me from the terrifying place [of samsara]. So today, I and all sentient beings equaling the expanse of space go for refuge to you, infallible refuge, the Three Precious Jewels.

f.d:
bdag sogs sems can thams cad spyir 'khor ba dang khyad par ngan song gsum gyi 'jigs pa chen po 'di las da lta nyid du bsrung zhing skyob tu gsol lo snyam pa'i blo 'gel gyi sems bskyed pa de'am/ de'i tshan gyis rang dbang med par ngag tu'ang bla ma la skyabs su mchi'o zhes sogs dper na rang gi lus la zug chen po skyes pa na rang dbang med par skad shor ba lta bu'i ngag gi rig byed de ni thun mong ba'i skyabs 'gro dang / khyad par
sems can las dang nyon mongs pa gnyis kyis rang dbang med par byas nas spyir 'khor ba dang khyad par ngan song gsum gyi 'jigs su rung ba'i g.yang kha mi bzad pa rab tu 'grims pa'i nyam thag pa'i gnas su gyur pa 'di dag kyang gcig tu skye ba nas tshe rabs thams cad du bdag la med du mi rung ba'i bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs sgrub pa'i mdza' bshes/ gnyis su gzhi dang lam dang 'bras bu gang gi gnas skabs na yang bdag la med du mi rung ba'i bdag gi phan bde'i legs tshogs bde blag tu ster ba'i yid bzhin gyi nor bu dang bla ma dang lhag pa'i lha rnams dang khyad par cung zad kyang med pa sha stag tu 'dug pa la/ da lta'i gnas skabs las dang nyon mongs pa gnyis kyis rang dbang med par byas te 'di ltar 'phral thes 'phugs thes su song zhing mgon med skyabs med du gyur pa 'di 'dra snying re rje/

Pray save us this very minute from the terrors of samsara in general and those of the lower realms in particular. In this way, cultivate the mind placing your entire trust [in the Three Jewels], and with your speech utter the phrases “I go for refuge to the guru” and so on.[853] Utter these phrases as if uncontrollably, as one would cry aloud when experiencing an acute physical pain. This act, including such verbal expressions, constitutes the common practice of going for refuge. There is, however, the following uncommon [Mahayana] way of going for refuge:
All these sentient beings caught in a desperate plight with no power remain trapped, owing to their karma and afflictions, in the terrifying abyss of cyclic existence in general and in the three lower realms in particular. They are truly, first of all, [368] my beloved ones indispensable throughout all my lives in securing my welfare. Second, with respect to being indispensable in the ordinary state, along the path, and in resultant state, they remain the source of my benefit and happiness. In this, there is no difference at all between sentient beings, who are wish-granting jewels, on the one hand and my gurus and meditation deities on the other. How tragic it is that sentient beings’ current situation should be so desperate: their freedom robbed by karma and affliction, their immediate and long-term fates so hopeless, and bereft of protector and refuge. How tragic indeed!

d.div: [853] The author is referring to the refuge formula: “I go for refuge to the guru, I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dharma, I go for refuge to the Sangha.”

f.d: sems can 'di rnams 'jigs pa chen po de las sgrol zhing skyob pa'i khur de yang nged rang gcig pu la bab mod kyang / da lta gnas skabs 'di 'dras ni sems can thams cad lta ci smos/ sems can gcig gi mgon skyabs byed pa'i nus pa'ang bdag la mi 'dug/ de'i nus pa su la yod na rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che thob na sems can thams cad kyi mgon skyabs byed pa'i nus mthu thogs pa med par 'jug pas go 'phang dam pa de thob byar bzung / mkhas grub tshad mar gyur pa rnams kyis nyid kyi sku dang srog la'ang mi gzigs par dka' ba brgya phrag gis ji ltar sgrub pa'i lam zab mo bla ma lha'i rnal 'byor gyi sgo nas phyag rgya chen po'i khrid dmigs skyong tshul 'di nyid nyams len gyi mthil du bzung nas mkhas grub tshad mar gyur pa de rnams kyi rjes su slob ste lus dang srog la'ang ltos pa med pa'i dka' spyod dang rlabs po che'i brtson 'grus kyi sgo nas tshul bzhin du bsgrub par bya'o snyam pa'i sems dung dung ba zhig bskyed pa ni/ theg pa chen po'i dkon mchog gsum rang gi thob byar bzung nas 'bras bur skyabs su 'gro ba'i theg chen gyi skyabs 'gro yin la/ 'di 'dra'i skyabs 'gro dang theg chen sems bskyed gnyis kyi khyad par shin tu 'byed dka' ba zhig yod gsungs/

Now although the responsibility to save these sentient beings from such terror rests upon me alone, my present situation is such that, let alone being a protector and refuge to all sentient beings, I cannot even be a protector and refuge for a single sentient being. Who then has such ability? If I were to attain the precious state of buddhahood, I would then have unimpeded ability to serve as a protector and refuge to all sentient beings. So I shall take such a state as the object of my attainment. I will embrace as my heart practice this mahāmudrā meditation taking the profound path of guru yoga as its basis — a path established by authoritative masters through hundredfold efforts and without concern even for their own body and life. In this way, I will follow the example of these authoritative masters, and without concern for even my body and life, I will strive in this practice with fortitude and with expansive waves of joyful perseverance. Generating such a thought in a fervent manner constitutes the practice of going for refuge according to the Mahayana in that it entails taking your own resultant Three Jewels as the object of attainment and then seeking refuge in them. The teacher said, in fact, that it is extremely difficult to differentiate between this type of going for refuge and the Mahayana generation of the awakening mind.

de nas bla ma dkon mchog rnams kyang rang gzhan sems can thams cad la brtse zhing byams pa'i tshul du bzhugs par dmigs pa dang / rang gzhan thams cad kyis kyang skyabs yul de rnams kyi yon tan dang bka' drin dran pa'i dad gus chen pos mgrin gcig tu skyabs 'gro'i tshig 'ur te bton pa'i tshe/ sbyang 'jug tshud gsum gyi dmigs pa yongs grags ltar dang / sdig pa sbyang skabs dbang chen gser gyi sa gzhi'i steng du 'chi bdag gshin rje srin po'i gzugs can gan rkyal du gnas pa'i khar sdig pa thams cad song ste kho tshim pa dang mnyam du kha sdig pa'i lhag ma las grub pa'i gser gyi 'khor lo rtsibs stong dang ldan pas bkag pa'i mos pa bya ba ni sdig pa sbyang ba'i zhor la tshe sgrub pa'i thabs ma gcig lab sgron gyi man ngag yin gsungs/

Then, visualizing the guru and the Three Jewels as residing with compassion and loving kindness for all sentient beings, and imagining both yourself and others generating [369] fervent faith in and reverence for these objects of refuge, inspired by contemplating their qualities and kindness, imagine chanting aloud in unison the words of the refuge practice. When you do, you can relate this to the well-known visualization practice of imagining purifying [your negative karma and obscurations], receiving the blessings, and being accepted [within the fold of care]. And when you purify the negative karma, you could imagine the lord of death takes the form of an ogre lying on its back on the ground and that all your negative karma enters his mouth and that his mouth then closes shut and is sealed by a thousand-spoked golden wheel. The teacher said this is an oral instruction of Machik Labdrön for ensuring that, while you purify negative karma, you are also cultivating longevity.

de nas sangs rgyas chos tshogs ma'i skabs rang gzhan sems can thams cad 'khor ba spyi dang khyad par ngan song gsum du 'jug cing khrid par byed pa dang / yar thar pa dang thams cad mkhyen pa thob tu mi ster ba ni nyon mongs pa'i sgrib pa dang shes bya'i sgrib pa 'di gnyis yin pas rang gzhan sems can thams cad 'jigs pa chen po de las da lta nyid du srung zhing skyob tu gsol lo snyam pa'i theg chen gyi skyabs 'gro dang /

Next, when chanting the lines “To the Buddha, Dharma, and the Excellent Assembly. . . ,”[854] contemplate how it is the two obscurations — the afflictive obscuration and the knowledge obscuration — that lead myself and all sentient beings to samsara in general and to the three lower realms in particular. It is these two that prevent us from attaining liberation and the state of omniscience. You appeal [to the objects of refuge] that you and all other sentient beings may be protected and saved from these two great sources of danger this very moment. This is the Mahayana practice of going for refuge.

d.div: [854] This is the well-known verse “To the Buddha, Dharma, and Excellent Assembly, / I go for refuge until enlightenment. / Through my virtue of engaging in giving and so forth, / may I attain buddhahood for the benefit of all beings.”

f.d: bdag gis sbyin pa las byung ba sogs gzhi gsum gyi dge ba dus gsum du bsags pa rnams kyi mthu las rang gzhan sems can thams cad kyis myur du rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che thob na ci ma rung / de lta bu'i go 'phang de myur du thob par gyur cig /sems can thams cad kyi don du rdzogs byang thob 'dod kyi sems 'di yang rmi lam du yang mi gtong snyam pa lta bu'i smon sems dam bca' can dang /

Then cultivate the thought:
Through the force of virtue I have gathered throughout all three times, such as through the three sources of virtue that include giving,[855] may I and all other sentient beings quickly attain the precious state of buddhahood. May we swiftly attain such a state, and may I never abandon, even in my dreams, this aspiration to attain buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings. In this way, you generate the aspirational awakening mind accompanied by a pledge.

d.div: [855] The “three sources” here are the virtuous acts of giving, practicing morality, and venerating the buddhas.

f.d: dkon mchog gsum la bdag skyabs mchi/ /zhes sogs kyi skabs skyabs 'gro gong dang 'dra/
When chanting the lines “I go for refuge to the Three Jewels” and so on,[856] going for refuge is the same as explained above.

d.div: [856] The full verse reads: “I go for refuge to the Three Jewels, / I confess all my negative karma, / I rejoice in the virtue of all beings, / and I uphold in my mind the buddha’s awakening.”

f.d: sdig bshags rang nyid tshe 'dir yang yon tan shes rgyud la skye ru mi ster zhing phyi mar ngan song du 'khrid par byed pa'i sdig pa'i phung po ji snyed yod pa thams cad phyogs bcu na bzhugs pa'i rgyal ba sras bcas khyed rnams kyi spyan sngar mthol lo 'chags so snyam pa dang /

The purification of negative karma is done through such contemplations as: “Whatever heaps of negative karma I may possess, which prevent me from enhancing qualities in this life and lead me to the lower realms in future lives, O buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the rest, I declare these in your presence and seek your forgiveness.”

rjes su yi rang ni 'jig rten 'di na skye 'phags thams cad kyis bsags pa'i dge ba ji snyed yod pa thams cad bdag gcig pus sems can gyi don du gsog nus pa zhig byung na ci ma rung snyam pa dang / sbyor ba de rnams sngon du btang nas dngos gzhi 'jug sems gzung tshul ni/
bdag gis ma sems can thams cad kyi don du rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang rin po che de ci nas kyang thob par bya/ de'i phyir du rgyal sras kyi spyod pa spyi dang bye brag mtha' dag la lus dang srog la'ang mi lta ba'i dka' spyod dang rlabs po che'i brtson 'grus kyi sgo nas tshul bzhin du slob par bya'o/ / de ltar byed nus pa bla ma lhas xxx

The practice of rejoicing involves contemplating, “How I wish I may accumulate on my own all virtues that have been gathered by all beings in the universe, both ordinary and ārya beings.” [370] With these as a preparation, here is how you uphold the engaging awakening mind:
For the sake of all mother sentient beings, I will by all means seek the attainment of the precious state of buddhahood. To this end, I will strive with fortitude and with expansive waves of joyful perseverance, with no concern even for my body and life, to engage in the general and specific deeds of the bodhisattva. O guru deity, bless me that I may be able to do this.

de yang theg pa gong 'og gi sdom pa thams cad skyabs 'gros rten gzhi byas nas blang dgos pa dang / sdig pa tshab chen rgyud la yod pa dang / bsod nams shin tu chung ba'i gang zag gi rgyud la byang chub kyi sems dang byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa skye bar mi 'gyur ba dang / brgya la skyes na'ang dgos pa sgrub nus su mi 'gyur bar sa gzhi tshwa sgo can dang / rtsa dang ldum bu sogs mang ba dang / lud dang drod gsher sogs mi 'dzom par sa bon btab kyang myu gu skye dka' ba dang / skyes su zin kyang phan mi thogs pa dang 'dra bas byang chub kyi sems gzung ba la skyabs 'gro sogs gsum nges can sngon du gtong dgos pa yin gsungs/

The teacher then makes the following points: That all the vows of both lower and advanced vehicles need to be received through taking the practice of going for refuge as their foundation; how the bodhisattva vow does not take root within those who possess grave negative karma within their mind stream and those whose store of merit is extremely small; even when it does arise in such individuals, it does not do so in a way that it can [effectively] serve its function. This, the teacher said, is analogous to how it is difficult for seeds to grow, even if planted, when the soil is fraught with problems like excessive salt, grass, and weeds and where there is lack of fertilizer and moisture; even when seeds do grow [in such soil], they are of little use. Therefore, to uphold the awakening mind, you definitely need to preface it with these three practices — going for refuge, [purifying negative karma, and rejoicing].

de ltar byang chub kyi sems dang sdom pa rgyud la skyes par rang nyid kyis dga' ba bsgom zhing / rang nyid la de lta bu'i dge ba rlabs po che skyes pa'i rkyen gyis bla ma thub pa'i dbang po dgyes nas mar me gcig las gnyis chad kyi tshul du rang 'dra gnyis pa zhig chad nas rang la thim pas/ rang gi lus ngag yid gsum bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i sku gsung thugs su lam gyis gyur pa'i mos pa bya zhing dar cig mnyam par 'jog

[Having generated the mind,] cultivate joy at the arising in you of the awakening mind and the bodhisattva vow. And imagine that, from having such a powerful virtuous state of mind arise in you, Guru Śākyamuni is pleased and that, in the fashion of one butter lamp being lit from another, a replica of guru Śākyamuni emerges and dissolves into you. Then imagine that your three doors — body, speech, and mind — transform instantly into the enlightened body, speech, and mind of Guru Śākyamuni. Then remain in equipoise on this thought for a little while.

rang gi sku las 'od zer nyi ma dang me shel gyi 'od lta bu tsha ba'i reg bya can dang / kha ba dang chu klung chen po'i reg bya lta bu grang ba'i reg bya can dpag tu med pa 'phros pas/ tsha grang gi dmyal ba'i snod dang bcud kyi sems can thams cad kyi skyon dang sdug bsngal thams cad sbyangs nas dag pa'i zhing dang thub dbang du gyur pa'i mos pa bya ba dang / yang 'od zer dgos 'dod kun 'byung gi nor bu dang zas gos gnas mal sogs yo byad mkho dgu'i rnam par spros pas yi dwags rnams dang / legs nyes 'byed pa'i blo gros dang / rjes yong sngon dran dang / dran shes ngo tsha khrel yod dang bag yod kyi byed las can dpag tu med par 'phros pas dud 'gro rnams dang / zas dang sman dang gos dang nor gyi bye brag sna tshogs pa'i rnam par spros pas mi rnams dang / byams dang snying rje dga' ba dang btang snyoms sogs kyi byed las dpag med 'phros pas lha min rnams dang / tshe dang bsod nams skyo shas nges 'byung bag yod sogs kyi byed las can dpag med spros pas khams gong 'og gi lha rnams kyi rang rang gi sdug bsngal thams cad nye bar zhi nas snod thams cad dag zhing dang bcud thams cad thub pa'i dbang po'i skur lam gyis gyur pa'i mos pa byas te/

Then imagine that immeasurable light radiates from your body — hot rays like sunlight or crystal and cool rays cold like snow or a great river stream — and that this cleanses the defects of the hot and cold hell realms and of the beings therein, turning them into perfect buddhafields inhabited by enlightened buddhas. Again, imagine emanating immeasurable light for the hungry ghosts in the form of wish-granting jewels, food, clothing, shelter, and all sorts of articles of everyday need. [371] For the animals, [imagine light] in the form of abilities, such as the intellect to distinguish what is good from what is bad, the capacity for forethought and mindfulness, a sense of shame and of consideration of others, heedfulness, and so forth. For humans, [imagine light] in the form of food, medicine, clothes, and diverse material things; for the demigods, [light] in the form of loving kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and so forth; and for the deva gods of lower and higher levels, [light] in the form of increased life span and merit and the capacity for disenchantment, renunciation, and heedfulness, and so forth. These help relieve the beings in the individual realms of their specific suffering; and both the environment and the beings within become purified, the environments turning into buddhafields and their inhabitants into enlightened buddhas.

da res bla ma'i dka' drin gyis rigs drug gi sems can thams cad 'di ltar bla ma thub pa'i dbang po'i go 'phang la bkod rgyu byung ba skal ba re bzang snyam pa'i dga' ba bsgom/ de yang gzhan phyogs pa dag gis ngan song dong sprugs dang / rigs drug gnas 'dren sogs zab dgu dang snyan dgur btags pa'i gdams pa thams cad kyang / rang cag gi rje bla ma'i bka' brgyud 'di la sems bskyed 'bras bu lam byed 'dis go mi chod pa ci yang med pas gzhan la 'gram chu ldang mi dgos gsungs/

With the thought that it is most fortunate indeed that today I have the opportunity to lead all these beings of the six realms to the state of Guru Buddha Śākyamuni, rejoice. The teacher said that when compared to what others label as “profound” and “beautiful” instructions, such as “stirring up the pit of the lower realms” and “lifting beings out of the six realms,”[857] there is nothing whose purpose is not satisfied by this practice of “generating the awakening mind by way of bringing the result on to the path” according to the sacred lineage of Master Tsongkhapa. So there is no need to find other such teachings tempting,[858] he said.

d.div: [857] Respectively, ngan song dong sprugs and rigs drug gnas ’dren.
[858] ’Gram chu ldang ba, “mouth-watering.”

f.d:
de nas tshad med bzhi bsgom pa'i mtshams sbyor dang / ji ltar bsgom pa'i tshul dang / bdud rtsi 'bebs sbyang sogs spyi ltar byas rjes/
ga na bdag gnas khang byi dor byas pa nas bzung ste da lta'i bar 'di yang ma rgan sems can ngan song gsum du lhung zin pa de rnams sdug bsngal brgya phrag du mas rtag tu gzir ba'i ngang tshul las ma 'das pas ngas ma rgan ches nyam thag pa'i gnas su gyur pa de rnams ci'i phyir yal bar 'dor/ des na bdag gis ma sems can thams cad kyang tshe 'di nyid la rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi go 'phang mchog la 'god thub pa zhig bya snyam pa'i zhe dam drag po blo phugs su bcug ste/ ngag tu ma sems can thams cad kyi don du myur ba myur bar zhes pa nas de'i phyir du lam zab mo bla ma lha'i rnal 'byor gyi sgo nas phyag rgya chen po'i 'khrid bsgom par bya'o zhes pa'i bar lan 'ga' brjod/

Next, following this [generation of awakening mind] with the practice of the four immeasurable thoughts, engaging in the actual cultivation of them, visualizing nectar descending and cleansing, and so forth — contemplate as follows:
Alas! From when I swept and cleaned my place of practice up to now, so many mother sentient beings have already plummeted into the three lower realms. Their fate is nothing but constant torment by hundreds of sufferings. How could I abandon these sentient beings? I will therefore strive to place all mother sentient beings in the precious state of buddhahood. In this way, generate a strong intention from the depths of your heart. Then with your voice chant the phrase “For the sake of all mother sentient beings, I will quickly, quickly, in this very life, actualize” up to the line “To this end, I will meditate on the guide to mahāmudrā on the basis of the profound path of the guru-deity yoga.”[859] Chant this several times.

d.div: [859] In Panchen’s root text, this last sentence reads “To this end, I will practice the profound path of the guru-deity yoga.”
