That said, generally speaking, the mind must be admitted to be a conditioned thing; it would be contradictory to say that it is a nonimplicative negation. That this is so is stated by the Essence of Eloquence, “For example, although the nonexistence of a vase both is a nonimplicative negation and shares a common locus with a physical location, this does not violate the fact that something cannot be both a nonimplicative negation and a conditioned thing.”[1037]

d.div: [104] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ pha_drangs nges legs bshad snying po/ shog_32_na6
[1037] This is the same passage from Tsongkhapa cited just above; see note 1035.

f.d:
de yang spyod 'jug las/
gang tshe rnam par dpyad pa yi/ / rnam dpyod kyis ni dpyad byas na/ / de'i tshe rnam dpyod de yang ni/ / rnam dpyod phyir na thug pa med/ /
dpyad bya rnam par dpyad byas na/ / rnam dpyod la ni rten yod min/ / rten med phyir na mi skye ste/ / de yang mya ngan 'das par brjod/[105] / ces pa'i man ngag yin nam snyam ste/ /mgo 'khor tshad gnas 'di la 'khor bar mchi'o/ /

This, I feel, echoes the insights of the following from the Guide to the Bodhisattva Way:
[Objection:] When things are subjected to analysis with a thorough and discerning intellect, at that point the analyzer too should be analyzed and so on, and there is no end.
[Reply:] When the thing under scrutiny is analyzed, the analyzing intellect will have no support, and with no support it can arise no more; this is what is referred to as nirvana.[1038] Everyone who is confused [about emptiness] seems to be confused on this issue.[1039]

d.div: [105] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_110_dang _111_shog_35_na3
[1038] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 9.110–11, Toh 3782 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 35a3.
[1039] The author is referring here to the crucial point of emptiness being a nonimplicative negation and that it must be perceived and experienced as such in one’s emptiness meditation.

f.d: man ngag de rnams ni grub chen rnams kyi gsung dang 'dra bas shin tu go dka' zhing / 'on kyang go nus pa zhig byung na dka' gnad kyi mdud pa mang po rang zhig rang grol du 'gro bas gces par gzung ngo / / las dang po pas mnyam gzhag nam mkha' lta bu'i stong nyid bsgom tshul 'di rnams ni/ 'khrul pa shin tu che zhing dka' ba'i gnas phra sa/ gzhung chen po rnams la lo mang por sbyangs pa'i mkhas par grags pa rnams kyang bla ma'i man ngag la ma brten par the tshom tsam yang bskyed mi nus pa'i gnas yin pas/ bdag 'dras rbad kham chen po byas na mi rigs pas gzur gnas dpyod ldan rnams kyi dpyod pa'i sgor smos pas btsan snga dor nas zhib tu dpyod par mdzod cig/

These instructions resemble the words of the mahāsiddhas and are thus extremely challenging to understand. Yet when one does comprehend them, many of the knots tightly binding difficult points seem to get undone on their own; so please treasure the instructions. There seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding of these points on how those on the beginner’s stage should engage in meditative equipoise on space-like emptiness. [484] They are indeed difficult and subtle, and without relying on the guru’s instructions, even those who have studied the great treatises for many years and are known to be learned are unable to even entertain discerning doubts on these matters [let alone attain realization]. So it would be inappropriate indeed for someone like me to speak on these matters with much confidence. What I have said here has been presented only as an opening for critical inquiry for those with discerning minds. So refrain from rushing to judgment and carefully analyze.
e. Illusion-like emptiness in post-equipoise

de nas rjes thob sgyu ma lta bu'i stong nyid bsgom tshul ni/ mnyam gzhag de las langs pa na sngar mnyam gzhag tu nga rang bzhin gyis med tshul zhib tu mthong ba de la blo rtse gtad nas/ tshogs drug gi yul du nga la sogs pa 'khor 'das kyi chos ci snang yang snang tshul de la tshad 'jog mi bya bar yod nas 'di ltar snang ngam/ med nas 'di ltar snang zhes zhib tu dpyad pas med bzhin du snang ba'i tshul la nges pa bskyed de rtse gcig tu bskyangs/ de lta bu'i nges pa 'char ma bde na thag khra'i sbrul dang me long nang gi byad bzhin gyi gzugs brnyan sogs las dpe blangs te zhib tu dpyad pas med bzhin du snang ba'i sgyu ma'i don la nges pa rnyed pa na rtse gcig tu bskyang bar bya'o/ /

Next, here is how you meditate on the illusion-like emptiness during periods of post-equipoise. When you rise from your meditative equipoise, maintain single-pointed focus on the absence of intrinsic existence of your “I” that you saw during your meditative equipoise, and then observe how the phenomena of both samsara and nirvana appear to your six senses. As phenomena appear to your senses, do not rely on how they appear to you but probe, “Do they appear to me in such terms because that is how they exist? Or do they take the form they appear to even though they do not exist like that?” In this way, cultivate the ascertainment that even though they appear to have such existence, they do not, and maintain this awareness single-pointedly. Should you find it difficult to develop such an ascertainment, contemplate analogies such as the snake in relation to a striped rope, the reflection of a face in the mirror, and the like and engage in careful analysis. When, as a result, you have generated ascertainment of the illusion-like character of things — the fact that despite their nonexistence, their appearances persist — maintain this awareness with single-pointedness.

tshul 'di ni dper na sngar dung kha dog dkar por mthong zin gyi nges pa dang / da ltar mkhris pa sogs kyis dung ser por mthong ba'i dbang shes gnyis la brten nas da lta'i snang tshul 'di 'khrul snang du nges par byar yod pa de bzhin du/ sngar mnyam gzhag tu nga rang bzhin gyis med tshul zhib tu rtogs zin rtogs pa'i nges pa dang / da ltar nga bsnyon med du snang ba'i tha snyad pa'i blo gnyis la brten nas nga'i snang tshul de med bzhin du snang ba'i tshul du nges par bya ba yin te/ sems can gyi rgyud la mnyam gzhag ma gtogs par blo gang la yul cir snang yang cha thams cad nas rang ngos nas grub par snang ba las gzhan ma 'khrul pa'i cha cung zad kyang med par gsungs shing / rje btsun blo bzang chos rgyan gyis/ rang cag so so skye bo'i snang tshul 'di thams cad dgag bya'i snang tshul yin par gsal bar gsungs/[106]

Thanks to two factors — (1) the conviction one has that conches are white because one has seen them in the past and (2) a present sensory experience of seeing a conch as yellow because one has jaundice — a specific instance of seeing a conch as yellow can be determined as delusory. Similarly, on the basis of two factors — (1) the ascertainment generated from deeply realizing the absence of intrinsic existence of your “I” in meditative equipoise and (2) your present everyday experience wherein you inescapably perceive an “I” — you should determine that your perception of “I” is such that what appears to it does so despite having no such existence. It has been said that sentient beings not in meditative equipoise perceive all objects of all classes of cognition wholly in terms of intrinsic existence; no aspect of the cognition remains unmistaken.[1040] The most revered Losang Chögyen also clearly states that for us ordinary beings, all our immediate perceptions are perceptions of the object of negation [i.e., intrinsic existence].[1041]

d.div: [106] paN chen blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan gyi gsung 'bum/ nga _dri ba lhag bsam rab dkar gyi dris lan blo bzang bzhad pa'i sgra dbyangs/ shog_2_na2
[1040] The author is referring here to Tsongkhapa’s Illuminating the Intent (trans.), 64.

[1041] Lamp So Bright, 681, where Panchen states, “For us near-sighted ordinary beings, it is precisely the way in which this or that subject — our mind and so on — appears to us that is itself the way we perceive the object of negation.” The critical Tibetan edition erroneously attributes this to Panchen’s Response to Queries.

f.d:
lcang skya rol pa'i rdo rjes/
da lta rang re yi blo gsal 'ga' zhig / tshugs thub bden grub sogs brda la zhen pas/ / snang ba ling ling de rang sor bzhag nas/ / dgag rgyu rwa can zhig 'tshol bar snang ste/ / sgrib bral a ma yi bzhin ras de na/ / lang lang ling ling de yod skad mi 'dug[107] / ces dang /

Changkya Rölpai Dorjé writes:
There seem to be among today’s scholars those who, caught in the web of words — “thoroughly withstanding,” “true existence,” and so on — seek only something with horns to be negated, leaving intact this everyday solid appearance. [485] But on my mother’s unveiled face such vivid dualism is not found, I believe. Through excessive discussions off the mark, my old mother is likely to run away![1042]

d.div: [107] lcang skya rol pa'i rdo rje'i gsung 'bum/ nga _lta ba'i gsung mgur zab mo/ shog_2_ba1
[1042] Recognizing My Mother, verses 10–11, 2b1. A full translation of this song on the view can be found at tibetanclassics.org.

f.d: pha bla ma de nyid kyis/ nged cag gi snang tshul 'di las gzhan pa'i dgag bya'i snang tshul gzhan btsal rgyu med pas/ yang yang brtags nas 'di nyid dgag bya'i snang tshul du ngo 'phrod pa zhig 'bad dgos gsungs/

Similarly, my father guru says, “There is no other way to perceive the object of negation except the very way we perceive things. We need to learn to recognize the way the object of negation appears through examining it repeatedly.”[1043]

d.div: [1043] An oral instruction from the author’s personal guru.

f.d: des na 'o skol gyi blo lhan skyes kyi snang tshul 'di nyid tshig gis rjes su 'brangs te 'khrul snang du kha tshom chod pa tsam ma gtogs/ gzu bor gnas pa'i blos brtags nas med bzhin du snang ba'i tshul la nges pa gting nas 'drongs pa zhig shin tu dka' bas/ bcom ldan 'das thugs rje can de nyid kyis kyang tshul 'di la dpe mtha' yas pa zhig gsungs shing / tshul 'di ni dbu ma thal 'gyur ba ma gtogs rang sde mkhas pa su zhig gi mkhyen pa'i yul du mi shong ba'i dka' gnas su gsungs pas tshig tsam gyis mgu bar mi rigs so/ /

In view of these points, other than by relying on words and concluding that this very perception of our [naïve] innate cognition is itself deluded, we would be hard pressed to develop conviction from the depths of our mind that, when examined with an unbiased mind, things appear to our mind despite not existing in the way they appear. The most compassionate Blessed One has presented countless similes to illustrate this [illusion-like character]. In fact, this key point is said to be so challenging that it is beyond the comprehension of the learned ones of any Buddhist school apart from the Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka. So it would be ill advised to remain content with mere words.

de ltar las dang po bas go ba'i steng nas sgyu ma lta bu'i stong nyid bskyangs pa ma gtogs mnyam gzhag tu stong nyid bsgom stobs kyis rjes thog tu yul gang snang yang ched du gnyer mi dgos par sgyu ma lta bur ngang gis 'char lugs med par gsungs/ sgyu ma lta bu'i nyams len 'di la rang gi sde pa gong 'og su yi lugs la'ang rang rang gis brtag pa'i dgag bya dkag pa'i nges shes blo phugs su 'tshangs pa zhig med na/ ting nge 'dzin 'ga' zhig bsgom pa'i mthus thogs rdugs bkag pa'i nyams snang bun long du song ba lta bu la ni sgyu ma lta bu'i don gang yang med do//

Thus it is said that those on the beginner’s stage can meditate on illusion-like emptiness in the form of an intellectual understanding, but it is impossible for them to perceive whatever appears to the mind as illusion-like purely through the force of having realized emptiness during meditative equipoise, without having to consciously generate the perspective. When it comes to this practice of cultivating illusion-like perception, the particular Buddhist school of thought, higher or lower, is immaterial if there is no integration of the ascertainment of the absence of what is to be negated in the very core of one’s mind. Simply experiencing a dissolution of appearances into some indistinct perception through the force of engaging in meditative concentration — whereby perceptions of [material attributes like] obstruction have been dismantled — is not the meaning of illusion-like [emptiness] at all.

gzhan yang bden gnyis zung 'jug dang / snang stong dbyer med dang / snang stong rgyu 'bras su 'char tshul dang / snang bas yod mtha' sel tshul dang / stong pas med mtha' sel tshul dang / stong pa rten 'brel dang rten 'brel stong pa'i don du 'char tshul zer ba sogs rang cag dga' ldan bka' brgyud pa'i bla ma rnams kyis tha snyad snyan dgu 'dogs pa'i zab chos de yang sgyu ma lta bu'i stong nyid bsgom tshul 'di la/ stong pa'i nges shes dang rten 'brel gyi nges shes gnyis phan tshun gcig la gcig mi gnod par ma zad/ gcig grogs su gcig 'gro ba'i tshul zhig yod pas de la zer ba yin no/ /

Furthermore, the profound teaching our sacred Ganden lineage calls “the union of two truths,” “the indivisibility of appearance and emptiness,” “the dawning of appearance and emptiness as cause and effect,” “appearance dispelling the extreme of existence and emptiness dispelling the extreme of nonexistence,” “the dawning of emptiness as dependent origination and dependent origination as emptiness,” and so on points to this: There is, in this meditation on illusion-like emptiness, a method that ensures that the two ascertainments — that of emptiness and that of dependent origination — [486] not only do not undermine each other, they actually complement [and reinforce] each other. Here is how this can be understood.

de'i tshul yang nga de gdags gzhi 'dogs byed phan tshun 'phrad pa'i dbang gis glo bur du snang zhing de gnyis gang rung zhig log pa na'ang de nyid du yal 'gro ba ma gtogs rang dbang du gnas pa'i mthu yang med cing / gzhan gshed du 'gro rgyu cung zad kyang med pa'i rten 'brel btags yod kyi tshul sngar bzhin thag pa la btags pa'i sbrul dper blang ste zhib tu bsam pas/ nga gdags gzhi 'dogs byed gang la'ang ltos pa med par kho rang gi ngos nas btsal bas gang du snang ba'i yul steng du grub lugs gtan nas med pa'i tshul la ched du ma bsam par yang nges pa ngang gis skye ba dang / nga gang la'ang ltos pa med par kho rang gi ngos nas grub lugs ji ltar 'dug btsal bas gang du snang ba'i yul steng du rdul tsam yang mi rnyed pa'i tshul zhib tu bsam pas nga rten 'brel btags yod kyi tshul la ched du bsam mi dgos par yang nges pa ngang gis skye ba ste/ rten 'brel dang stong pa'i nges pa gnyis phan tshun gcig grogs su gcig 'gro ba'i rgyu 'bras lta bur 'char ba zhig yin te/

Taking the snake conceived in relation to a rope as an analogy, as you contemplate deeply the way your “I” is a dependently originated construct and how there is not even the slightest possibility it is otherwise — that its perception arises suddenly when the designative basis meets the designating mind and that, when one of the two ceases, [the perception] cannot sustain itself — and the way, when you search on this basis for an “I” that is not contingent on factors like the designative basis and the designating mind, the ascertainment will arise naturally and without deliberate effort that your “I” simply does not possess any objective existence at the locus where it appears. And as you contemplate deeply based on searching for your “I” in its own right — as something independent of any other factors — and you realize that not even a speck the size of an atom can be found at the locus where it appears, the ascertainment will arise in you naturally, without your having to make any deliberate effort, that its character is as a dependently originated nominal reality. This is how the two ascertainments — that of dependent origination and that of emptiness — reinforce one another as if they are cause and effect of each other.

rje thams cad mkhyen pas/
snang ba rten 'brel bslu ba med pa dang / / stong pa khas len bral ba'i go ba gnyis/ / ji srid so sor snang ba de srid du/ / da dung thub pa'i dgongs pa rtogs pa min/ /
nam zhig res 'jog med par cig car du/ / rten 'brel mi bslur mthong ba tsam nyid na/ / nges shes yul gyi 'dzin stangs kun 'jig na/ / de'i tshe lta ba'i dpyad pa rdzogs pa lags/ /
gzhan yang snang bas yod mtha' sel ba dang / / stong pas med mtha' sel ba'i stong pa gnyis/ / rgyu dang 'bras bur 'char ba'i tshul rtogs na/ / mthar 'dzin lta bas 'phrog par mi 'gyur ro/[108] / zhes dang /

The omniscient Jé Tsongkhapa states:
As long as the two understandings — of appearance, undeceiving dependent origination, and of emptiness, the absence of all positions — remain separate, then you have not realized the intent of the Sage.
However, if at some point, not in alternation but at once, the instant you see that dependent origination is undeceiving, this dismantles the entirety of the object of grasping at certitude, then your analysis of the view is complete.
Furthermore, when appearance dispels the extreme of existence and when emptiness dispels the extreme of nonexistence, and you understand how emptiness arises as cause and effect, you will never be swayed by views grasping at extremes.[1044]

d.div: [108] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ kha_gsung thor bu/ lam gtso rnam gsum/ shog_194_ba1
[1044] Three Principal Elements of the Path, verses 11–13, 194b1. See chapter 2 above.

f.d:
rje btsun blo bzang chos rgyan gyis/
snang bas stong pa mi sgribs shing / / stong pas snang ba mi 'gog pa'i/ / stong dang rten 'byung don gcig par/ / lam bzang de'i tshe mngon sum 'gyur/[109] / zhes dang /

Similarly, the most revered Chökyi Gyaltsen writes:
When appearance does not obscure emptiness and when emptiness does not obstruct appearance, the excellent path — where emptiness and dependent origination share the same meaning — will then manifest.[1045]

d.div: [109] paN chen blo bzang chos rgyan gsung 'bum/ nga _dge ldan bka' brgyud rin po che'i phyag chen rtsa ba rgyal ba'i gzhung lam/ shog_4_ba2
[1045] Panchen Losang Chögyen, Highway of the Conquerors, verse 45. See below, page 685.

f.d:
lcang skya rol pa'i rdo rjes/
pha rgan btsal bas ni ma rnyed pa de/ / ma rgan rnyed pa kho yin par 'dug pas/ / a ma'i pang nas ni pha rgan rnyed pas/ / pha ma drin can gyis bu nga skyob skad/[110] / ces dang /

Changkya Rölpai Dorjé too writes:
Not finding my father when sought is, in fact, the finding of my mother, and my father is found on my mother’s lap! That’s how the kind parents save their child, I am told![1046] [487]

d.div: [110] lcang skya rol pa'i rdo rje'i gsung 'bum/ nga _lta ba'i gsung mgur zab mo/ shog_2_na2
[1046] Recognizing My Mother, verse 7, 2a2.

f.d: pha bla ma de nyid kyis/ stong pa dang rten 'brel gyi don la bsam pa na/ dper na rta gnyis kyis shig phrug res byas pa dang 'dra bar nges pa phan tshun ngang gis 'jug pa zhig dgos gsungs/[111]

And my father guru says, “When you contemplate the meanings of emptiness and dependent origination, the ascertainments of the two should mutually reinforce one another like two horses who take turns grooming each other.”[1047]

d.div: [111] 'dir yang pha bla de nyid ces pa lha rtse ye shes bstan 'dzin yin nges pas de'i zhal shes bkod par snang /
[1047] An oral teaching from the author’s guru.

f.d: de ltar dmigs rten 'tshol ba'i dpyad sgom dang / dpyad mthar nges pa'i 'jog bsgom gnyis res 'jog tu bskyangs pas nges pa'i ngang du dpyad pa phra mo byas pas nges pa la mi gnod pa'i brtan pa rnyed pa na nges pa'i ngang du dpyad pa bya dgos pas/ de yang sngar ltar dmigs rten 'tshol ba'i dpyad pa rags pa de 'dras dpyad na nges pa 'thor 'gro bas/ dper na chu dwangs shing mi g.yo bar gnas pa'i nang du nye'u chung 'khyug 'khyug 'gro ba lta bur sems khyad par gnyis ldan gyi nges shes kyi ngang du rtse gcig tu 'dzin pa'i dran pa thu re bsten pa'i ngang las cung zad kyang ma g.yos par sems kyi cha shas phra mo zhig gis gnad bzhi'i phyogs dran pa tsam mam/ sems kyi cha shas phra mo zhig gnad bzhi'i phyogs la ston tsam byas pas nges shes kyi 'dzin stangs kyi ngar yang yang gso bar byas pas/ dpyad pa ji tsam byas kyang nges pa la mi gnod par ma zad nges pa'i 'dzin stangs kyi ngar shugs drag la yun ring bar gnas pa'i grogs su gyur pa na lta ba la myong ba legs par thon pa yin no/ /

Thus maintain the two forms of meditation — analytical meditation searching for the meditative object and placement meditation subsequently resting on the ascertainment arisen from such analysis — and when you have attained such stability that subtle analysis while settled on the ascertainment does not undermine your ascertainment, then continue to engage in analysis while sustaining your ascertainment. Note that if you were to apply here the coarse level of analysis you applied earlier, when you were searching for the meditative object, you would risk dismantling your ascertainment. So your analysis here needs to be similar to the way a minnow swims about in a clear and calm body of water. You do this by maintaining continuous mindfulness with your mind resting single-pointedly on the ascertainment endowed with the two features and, not wavering even slightly from such a state, engaging in analysis with a small part of your mind. Do this either by simply recalling the four key points [of emptiness meditation] or by simply directing a small part of your mind to the four key points. When you proceed in this way, constantly refreshing the mode of apprehension of your ascertainment, then no matter how much you analyze, not only is your ascertainment not undermined, your analysis in fact helps ensure that the mode of apprehension of your ascertainment remains strong and enduring. When this happens, you have gained good experience of the view.

de yang sngar dmigs rten 'tshol ba'i skabs gnad bzhi'i dpyad pa mang du byas pas 'byongs pa'i dbang gis gnad bzhi'i phyogs la blo kha ston pa tsam mam/ dran pa tsam gyis gnad bzhi'i dpyad pa dngos byas pa dang 'dra b.re sang shes shugs drag bskyed nus pa'i gnad kyis so/ / 'on kyang lta ba la myong ba phul phyin skyes pa la ni lhag mthong thob dgos pa 'dra'o/ / de ltar na dpyad pa byed lugs dang dpyad pa snga phyi gnyis kyi bar du 'gyangs ring thung yang sngar dmigs rten 'tshol ba'i skabs dang ye mi 'dra bas/ nges shes kyi shugs zhan du 'gro bar dogs pa na dpyad pa phyi ma byed pa yin gyi/ nges shes kyi shugs zhan du song ba na byed pa min la/ dpyod pa na'ang nges pa'i 'dzin stangs btang ba min no/ /

Thanks to the repeated analysis you engaged in previously when you were searching for the object of meditation and thus becoming trained, you are now capable of generating a strong ascertainment, one that is comparable to engaging in full-fledged analysis of the four key points, by simply directing your mind to it or simply recalling it. Of course, for an optimal experience of the view, you need to attain insight (vipaśyanā). But now when it comes to engaging in analysis and the intervals you need between earlier and subsequent analyses, the situation is entirely different compared to when you were first seeking the meditative object. Here, subsequent analyses should be brought in when you sense that the force of your ascertainment is beginning to wane, not when its strength has already decreased. Also, when you engage in analysis, you should do so without losing the mode of apprehension [of the ascertainment].
de lta bu'i tshul gyis mnyam gzhag tu nam mkha' lta bu'i stong nyid bsgom pa'i rjes thob tu sgyu ma lta bu'i stong nyid kyang bsgom dgos so//

In brief, in the wake of having engaged in meditation on the space-like emptiness during equipoise, you also need to meditate, in ways such as those outlined here, on the illusion-like emptiness of the post-equipoise period. [488]

d.b: sems kyi don dam pa'i ngo sprod/

f.d: f. The selflessness of phenomena: Introducing the mind’s ultimate nature

de dag ni gang zag gi bdag med kyi dbang du byas pa'i mnyam rjes bskyang tshul yin la/ de nas chos kyi bdag med kyi dbang du byas pa ni nga'i phung po lnga po gang gi steng du sngar gyi gnad bzhi'i dpyad pa kha spos nas bsgom yang chos kyi bdag med bsgom par 'gyur mod/ 'on kyang gdams pa 'di'i bsgrub bya gtso bo sems kyi don dam pa'i ngo sprad yin pas de'i tshul cung zad brjod na/

What has been presented thus far is how you maintain meditative equipoise and post-equipoise states from the standpoint of the selflessness of persons. To meditate on the selflessness of phenomena, you could simply extend the same analysis — in terms of four key points — to the five aggregates, and this would indeed constitute a meditation on the selflessness of phenomena. In this [mahāmudrā] instruction, however, the primary aim is to introduce the ultimate nature of the mind. So I will briefly explain here such an introduction.

sngar ltar sems la dmigs pa'i gnas cha rnyed pa na/ mnyam gzhag de'i ngang las cung zad kyang ma g.yos par shes pa'i cha shas phra mo zhig gis rang gi sems kyi kun rdzob pa'i ngo bo gzugs can gang du'ang ma grub pa'i stong sangs nam mkha' lta bu bying rgod sogs kyis ma sgrib pas yul snang sna tshogs ngang gis 'char zhing yul gang la'ang 'gyur zhing 'phro sla ba/ phral du snang ba 'gags pa med par gsal zhing rig pa phugs su rgyun chad pa med par 'jug pa'i rnam shes breng tsam de rang gi sems la 'char tshul ji ltar 'dug phra zhing mdzangs pa'i rig pas brtag pa na/ gdags gzhi 'dogs byed skad cig snga phyi gang la'ang ltos pa med par kho rang gi ngos nas btsal bas gang du snang ba'i yul steng du rnyed rgyu yod pa 'dra ba zhig snang ba bsnyon du med do/ / de ltar snang ba bzhin du don la yod na rang gi skad cig snga phyi rnams dang rang ngos nas grub pa'i gcig tha dad gang rung du nges par grub dgos pa dang / gcig tha dad gang du grub par khas blang yang gnod byed du ma 'bab tshul rnams zhib tu brtag pa'i dpyad sgom dang / dpyad mthar nges pa'i 'jog sgom dang / mnyam gzhag de las langs pa na/ rang gi sems gang la'ang ltos pa med par tshugs thub tu grub pa bsnyon med du snang ba'i tha snyad pa'i shes pa dang / sems rang ngos nas ma grub par rtogs zin nges pa'i shes pa gnyis la brten nas sgyu ma lta bu'i nyams len bskyang tshul rnams sngar ltar bya'o//

As practiced earlier, once you have attained stability in your focus on the mind, remain unwavering in this meditative equipoise but with a small part of your mind observe the mind’s conventional nature — this space-like vacuity with no material existence whatsoever. When it is unobscured by mental laxity and excitation, all sorts of diverse objects can naturally appear to it, and it can also easily move to any object whatsoever; its immediate perceptions are unstoppable, and luminous and aware, its continuity is unceasing.[1048] As you observe how this mere stream-like consciousness[1049] appears to your mind and examine it with subtle and skillful awareness, it will undeniably appear to exist without depending on such factors as a designative basis, a designating mind, temporal instances, and so on; it will appear to exist in its own right, as something that could be found to exist objectively at the very locus where it is being perceived. Now were the mind to actually exist as it is perceived, it would have to be either intrinsically identical with or different from its temporal instances, yet asserting it to exist in either of these two terms leads to numerous logical objections. In this way, engage in analytical meditation, carefully examining these points, and engage in placement meditation resting on the ascertainment arrived at following such analysis. And when you arise out of such meditative equipoise, maintain the practice of illusion-like emptiness based on the convergence of the two factors — (a) an awareness of how, to your everyday cognition, your mind appears to exist in its own right, without being contingent on any other factors, and (b) the ascertainment rooted in your realization that your mind lacks such intrinsic existence. Practice all of these as explained above [in the context of the selflessness of persons].

d.div: [1048] The italicized emphasis is mine. The author is referring to three key characteristics of the mind that are said to constitute the mind’s conventional nature: space-like vacuity (stong pa), luminous clarity (gsal ba), and awareness (rig pa).

[1049] Rnam shes breng tsam de. The idea here is to settle your mind to a point where what you are perceiving is a kind of bare awareness characterized by vacuity, clarity, and awareness and stripped of any kind of object orientation.

f.d: de dag ni las dang po pas lta ba la myong ba 'don tshul gyi man ngag zhal shes dang bcas pa med du mi rung ba rnams gsal bar bkod pa yin gyi/ skyong tshul de rnams gong nas gong du khyad par du gyur pa'i gnas skabs kyi dbye bas zhi gnas rjes mthun pa la brten nas lhag mthong rjes mthun pa bsgom tshul/ zhi gnas mtshan nyid pa la brten nas lhag mthong rjes mthun pa dang / zhi gnas mtshan nyid pa la brten nas lhag mthong mtshan nyid pa dang / bde ba skyong tshul dang / zab gsal gnyis med kyi rnal 'byor skyong tshul sogs mang du yod kyang bdag dang bdag 'dras skyong tshul de rnams la go ba rnam dag btsal ba tsam ma gtogs nyams steng du phab nas ji ma ji bzhin bskyangs pa zhig skye ba 'dir yong mdog mi snang bas bris pa'i ngal ba ma byas kyang gzhung chen mo rnams kyi steng nas go ba 'tshol bar bya'o//

In the above I have scribed in clear terms the indispensable pith instructions, together with oral teachings, on how those on the beginner’s stage can bring about an experience of the view [of emptiness]. There are, of course, numerous other important matters, such as [489] how, based on distinctions among the progressive levels of these practices, (1) you engage in the meditative practice of cultivating semblance insight in dependence on semblance tranquil abiding, (2) how you attain semblance insight on the basis of actual tranquil abiding, (3) how you attain actual insight on the basis of attaining actual tranquil abiding, (4) how you cultivate bliss, (5) how you cultivate the nondual yoga of profundity and clarity, and so on.[1050] As for these, other than seeking to develop a correct [conceptual] understanding of them, it does not appear that those like me have the good fortune to attain them through cultivating them exactly as they are at the experiential level. I have therefore not endeavored to write about them here; please seek to understand them on the basis of the great treatises.

d.div: [1050] Our author may be thinking here of a famed oral teaching of Jé Tsongkhapa entitled Vajra Lines on the View, which mentions five distinct levels of meditative experience of emptiness. See Jinpa, Tsongkhapa, 310–11. On Tsongkhapa’s list, the last two are meditation on emptiness in an ārya’s direct realization of emptiness and meditation on emptiness in the completion stage of tantra, where the meditating subject is the gnosis conjoined with innate bliss.

f.d: dmigs skor de rnams la thog mar blo sbyong ba na thun re rer thams cad rgyas par bskyang khul byas kyang lam du 'gro ba zhig mi yong bar ma zad sun par 'gyur ba'i gegs che bas/ thun dang por thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'i sngon 'gro'i skor rnams rgyas par skyong zhing / dmigs skor 'og ma rnams tshig gi rjes su 'brang ba'i shar sgom gyis bskyangs/ gnyis par tshogs zhing gsal 'debs pa dang / de la yan lag bdun pa 'bul ba'i skor rnams rgyas pa dang gong 'og gi dmigs skor rnams shar sgom gyis bskyangs/ gsum par nye brgyud gsol 'debs sogs gsol 'debs kyi skor dang / ting nge 'dzin gyi dbang bzhi len tshul rnams rgyas pa dang / gong 'og gi dmigs skor rnams shar sgom gyis bskyang / bzhi par mdo sngags kyi lam gyi lus yongs su rdzogs par shar sgom gyi sgo nas byin rlabs zhu ba'i tshul rnams rgyas pa dang / gong gi dmigs skor rnams shar sgom gyi tshul du bskyang bar bya'o/ /

When you are first training your mind in these meditation topics, even if you try to cultivate them extensively in each and every session, you are not likely to have much success. You actually risk becoming discouraged. So, in the first session, for example, you may be better off practicing the meditation topics of the common and uncommon preliminary practices more extensively and practicing the subsequent meditation topics more in the manner of a review, scanning through the words. In the second session, you could focus more on the merit-field practice and the offering of the seven limbs to the merit field, approaching the prior and subsequent meditation topics in the manner of a review. In the third session, you could focus extensively on the supplications, such as to the lineage gurus of the near transmission, followed by the meditative concentration of receiving the four empowerments, cultivating the preceding and subsequent meditation topics in the manner of a review. In the fourth session, you would then focus extensively on reviewing the entire path of sutra and tantra and receiving the blessings, cultivating the preceding meditation topics in the form of a review.

de yang sngon 'gro bla ma'i rnal 'byor gtsor 'don byas na thun bzhi gang rung gi mjug tu phyag chen gyi khrid dmigs rgyas bsdus 'tshams pa re skyong / phyag chen gtsor 'don byas na thun bzhi ka'i gsham du phyag chen gyi dmigs skor skyong bar bya'o/ / 'di dag ni kho bo ri khrod 'grims pa'i thog mar bla ma'i rnal 'byor bskyangs pas/ 'bad rtsol ji ltar bskyed kyang nyi ma gcig la bla mchod tshar re'ang thon mi thon gyi tshod du song bas bskyal tshul gyi gnad zhus pa'i lan du pha bla ma de nyid kyis stsal ba'i man ngag yin no//

If your primary focus is the preliminary guru-yoga practice, then at the end of one of the four sessions, review the meditation topics of mahāmudrā for an appropriate length. In contrast, if your primary focus is mahāmudrā, then at the end of each of the four sessions, engage in substantial meditative practice of the topics pertaining to mahāmudrā. When I first began my life as a hermit in the mountains, I engaged in guru-yoga practice. At that time, regardless of how much effort I made, I found it difficult to complete even one round of Offering to the Guru. [490] So I asked my father guru’s advice on how best to undertake the practice [pertaining to these meditation topics]. What I have shared here is the advice he gave me.
gsum pa mjug tu ji ltar bya ba ni/
3.1.3. Concluding activities

bsgom bya'i lam dang sgom byed sgrub pa po'i sems dang / sgom pa po rang nyid de 'khor gsum po de sgrub pa po rang gi tha snyad pa'i shes pa la tshul ji ltar snang brtag pa na/ rang gi sems kyis bzos pa lta bu ma yin par don de rnams rang rang gi ngos nas btsal bas gang du snang ba'i yul steng du rnyed rgyu yod pa 'dra ba zhig snang ba bsnyon du med do/ / de rnams snang ba ltar du yod na bsgom bya de sgom pa po rang gi sems kyis bsgom pa la ma ltos par ngo bo nyid kyis bsgom byar 'gyur la/ de ltar na sgom pa po med pa'i bsgom bya dang / sgom pa po yang sgom byed kyi sems kyis bsgom bya sgom pa la ma ltos par ngo bo nyid kyis sgom pa por 'gyur la/ de ltar na bsgom bya med pa'i sgom pa po 'gyur te/ rtsa shes las/
yin par gyur la bya ba med/ / byed po med pa'i las su 'gyur/ / yin par gyur la bya ba med/ / las med byed pa por yang 'gyur/[112] / zhes gsungs so/ /

As you examine the three spheres of your meditation practice — the path being practiced, the meditating mind of the practitioner, and the meditator yourself — all three undeniably appear as not constructed by your own mind; they appear to exist objectively, findable at the site where they are perceived to be. Contemplate how, if they were to exist in such a manner, then the topic being meditated on would not be contingent on your mind meditating on it; they would be independent. In that case, there would be something being meditated upon without there being a meditator, and the meditator too would become an intrinsically real meditator with no dependence on the meditating mind meditating. For example, Fundamental Wisdom states:
For an agent that is real, there is no activity, so the object would be without an agent. For an object that is real, there is no activity, so the agent too would have no object of action.[1051]

d.div: [112] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_slob dpon klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa shes rab/ rab byed/ 8_sh+loka_5_shog_6_na1
[1051] Nāgārjuna, Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), 8.2; Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 6a1.

f.d:
de ltar na 'khor gsum po de dag phan tshun ltos btags kyi rten 'brel tsam ma gtogs don rang ngos nas btsal pas rnyed rgyu rdul tsam yang med do/ / de nyid las/
byed po las la brten byas shing / / las kyang byed pa po nyid la/ / brten nas 'byung ba ma gtogs par/ / grub pa'i rgyu ni mi mthong ngo /[113] / zhes gsungs/

Thus, when these three spheres of activity are searched for objectively, apart from conceptual imputations of them defined through mutual dependence, not even the minutest particle can be found to exist. The same text states:
The agent exists in dependence on the object, and the object in turn depends on the agent. Apart from this, we find no other cause of their establishment.[1052]

d.div: [113] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_slob dpon klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa shes rab/ rab byed/ 8_sh+loka_12_shog_6_na6

f.d: des na ltos btags kyi rten 'brel yin pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis bya byed kyi rnam gzhag thams cad ches 'thad pas bdag gi dge ba'i rtsa ba 'di dag thams cad kyang bsngo ba smon lam ji ltar btab pa de bzhin du 'grub pa'i rgyur gyur cig snyam du bsam ste/ gsang 'dus smon lam dang / phyag chen smon lam sogs kyis dge rtsa rnams gnas skabs dang mthar thug gi phan bde'i rgyur 'dun pa drag pos bsngo bar bya'o//

Contemplate the following: In light of the above, the fact that all things are dependent originations of mutually dependent conceptual imputations makes presentations of everyday function tenable. So, through dedicating all my roots of virtue here, may the aims of my aspirations be fulfilled just as prayed for. With this thought, and through prayers of dedication such as those of the Guhyasamāja sādhana or of mahāmudrā,[1053] dedicate with fervent intention all your roots of virtue that they may become conditions for realizing both temporary and ultimate benefit and happiness.

d.div: [1053] For the Guhyasamāja prayers referred to here, see Tsongkhapa, Guhyasamāja Dedication Prayer and Verses of Auspiciousness. These are the standard dedication prayers recited at the end of Guhyasamāja sādhana practice in the Geluk tradition. The mahāmudrā prayer (phyag chen smon lam) referred to here is the one by Yongzin Yeshé Gyaltsen.

f.d: gnyis pa thun mtshams su ji ltar bya ba ni/
3.2. How to practice between sessions

spyod 'jug las/
lus kyis 'di ltar gnas bya zhes/ / bya ba bsdogs nas de nas ni/ / skabs su lus 'di ji lta bur/ / gnas pa yin zhes blta bar bya/ /
sems kyi glang chen myos pa ni/ / chos la sems pa'i ka chen la/ / ji ltar btags pa mi 'chor bar/ / de ltar 'bad pa kun gyis brtag /
cis nas ting 'dzin brtson pa ni/ / skad cig gcig kyang mi 'chor bar/ / bdag gi yid 'di gang spyod ces/ / de ltar yid la so sor brtag /
'jigs dang dga' ston sogs 'brel bar/ / gal te mi nus ci bder bya/[114] / zhes gsungs pa ltar sems rnam par g.yeng ba'i nyes dmigs dang / mnyam par gzhag pa'i phan yon rnams zhib tu shes par byas te/ sems don med dang don ma yin pa'i phyogs las bsrung zhing / skyong rgyu'i dge ba'i phyogs su bkol bar bya'i snyam pa'i 'phen pa yang yang gtong nas/ ji ltar 'phen pa btang ba ltar rtag tu dran pa dang / skabs su skabs su 'phen pa btang ba ltar gnas mi gnas brtag pa'i shes bzhin gyis bya ra byas te/ phan yon dang nyes dmigs dran pas sems skyong rgyu'i dge ba'i phyogs su bkol zhing / don med dang don ma yin pa'i phyogs las bsrung ba la rab tu sgrim pa'i bag yod bsten pa ni thun mtshams su ji ltar bya ba thams cad kyi rtsa ba lta bu yin te/

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way says:
Having initiated an action with the intention “I shall conduct with my body in this way,” you should periodically observe thereafter how your body is positioned.
With your mind, the rutting elephant, tied to the great post of Dharma contemplation, while ensuring that it does not break loose, you should examine it with all your effort.
Never abandon, even for an instant, this striving for concentration. And thinking, “Where is mine wandering to?” observe your mind with discernment.
If you are not able to do so because of danger, festivities, and so on, then just follow your inclination.[1054] Just as stated above, you should understand deeply the faults of the distracted mind and the benefits of the settled mind and repeatedly set your intention to guard your mind against fruitless activities and inappropriate pursuits. Maintain continuous mindfulness of the intentions you have set, and every now and then, applying meta-awareness, monitor if your mind is on course with the intentions you have set. Also, mindful of the pros and cons, cultivate heedfulness that helps you direct your mind toward virtue and vigilantly guard against fruitless activities and inappropriate pursuits. This [application of heedfulness] is like a foundation for all the practices you do in between sessions.

d.div: [114] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_39_nas _42_shog_11_ba5
[1054] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 5.39–42b, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 11b5.

f.d:
de ltar byas pas bslab pa'i gnas rnams dag par 'gyur ba dang / skyong rgyu'i dmigs rnam la dmigs pa'i ting 'dzin myur du 'grub pa'i phan yon yod de/ de yang thog mar ting nge 'dzin gyi phan yon mthong ba'i dad pa bskyed de/ de la brten nas ting nge 'dzin don du gnyer ba'i 'dun pa ngang gis skye zhing / ting nge 'dzin de yang rtsa ba tshul khrims la rag las par mthong nas bslab pa'i gnas rnams la gus pa dang / de las bslab bya'i gnas la 'jug ldog tshul bzhin du bya ba'i dran pa dang shes bzhin rtag tu 'jug cing / 'jug ldog byed par yang mi 'dod pa'i mtsher snang med par rab tu sgrim pa'i bag yod kyi mthus sgo gsum gyi g.yeng ba thams cad zhi nas ting nge 'dzin myur du 'grub pa dang / bslab pa'i gnas rnams dag par 'gyur bar dgongs nas/ rgyal sras zhi ba lhas bslab btus su/
de kun gang gis 'thob ce na/ / 'bras bu med pa'i byed spong bas/ / de yang rtag tu dran pas 'grub/ / de yang shin tu gus las 'byung / / de ni zhi ba'i che ba nyid/ / shes par 'gyur nas brtun pa bskyed/[115] / ces dang /
phyi rol g.yo ba zlog pa yis/ / yid ni zhi las g.yo mi 'gyur/[116] / zhes gsungs/

Conducting yourself like this benefits you in these [two] ways: you ensure the purity of all facets of your precepts, and you swiftly attain meditative concentrations on your chosen meditation topics. Here is how these benefits emerge. First, seeing the benefits of meditative concentration, you generate admiration for it, and on this basis, an interest in pursuing meditative concentration arises in you naturally. Then, when you see that [success in] meditative concentration is rooted in morality, you develop respect for the precepts. This in turn gives rise to constant application of mindfulness and meta-awareness, as these help you conduct yourself in accord with your precepts of what is to be engaged in and what is to be avoided. And thanks to the power of resolute heedfulness, which helps prevent any kind of apprehensiveness regarding what is to be engaged in and what is to be shunned, all the distractions of the three doors come to cease. In this way, meditative concentration [492] is quickly attained and all the precepts come to be perfected. Thus, says the great bodhisattva Śāntideva:
By what means will all of these be attained? They are attained through mindfulness because it prevents fruitless pursuits. They arise too from deep respect, which in turn comes from knowing the benefits of serenity, giving rise to effort.[1055] And:
By ceasing distractions to the external, the mind will not sway from serenity.[1056]

d.div: [115] sde dge_3939_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ bslab btus/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_7_shog_2_na2
[116] sde dge_3939_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ bslab btus/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_9_shog_2_na2
[1055] Verses on the Compendium of Training (Śikṣāsamuccayakārikā), verse 7, Toh 3939 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 2a2.
[1056] Ibid., verse 9, 2a2.

f.d: gzhan yang khrus dang kha zas sogs kyi rnal 'byor/ zas kyi tshod rig pa/ nam gyi cha stod smad la mi nyal bar rnal 'byor la brtson pa/ nyal ba'i tshe ji ltar bya ba sogs ni gzhan du shes par bya'o//

As for other activities, such as the yogas of washing and eating, moderation with respect to food, not sleeping at the start and end of the night but striving in practice, the proper way to sleep, and so forth, understand these from elsewhere.[1057]

d.div: [1057] For a detailed explanation of the practices to be engaged in between the sessions, such as guarding the doors of your senses, engaging in everyday activities with awareness, and disciplines pertaining to habits of diet and sleep, see Tsongkhapa, Great Treatise (trans.), 1:100–108.

f.d: bla mchod bde stong dbyer med ma dang / phyag chen rtsa ba rgyal ba'i gzhung lam gnyis kyi tshig don rnams la mdo rgyud kyi khungs dang sbyar nas nges pa 'tshol lugs rnams bla ma yongs 'dzin rin po che'i sngar med kyi rmad du byung ba'i legs bshad gnyis kyi steng nas shes par bya dgos shing /[117] 'dir ni legs bshad de gnyis nas man ngag gi gnad mang po zhig bla ma'i zhal nas shes dgos par gsungs pa rnams las/ rang gis pha bla ma de nyid kyi zhal gyi bum bzang las gang thob pa rnams kho bo dus kyi pho nyas khrid pa na ming tsam yang med par 'gyur du dogs nas yi ger bkod pa'i phyir dang / lung rigs kyi spros pa'i gseb na dmigs rnam yid la byed tshul ngos 'dzin dka' ba rnams gzung sla bar bya ba'i phyir dang / rang gis kyang bla ma'i man ngag la brten nas gdams pa de gnyis kyi tshig don rnams la go ba ji ltar blang ba'i tshul dang / dmigs rnam yid la byed tshul ji ltar byas pa rnams kha chems rlung la bskur ba'i phyir du bris pa yin gyi bris pa'i ngal ba tsam bsten par song ma song ni btsan ma snga bar zhib tu gzigs dang shes par 'gyur ro//

You should learn how to relate the words and meaning of Offering to the Guru: Union of Bliss and Emptiness and the mahāmudrā root text Highway of the Conquerors to their sources in the sutras and tantras and understand them on the basis of two unparalleled works of excellence by Guru Yongzin Rinpoché.[1058] Both of these two excellent texts contain, in relation to many key points of instruction, the statement that they need to be learned from the mouth of one’s guru. So what I have done here is to put into words what I myself have received from the excellent vase that is my own father guru’s mouth, fearing that not even their names will survive after I have been led away by time’s messenger. I have also written this work to help make it easier for others to know how to bring into their practice some of the more difficult aspects of the meditation topics buried amid elaborate scriptural citations and reasoning, and also to send upon the wind a testament of how I have myself developed an understanding of the words and meanings of these two instructions on the basis of my guru’s pith instructions and of how I have approached the practice of the relevant meditation topics. As to whether what I have done remains just an effort [with no benefit], please do not rush to judge; read carefully and you will come to appreciate.

d.div: [117] 'dir legs bshad gnyis gsungs pa yongs 'dzin ye shes rgyal mtshan gyi gsung 'bum/ papar bzhugs pa bla ma mchod pa'i khrid yig gsang ba'i gnad rnam par phye ba snyan rgyud man ngag gi gter mdzod dang / gsung 'bum _tsa_par bzhugs pa dga' ldan phyags rgya chen po'i khrid yig lam bzang gsal sgron/
[1058] These are, respectively, Yongzin Yeshé Gyaltsen’s Treasure House of Instructions and his Bright Lamp of the Excellent Path.

f.d:
smras pa/
zhing 'dir rgyal dang rgyal sras grangs med byon pas ma thul ba/ / sems can nyon mongs lta ba che dang dus kyi snyigs ma lngas/ / rab tu bdo zhing 'dul dka' mgon skyabs bral ba bdag cag kyang / / gang gis slob mar bdag gir bzhes pa'i snying stobs de rmad byung / /

Thus I say:
Not tamed by conquerors and their children who have appeared in this realm, sentient beings rife with afflictions and false views, and so hard to tame owing to a proliferation of the five degenerations, even for such beings bereft of guardian and refuge like us, your courage in embracing us as yours is most excellent indeed!

d.div: gang gi man ngag mnyen zhing rno ba des/ / phyugs 'dra rmongs pa bdag gi rna khung du'ang / / brgyud de sems kyi gting du chos don gyi/ / go ba bskyal ba'i mdzad pa de bas rmad/ /

Your pith instructions supple and sharp, on entering the ears of an ignorant beast-like person like me, can bring the meaning of Dharma to the mind’s core; this enlightened deed is most amazing indeed!

rmad byung ngo mtshar gnas gyur bshes gnyen gyi/ / man ngag grub pa'i mig sman la brten nas/ / mdo rgyud zab cing brling ba'i sa 'og tu/ / lkog gyur gnas pa'i nyams len gter chen por/ / legs par brtags pas rang gis mthong tshod dang / / sbyar ba'i legs bshad gtam du byas mod kyang / / bdag blo rang bzhin mi gsal nyams chung bas/ / ma bshad log bshad ha cang bshad pa dang / / rang bzo sogs kyis nongs pa gang mchis pa/ / chos kyi spyan ldan rnams kyi spyan sngar 'chags/ /
bu chung shed ma bye ba'i 'khrul ba kun/ / brtse ldan pha mas 'bad de bsal ba bzhin/ / bdag la sgrib par mi 'gyur mdzad du gsol/ /

By relying on the eye lotion prepared through cultivating the instruction of my teacher, the source of such excellent wonder, I have searched the subterrains of sutra and tantra and examined the great treasures of meditative practice that are found hidden there; the insights gleaned I have brought into a discourse here. Yet as my mind is naturally hazy and feeble, whatever faults there might be of insufficient explanation, distorted explanation, explaining too much, or self-fabrication, I seek forgiveness in the presence of those with Dharma eyes.
Just as when a child commits all sorts of errors, his loving parents strive with effort to rectify them, likewise, help me so that these faults do not obscure me.

'on kyang rje btsun bla ma'i bka' drin gyis/ / legs par bshad pa than thun mchis na yang / / bu chung kha nas don ldan tshig smras par/ / pha mas ya mtshan gzung zhing dga' ba ltar/ / byams brtse'i thugs kyis bdag la dgyes par mdzod/ /

If, thanks to the kindness of my most revered teacher, there are nuggets of insight here and there, then just as when a toddler utters meaningful sentences, it brings wonder and joy to her parents, likewise, with compassion in your heart, do be pleased with me.
'dir 'bad las byung bsod nams phung po des/ / 'gro ba kun kyang yang dag bshes gnyen gyis/ / rjes su gzung zhing man ngag sbyin pa'i snod/ / skal ldan slob ma kho nar 'gyur bar shog /
Through the heap of merit arising from this effort, may all beings be sustained by perfect spiritual mentors and become their fortunate disciples, vessels into which instructions are granted.

bdag kyang skye ba kun tu yang dag pa'i/ / bshes gnyen dam pas nam yang mi phongs shing / / sangs rgyas dngos su mthong ba'i dad gus gyis/ / gang gi don du lus srog longs spyod gang / / ltos pa med par gtong ba'i bsam sbyor gyis/ /

mnyes par byas pas dgyes bzhin rjes bzung ste/ / thugs kyi bcud kun phyung ba'i man ngag rnams/ / sbas gsang med par stsol zhing su la yang / / mngon par mi mdzad gsang ba'i rnam thar kun/ / lhug par gsung ba'i sras kyi thu bor gyur/ /

lus srog khyad du gsod pa'i dka' spyad dang / / drag la rgyun mi 'chad pa'i brtson 'grus kyis/ / bla ma'i man ngag tshul bzhin sgrub pa yis/ / lung dang rtogs pa'i chu klung rab brdol bas/ / bla ma'i thugs kyi chu gter 'gengs par shog /

May I too never be deprived throughout all my lives of the presence of sublime spiritual mentors, and with faith and reverence that sees them as actual buddhas, may I please them with my thoughts and actions and be willing to sacrifice my body, life, and resources for their sake.

May I thus be sustained by them with joy, and may they grant me instructions distilling the entire essence of their heart without concealment or secrecy. May I become their chief disciple, with whom they share all the secret and invisible aspects of their liberating life.

Through ascetic practice sacrificing even life and limb, through diligence concerted and uninterrupted, and through practicing according to the guru’s instructions, may the stream of scripture and realization surge within me. May I become like this the reservoir of my guru’s heart.

deng dus phal cher gang gi skyon yon rnams/ / legs par 'byed pa'i blo mig rab ldongs pas/ / gang la thogs pa'i ming snyan rna ba yis/ / thos pa tsam gyi rjes su yid rton pa'i/ / dad dang don gnyer can gyi longs ba mang / /
rnam par dpyod pa'i mig can phal cher yang / / phrag dog gdon gyis sems la rang dbang med/ / chos dang chos smra ris su ma bcad par/ / cig car spong ba'i smyon pas phyogs kun khyab/ /

Today, for most people, the eyes of intelligence that properly distinguish faults from virtue seem blinded. As such, they develop a reliance on someone as a teacher based simply on hearing of their renown. There thus are many faithful aspirants who seem blind. [494]

Yet even among those with eyes of analysis, many seem robbed of their autonomy by the demon of envy, and with no discernment as to teachings and teachers, they reject them impulsively; such crazed people seem to be everywhere.

des na bdag gi ngal ba 'bras bu chung / / 'on kyang bla ma'i man ngag thob pa rnams/ / kha chems rlung la bskur ba'i 'phrin yig 'di/ / blo ldan gzur gnas 'ga' yi phyag brgyud de/ / thos bsam bsgom pas mi sha ldon par shog /

Thus, though the fruits of this effort of mine may be small, for those who have received a guru’s instructions, may this epistle, a testament I have sent upon the wind, be transmitted through the hands of a few who are wise and unbiased and help them prove their worth as humans through study, reflection, and meditation.
de'i tshe chos 'di'i sgos kyi srung ma'i gtso/ / phyag drug mgon dang dam can chos kyi rgyal/ / rgyal po chen po rnam thos sras rnams kyis/ / g.yel ba med par rtag tu grogs mdzod cig/ /
At that point may the special protectors of this teaching — the six-armed Mahākāla, the Dharma king Kālarūpa, as well as the great kind Vaiśravaṇa — be their allies at all times.
gzhan yang rgyal dang rgyal sras gang gis kyang / / 'dul ba'i spyod yul ma gyur 'dul dka' yang / / bdag gi legs bshad 'di yi spyod yul du/ / gyur nas ji zhig ltar stes 'dul bar shog/ /
Also, may even those so hard to tame who have not been pacified by any conqueror or bodhisattva become beneficiaries of this work of mine, and may they become tamed on the basis of it.
gal te 'ga' zhig gang zag skyon gyis 'dir/ / phral du yid mi bde'am 'khrugs gyur kyang / / dam chos spong ba'i sdig tu mi 'gyur bar/ / slad nas phan zhing bde ba'i rgyur gyur cig/

If some, owing to their individual faults, come to experience, in the near term, frustration and disturbance [from this work], may this not cause them to abandon the Dharma but may it ultimately become a source of benefit and joy.

f.d: Colophon

ces phyag chen gyi khrid dmigs skyong tshul dang de'i sngon 'gro thun mong min pa'i bla ma'i rnal 'byor gyi 'khrid dmigs skyong tshul man ngag zhal shes dang bcas pa'i kha chems rlung la bskur ba'i 'phrin yig ces bya ba 'di ni/ mkhas btsun bzang gsum gyi yon tan thams cad phan tshun 'gran pa bzhin du dar ba'i dpal ldan bla ma dam pa rje btsun ye shes bstan 'dzin dpal bzang po'i zhal snga nas gdams pa 'di gnyis kyi bka' drin legs par mnos pa'i bya bral tshul khrims nyi mas dga' ldan blo 'phel ri khrod du sbyar ba'o/ /

This Letter of Final Testament Sent upon the Wind, containing pith instructions as well as oral teachings on how to undertake the meditative practice of mahāmudrā and its uncommon preliminary, the practice of guru yoga, was composed by the do-nothing[1059] Tsultrim Nyima, someone blessed with both of these instructions from the glorious and sublime guru, the most revered Yeshé Tenzin. It was composed at Ganden Lophel mountain hermitage.

d.div: [1059] The Tibetan word bya bral, literally “do-nothing,” or “someone with nothing to do,” is a common term for a hermit who has chosen the path of single-pointed meditative practice, often in a place of solitude. Another term, ri khrod pa, or “one who is from a mountain hermitage,” is the Tibetan equivalent of the term hermit.

f.d: 'dis kyang rje bla ma'i snyan brgyud kyi gdams pa'i me ro slong bar gyur cig/ // sarba mang+ga laM//
May it help revive from its embers the fire of instructions of Jé Tsongkhapa’s oral transmission. Sarva maṅgalaṃ (May auspiciousness prevail everywhere!)
dge ldan phyag rgya chen po dang / dbu ma'i lta khrid/
Part 3: Geluk Mahāmudrā and Guide to the View
@#/ /dge ldan bka' brgyud rin po che'i phyag chen rtsa ba rgyal ba'i gzhung lam zhes bya ba bzhugs so/ /
9. Highway of the Conquerors: Mahāmudrā Root Text According to the Precious Geden Lineage
paN chen blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan/
Panchen Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen [497]
@#/ /na mo mahA mu drA ya/ /
Namo mahāmudrāya.
kun khyab kun gyi rang bzhin phyag rgya che/ / dbyer med brjod bral sems kyi rdo rje'i dbyings/ / rjen par ston mdzad khyab bdag grub pa'i rje/ / zla med bla ma'i zhabs la gus pas 'dud/ /[1]

1 I bow at the feet of my peerless guru, the sovereign lord among siddhas, who reveals naked mahāmudrā, the all-pervading nature of everything, indivisible, and the ineffable expanse of the vajra mind.[1060]

d.div: [1060] In the collected works of Panchen Losang Chögyen, the verses of the root text are not numbered. We have introduced verse numbers here in the translation for the benefit of the reader. Please note the numbering here differs slightly from the Tibetan critical edition. In editing my translation, I have benefited from Roger Jackson’s eloquent translation in his Mind Seeing Mind.

f.d: mdo rgyud man ngag rgya mtsho'i bcud bsdus nas/ / legs par 'doms mdzad dge ldan bka' brgyud pa/ / grub mchog d+ha rmA badz+ra yab sras kyi/ / bka' srol phyag rgya chen po'i gdams pa bri/ /[2]

2 I will compose here the instructions of the mahāmudrā oral tradition of the most realized Dharmavajra, father and son, the upholders of the sacred Geden lineage who distilled the essence of the sea of sutra, tantra, and pith instructions and transmitted it well.
'di la sbyor dngos mjug gsum las/ / dang po bstan dang theg chen la/ / 'jug pa'i sgo dang gzhung shing phyir/ / kha tsam tshig tsam ma yin pa'i/ / skyabs 'gro sems bskyed nan tan bya/ /[3]

3 Here, of the three — preparation, main practice, and conclusion — since it’s the doorway and support beam of the teaching and the Mahayana, strive first in going for refuge and arousing awakening, not just with your mouth and with words alone.
sems kyi chos nyid mthong ba yang/ / tshogs bsags sgrib sbyang la bltos pas/ / yig brgya 'bum tsam ltung bshags ni/ / brgya phyag gang mang sngon btang nas/ /[4]

4 And since seeing the mind’s true nature depends on gathering merit and purifying obscurations, proceed first by reciting the hundred-syllable mantra a hundred thousand times and repeating hundreds of times the Confession of Downfalls with prostrations.
dus gsum sangs rgyas thams cad dang / / dbyer med rtsa ba'i bla ma la/ / snying nas gsol 'debs yang yang bya//[5]
5 To your root guru, who is inseparable from all the buddhas of the three times, make heartfelt supplications again and again.
dngos gzhi phyag rgya chen po la/ / bzhed tshul mang du 'dug na yang / / mdo sngags dbye bas gnyis su yod/ /[6]
6 With regard to the main practice of mahāmudrā, though there seem to be numerous perspectives, it is divisible in terms of two: sutra and tantra.
phyi ma rdo rje'i lus nyid la/ / gnad du bsnun sogs thabs mkhas las/ / byung ba'i bde chen 'od gsal te/ /
7 The latter is the clear light of great bliss that arises from skillful means such as penetrating the vital points in the vajra body.
sa ra ha dang klu sgrub zhabs/ /[7] nA ro mai tri'i phyag chen te/ / grub snying skor nas bstan pa yi/ / bla med rgyud sde'i yang snying yin//[ 8]
8 This is the mahāmudrā of Saraha and Nāgārjuna, of Nāropa and Maitripa, taught in the Attainment and Essence texts[1061] and is the quintessence of unexcelled tantras.

d.div: [1061] These refer to the Seven Attainment Texts (grub pa sde bdun) and the Essence Trilogy (snying po skor gsum). On the identification of these texts, see the Lamp So Bright autocommentary below, page 686.

f.d: sngon ma rgyas 'bring bsdus gsum gyis// dngos bstan stong nyid bsgom tshul te/ / 'di las gzhan pa'i thar pa'i lam/ / med ces 'phags mchog klu sgrub gsungs/ /[9]

9 As for the former, this refers to the way of meditating on emptiness taught explicitly in the long, medium, and short [Perfection of Wisdom]. The supreme ārya, Nāgārjuna, has stated that there is no path to liberation apart from this.
'dir ni de yi dgongs pa bzhin/ / phyag rgya chen po'i khrid phog ste/ / sems kyi ngo sprod byed pa'i tshul/ / rgyud ldan bla ma'i gsung bzhin brjod//[10]
10 Here I will present a guide to mahāmudrā that accords with his thought [498] and expound a way to introduce the mind’s nature that accords with the teaching of the lineage gurus.

lhan cig skyed sbyor ga'u ma/ / lnga ldan ro snyoms yi ge bzhi/ / zhi byed gcod yul rdzogs chen dang / / dbu ma'i lta khrid la sogs pa/ /[11] so sor ming 'dogs mang na yang / / nges don lung rigs la mkhas shing / / nyams myong can gyi rnal 'byor pas/ / dpyad na dgongs pa gcig tu 'bab/ /[12]

11–12 The Innate Union, the Amulet Box, the Fivefold, Equal Taste, and the Four-Lettered, Pacification, Cutting Off, and the Great Perfection, the Guide to the Middle Way View, and so on — though many teachings exist, each with a different name, when examined by a yogi who is versed in definitive scriptures and reasoning and who possesses meditative experience, they come down to a single intention.
des na 'di la lta thog nas/ / sgom pa 'tshol dang sgom thog nas/ / lta ba 'tshol ba'i lugs gnyis las/ / 'dir ni phyi ma'i lugs bzhin yin//[13]
13 Thus, of two approaches — seeking meditation on the basis of the view and seeking the view on the basis of meditation — the presentation here is the latter approach.
bsam gtan bde ba'i stegs bu la/ / lus gnad bdun dang ldan byas la/ / rlung ro dgu phrugs dag tu bsal/ / rig pa dwangs snyigs legs par phye/ /[14]

14 On a platform conducive to meditative absorption, your body maintaining the seven-point posture, dispel the stale winds through the nine-round breathing and distinguish well the fresh and sullied awareness.
/rnam dag dge ba'i sems ldan pas/ / skyabs 'gro sems bskyed sngon du btang / / zab lam bla ma'i rnal 'byor bsgom/ / shugs drag gsol 'debs brgya rtsa sogs/ / byas nas bla ma rang la bstim/ /[15]

15 With a pure virtuous state of mind, proceed first with going for refuge and arousing the awakening mind, and then practice the profound path of guru yoga. After performing fervent supplications a hundred times or so, dissolve the guru into you.
snang ba ban bun ngang de la/ / re dogs la sogs rnam rtog gis/ / bcas bcos gang yang mi byed pa/ / g.yo med cung zad mnyam par gzhog /[16]
16 While in that state where appearances are indistinct, do not alter it or add anything to it by thoughts of hope, fear, and so on, but rest unwavering in equipoise for a while.

brgyal dang gnyid log lta bu yi/ / yid byed bkag pa ma yin pa/ / ma yengs dran pa'i rgyang so tshugs/ / 'gyu ba rig pa'i shes bzhin sdogs/ /[17] rig cing gsal ba'i ngo bo la/ / hrim gyis bsgrims la gcer gyis ltos/ /

17 Do not cease mental activity as in fainting or falling asleep; post the sentry of undistracted mindfulness and station meta-awareness to detect any movement. Hold the clear and aware nature of mind with a firm focus and starkly look at it.
rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa/ / de dang de nyid ngos zin bya/ /[18] yang na ral bskor mkhan bzhin du/ / rnam rtog ci skyes rbad rbad gcod/ /
18 Whatever thoughts arise, any thought, note it as that and just that. Alternatively, like a skilled swordsman, swiftly cut down the thoughts as they arise.
bcad mthar gnas pa de yi tshe/ / dran pa ma shor lhod kyis glod/ /[19] hrim gyis bsgrims la lhod kyis glod/ / sems kyis 'jog sa de na gda'/ /
19 When, after cutting down, your mind is stable, then, without losing mindfulness, loosen and relax: “Focus with firmness but loosen and relax; there lies the spot to rest your mind.”[1062]

d.div: [1062] In Lamp So Bright, Panchen attributes this to Machik Labdrön; see page 661.

f.d: zhes dang gzhan yang ji skad du/ / 'jur bus bcings pa'i sems nyid ni/ / glod na grol ba the tshom med/[1] / ces gsungs pa ltar ma yengs glod//[20]
20 So it is stated; and elsewhere it says, “This mind, bound in its own entanglement, when relaxed becomes free, no doubt.”[1063] As taught here, relax without distraction.

d.div: [1] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod kyi glu/ shog_73_na4
[1063] Saraha, Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti), Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 73a4.

f.d: rnam rtog gang skyes ngo bo la/ / bltas tshe rang yal stong sang 'char/ / de bzhin gnas tshe'ang brtags pa na/ / ma bsgrib stong gsal hrig ge ba/ /[21]

21 Whatever thoughts arise, when you observe their nature, they naturally disappear, and a pure vacuity appears. Likewise, when you examine the settled mind as well, you see an unobstructed vacuity and vivid clarity.
mthong ba gnas 'gyu 'dres pa zhes/ / grags shing rnam rtog ci skyes kyang / / mi 'gog 'gyu ba ngos zin par/ / byas te de yi ngo bo la/ /[22]
22 This is called “merging of stillness and movement.” And whatever thoughts may arise, do not stop them, but recognize their movement and place your mind upon their nature.
'jog pa rdzings kyi bya brtson ni/ / 'phur ba'i dpe dang mtshungs pa yin/ / ji ltar gzings nas 'phur ba'i bya rog ni/ / phyogs rnams bskor nas slar yang der 'bab bzhin/[2] /[23]
23 This is analogous to the flights of a bird captive on a ship: “It’s like the raven that takes off from a ship, [499] flies to every direction, and lands there again.”[1064]

d.div: [2] sde dge_2273_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod ces bya ba phyag rgya chen po'i man ngagashog_123_na6
[1064] Ibid., 74b5; a slightly different version appears in Saraha’s Treasury of Dohās (Dohākoṣamahāmudropadeśa, Toh 2273).

f.d: zhes pa ji bzhin bskyangs pa las/ / mnyam gzhag ngo bo gang gis kyang / / ma sgribs dwangs shing gsal ba dang / / gzugs can gang du ma grub pas/ / stong sang nam mkha' lta bu dang / / ci yang 'char bas hrig ge ba/ /[24]

24 In this way, as you maintain meditative equipoise, its essence will dawn as unobscured by anything, as lucid and clear and, since it does not exist in any physical way, as a pure vacuity just like space, where everything appears vividly.
de ltar sems kyi chos nyid ni/ / mngon sum lhag gis mthong mod kyang/ / 'di zhes gzung zhing bstan du med/ / gang shar 'dzin med lhug par 'jog /[25]
25 Thus though the mind’s true nature may be seen as if in a direct manner, it cannot be grasped at or shown as “this.” Whatever appears, without grasping, rest your mind.
'di ni sangs rgyas sbar bcangs su/ / gtod pa'i gdams ngag yin no zhes/ / deng sang gangs ri'i sgom chen pa/ / phal cher dgongs pa gcig gis sgrog /[26]
26 “This is the special instruction to grab buddhahood with one’s bare hands.” So proclaim most present-day meditators of the Land of Snows, with a shared understanding.
de ltar mod kyi tshul 'di ni/ / dang po'i las can sems gnas pa/ / bsgrub pa'i rmad byung thabs mkhas dang / / sems kyi kun rdzob ngo sprod tshul/ / yin zhes chos kyi rgyal mtshan smra/ /[27]

27 Be that as it may, I, Chökyi Gyaltsen, would say the following: “This is an excellent method for the beginner to cultivate mental stillness and the way to introduce the mind’s conventional nature.”

da ni sems kyi chos nyid la/ / ngo sprod ji ltar bya ba'i tshul/ / sangs rgyas rnams kyi ye shes kun/ / ngur smrig 'dzin pa'i tshul bzung dang / / bdag blo rmongs pa'i mun sel ba'i/ / rtsa ba'i bla ma'i zhal gdams 'god/ /[28]

28 Now, as for the way to introduce the mind’s true nature, I will set this forth following the oral instructions of my root guru: as a saffron-clad monk, the embodiment of the gnoses of all the buddhas,[1065] dispelling the darkness of ignorance from my mind.

d.div: [1065] “Gnoses of the buddhas” is a gloss on the name of Panchen’s root guru, Sangyé (buddha) Yeshé (gnosis).

f.d: sngar gyi mnyam gzhag ngang nyid las/ / ma g.yos dwangs pa'i chu nang du/ / ji ltar nye'u chung 'khyug pa ltar/ / phra mo'i shes pas sgom pa po'i/ / skyes bus rang bzhin mdzangs par brtag /[29]
29 While in that foregoing meditative equipoise, unwavering, and just like a minnow darting about in clear water, analyze skillfully with subtle awareness the nature of that person who is meditating.
'phags pa klu sgrub skyob nyid kyis/ / skyes bu sa min chu ma yin/ / me min rlung min nam mkha' min/ / rnam shes ma yin kun min na/ / de las gzhan na skyes bu gang / /[30]
30 The savior Ārya Nāgārjuna himself says: “The person is not earth nor water, is not fire, wind, nor space, is not consciousness — nor is it all of them. Where then, apart from these, is the person?
skyes bu khams drug 'dus pa'i phyir/ / yang dag ma yin ji lta bar/ / de bzhin khams ni re re yang / / 'dus phyir yang dag nyid du min/[3] /[31]
31 The person is a composite of six elements; as such it has no real existence. Likewise, each element too is in turn a composite and hence has no real existence.”[1066]

d.div: [3] sde dge_1458_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_80_dang _81_shog_9_ba7
[1066] Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī), 1.80–81, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109b7.

f.d: gsungs pa ji bzhin btsal ba na/ / mnyam gzhag mnyam par 'jog mkhan sogs/ / rdul phran tsam yang ma rnyed pa/ / de tshe g.yeng med rtse gcig tu/ / nam mkha' lta bu'i mnyam gzhag skyong / /[32]

32 In accordance with this statement, when you search, not even a minute particle will be found of the meditative equipoise, the one who is in equipoise, and so forth. At that point, maintain the space-like equipoise without distraction and single-pointedly.

yang na mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngang / / gzugs su ma grub stong sang nge / / sgrib med sna tshogs 'char zhing 'phro/ / 'gag med gsal zhing rig pa'i rgyun/ /[33] chad pa med pa 'jug pa'i sems/ / ltos med snang zhing 'dzin pa yi/ / zhen yul mgon po zhi ba lhas/ /

33–34 Alternatively, while in meditative equipoise, observe your mind as thus characterized: pure vacuity because it does not exist as physical; unobscured as diverse appearances arise to it; and unceasing, a luminous and aware continuum that is uninterrupted in its engagement. Such a mind appears and is conceived as independent, but with respect to such objects of clinging, the guardian Śāntideva states:
rgyud dang tshogs zhes bya ba ni/ /[34] phreng ba dmag sogs bzhin du brdzun/[4] / zhes gsungs lung dang rigs pa yis/ / snang tshul ltar du ma grub pa'i/ / ngang du rtse gcig mnyam par gzhog /[35]

35 “The so-called continuums and collections, just like rosaries, armies, and so on, are false.”[1067] So through scripture such as this and reasoning, [500] establish this truth of how things do not exist as they appear and rest your mind single-pointedly in this meditative equipoise.

d.div: [4] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_101_shog_27_ba1
[1067] Guide to the Bodhisattva Way (Bodhicaryāvatāra), 9.101, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 27b1.

f.d: mdor na bdag gi dge ba'i bshes/ / don dang mthun pa'i thams cad mkhyen/ / sangs rgyas ye shes zhal snga nas/ /[ 36]
36 In brief, as my spiritual mentor, the omniscient Sangyé Yeshé, who is in accord with reality, states:
gang shar rnam rtog 'dzin par yongs rig na/ / don dam chos dbyings gzhan la ltos med 'char/ / shar ba'i ngang du rig pa zhugs pa la/ / rtse gcig mnyam par 'jog pa e ma ho/[5] /[37]

37 “When you are fully aware that whatever appears is conceived by thoughts, then the ultimate expanse dawns independently of anything else. When your awareness enters into what has thus dawned, you rest in single-pointed meditative equipoise — E ma ho!”[1068]

d.div: [5] mkhas grub sangs rgyas ye shes kyi gsung 'bum/ le tshan ca/ gsung mgur chab shogadris lan sogs phyogs gcig tu sdebs pa/ shog_67_ba6
[1068] Khedrup Sangyé Yeshé, Collection of Experiential Songs, Letters, and Replies to Queries, 67b6.

f.d: zhes gsungs de bzhin dam pas kyang / / stong pa'i ngang du rig pa'i mdung bskor bya/ / lta ba la thogs thug med do ding ri ba/[6] / zhes sogs dgong pa gcig tu gnas//[38]
38 In the same vein, Dampa Sangyé says: “Whirl the spear of awareness within emptiness; the view, O people of Dingri, is unobstructed.”[1069] These statements and their likes make the same point.

d.div: [6] dam pa sangs rgyas kyi zhal gdams ding ri brgyad cu pa/ dpal spungs dpar ma'i gdams ngag mdzod pod dgu pa/ shog_17_ba4_stong pa'i ngang du rig pa'i mdung skor gyis/ /lta ba thogs rdugs med do ding ri ba//
[1069] Dampa Sangyé, Hundred Verses of Advice, verse 51, 17a4.

f.d: rjes ni phyag chen bsgom pa las/ / byung ba'i rnam dkar ci mchis pa/ / dus gsum dge tshogs rgya mtshor bcas/ / bla med byang chub chen por bsngo/ /[39]
39 At the conclusion, the virtues that have emerged from meditating on mahāmudrā together with the ocean of virtues of all three times, dedicate these all to the great, unexcelled enlightenment.
de ltar goms nas tshogs drug gis/ / yul du snang ba ci shar yang / / snang tshul zhib mor rtogs shig dang / / gnas tshul rjen par lhang gis 'char/ / gang shar ngos 'dzin lta bu'i gnad/ /[40]

40 Thus, having gained familiarity [with this practice], realize precisely the mode of appearance of any object that appears within the field of your six senses, and its mode of being will dawn naked and vivid. Recognizing whatever appears is the key point of the view.[1070]

d.div: [1070] This line is part of a well-known instruction attributed to the Indian mystic Mitrayogi; see page 722.

f.d: mdor na rang sems la sogs pa/ / gang gang snang ba'i don de ni/ / ma 'dzin de de'i gnas tshul de/ / nges par gyis la rtag tu skyong //[41] 'di ltar shes nas 'khor 'das kyi/ / chos kun rang bzhin gcig tu sbyor/ /

41 In brief, whatever appears — be it your own mind or something else — do not grasp but ascertain its mode of being and always maintain that awareness. Knowing this, bring all phenomena of samsara and nirvana into a single nature.
de skad du yang 'phags pa lhas/ /[42] dngos po gcig gi lta po gang / / de ni kun gyi lta por bshad/ / gcig gi stong nyid gang yin pa/ / de ni kun gyi stong nyid yin/[7] /[43]
42 Here, Āryadeva says: “The viewer of one thing is stated to be the viewer of all, and the emptiness of one is the emptiness of all.”[1071]

d.div: [7] sde dge_3846_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsha_'phags pa lha/ bzhi brgya pa/ rab byed/ 8_sh+loka_16_shog_9_ba6
[1071] Four Hundred Verses (Catuḥśataka), 8.16, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 9b6.

f.d: ces gsungs de ltar chos nyid la/ / tshul bzhin mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngor/ / yod med la sogs 'khor 'das kyi/ / spros pa'i mtha' dang bral med kyi/ /[44]
43 Thus, within the perfect meditative equipoise on this ultimate nature of reality, you are free from the elaborated extremes of existence and nonexistence and of samsara and nirvana.
de las langs nas brtag pa'i tshe/ / ming kyang btags yod tsam zhig gi / bya byed rten 'brel bsnyon med par/ / rmi lam smig rgyu chu zla dang / / sgyu mar lta bur ngang gis 'char/ /[45]

44 Yet when you arise from that equipoise and examine, it is undeniable that actions, agents, and dependent originations of mere labels and mere concepts naturally appear — like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon in water, or like a magician’s illusion.
snang bas stong pa mi bsgrib cing / / stong pas snang ba mi 'gog pa/ / stong dang rten 'byung don gcig pa'i/ / lam bzang de tshe mngon sum 'gyur//[46]

45 When appearance does not obscure emptiness and when emptiness does not obstruct appearance, the excellent path — where emptiness and dependent origination share the same meaning — will then manifest.
de skad smra ba mang thos spong ba pa/ / blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan zhes bya ste/ / dge bas 'gro kun zhi sgo gnyis pa dang / / bral ba'i lam 'dis myur du rgyal gyur cig/[47]

46 These were uttered by a renunciant who has heard widely, someone who is called Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen. From this virtue may all beings swiftly become victorious through this path, for there is no second path to peace.

ces phyag rgya chen po'i ngo sprod byed tshul 'di yang / 'di nang gi chos brgyad smyon pa'i zlos gar ltar mthong nas/ dben pa'i ri sul du drang srong gi spyod tshul gyis 'dug nas/ lam 'di la nyams len snying por byed pa gnas bcu rab 'byams pa dge 'dun rgyal mtshan dang ha mthong ka bcu pa shes rab seng ge gnyis kyis snga mo nas yang yang bskul zhing / gzhan yang nges don phyag chen gyi nyams len byed par 'dod pa'i rang gi slob ma mang pos bskul ba dang / khyad par rje grub pa'i dbang phyug thams cad mkhyen pa rgyal ba dben sa pa chen po de nyid kyis/ rang gzhan la 'doms par mdzad pa'i nyams mgur zhig tu bshes gnyen bsten tshul zhi lhag gi bar bka' gdams lam rim ltar gdams nas/ mjug tu
bshad ma thag pa'i lam 'di ma yin pa/ da lta'i gangs can sa la ma grags pa'i/ phyag rgya chen po'i gdams ngag mthar thug pa/ da lta yi ger 'god par mi nus so/[8] / zhes de dus dgag bya'i dbang gis mi 'god pa phyi dus la dgongs pa/

This method of pointing out mahāmudrā was written in response to long-standing repeated requests from the master of ten topics Rabjampa Gendun Gyatso and the master of ten treatises Hamdong Sherab Sengé, who, having seen the eight worldly concerns of this life as the play of a madman, live in mountains of solitude as wandering mendicants embracing this path as their heart practice. I have also been approached by many students who have the desire to engage in the practice of definitive mahāmudrā. In one of his experiential songs addressed to both himself and to others, the lord among the siddhas, the omniscient Ensapa the Great himself, gives instructions on the stages of the path according to the Kadam teachings, beginning from the topic of proper reliance on the spiritual mentor up to tranquil abiding and insight. At the end he says:
Not the path I have just outlined, and not known at present in this Land of Snows, there is the definitive instruction on mahāmudrā. At this point, though, I dare not commit it to writing.[1072] There are examples of teaching that, on account of present obstacles, may not be committed to writing but are intended for a later time.

d.div: [8] dben sa ba blo bzang don grub kyi gsung 'bum/ ka_rang la gdams pa bde chen gter mdzod sogs thor bu'i skor/ shog_23_ba6

[1072] Ensapa Losang Döndrup, Great Bliss Treasury (in Miscellaneous Writings), 52. I have read the first line according to how it appears in Ensapa’s own text, where the first line, in fact, reads: “Not included in the path I have just outlined” (bshad ma thag pa’i lam ’dir ma gtogs pa).

f.d:
dper na dam chos pad dkar du/
sangs rgyas ye shes rab tu rtogs bya'i phyir/ / thabs 'di rang byung gis ni mdzad gyur gyi/ / de dag rnams la khyed cag sangs rgyas su/ / 'gyur ro zhes ni nam yang mi gsung ngo / / ci phyir zhe na skyob pa dus la gzigs/[9] /zhes gsungs pa dang 'dra ba'i bzhed pa bsgrub pa'i phyir/ ston pa mnyam med shAkya'i rgyal po nas bzung ste/ bdag gi rtsa ba'i bla ma thams cad mkhyen cing gzigs pa sangs rgyas ye shes zhabs kyi zhal snga nas kyi bar/ lam 'di mngon sum du thugs nyams su bstar ba'i byin rlabs kyi brgyud pa ma nyams shing / dam tshig la sel ma zhugs pa'i rigs su byung zhing mdo rgyud dam pa'i man ngag 'dzin pa'i spong ba pa blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan gyis/ dge ldan rnam par rgyal ba'i gling du sbyar ba'o// //

There is, for example, the following statement in the Sublime Dharma of the White Lotus:
