When illnesses arise in your body, it’s to fuse the expanse and your awareness into one. When subtle conceptualization arises, it’s to level out and destroy the afflictions. When sleeping alone in private, it’s to place yourself in bare awareness. When in the midst of others, it’s to behold the nature of whatever arises. When becoming lax, it’s to rouse yourself with the sound of phat! When your mind is dispersed, it’s to cut its very root. When excitation arises, it’s to rest your mind in the expanse. When the mind is chasing an external object, it’s to behold the real nature of the object.
This sublime teaching, the pacification of suffering: when bad omens occur, embrace them as lucky charms; whatever concepts arise, just delight in them; when sickness occurs, take them as boons; [520] whatever befalls you, just delight in it; when death occurs, take it into the path; whatever pleases the lord of death, just delight in it.
This sublime teaching, the pacification of suffering, is the intent of the conquerors of the three times.[1144]

d.div: [50] dam chos sdug bsngal zhi byed kyi snying por dril ba'i rdo rje'i mgur/ pha dam pa sangs rgyas kyis rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug mi la ras pa la gdams pa/ gdams ngag mdzod pod dgu ba/ shog_18_ba6
[1144] Dampa Sangyé, Vajra Song, 18b6.

f.d:
gcod yul ni dam pa'i gdams pa ma cig gi zab chos te yongs su grags pa ltar dang / rdzogs chen man ngag lta ba'i 'phreng ba sogs slob dpon pad+ma'i thugs kyi bcud phyung ba rnams dang / zab mo dbu ma'i lta khrid ces bya ba la sogs pa/ gdams don la so sor 'dogs byed kyi ming mi 'dra ba sna tshogs pas btags na yang / drang nges ji bzhin 'byed pa'i lung rigs mkhas pas legs par dpyad na/ phan tshun tsha grang ltar mi 'gal bar dgongs pa gcig tu 'bab ste/ dri med 'od las/
ji ltar sa la rin chen ming / / dbye ba tha dad tha dad ni/ / yul dang yul gyi dbang gis brjod/ / rin chen dbye ba 'gar yang med/[51] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro//

As for Cutting Off, it is the profound teaching of Machik representing the instruction of Dampa and is quite widely known. In addition, there are instructions such as the Great Perfection — distilling the heart teachings of Guru Padmasambhava, including his Garland of Views: A Pith Instruction — the Guide to the Middle Way View, and so forth. Although all these instructions are given varied and different names, when the wise who are versed in the scriptures and reasoning distinguish the provisional and the definitive meanings exactly as they are, they see that they all come down to a single intention and are not in contradiction, like heat and cold. This is as stated in Stainless Light:
The same jewel is called on the earth by different names from one region to the next, yet no difference exists in its preciousness.[1145]

d.div: [51] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_rigs ldan pad+ma dkar po'i 'grel chen dri med 'od/ khams kyi le'u/ shog_22_na3
[1145] Puṇḍarīka, Vimalaprabhā, Toh 845 Kangyur, dus ’khor, shrī, 22a3.

f.d: bsgom pa'i rim pa
2.2.1.1. The actual meditation

'o na phyag rgya chen po de bsgom pa'i rim pa ji ltar zhe na smras pa/
des na 'di la lta thog nas/ / bsgom pa 'tshol dang sgom thog nas// lta ba 'tshol ba'i lugs gnyis las/ / 'di ni phyi ma'i lugs bzhin yin//[13]
ces pa ste/

If asked, “What then is the sequence in mahāmudrā meditation?” I say:
13 Thus, of two approaches — seeking meditation on the basis of the view and seeking the view on the basis of meditation — the presentation here is the latter approach.

lugs gnyis po ji ltar byas kyang yod mod/ 'on kyang mgon po zhi ba lhas/
zhi gnas rab tu ldan pa'i lhag mthong gis/ / nyon mongs rnam par 'joms par shes byas nas/ / thog mar zhi gnas btsal bya/[52] / zhes dang / dkon brtsegs las kyang /
tshul khrims la ni gnas nas ting nge 'dzin thob ste/ ting nge 'dzin thob nas kyang shes rab sgom par byed/[53] ces bka' stsal pa ltar sgom thog nas lta ba 'tshol ba'i lugs so//

There are thus two approaches, and either of them may be adopted. As the guardian Śāntideva says:
Knowing that insight endowed with tranquil abiding destroys the afflictions completely, first seek tranquil abiding.[1146] And the Heap of Jewels Sutra says:
Abiding in morality, you achieve meditative absorption, and having attained absorption, cultivate wisdom.[1147] As stated in these citations, the approach presented here is to seek the view on the basis of meditation.

d.div: [52] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha'i spyod 'jug_le'u brgyad pa/ sh+loka bzhi pa/ shog_23_ba1
[53] sde dge_87_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ cha_'od srung gi le'u bzhi bcu rtsa gsum pa/ shog_46_ba5
[1146] Guide to the Bodhisattva Way (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 8.4, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23b1.
[1147] Questions of the Bodhisattva Jñānottara (Jñānottarabodhisattvaparipṛcchā), Toh 82 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, cha, 46b5.

f.d: [zhi gnas sgom tshul ]
2.2.1.1.1. Cultivating tranquil abiding
de ltar yin na thog mar zhi gnas sgom tshul gang zhe na/ 'di la sbyor ba dang / dngos gzhi gnyis las/
Since this is the case, what is the way to cultivate tranquil abiding first? This is twofold: the preparation and the main practice. [521]
dang po [sbyor ba ]ni/
2.2.1.1.1.1. The preparation

rje btsun byams pas/
blo ldan gang du bsgrub pa'i yul/ / legs par rnyed dang gnas bzang dang / sa bzang ba dang grogs bzang dang / / rnal 'byor bde ba'i yo byad ldan/[54] / zhes gsungs pa'i gnas su tshul khrims rnam par dag pa la gnas bcas shing / 'dod chung chog shes dang ldan pas/ zhi gnas kyi yan lag gam tshogs bsten pa sogs dang / sbyor ba'i chos drug rnams nges par bsgrub dgos so zhes bshad pa/

The exalted Maitreya says:
In what sort of place do the wise practice meditation? It should be easily accessible and have a pleasant environment, where the ground is good and companions good and where the yogi has the necessities for comfort.[1148] So in a place thus described, abide with pure morality, with few desires and content with what you have, and seek the conditions or collections relevant to tranquil abiding. Certainly, you should also engage in the six preparatory practices. So I say:

d.div: [54] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u bcu bzhi pa/ sh+loka bdun pa/ shog_17_ba7
[1148] Ornament of Mahayana Sutras (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra) 14.7, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 17b7.

f.d:
bsam gtan bde ba'i stegs bu la/ / lus gnad bdun dang ldan byas nas// rlung ro dgu phrugs dag tu bsal/ / rig pa dwangs snyigs legs par phyed//[14]
rnam dag dge ba'i sems ldan pas/ / skyabs 'gro sems bskyed sngon du btang // zab lam bla ma'i rnal 'byor bsgom/ / shugs drag gsol 'debs brgya rtsa sogs/ / byas nas bla ma rang la bstim/ /[15]
zhes pa ste

div.div: 14 On a platform conducive to meditative absorption, your body maintaining the seven-point posture, dispel the stale winds through the nine-round breathing and distinguish well the fresh and sullied awareness.

15 With a pure virtuous state of mind, proceed first with going for refuge and arousing the awakening mind, and then practice the profound path of guru yoga. After performing fervent supplications a hundred times or so, dissolve the guru into you.

f.d: rnam dag dge sems ni byang chub kyi sems dang / zab lam bla ma'i rnal 'byor ni lam gyi cha yongs su rdzogs pa'i bla ma'i rnal 'byor te zur du bkod pa lta bu yin la gzhan ni go bar zad do/ /

“A pure virtuous state of mind” refers to the awakening mind, while “the profound path of guru yoga” is a guru yoga that encompasses all aspects of the path, such as the one I have composed separately.[1149] The rest can be understood easily.

d.div: [1149] That is, the Offering to the Guru (Guru Pūjā), chapter 7 in the present volume.

f.d: [dngos gzhi ]
2.2.1.1.1.2. The main practice the method for cultivating mental stillness
de ltar sbyor ba'i rim pa sngon du btang nas/ sems gnas bsgrub pa'i thabs bshad pa/
Having begun first with the preparatory stages, I will explain the method for cultivating mental stillness:

div.div: snang ba ban bun ngang de la/ / re dogs la sogs rnam rtog gis// bcas bcos gang yang mi byed pa/ / g.yo med cung zad mnyam par zhog/[16]
16 While in that state where appearances are indistinct, do not alter it or add anything to it by thoughts of hope, fear, and so on, but rest unwavering in equipoise for a while.

brgyal dang gnyid log lta bu yi/ / yid byed bkag pa ma yin pa// ma yengs dran pa'i rgyang so tshugs/ / 'gyu ba rig pa'i shes bzhin bsngogs//[17] rig cing gsal ba'i ngo bo la/ / hrim gyis bsgrims la gcer gyis ltos//

17 Do not cease mental activity as in fainting or falling asleep; post the sentry of undistracted mindfulness and station meta-awareness to detect any movement. Hold the clear and aware nature of mind with a firm focus and starkly look at it. [522]
rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa/ / de dang de nyid ngos zin bya//[18] yang na ral skor mkhan bzhin du/ / rnam rtog ci skyes rbad rbad gcod//
18 Whatever thoughts arise, any thought, note it as that and just that. Alternatively, like a skilled swordsman, swiftly cut down the thoughts as they arise.
bcad mthar gnas pa de yi tshe/ / dran pa ma shor lhod kyis glod//[19] hrim gyis bsgrims la lhod kyis glod/ / sems kyi 'jog sa de na gda'//[55]

div.b: 19 When, after cutting down, your mind is stable, then, without losing mindfulness, loosen and relax: “Focus with firmness but loosen and relax; there lies the spot to rest your mind.”

d.div: [55] ma cig gi lung 'tshol zhib byed kyang ma rnyed/

div.div: zhes dang gzhan yang ji skad du/ / 'jur bus bcings pa'i sems nyid ni// glod na grol bar the tshom med/[56] / ces gsungs pa ltar ma yengs glod/ /[20]
20 So it is stated; and elsewhere it says, “This mind, bound in its own entanglement, when relaxed becomes free, no doubt.” As taught here, relax without distraction.

d.div: [56] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod kyi glu/ shog_73_na4

div.div: rnam rtog gang skyes ngo bo la/ / bltas tshe rang yal stong sang 'char// de bzhin gnas tshe'ang brtags pa na/ / ma bsgribs stong gsal hrig ge ba//[21]

21 Whatever thoughts arise, when you observe their nature, they naturally disappear, and a pure vacuity appears. Likewise, when you examine the settled mind as well, you see an unobstructed vacuity and vivid clarity.

f.d: mthong ba gnas 'gyu 'dres pa zhes/ / grags shing rnam rtog ci skyes kyang // mi 'gog 'gyu ba ngos zin par/ / byas te de yi ngo bo la/ /[22] 'jog pa rdzings kyi bya btson ni/ / 'phur ba'i dpe dang mtshungs pa yin// ji ltar gzings nas 'phur ba'i bya rog ni/ / phyogs rnams bskor nas slar yang der 'bab bzhin//[23] zhes pa ji bzhin bskyangs pa las//[57] zhes so/ /

div.div: 22 This is called “merging of stillness and movement.” And whatever thoughts may arise, do not stop them, but recognize their movement and place your mind upon their nature. 23 This is analogous to the flights of a bird captive on a ship: “It’s like the raven that takes off from a ship, flies to every direction, and lands there again.”

d.div: [57] sde dge_2273_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod ces bya ba phyag rgya chen po'i man ngag_shog_123_na6

f.d:
de yang 'dir bsgrub par bya ba'i ting nge 'dzin gyi ngo bo ni gsal ba'i ngar dang ldan pa dang / rtse gcig pa'i mi rtog pa yan lag gnyis dang ldan pa'i ting nge 'dzin yin no/ / de lta bu'i zhi gnas mtshan nyid pa ni/ mnyam par ma gzhag pa'i sa pa 'dod sems rtse gcig pa'i ting nge 'dzin las byung ba yin la/ de ni mgon po byams pas/
nyes pa lnga spong 'du byed brgyad/ / bsten pa'i rgyu las byung ba'o/[58] / zhes nyes pa lnga spong ba'i gnyen po 'du byed brgyad bsten pa las byung ba'i sems gnas pa dgus 'grub par gsungs la/ sems dgu po de yang 'phags pa thogs med kyis sa sder stobs drug gis 'grub cing / yid byed bzhi dang ldan par gsungs so/ /[59]

The concentration being cultivated here is a meditative state with two limbs: vibrant clarity and nondiscursive single-pointedness.[1150] Such authentic tranquil abiding arises based on single-pointed concentration of a desire-realm mind, a state of mind that belongs to the non-equipoised class.[1151] Here, Lord Maitreya says:
It results from reliance on the eight applications that reject the five faults.[1152] Maitreya states how tranquil abiding is attained through nine stages of stilling the mind, which in turn arise through reliance on the eight applications that are the antidotes against the five faults. In his collection on the grounds, Ārya Asaṅga explains how these nine mental stages are attained through the six powers and are characterized by four types of mental application.

d.div: [58] sde dge_4021_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ dbus dang mtha' rnam par 'byed pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa/ sh+loka_3_shog_4_na3
[59] sde dge_4036_bstan/ sems tsam/ dzi_'phags pa thogs med/ rnal 'byor spyod pa'i sa las nyan thos kyi sa/ bam po bcu gsum pa/ shog_133_ba1

[1150] The Tibetan phrase here, gsal ba’i ngar dang ldan pa dang rtse gcig pa’i mi rtog pa, could be more accurately rendered as “vibrancy born of clarity and nondiscursiveness born of single-pointedness.” In any case, Panchen is referring here to two well-known attributes of a meditative mind known more classically as clarity (gsal cha) and stability (gnas cha).

[1151] Mnyam par ma bzhag pa’i sa pa. By nature, states of mind in the desire realm are characterized by a lack of focus because of excessive attraction to sense objects. In contrast, states of mind in the form and formless realms are characterized by an absence of such distraction. They are thus said to belong to the equipoised class (mnyam par bzhag pa’i sa pa).
[1152] Differentiation of the Middle and Extremes (Madhyāntavibhāga) 4.3, Toh 4021 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 43a2. See the Fifth Dalai Lama’s explanation of these on pages 342–46 above.

f.d: 'o na dmigs rten ci 'dra zhig la dmigs nas ting nge 'dzin bsgom zhe na/ spyir bcom ldan 'das kyis ting nge 'dzin skyon med bsgrub pa'i dmigs rten la/ khyab pa'i dmigs pa/ dpyad pa rnam sbyong gi dmigs pa/ mkhas pa'i dmigs pa/ nyon mongs rnam sbyong gi dmigs pa sogs mtha' yas pa gsungs kyang /[60] gdams pa 'di'i bla ma gong ma phal cher sems la dmigs nas ngo sprod par bzhed pa ltar 'dir yang tshul de nyid do//

What kind of object does one focus on to cultivate meditative absorption? In general, the Blessed One spoke of countless types of meditation objects in the context of cultivating faultless concentration, such as the universal objects, objects that purify behavior, objects of expertise, objects that purify the afflictions, and so forth. This said, given that most gurus of this particular instruction lineage [of mahāmudrā] uphold the tradition of conducting the introduction [to tranquil abiding] by taking the mind as the focal object, I will do the same here.

d.div: [60] sde dge_106_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca_'phags pa dgongs pa nges par 'grel ba zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u brgyad pa/ shog_26_na1

f.d: de yang bla ma la mig nas mchi ma 'khrug cing lus kyi ba spu g.yo ba dang / yid mos gus drag pos snying khong rus pa'i gting nas gdung shugs drags pos gsol ba rgyun ring du btab pa'i mthar bla ma rang la thim pas byin gyis brlabs par bsam zhing snang ba ban bun du gyur pa'i ngang de la gnas skabs dang mthar thug gi don 'di 'dra zhig grub na snyam pa'i re ba dang / 'phral phugs su mi 'dod pa 'di lta bu mi yong ngam snyam du dogs pa la sogs pa'i rnam rtog gis bcas bcos gang yang mi byed pa/ sngar 'das kyi rjes mi gcod/ ma 'ongs pa'i sngun mi bsu bar/ da lta 'gyu ba gang yang med pa de'i ngang du cung zad mnyam par 'jog go /

With tears in your eyes and the hairs of your body standing up in their pores, and with your mind fervently moved by devotion and reverence, supplicate your guru for a long time from the very core or bone of your heart. At the end, when your guru dissolves into you, imagine that you have been blessed. Then, within this state where all appearances have become somewhat indistinct, do nothing by way of contrivance of conceptualization, such as entertaining the hopeful thought “If only I could accomplish such and such immediate and ultimate goals” or having anxious thoughts like “What if such and such undesirable events befall me?” Neither chasing the past nor anticipating the future, rest your mind in equipoise in the present, with no movement at all.

de ltar 'jog pa'i tshe brgyal ba dang / gnyid log pa lta bu yi yid la byed pa thams cad bkag pa ma yin pa/ sems g.yo med du gnas pa de nyid ma yengs pa ste cung zad kyang brjed pa med pa'i dran pa'i rgyang so tshugs par byed/ de ltar dmigs pa dran pa'i thag pas bcings kyang / dran pa nyams na sems 'gyu ba'i rnam rtog 'phro nyen che bas/ dran pa'i shugs zhan du song nas sems gzhan du 'gyu ba'am mi 'gyu ba rig pa'i shes bzhin bya ra ba lta bu bsdogs nas 'jog dgos te/ dbu ma snying po las/
sems kyi glang chen log 'gro ba/ / dmigs pa'i ka ba brtan po la/ / dran pa'i thag pas nges bcings te/ / shes bzhin lcags kyus rim dbang bya/[61] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro//

At the time of resting your mind in this way, unlike the total cessation of all mental engagement during fainting or falling asleep, post the sentry of mindfulness ensuring the mind that is abiding unwavering remains undistracted — that is to say, it is not lost to even the slightest forgetfulness. Even though you may tie the meditation object with the rope of mindfulness, if your mindfulness weakens, there is great danger that thoughts involving the mind’s movement could proliferate. So you need to place your mind [on the focal object] by stationing the watchman of meta-awareness, monitoring whether your mind has wandered elsewhere due to a weakening of the force of mindfulness. This is as stated in the following in Essence of the Middle Way:
This wandering elephant of mind, tie it firmly to a sturdy post, its object, with the rope of mindfulness and gradually tame it with the hook of meta-awareness.[1153] [524]

d.div: [61] sde dge_3855_bstan/ dbu ma/ dza_slob dpon legs ldan 'byed/ dbu ma snying po/ de kho na nyid kyi shes pa tshol ba'i le'u gsum pa/ shog_4_na6
[1153] Bhāviveka, Madhyamakahṛdaya, 3.16, Toh 3855 Tengyur, dbu ma, dza, 4a6 (critical edition, 62).

f.d: mdor na ting nge 'dzin skyon med bsgrub pa dran shes skyong tshul las ma 'das shing / de yang dran pa gtso bo yin te/ de byung na shes bzhin dran pa'i 'bras bur gsungs pas zhar la 'ong ngo / /

In brief, the cultivation of flawless meditative absorption constitutes nothing but the maintenance of mindfulness and meta-awareness. Here too, mindfulness the key: when mindfulness is present, meta-awareness arises as a byproduct, for meta-awareness has been described as a result of mindfulness.

de'i tshe rnam rtog gzhan 'gags nas/ sems rig cing gsal ba nges byung na de kha'i ngo bo la/ dran pa hrim gyis bsgrims la rtse gcig tu gcer gyis ltos shig de ltar bltas nas 'gyu ba'am rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa/ de dang de nyid ngos zin par bya ste/ /de ltar byed pa ni shes bzhin la rag las so/ / yang na ni 'dul ba lung las/ mda' mkhan dang ral bskor mkhan 'thab tshul gsungs pa ltar/[62] dran shes stobs bskyed nas thog brdzis su rnam rtog ci skyes pa de 'phral du rbad rbad bcad de 'phro 'thud mi 'jug pa'o// rnam rtog gi 'phro bcad pa'i mthar 'gyu ba med par gnas pa de'i tshe dran shes ma shor ba khong grims la 'phral du lhod chags pa zhig byas la mnyam gzhag gi ngang du glod dgos te/

At that point, when all other thoughts have ceased and that aware and clear mind is perceived, fasten your mindfulness with a firm focus on its nature and starkly observe it with single-pointedness. Observing in this manner, note whatever movement or thought arises and recognize it as just this or that. Doing this depends, of course, on meta-awareness. Alternatively, as explained in a Vinaya text, meditate in way in which an archer and a swordsman fight in a duel: applying the force of your mindfulness and meta-awareness, tread on whatever thoughts arise, instantly cutting them down and thus preventing them from gaining momentum. When, in the aftermath of severing the proliferation of thought, you abide free of movement, ensure that you do not lose mindfulness and meta-awareness, maintaining a state that is alert at the core and relaxed on the surface. In this manner, settle your mind relaxed in meditative equipoise.

d.div: [62] 'dul ba lung la zhal 'phangs mdzad pa de gzhung gang la dngos ngos 'dzin ma thub/

f.d:
ma cig gis/
hrim gyis bsgrims la lhod kyis glod/ / sems kyi 'jog sa de na gda'/[63] / zhes dang / gzhan yang ji skad du/ bram ze chen pos kyang /
'jur bus bcings pa'i sems nyid ni/ / glod na grol bar the tshom med/[64] / ces gsungs pa ltar khong grims la lhod chags pa zhig byas te/

As Machik writes:
Focus with firmness but loosen and relax; there lies the spot to rest your mind.[1154] Also, the Great Brahman, Saraha, says:
This mind, bound in its own entanglement, when relaxed becomes free, no doubt.[1155] So, as suggested in the above, inwardly alert, stay relaxed.

d.div: [63] ma cig gi lung 'di 'tshol zhib byed kyang ma rnyed/
[64] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod kyi glu/ shog_73_na4
[1154] Source of Machik’s quote not located.
[1155] Saraha, Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti), Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 73a4.

f.d:
'di tsam las sgrims drags na rgod pa skye ba 'dug snyam pa las cung zad glod/ 'di tsam las glod drags na bying ba skye ba 'dug snyam pa las cung zad bsgrims na ran par 'gyur bas/ de gnyis kyi mtshams su rnam rtog gi 'gyu ba las sems blan/ gnas cha byung res kyi bying zon byas nas 'jog dgos te/ slob dpon tsan+t+ra gau mis/
brtson pa babasten na rgod pa 'byung 'gyur zhing / / de spangs na ni zhum pa skye bar 'gyur/ / 'di yi rigs par mnyam 'jug rnyed dka' na/ / bdag gi sems dkrugs pas ni ci zhig bgyi/[65] / zhes 'byung ba bzhin no/ /

And when you sense your mind becoming too alert, such that excitation may arise, relax a little; and when you sense your mind becoming too relaxed, such that mental laxity may arise, strengthen your alertness a little. This way you will find just the right balance. So between those two extremes, relax your mind from the movements of thought, and watch out for occurrence of mental laxity every time stability arises. Master Candragomin writes:
If effort is applied excitation arises; if shunned slackness occurs. When it is hard to find a proper balance, my mind is perturbed, so what should I do?[1156]

d.div: [65] sde dge_1159_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon tsan dra go mi/ bshags bstod/ shog_205_ba5
[1156] Praise in the Form of a Confession (Deśanāstava), Toh 1159 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 205b5.

f.d: de dag gi dus su rnam rtog la thog brdzis byas pa dang / rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa de'i ngo bo la bltas pa de dang de'i tshe rnam rtog de dag rang yal du song ba'i stong sang 'char la/ de bzhin du sems g.yo med du gnas pa'i tshe'ang brtags pa na ma sgribs stong sang gsal hrig ge ba/ snga phyi gnyis khyad par med par mthong ba de la gnas 'gyu 'dres pa yin ces sgom chen pa rnams la grags shing tha snyad mdzad do//

During these times when you are trampling on the thoughts or looking at the face of each thought as it arises, right there and then, the thoughts will vanish on their own accord, giving rise to the dawning of a pure vacuity. Similarly, when you examine the mind as it remains without wavering, [525] you will see an unobstructed pure vacuity, a vivid clarity, with no differentiation between the earlier and the latter instances. This is known to the great meditators as “the merging of stillness and movement,” and they refer to it by such a phrase.

yang na sems gnas pa skyong thabs 'di ltar bya ste/ rnam rtog ci 'dra zhig skyes kyang / mi 'gog par gang du 'gyu gang la 'gyu ngos zin par byas te rnam rtog de'i ngo bo la blta zhing 'jog la/ de ltar bzhag pas mthar 'gyu ba 'gags nas gnas pa ni rgya mtsho chen por rdzings nang du yun ring por bzungs pa'i bya btson ni/ rgya mtsho'i nang du 'phur ba'i dpe dang mtshungs pa yin pa'i phyir te/ do ha las/
ji ltar gzings nas 'phur ba'i bya rog ni/ / phyogs rnams bskor nas slar yang der 'bab bzhin/[66] / zhes gsungs pa ji bzhin bskyang bar bya ste/ yang dgon pas/
blo rnam rtog la skyon du mi lta zhing / / mi rtog pa ched du mi sgom par/ / sems rang lugs su zhog la rgyang so tshugs dang / / sgom zhi gnas kyi steng du phebs pa cig 'ong gi/[67] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro//

Alternatively, you could engage in the following method for stilling the mind: Whatever thought arises, do not suppress it but note where it comes from and where it moves to and rest your mind by simply looking at the nature of that thought. As you rest your mind in this way, movement will eventually cease and your mind will become still. This is analogous to the flights of a bird long captive aboard a ship sailing across a vast ocean. The Dohā Treasury of Songs says:
It’s like the raven that takes off from a ship, flies to every direction, and lands there again.[1157] Maintain your meditation exactly as described here. So Yangönpa says:
Not viewing the thoughts as faults, not deliberately meditating on nonconceptuality, rest your mind in its natural mode and post a sentry, and your meditation will reach tranquil abiding.[1158]

d.div: [66] sde dge_2273_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod ces bya ba phyag rgya chen po'i man ngag_shog_123_na6

[67] phyag rgya chen po lhan cig skyes sbyor gyi thon chos/ rgyal ba yang dgon pa rgyal mtshan dpal gyi gsung 'bum/ ka_shog_11_na2_blo rtog pa la skyon du ma blta bar/ /mi rtog pa ched du ma bsgom par/ /sems rang lugs su zhog la rgyangs so tshugs dang / /sgom zhi gnas kyi thil du phebs pa cig 'ong gis//
[1157] Saraha, Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti), Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 73a4.
[1158] Yangönpa, Parting Teaching on Mahāmudrā Innate Union, 11a2.

f.d:
gzhan yang deng sang gi gdul bya rnams kyis sems kyi gzhag thabs drug gi sgo nas bskyangs na gdams pa'i rgyal por 'gyur ro/ / ji ltar zhe na/
sprin dang bral ba'i nyi bzhin bzhag / khyung chen mkha' la lding bzhin bzhag / rgya mtsho chen po'i gzings bzhin bzhag / bu chung lha khang blta bzhin bzhag / mkha' la bya 'phur rjes bzhin bzhag / ras bal brdal ba bzhin du bzhag / sems kyi bzhag thabs 'di dag gis/ / rnal 'byor don dang ldan par 'gyur/[68] / ces pa ste/

Furthermore, if today’s trainees maintain their meditation practice by means of the six methods of resting the mind, theirs will be a king among instructions. How are they done? It is said:
Rest it like the sun free from the clouds. Rest it like a great garuḍa soaring in the sky. Rest it like a ship on the great ocean. Rest it like a small child looking inside a temple. Rest it like the tracks of a bird flying in the sky. Rest it like fluffed cotton wool. By these methods of resting the mind, your yoga will be meaningful.[1159]

d.div: [68] 'di gzhung gzhan zhig nas drangs sam paN chen rang nyid nas sdom tshig tu mdzad zhu dka'/

[1159] Panchen does not cite his source. A similar citation is found, though with slightly different order of the six, in Dakpo Tashi Namgyal’s Moonbeams of Mahāmudrā, 329, where he identifies Milarepa as its source.

f.d: dang po ni/ dper na sprin dang bral ba'i nyi ma de mchog tu gsal zhing dwangs par gnas pa ltar sems kyi rang bzhin 'od gsal ba de la mtshan 'dzin gyi rnam rtog dang bying rgod sogs kyis ma sgribs pas 'gog pa'o/ /

Just as the sun when free of clouds remains supremely bright and brilliant, in the same manner, rest your mind in the luminous nature of mind unobscured by conceptual apprehension of signs, by mental laxity and excitation, and so forth.

gnyis pa ni/ dper na/ mkha' lding ni nam mkhar rgyu ba'i tshe gshog pa rdeb pa sogs rtsol ba ha cang mi dgos pa rang shugs kyis rgyu ba bzhin du/ sems ha cang grims pa dang ha cang lhod drags pa ma yin par/ khong grims pa'i gsal cha'i ngar dang ldan cing / /'phral lhod chags pas dran shes kyi rgya dang ma bral bar skyong ba'o/ /

Just as a garuḍa flying across the sky does so naturally, soaring high without needing much exertion of flapping its wings, in the same manner, maintain your meditation without straying outside the seal of mindfulness and meta-awareness — in such a way that your mind is neither too alert nor too relaxed but possesses vibrant clarity due from being alert at the core yet relaxed on the surface.

gsum pa ni/ dper na rgya mtsho chen po rlung gis bskyod kyang khar rlabs cung zad byung yang g.yo bar mi nus pa bzhin du/ sems dmigs pa la 'jog pa'i tshe/ rnam rtog phra mo 'gas cung zad g.yos kyang / rnam rtog rags pas cung zad kyang mi g.yo bar 'jog go /

Just as waves rise a little on the surface when a great ocean is stirred by winds, but the sea is not moved in its depths, [526] in the same manner, rest your mind in such a way that even if some subtle level of thought does elicit movement when you place your mind on the meditation object, it is not swayed even slightly by the coarse levels of thought.

bzhi pa ni/ dper na bu chung lha khang blta ba'i tshe/ ri mo'i cha shas phra ba la rtog dpyod mi 'jug cing / cha rags par bkra ba la mi g.yeng bar blta ba bzhin sems dmigs pa la 'jog pa'i tshe sgo lnga'i dbang shes kyi yul yid du 'ong mi 'ong ci shar yang rtog dpyod dang chags sdang mi byed par dmigs pa la rtse gcig tu 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as a small child looking inside a temple does not consider the details of the murals but stares undistracted at the large vibrant patterns, in the same manner, when your mind is focused on the meditation object, whatever objects — attractive or unattractive — may appear to your five senses, simply rest your mind single-pointedly on the meditation object without judgment and without emotions of attachment or aversion.

lnga pa ni/ dper na bya nam mkhar 'phur ba'i rjes mi 'byung ba ltar/ tshor ba bde sdug btang snyoms ci 'dra zhig byung yang / chags sdang rmongs gsum gang gi'ang dbang du mi gtong bar mnyam par 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as birds cruising across the sky leave no track, in the same manner, whatever feelings you might be experiencing, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, rest your mind in equipoise without giving in to any of the three poisons of the mind — attachment, aversion, and delusion.

drug pa ni/ dper na ras bal brdal ba'i tshe 'jam zhing khong lhod lhod por yod pa bzhin du/ mnyam par 'jog pa'i tshe sems dug gsum mngon gyur ba dang bying rgod kyi rtsub reg dang bral bar byas te mnyam par 'jog pa yin no/ /

Just as when cotton wool is fluffed it becomes softer and freer, in the same manner, when you rest your mind in equipoise, you do so free of manifest levels of the three poisons and the rough and hard textures of mental laxity and excitation.
a. Imprints resulting from maintaining meditative equipoise in this way
de ltar bskyangs pa las lag rjes ci 'dra zhig 'byung zhe na/
What imprints will emerge from maintaining meditative equipoise in the way presented above? Here I say:
mnyam gzhag ngo bo gang gis kyang / / ma sgribs dwangs shing gsal ba dang // gzugs can gang du'ang ma grub pas/ / stong sang nam mkha' lta bu dang // ci yang 'char bas hrig ge ba/ /[24] zhes pa'o//

div.div: 24 In this way, as you maintain meditative equipoise, its nature will dawn as unobscured by anything, as lucid and clear and, since it does not exist in any physical way, as a pure vacuity just like space, where everything appears vividly.

f.d: de ltar bskyangs pas mnyam gzhag gi ngo bo gang gis kyang ma sgribs pa dwangs shing shin tu gsal ba dang / gzugs can gyi dngos po gang du yang ma grub pas stong sang nam mkha' lta bu dang 'dra ba yin pa la/ yang bzang ngan gyi yul lnga ci byung yang me long dwangs pa la gzugs brnyan ltar gsal hrig ge bar ci yang 'char ba/ 'di yin 'di min gyi ngos bzung dang bral ba'i nyams 'char/ 'di 'dra ba'i ting nge 'dzin ji ltar brtan yang lus sems shin sbyangs kyi bde bas ma zin na 'dod sems rtse gcig pa dang / des zin pa'i ting nge 'dzin zhi gnas su gsungs shing / mngon shes rdzu 'phrul sogs yon tan mang po'i 'byung khungs yin pa dang / khyad par theg pa gsum ga'i 'phags lam rnams kyang 'di la brten nas 'thob pa yin no//

When you maintain meditative equipoise in this way, the following will unfold: You will experience the nature of your meditative equipoise as unobscured by anything, as lucid and utterly clear. As it does not exist in any physical way, it is a pure vacuity like space, yet like reflections appearing in an unblemished mirror, whatever objects it encounters — good or bad — appear clearly and vividly. It is undefinable by any identifications of “it is this” or “it is not that.” Now, however stable such a meditative concentration may be, if it is not imbued with physical and mental pliancy, it is said to be a single-pointedness of mind belonging to the desire realm. A meditative concentration imbued with [physical and mental pliancy, on the other hand] is described as tranquil abiding. [527] Tranquil abiding will be the source of numerous higher qualities such as clairvoyance and other supernatural feats. In particular, all the paths of the three vehicles are attained on the basis of tranquil abiding.
b. Identifying this path in terms of its own nature
'o na lam 'di nyid rang gi ngo bo'i sgo nas ci 'drar ngo sprod ce na smras pa/
How is this path to be identified with respect to its own nature? Here I say:

de ltar sems kyi chos nyid ni/ / mngon sum lhag gis mthong mod kyang / / 'di zhes gzung zhing bstan du med/ / gang shar 'dzin med lhug par 'jog /[25]
'di ni sangs rgyas sbar bcangs su/ / gtod pa'i gdams ngag yin no zhes// deng sang gangs ri'i sgom chen pa/ / phal cher dgongs pa gcig gis sgrogs//[26]
de lta mod kyi tshul 'di ni/ / dang po'i las can sems gnas pa// sgrub pa'i rmad byung thabs mkhas dang / / sems kyi kun rdzob ngo sprod tshul// yin zhes chos kyi rgyal mtshan smra/ /[27] zhes de skad du brjod do//

25 Thus though the mind’s true nature may be seen as if in a direct manner, it cannot be grasped at or shown as “this.” Whatever appears, without grasping, rest your mind.
26 “This is the special instruction to grab buddhahood with one’s bare hands.” So proclaim most present-day meditators of the Land of Snows, with a shared understanding.
27 Be that as it may, I, Chökyi Gyaltsen, would say the following: “This is an excellent method for the beginner to cultivate mental stillness and the way to identify the mind’s conventional nature.”
This is how I would respond to the question.
[sems kyi chos nyid la ngo sprod ]
2.2.1.1.2. Cultivating insight
da ni bye brag tu sems kyi chos nyid la ngo sprod ji ltar byed tshul ston par dam bca' ba/
Now, to state the promise to present the method of how to introduce the mind’s true nature, I say:

da ni sems kyi chos nyid la/ / ngo sprod ji ltar bya ba'i tshul// sangs rgyas rnams kyi ye shes kun/ / ngur smrig 'dzin pa'i tshul bzung nas// bdag blo rmongs pa'i mun sel ba'i/ / rtsa ba'i bla ma'i zhal gdams dgod//[28]
ces pa ste/

div.div: 28 Now, as for the way to introduce the mind’s true nature, I will set this forth following the oral instructions of my root guru: as a saffron-clad monk, the embodiment of the gnoses of all the buddhas,[1160] dispelling the darkness of ignorance from my mind.

d.div: [1160] “Gnoses of the buddhas” is a gloss on the name of Panchen’s root guru, Sangyé Yeshé.

f.d: gzhan rtogs sla zhing dam 'cha' tshul mi 'dra bas sngon ma rnams dang zlos pa'i skyon med do/ / des na 'di la ngo sprod tshul gyi dbye ba spyir bstan pa dang / de dag gi snying po dril nas bstan pa'o/ /

The meaning here is easy to comprehend. Since the promise here is of a different nature, there is no fault of redundancy with respect to the earlier ones.[1161] Thus here there is (1) a general presentation of the various ways of introducing [the mind’s ultimate nature] and (2) the distilled essence of those ways of introducing. [528]

d.div: [1161] Panchen is saying that, even though the reader has encountered two earlier promises for what he intends to present — one at the start of the text and a second one before beginning sutra mahāmudrā — having a new promise here should not be seen as redundant because it relates to the specific topic of introducing the mind’s ultimate nature.

f.d: dang po [ngo sprod tshul gyi dbye ba spyir bstan pa ]ni/
2.2.1.1.2.1. A general presentation of the various ways of introducing [the mind’s ultimate nature]

ston pas/ sems rtogs na sangs rgyas yin pas/ sangs rgyas gzhan du mi btsal ces pa dang /[69] sa ra has kyang /
sems nyid gcig pu kun gyi sa bon te/ / gang la srid dang mya ngan 'das 'phro ba/ / 'dod pa'i 'bras bu thams cad ster byed pa/ / yid bzhin nor 'dra'i sems la phyag 'tshal lo/[70] / zhes pa dang / gling ras kyis kyang /
rang gi sems nyid rtogs na sangs rgyas yin/ / sgro 'dogs nang nas chod na yongs kyang yin/[71] / zhes bshad pa ltar/ rang gi sems kyi chos nyid ji bzhin du rtogs pa dang / ma rtogs pa las 'khor 'das gnyis su 'gyur ba'i khe nyen shin tu che bar mdo rgyud dam pa thams cad dgongs pa mthun la/

The Teacher has stated that when the nature of the mind is realized, that is Buddha,[1162] so buddhahood is not to be sought elsewhere. Saraha too says:
Mind itself is the seed of everything, the source of both samsaric existence and nirvana and that which grants all desired goals — to this wish-granting jewel mind, I pay homage.[1163] And Lingrepa says:
When you realize your own mind, buddhahood will arise. When you cut reifications from within, fulfillment will arise.[1164] As stated in these lines, all excellent sutras and tantras converge on the understanding that it is on the basis of whether one has realized the mind’s true nature as it is that samsara and nirvana come into being, and that this is a matter of great gain or loss.

d.div: [69] 'di mdo rgyud gang gi lung yin ngos 'dzin ma thub pas 'tshol zhib byed kyang 'di'i khungs ma rnyed/
[70] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod kyi glu/ shog_72_ba5

[71] rje grub thob chen po'i bka' 'bum las mgur gyi rim pa/ gling chen ras pa pad+ma rdo rje'i gsung 'bum/ pod dang po/ shog_28_na6_rang gi sems nyid rtogs na sangs rgyas 'byung / /sgro 'dog nang nas chod na yongs kyang 'byung / /mnyam bzhag rjes thob med par brtan byas nas/ /gzhan phan rgya cher mod cig rnal 'byor pa/ /

[1162] The “Teacher” here is the Buddha, and what Panchen has in mind follows texts such as the Gnosis at the Point of Death Sutra when it says, “If you realize the mind, this is gnosis, so cultivate the thought of not seeking buddhahood elsewhere.” Ātajñānasūtra, Toh 122 Kangyur, mdo sde, tha, 153a5.
[1163] Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti) verse 41, Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 72b5.

[1164] Lingrepa, Experiential Songs (nyams mgur gyi rim pa), 28a6. The full stanza reads: “When you realize your own mind, buddhahood will arise. / When you cut reifications from within, fulfillment will arise. / With stability and no differentiation between equipoise and post-equipoise, / engage extensively in other’s welfare, O yogi.”

f.d:
sems kyi gzhi rtsa bcad nas bsgom tshul/ kha cig ni mnyam gzhag gi ngang nas rang gi sems phyi dang nang dang skye ba dang gnas pa dang 'gag pa gang du grub dpyad pa na/ gang du yang ma grub par mthong ba'i tshe/ sems kyi gzhi rtsa chod pa dang / sems ngo 'phrod pa dang / phyag chen gyi don thob pa yin te/ do ha las/
sems dang snang ba thams cad ni/ / btsal na mi rnyed 'tshol mkhan gang na'ang med/ / med pa dus gsum ma skyes ma 'gags pas/ / de nyid gzhan du 'gyur ba med pa ni/ / rang bzhin bde ba chen po'i gnas lugs yin/ / de phyir snang ba thams cad chos kyi sku/[72] / zhes pa'i don du 'dod/

As for the way to meditate by cutting the root basis of the mind:[1165] (1) Some maintain that as you examine, from within the state of meditative equipoise, whether the mind exists anywhere — outside, inside, when arising, abiding, ceasing, and so on — and see that it does not exist anywhere, you have then cut the root basis of the mind, recognized the mind, and attained the goal, mahāmudrā. They maintain this to be meaning of the following passage from the Treasury of Dohās: A Pith Instruction on Mahāmudrā:
The mind as well as all appearances, when sought, nothing is found; the searcher too is nowhere. The nonexistent does not arise nor cease at any time, and it cannot turn into something else. This is the abiding nature of natural great bliss. Thus all appearances are dharmakāya indeed.[1166]

d.div: [72] sde dge_2273_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod ces bya ba phyag rgya chen po'i man ngag_shog_122_ba1
[1165] Numbering of these five different explanations has been introduced to assist the reader.
[1166] Saraha, Dohākoṣamahāmudropadeśa, Toh 2273 Tengyur, rgyud, zhi, 122b1.

f.d:
yang 'ga' zhig ni sems btsal bas rang gi lus 'di'i spyi bo nas rkang mthil gyi bar gyi cha shas gang du yang ma grub pa dang / kha dog dang dbyibs sogs gzugs can gang du yang ma grub par mthong ba de sems kyi chos nyid mthong ba sogs yin te/ zhang rin po ches/
kun gyi sa bon rang sems gnas lugs ni/ / rgyal ba sras bcas kun gyi thugs dang ni/ / ye nas khyad med ye shes chos skur snang / / bem po ma yin rang gi ngang gis gsal/ / dngos por ma grub kha dog tshad kyis stong /[73] / zhes gsungs pas so snyam du dgongs/

(2) Now some assert that as you search for the mind and find that it does not exist anywhere — in any part of the body, from the top of your crown to the soles of your feet — and see that it exists nowhere as a material entity with color, shape, and so forth, you have seen the mind’s true nature. They understand this to be so because Shang Rinpoché says:
The abiding nature of your own mind, which is the seed of all, is not different whatsoever from the mind of the buddhas as well as of their children: they appear as dharmakāya. It is not material and is self-luminous; not existing as a thing, it is devoid of color and dimension.[1167]

d.div: [73] skye med zhang rin po che'i gsung phyag rgya chen po'i lam mchog mthar thug_lta ba'i le'u/ 2_ba1_gdams ngag mdzod pod lnga pa/ le tshan nyer dgu pa/
[1167] Lama Shang, Ultimate Supreme Path of Mahāmudrā, 2b1. For a translation of Shang’s entire text, see Roberts, Mahāmudrā and Related Instructions, 83–134.

f.d:
yang la la ni/ sngar 'das kyi shes pa'i rjes mi gcod/ ma 'ongs pa'i shes pa'i sngun mi bsu/ da ltar gyi shes pa so ma ma bcos pa de'i ngang du lhan ne bzhag pas sems kyi ngo bo rjen cher gyi mngon sum du mthong la/[74] de'i tshe sems kyi rtsa ba chod cing sems ngo 'phrod pa yin te/ sa ra has/ so ma ma bcos lhug par bzhag[75] /ces sogs dang / grub chen gling gis/
ma bcos so mar bzhag na rtogs pa 'char/ / chu bo'i rgyun bzhin bskyangs na yongs kyang 'char/ / dmigs gtad mtshan ma thams cad yongs spongs la/ / rtag tu mnyam par zhog cig rnal 'byor pa/[76] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

(3) Some maintain: Neither chasing the past nor anticipating the future but resting your mind in the present-moment awareness, which is fresh and uncontrived, you will directly perceive the mind’s bare nature. At that point you have cut the root basis of mind [529] and have recognized the mind’s nature. Saraha says, “Rest naturally in the fresh, uncontrived mind.”[1168] The great siddha Lingrepa too says:
When you rest in the uncontrived, fresh awareness, realization dawns; when you maintain realization like a flowing river, fulfillment occurs. Shunning utterly all objectifiable loci and signs, abide always in meditative equipoise, O yogi.[1169]

d.div: [74] skye med zhang rin po che'i gsung phyag rgya chen po sgom ma mo sngon 'gro dngos gzhi/ 8_ba3_dbyin ji'i shog grangs _793_gdams ngag mdzod pod lnga pa/
[75] 'dir sa ra ha'i gsung lung tshig zin bzhin drangs par mi snang la de'i do ha mdzod du sems ma bcos pa gnyug ma'i skor mang tsam gsungs pa la zhal 'phangs mdzad sam snyam/

[76] rje grub thob chen po'i bka' 'bum las mgur gyi rim pa/ gling chen ras pa pad+ma rdo rje'i gsung 'bum pod dang po/ 28_na6_khams pa sgar gsung rab nyams gso khang nas _1985_lor ldi lir dpar du bskrun pa/ ma bcos gnyug mar bzhags na rtogs pa 'char/ /chu bo'i rgyun bzhin bsgom na yongs kyang 'char/ /dmigs gtad mtshan ma thams cad yongs spangs la/ /rtag tu mnyam par zhog cig rnal 'byor pa/ /
[1168] Exact source not located.
[1169] Lingrepa, Experiential Songs, 28a6.

f.d:
gsung gzhan dag ni/ sems la gzugs sgra sogs yul gang dang gang gi rnam par shar ba dang / dge mi dge sogs bzang ngan gyi rnam rtog ci shar kyang / dgag bsgrub cung zad kyang mi byed par/ de kha'i ngo bo la gcer gyis bltas pas rang yal du 'gro /de rjes gang du'ang ngos gzung med pa'i stong sang hang nge ba de la 'jog cing / de ltar mthong ba chos nyid rtogs pa dang sems ngo 'phrod pa yin te/ gang+gA ma las/
blo 'das byar med don de rtogs 'dod na/ / rang sems rtsad chod rig pa gcer pur zhog / rtog pa dri ma'i chu de dwangs su chug / snang ba dgag bsgrub mi bya rang sor zhog / spong len med na phyag rgya chen po yin/[77] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro zhes bzhed/

(4) In other teachings it says: Whatever sensory objects such as form, sound, and so forth appear to the mind, or whatever thoughts of good or bad such as of virtue and nonvirtue arise, as you starkly look at their nature without reacting, neither with rejection nor with affirmation, they will vanish on their own. Following this, rest your mind in that pure vacuity, not identifiable in any way, with a sense of wonder. Seeing thus they assert is to realize the ultimate nature and to recognize the nature of mind. [Tilopa’s] Mother Ganges says:
If you wish to realize the truth that transcends thought and activity, cut the root of your mind but leave your awareness naked: let the muddied water of thoughts turn clear. Neither reject nor affirm appearances, leave them alone: when you do not reject or affirm, that is mahāmudrā.[1170]

d.div: [77] sde dge_2303_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_ti l+li pa/ phyag rgya chen po'i man ngag_243_na3_'di la phyag chen gang+ga ma'ang zer/
[1170] Instruction on Mahāmudrā (Mahāmudropadeśa, Toh 2303 Tengyur, rgyud, zhi, 243a3.

f.d:
yang mang po zhig ni/ rnam rtog gi ris ci skyes kyang rang yal du mi gtong bar thog rjis byas/ de kha'i steng du je rgyas su btang bas rang grol du 'gro bas/ shar grol dus mnyam pa ste/ rnam rtog ji tsam mang ba tsam gyis chos sku grangs mang ba yin te/ bla ma zhang gis/
de ltar bzhag pa'i ngang nyid nas/ / rnam rtog thol gyis byung gyur na/ / de nyid 'od gsal chos sku las/ / gzhan zhig snyam du ma sems shig /
de phyir rnam rtog 'phro ba de/ / stong nyid las ni stong nyid 'phro/ / chos sku las ni chos sku 'phro/ / zung 'jug las ni zung 'jug 'phro/[78] / zhes pa'i don du 'doms so//

(5) Again, many others say: Whatever thoughts may arise, rather than letting them vanish on their own, trample on them and then let them rise back up, at which point they will release themselves. There will, in this way, be a simultaneity of arising and release. And the more thoughts, the more dharmakāyas. They instruct thus by understanding it to be the meaning of the following passage from Lama Shang:
While resting your mind in this way, if thoughts happen to arise suddenly, think not of them as anything else other than the dharmakāya clear light.
Thus the proliferation of thoughts is emptiness emanating from emptiness, dharmakāya radiating from dharmakāya, union springing from union.[1171]

d.div: [78] skye med zhang rin po che'i gsung phyag rgya chen po'i lam mchog mthar thug_lta ba'i le'u/ 7_na3_gdams ngag mdzod pod lnga pa/ le tshan nyer dgu pa/ dpal spungs dpar ma/ de ltar bzhag pa'i ngang nyid las/ /rnam rtog tal gyis byung ba de/ /de nyid 'od gsal chos sku las/ /gzhan zhig yin snyam ma sems shig /g.yo med rgya mtsho dwangs pa las/ /rba rlabs chil gyis langs pa de/ /gzhan zhig min pa ji bzhin du/ /rtog pa'i gzhi ma sems yin la/ /sems kyi mtshan nyid gsal rig yin/ /gsal rig rang bzhin stong pa ste/ /stong pa'i ngo bo bde chen yin/ /sems kyi rang bzhin de la ni/ /mtshan ma'i mun pa gtan med pas/ /'od gsal bya ba ming du btags/ /chos rnams kun gyi bdag nyid de/ /rang sems rig pa'i ngo bo yin/ /rang sems rig pa'i ngo bo de/ /mtshan ma'i lus kyis stong pas na/ /lus med lus te lus kyi mchog /lus med chos nyid lus yin phyir/ /chos kyi sku zhes btags pa yin/ /phyi ru rnam rtog 'phros pa de/ /chos sku las ni chos sku 'phro/ /zung 'jug las ni zung 'jug 'phro/ /ces byung /
[1171] Lama Shang, Ultimate Supreme Path, 7a3. In the source as featured in Treasury of Instructions anthology, there are four intervening stanzas between these two verses.

f.d: gnyis pa [de dag gi snying po dril nas bstan pa ]ni/
2.2.1.1.2.2. The distilled essence of those ways of introducing

'phags pa yul 'khor skyong gis zhus pa las/
stong pa zhi ba skye ba med pa'i tshul/ / mi shes pas ni 'gro ba 'khyams gyur pa/ / de dag thugs rje mnga' bas thabs tshul dang / / rigs pa brgya dag gis ni 'jug par mdzad/[79] / ces zab mo stong pa nyid bdag med pa'i tshul ma shes pas/ 'gro ba rnams 'khor bar 'khyams pa yin la/ de dag 'khor bar 'khyams pa la thugs rje chen po mnga' ba'i ston pas 'khor ba las bsgral ba'i phyir du/ bdag med rtogs pa'i thabs tshul dang / bdag med gtan la 'bebs pa'i rigs pa brgya phrag dag gis dngos dang brgyud pas bdag med rtogs pa'i lam la 'dzud par mdzad ces gsungs so/ /

In the Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla sutra it says:
This way of emptiness, peace, and no-arising — ignorant of it, beings wander samsara’s realms. The Compassionate One effects their entry into this truth through hundreds of methods and reasons.[1172] [530] The sutra states that beings wander in samsaric existence owing to their ignorance of the way of emptiness, selflessness. To help free them from samsara, the Teacher, who has great compassion for these beings wandering samsara’s realms, effects their entry onto the path of realization of selflessness through hundreds of methods and lines of reasoning that directly or indirectly establish the absence self-existence.

d.div: [79] sde dge_62_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _'phags pa yul 'khor skyong gis zhus pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ shog_252_ba2
[1172] Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā, Toh 62 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 252b2.

f.d:
de bzhin du mgon po zhi ba lhas kyang /
yan lag 'di dag thams cad ni/ / thub pas shes rab don du gsungs/[80] / zhes dang / jo bo rjes kyang /
chos kyi phung po brgyad khrid dang / / bzhi stong gsungs pa thams cad kyang / / chos nyid 'di la gzhol cing 'bab/[81] / ces rgyal bas chos phung brgyad khri bzhi stong gsungs pa thams cad kyang mthar gdul byas chos nyid dam bdag med mngon sum du rtogs pa mthar phyin pa'i thabs su 'bab par gsungs pa yin no//

Along the same lines, the guardian Śāntideva says:
All these limbs of practice the Sage taught for the sake of wisdom.[1173] Atiśa too writes:
All the eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma that have been taught are for arriving at this ultimate reality.[1174] This says that all eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma taught by the Conqueror were taught as methods whereby spiritual aspirants can, in the end, perfect the realization of ultimate reality — selflessness.

d.div: [80] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u dgu pa/ sh+loka_1_shog_30_ba7
[81] sde dge_3902_bstan/ dbu ma/ a_jo bo rje/ bden pa gnyis la 'jug pa/ sh+loka_16_dang _17_shog_72_ba5
[1173] Guide to the Bodhisattva Way (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 9.1, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 30b6.
[1174] Entering the Two Truths (Satyadvayāvatāra) verse 16–17, Toh 3902 Tengyur, dbu ma, a, 72b5.

f.d:
de yang bdag med mngon sum du rtogs pa la sngon du bdag med thos bsam gyis gtan la phab nas bsgom dgos shing / sgom pa yang zhi gnas tsam gyis mu stegs can 'ga' zhig ltar nyon mongs spong mi nus te/ ting nge 'dzin rgyal po las/
'jig rten dag na ting 'dzin sgom byed kyang / de ni bdag tu 'du shes gzhig mi byed/ / de yi nyon mongs phyir yang rab tu ldang / / lhag spyod kyis ni ting 'dzin 'dir bsgoms bzhin/[82] / zhes gsungs/

As for the realization of selflessness by direct perception, you first need to establish it through study and reflection and then meditate upon it. With respect to meditation, too, if you have merely tranquil abiding, you will be like those non-Buddhists [who have attained tranquil abiding but are] unable to eliminate the afflictions. The King of Meditations Sutra says: [531]
Although, in the world, they cultivate concentration, they will not destroy the notion of selfhood, and their afflictions will rise back again, as when Udraka cultivated concentration.[1175]

d.div: [82] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u dgu pa/ shog_27_na7
[1175] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 9, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 27a7.

f.d:
'o na thar pa dngos su thob byed kyi ting nge 'dzin de ci zhe na/
gal te chos la bdag med so sor rtog / so sor de brtags gang zhig sgom byed pa/ / des ni mya ngan 'das thob 'bras bu'i rgyu/ / rgyu gzhan gang yin des ni zhi mi 'gyur/[83] / zhes bdag med pa'i chos la so sor brtags te/ brtags don bsgoms pas 'bras bu myang 'das 'thob par gsungs so/ /

What then is the meditative concentration that directly brings about the attainment of liberation? The same sutra says:
If you discern selflessness in relation to phenomena and meditate on what has been discerned, this would be the cause for attaining the fruit, nirvana. No other cause will bring about peace.[1176] This states that one who discerns phenomena to be devoid of selfhood and meditates on the truth thus discerned will attain the fruit of nirvana.

d.div: [83] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa ting nge 'dzin gyi rgyal po'i mdo/ bam pa/ 3_le'u/ 9_shog_27_na7

f.d:
de lta bu'i bdag med pa la yang ngo bo'i sgo nas phra rags med kyang chos dang gang zag gi dbye bas gnyis su 'gyur te/ dpal ldan zla bas/
bdag med 'di ni 'gro ba rnam sgrol phyir/ / chos dang gang zag dbye bas rnam gnyis gsungs/[84] / zhes gsungs pa bzhin no/ /

As for selflessness, there is no difference in the subtlety of its nature, but because of the differentiation [of bases] into persons and phenomena, it is twofold. The glorious Candrakīrti writes:
To help free beings, the Buddha taught no-self in twofold terms — that of phenomena and that of persons.[1177]

d.div: [84] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_179_shog_213_na6
[1177] Entering the Middle Way (Madhyamakāvatāra), 6.179ab, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 213a6.

f.d: gnyis po
a. [The selflessness of persons]

de yang gsung rab dgongs 'grel dang bcas pa las/ thog mar chos kyi bdag med gtan la phab kyang / sgom pa'i tshe thog mar gang zag gi bdag med sgom dgos te/ ting nge 'dzin rgyal po las/
ji ltar khyod kyis bdag gi 'du shes ni/ / shes pa de bzhin kun la blos sbyar bya/ / chos rnams thams cad de yi ngo bo nyid/ / yongs su dag pa nam mkha' lta bu yin/ / gcig gis kyang ni thams cad shes/ / gcig gis kyang ni thams cad mthong /[85] / zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro//

The scriptures and their commentaries present the selflessness of phenomena first, but when it comes to engaging in meditative practice, you should first meditate on the selflessness of persons. The King of Meditations Sutra states:
Just as you have discerned in relation to self, extend this with your mind to all. This is the nature of all phenomena: it is utterly pure like space. So by knowing one, you know all; by seeing one, you see all.[1178]

d.div: [85] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 12_shog_44_na2_ji ltar bdag gi 'du shes rig /de bzhin kun la blo yang gtod/ /chos kun de yi rang bzhin te/ /rnam par dag pa nam mkha' bzhin/ /zhes pa 'di yin nam snyam/
[1178] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 12, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 44a2.

f.d:
des na gang zag gi bdag med sgom pa la/ sngon du 'gog rgyu'i dgag bya ngos 'dzin dgos te/
spyod 'jug las/ brtags pa'i dngos la ma reg par/ / de yi dngos med 'dzin ma yin/[86] / zhes gsungs pa ltar/ dgag bya ngos ma zin na 'ben ma mthong bar mda' rgyag pa dang / dgra ngos ma zin par dmag 'dren pa dang 'dra bas so/ /

Thus, when meditating on the selflessness of persons, you must first identify the object of negation. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way says:
Without touching upon the imputed entity, the absence of its reality cannot be grasped.[1179] If you fail to identify what is to be negated, it will be like shooting an arrow without seeing the target or waging a battle without knowing who the enemy is.

d.div: [86] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_140_shog_36_na6
[1179] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 9.140, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 36a6.

f.d:
dgag bya ngos 'dzin kyang ha cang khyab che na ni chad mthar ltung zhing / ha cang khyab chung na ni/ dgag bya phra mo mi khegs pas rtag mthar ltung bas nyen yang shin tu che ste/ rtsa she las/
stong pa nyid la blta nyes na/ / shes rab chung rnams phung par 'gyur/ / ji ltar sprul la bzung nyes dang / / rig sngags nyes par bsgrub pa bzhin/ /
de phyir zhan pas chos 'di yi/ / gting rtogs dka' bar mkhyen gyur nas/ / thub pa'i thugs ni chos bstan las/ / rab tu log par gyur pa yin/[87] / ces gsungs so//

Also, when identifying the object of negation, if you identify it too broadly you will fall into the extreme of nihilism, and if you identify it too narrowly you will fall into the extreme of eternalism. So the danger is very great indeed. Fundamental Wisdom states:
If emptiness is viewed wrongly, those of small intellect will be destroyed, like handling a snake in the wrong way or like a spell wrongly executed.
Therefore, knowing that it would be hard for the feeble-minded to fathom this truth, the Sage turned his mind away [at first] from teaching the Dharma.[1180]

d.div: [87] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_slob dpon klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 24_sh+loka_11_dang _12_shog_15_na2
[1180] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, 24.11–12, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 15a2.

f.d: de yang brgyad stong par nga dang nga yir 'dzin pas sems can thams cad 'khor ba na 'khor bar gsungs pa bzhin/[88] nyes pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba mthar thug pa bdag 'dzin lhan skyes sam/ ngar 'dzin lhan skyes yin la/ spyir nga'o snyam du 'dzin pa'i blo la/ nga bden grub kyis khyad par du byas pa dang / nga bden med dam ming tsam rtog pas btags tsam du byas pa dang / de gnyis gang gis kyang khyad par du ma byas par nga'o snyam du 'dzin pa'i tshul gsum las/ phyi ma ni nga tsam zhig 'jog pa'i tha snyad pa'i tshad ma dang / bar pa ni dbu ma'i lta ba la nges pa rnyed pa yan chad kho na'i rgyud la 'byung gi gzhan la mi 'byung zhing / dang po de gang zag gi bdag 'dzin yin no/ / gang zag gzhan dmigs yul du byas nas bden par 'dzin pa ni gang zag gi bdag 'dzin yin kyang ngar dzin lhan skyes ma yin la/ ngar 'dzin lhan skyes sam/ 'jig lta ni/ dmigs pa rang rgyud kyi nga la dmigs nas rnam pa rang bzhin gyis grub par 'dzin pa'i shes rab nyon mongs can no/ / de ni rang rgyu chos kyi bdag 'dzin phra mo zhig gis bskyed pa yin te/

Also, as the Eight Thousand Lines states, it is through grasping at “I” and “mine” that sentient beings wander in the cycle of existence, and so the ultimate root of all faults is the innate self-grasping or the innate grasping at “I.” Within the thought “I am” there are, generally speaking, three kinds: (1) one that takes the “I” qualified by true existence, (2) one that takes it qualified by absence of true existence as a mere name or a mere construct of thought, and (3) one that is the simple thought “I am” without qualifying it in either of these two terms. Of these, the last is a veridical conventional cognition that posits the mere “I,” the second arises only within the mental continuum of those who have found the Madhyamaka view and not in others, and the first is the grasping at selfhood of persons. Taking another person as your referent object and grasping at his or her true existence is indeed a grasping at a selfhood of persons; it does not, however, constitute the innate grasping at “I.” Innate grasping at “I” or identity view is an afflicted intelligence that focuses upon your own “I” [532] and grasps it as existing by virtue of an intrinsic nature. And it is engendered by its cause, a subtle level of grasping at the selfhood of phenomena.

d.div: [88] sde dge_12_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_brgyad stong pa/ le'u/ 1_shog_3_na3

f.d:
mgon po klu sgrub kyis/
ji srid phung por 'dzin yod pa/ / de srid de la ngar 'dzin yod/ / ngar 'dzin yod na yang las te/ / las las kyang ni skye ba yin/[89] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/

The guardian Nāgārjuna states:
As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, there will be grasping at an “I,” when there is “I”-grasping, there is also karma, and from karma, there will be birth.[1181]

d.div: [89] sde dge_4158_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_35_shog_108_na5
[1181] Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī) 1.35, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 108a5.

f.d:
de nyid 'khor ba'i rtsa ba yin pas de'i 'dzin stangs kyi yul lam zhen yul de sun ma phyungs par bdag 'dzin spong mi nus te/ rig pa'i dbang phyug gis/
'di yul sun dbyung med par ni/ / de spong ba ni nus pa ma yin/[90] / zhes gsungs pa'i phyir/

Since it is the root of samsaric existence, you cannot eliminate self-grasping without repudiating its object of apprehension, its object of clinging. The lord of reasoning [Dharmakīrti] states:
Without repudiating its object, it [the erroneous subject] cannot be eliminated.[1182]

d.div: [90] sde dge_4210_bstan/ tshad ma/ ce_slob dpon chos grags/ tshad ma rnam 'grel/ tshad ma grub pa'i le'u/ sh+loka_223_shog_116_na3
[1182] Exposition of Valid Cognition (Pramāṇavārttika) 2.223, Toh 4210 Tengyur, tshad ma, ce, 116a3.

f.d: skyes bu bden par 'dzin pa'am/ nga bden par 'dzin pa'am/ gang zag bden par 'dzin pa de yi zhen yul ni/ skyes bu bden par grub pa dang / nga bden par grub pa dang / gang zag bden par grub pa sogs yin pas sun dbyung dgos la/ de dag sun 'byin pa ni/ de dag bden med du blta ba nyid yin te/ gang zag bden med du nges nas goms par byas pas/ gang zag bden par 'dzin pa bzlog par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ /

The objects of clinging in grasping at the true existence of the individual, grasping at the true existence of “I,” and grasping at the true existence of the person are, respectively, the truly existing individual, the truly existing “I,” and the truly existing person. It is these that must be eradicated. This eradication is accomplished only through viewing these as lacking true existence. For it is by ascertaining the person as devoid of true existence and cultivating this familiarity that the grasping at the true existence of the person will come to cease.
b. [Space-like meditative equipoise]
rgyu mtshan de dag gis na sngon du dgag bya'i snang tshul dang / 'dzin tshul man ngag myong 'khrid du bstan pa'i phyir bshad pa/
For these reasons, to first present the instruction by way of an experiential guidance on how the object of negation appears and how is grasped, the text says:

sngar gyi mnyam gzhag ngang nyid nas/ / ma g.yos dwangs pa'i chu nang du// ji ltar nye'u chung 'khyug pa ltar/ / phra mo'i shes pas sgom pa po'i// skyes bu'i rang bzhin mdzangs par brtag /[29] ces pa'o//

div.div: 29 While in that foregoing meditative equipoise, unwavering, and just like a minnow darting about in clear water, analyze skillfully with subtle awareness the nature of that person who is meditating.

f.d: 'di ltar sngar gyi zhi gnas kyi ting nge 'dzin la rtse gcig tu mnyam par gzhag pa'i mnyam gzhag gi ngang nas cung zad kyang ma g.yos par dper na dwangs pa'i chus gang ba'i mtsho nang du chu mi g.yo bar nye'u chung khyug khyug 'khyug pa ltar/ mnyam gzhag gi ngang nas phra mo'i shes pa zhig gis ting nge 'dzin sgom pa po'i skyes bu'am/ nga'am bdag nyid kyi rang bzhin te gnas tshul dang / blo la snang tshul dang / 'dzin tshul ji ltar 'dug phra zhing mdzangs pa ste so sor 'byed pa dang zhib pa'i blos brtag par bya'o/ /

Thus, while in meditative equipoise resting single-pointedly in the concentration of tranquil abiding you have cultivated, without wavering — like a minnow that swims in a pool of clear water without disturbing it — from within that meditative equipoise and with a subtle cognition, analyze what is the true nature of the one who is engaged in meditation — the individual, the “I,” or the self — how it appears to your mind and [533] how you apprehend it. Examine all this subtly and astutely — that is to say, with precise and discriminating awareness.

de ltar brtags pa na/ gnas tshul ni/ skyes bu dang / nga dang / gang zag la sogs pa chos thams cad ming tsam dang / rtog pas btags pa tsam dang / thag khra la sbrul lam/ mtho yor dang / shing phung la ming btags pa tsam ste/ mdo las/
dri za'i grong khyer ji ltar snang gyur kyang / / grong khyer de ni phyogs bcu kun na med/ / gzhan du grong khyer de ni ming tsam ste/ / de bzhin bde bar gshegs pas 'gro 'di gzigs/[91] / zhes de bzhin gshegs pas ji ltar gzigs pa ltar ro//

As you examine in this way, you will discern that the true mode of being is this: the “individual,” the “I,” the “person” — in fact, all phenomena — are mere names, they are mere constructs of thought, merely imputed, like a snake on a striped rope or like a man conceived upon a cairn or a pile of sticks. A sutra says:
However much a ghost town may appear, such a town exists in none of the ten directions; in other words, such a town is just a name. Likewise the Sugata sees this world.[1183] Such is the mode of being [of phenomena] seen by tathāgatas.

d.div: [91] sde dge_60_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _yab sras mjal ba'i mdo/ shog_43_na2
[1183] Meeting of Father and Son Sutra (Pitāputrasamāgamanasūtra), Toh 60 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 43a2.

f.d: des na rang cag rnams kyang ma 'khrul na/ chos thams cad ming rkyang btags yod tsam du snang dgos pa las/ de ltar mi snang bar ma rig pa'i gdon gyis brlams pas/ gnas tshul de log par snang zhing zhen pas las bsags/ las de'i dbang gis 'khor bar 'khyams nas sdug bsngal sna tshogs myong ba yin pas na/ da snying po rjen cher gyis bstan na/ de lta bu'i snang tshul dang zhen tshul la dgag bya'i snang tshul zhes pa'am bden grub tu snang tshul dang bden grub tu 'dzin tshul lam zhen tshul du 'dod pa yin no/ /

Thus, were we not deluded, all phenomena would appear to us as merely nominal, with merely imputed existence. But this is not how they appear to us. Instead, possessed by the demon of ignorance, we perceive the mode of being [of phenomena] in a distorted way and cling to it. Through this we create karma, and by the power of that karma we wander in samsara and experience all manner of suffering. Let me reveal here the essence of the matter in a stark way: this very mode of appearance and mode of apprehension [we experience] are, in fact, “the mode of appearance of true existence” and “the mode of apprehension of clinging to true existence.”

des na rang cag so skye la da lta'i snang ba 'char tshul 'di las gzhan pa'i rtags kyi dgag bya'i snang tshul gzhan med de/ so skye'i rgyud kyi shes pa thams cad ma rig pas bslad pa'i dbang gis yul ci snang yang bden par snang ba'i phyir/ de bas na/ 'di ltar gang zag dang chos btags yod tsam du nges pa la brten nas/ 'khor ba'i rtsa ba ngar 'dzin lhan skyes kyi nga'i 'dzin tshul ji bzhin du nges 'ong ste/ de ltar rtogs pa la brten nas dgag bya phra mo'i 'dzin tshul ma lus par nges nus pa'i phyir te/ rje thams cad mkhyen pas kyang / chos thams cad btags yod du bstan pa dang / de las zlog pa'i dgag bya ngos 'dzin tshul lo/[92] /zhes mang du gsungs so//

For us ordinary beings, therefore, apart from the present way in which things appear to us, there is no other different mode in which the object of negation of the reasoning might appear to us. Given that all instances of cognition of ordinary persons are tainted by ignorance, whatever object appears to us we perceive as truly existent. In view of these points, it is on the basis of ascertaining persons and phenomena as nominal existences that one comes to ascertain the exact manner in which the innate “I”-grasping — the root of samsaric existence — grasps an “I.” For it is through such realization that one will be able to ascertain all aspects of the manner in which the subtle object of negation is grasped. The omniscient Tsongkhapa too, on numerous occasions, has demonstrated “how all phenomena are nominal existences and how the object of negation, which is the contrary, is identified.”[1184]

d.div: [92] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ ma_dbu ma dgongs pa rab gsal/ shog_75_ba1

[1184] This is most probably a paraphrase of the following from Tsongkhapa’s Illuminating the Intent (trans., 181): “(1) how phenomena are posited through conceptualization and (2) presenting grasping at true existence, the contrary apprehension.

f.d:
tshul 'di dag la ni mkhas pa'i dbang por grags pa 'gro ba mang po'i 'dren par rlom pa 'ga'i yi ge la'ang nges pa ma mchis mod/ 'on kyang sgrub pa snying por mdzad pa'i dam pa rnams kho na thugs rgyus che ba 'dug ste/ mkhas grub nor bzang rgya mtshos/
'on kyang blo bzang nyin byed dbang po yi/ / rjes 'brang mkhas rlom rgyu skar du ma'i tshogs/ / rang mtshan rang bzhin grub dang bden dngos zhes/ / tha snyad tshig gis bcings pa'i dgag bya dag/ / rang blos bzhag pa rig pas bkag pa'i don/ / mtha' bral dbu ma chen por 'dod pa mthong / / rmi lam gzugs dang sgyu ma'i rta glang gang / / rang snang blo la snang tsam ma gtogs par/ / de las logs su cung zad yod min ltar/ / srid pa'i rtse mo nas bzung dmyal ba'i bar/ / sems can ji snyed rang rang so so yi/ / rtogs pas btags pa tsam zhig ma gtogs pa/ / yod pa'i dgag bya phra mo ma khegs na/ / ji tsam dpyad kyang nye tshe'i lta ba las/ / cung zad 'phags pa med par bdag gis khums/[93] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

With regard to these matters, there does not seem to be that much certainty even in the writings of some of those reputed as master scholars who claim to be guides of many beings; it is only sublime masters who have made meditative practice the heart of their life’s activity who possess the greatest familiarity. For example, Khedrup Norsang Gyatso says:
I see within the constellations trailing the Losang sun some with pretense of being learned who, parroting the phrases “intrinsic characteristics,” “intrinsic existence,” and “true being,” take reasoned negation of something constructed by their own mind — [534] an object of negation bound up in words — to be the great middle way free from extremes. Just as with dream objects or illusory horses and elephants, apart from the mere appearances perceived by the mind, they have no existence even to the slightest degree. Likewise, from the peak of samsara all the way to the hells, however many sentient beings there may be, if they do not negate the subtle object of negation, the existence beyond the mere imputations of each and every being’s mind, however much they may analyze, they do not in the slightest move beyond a superficial view. This is what I think.[1185]

d.div: [93] mkhas grub nor bzang rgya mtsho'i gsung rtsom mang che ba da bar dpe lag son ma gyur stabs gsung 'di'i khungs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[1185] Source not located.

f.d: de ltar brtags pa na/ skyes bu'am/ gang zag gam/ nga 'o snyam pa'i blo la snang ba ltar gyi skyes bu sogs yod na bden par yod pa las 'os med yin na'ang / de ltar snang ba ltar gyi skyes bu yod pa ma yin te/ skyes bu'i lus sems gnyis re re ba yang skyes bu ma yin/ lus sems gnyis tshogs pa yang skyes bu ma yin/ khams drug re re ba yang skyes bu ma yin/ khams drug tshogs pa tsam yang skyes bu ma yin/ khams drug las gzhan du yang skyes bu yod pa ma yin zhes ston pa la/

Thus if, under analysis, the individual and so forth do exist the way they appear to the mind as the “individual,” the “person,” and the “I,” there is then no alternative for them but to possess true existence. Yet no such individual as perceived exists. The person’s body and mind are each not the person, and the individual’s combined body and mind is also not the person. Neither is each of the six elements the person, nor is the combined six elements the person; yet apart from the six elements, there is also no person. To illustrate this point,

skyob pa bla na med pa mgon po klu sgrub nyid kyis/
skyes bu sa min chu ma yin/ / me min rlung min nam mkha' min// rnam shes ma yin kun min na/ / de las gzhan na skyes bu gang /[94] /[30]
zhes gsungs shing /

the peerless savior Nāgārjuna says:[1186]
30 “The person is not earth nor water, is not fire, wind, nor space, is not consciousness — nor is it all of them. Where then, apart from these, is the person?”[1187]

d.div: [94] sde dge_4158_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_80_shog_109_ba7
[1186] This is a gloss on the root-text line “The savior Nāgārjuna himself says.”
[1187] Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī) 1.80, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109b7.

f.d:
de dang mthun par spyod 'jug las kyang /
so dang skra sen bdag ma yin/ / bdag ni rus pa khrag ma yin/ / snabs min bad kan ma yin la/ / chu ser dang ni rnag kyang min/ /
bdag ni zhag dang rdul min te/ / glo mchin dag kyang bdag ma yin/ / nang khrol dag kyang bdag min te/ / bdag ni phyi sa gcin ma yin/ /
drod dang rlung yang bdag ma yin/ / bu ga ma yin rnam kun tu/ / rnam shes drug kyang bdag ma yin/[95] / zhes skyes bu'am/ bdag gam/ nga de rang gi lus kyi sa'i khams rus pa sogs sra ba'i cha yang nga min/ chu'i khams khrag sogs gsher ba'i cha yang bdag ma yin/ spyi bo nas rkang mthil gyi bar gyi me khams drod kyi cha yang bdag ma yin/ lus kyi rlung khams rtsa nang nas rgyu ba'i yang zhing g.yo ba yang skyes bu ma yin/

d.div: [95] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_58_nas _60_shog_33_na2
[1188] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 9.58–60, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 33a2.

f.d: lus kyi khong stong sogs bu ga rnams kyang skyes bu ma yin/ mig gi rnam par shes pa la sogs pa'i rnam shes thams cad kyang bdag ma yin cing bdag kyang de dag ma yin/ de dag tshogs pa yang nga ma yin/ nga yang de dag tshogs pa ma yin/ de rnams las gzhan na yang / sgom pa po'i skyes bu'o snyam du 'dzin pa'i blo la snang ba ltar gyi skyes bu med pa'i phyir/ mdo las kyang / gzugs bdag ma yin/ tshor ba bdag ma yin/ 'du shes bdag ma yin/ 'du byed bdag ma yin/ rnam par shes pa bdag ma yin/[96] zhes gsungs pa'i phyir/

Hollow spaces within the body such as the orifices are not the person, and classes of consciousness such as visual consciousness are not the self, nor is the self these factors. Their collection too is not the “I,” nor is the “I” the collection of these. Yet apart from these there is no such person, the meditator, as it appears to your mind. In the sutras too it says, “Form is not self, feelings are not self, discrimination is not self, mental formations are not self, and consciousness is not self.”[1189]

d.div: [96] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_mngon par byung ba'i mdo/ shog_62_na4
[1189] For example, Manifest Renunciation Sutra (Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra), Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 62a4.

f.d:
de lta na sgom pa po'i skyes bu'i phung po lnga dang / khams drug re re pa dang / tshogs pa dang / tshogs pa'i dbyibs sogs gang yang / sgom pa po'i skyes bu ma yin te/ gal te yin na/ gdags gzhi btags chos/ blang bya len pa po/ yan lag yan lag can rnams gcig tu 'gyur zhing /
gal te phung po bdag na de phyir de/ / mang bas bdag de dag kyang mang por 'gyur/[97] / zhes sogs kyi skyon du'ang 'gyur ro/

In view of the above, the meditating person’s five aggregates, each of the six elements, their collection, and the configuration of the collection — none of these constitutes the meditating person. For if any of these were the person, there would be such consequences as the oneness of the designative base and the designation, the appropriated and the appropriator, and the constituents and the constituted. There would also be the following problem:
Now if the aggregates are the self, then since they are multiple, the self would be multiple.[1190]

d.div: [97] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_127_shog_210_ba1
[1190] Candrakīrti, Entering the Middle Way, (Madhyamakāvatāra), 6.129ab, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 210b1.

f.d: khyad par rnam par shes pa skyes bu yin na/ skyes bu na ba dang / smras pa dang / mthong ba dang / bu bskyed pa sogs mi 'thad cing / skyes bu gcig kyang rnam shes drug ltar skyes bu drug tu 'gyur ba dang / yang na skyes bu gcig ltar rnam shes drug cha med gcig tu 'gyur ro/ / de dag tshogs pa'i dbyibs skyes bu yin na/ gzugs can du 'gyur bas gzugs med khams na skyes bu med par 'gyur ro/ /

In particular, if consciousness were the person, phenomena such as the person being ill, speaking, seeing, and procreating would become untenable. Also, although the person is one, just as there are six classes of consciousness, there would be six persons; conversely, just as the person is one, the six classes of consciousness would also be partless and one. If the shape of the collection [of the aggregates] were the person, since it would be a material entity, there would be no persons in the formless realm.

phung po lnga las gzhan du'ang skyes bu med de/ rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i 'brel med gzhan yin pas phung po 'dus byas su mtshon pa'i mtshan nyid dang mi ldan par 'gyur te/
gal te phung po las gzhan na/ / phung po'i mtshan nyid med par 'gyur/[98] / zhes gsungs shing / glang po'i rtsal gyi mdo las kyang /
gal te chos rnams rang bzhin yod gyur na/ / rgyal ba nyan thos bcas pas de mkhyen 'gyur/ / thar zug chos rnams mya ngan 'das mi 'gyur/ / mkhas rnams nam yang spros dang bral mi 'gyur/[99] / zhes gsungs pa'i nyes par yang 'gyur ro//

Yet there can be no person apart from the five aggregates. If there were, it would be intrinsically unconnected with and separate [from the aggregates] and would thus be devoid of the characteristics that define the aggregates as conditioned phenomena. It is said:
If it were separate from the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates.[1191] There would also be the faults pointed in the Elephant’s Skills Sutra:
If things were to possess intrinsic existence, the conquerors and śrāvakas would know this; things would be absolute and there will no nirvana, and the wise will never be free from conceptual elaboration.[1192] [536]

d.div: [98] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_slob dpon klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa shes rab ces bya ba/ rab byed/ 18_sh+loka_1_shog_10_ba6

[99] sde dge_131_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_de bzhin gshegs pa ye shes kyi phyag rgya'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo/ shog_251_ba2_gal te 'di ni rang bzhin 'ga' yod na/ /rgyal ba nyan thos bcas pa'i de nyid 'gro/ /ther zug chos rnams mya ngan 'da' ma yin/ /spros pa med pa nams kyang mkhas mi 'gyur/ /zhes gsal bas 'dir bkod pa yin/ ma dper glang po'i rtsal gyi mdor gsungs kyang glang po'i rtsal zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ sde dge_207_bka'/ mdo sde/ tsha_95_ba1_nas _109_bar bzhugs pa 'di'i nang 'tshol zhib byed kyang lung tshig 'di rnams brnyed son ma byung /
[1191] Nāgārjuna, Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), 18.1, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 10b6.

[1192] The passage is not found in the version of the Hastikakṣya Sutra found in the Kangyur (Toh 207). However, an almost identical passage is found in another sutra, the Concentration of the Gnosis Seal of the Tathāgatas (Tathāgatajñānamudrāsamādhi), Toh 131 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 251b2.

f.d: de ltar mnyam gzhag gi ngang nas/ shes pa phra mo zhig gis dpyad pas/ nged rang la ji ltar snang ba'i mnyam par 'jog mkhan gyi skyes bu'am/ bdag gam/ gang zag gam/ nga rdul tsam yang med par stong cham gyis 'gro la/ de lta bu'i stong sang de'i don spyi blo la gsal bar byas nas/ gzhan ma spros pa gang yang yid la mi byed pa rtse gcig tu mnyam par gzhag/ / med dgag stong sang de'i 'dzin stangs cung zad zhan du song na mnyam gzhag gi ngang nas sngar ltar dpyad la rtse gcig tu sgom pa ni mnyam gzhag nam mkha' lta bu'i skyong tshul yin no/ / thog mar de ltar nges pa na/ sngar lta ba la goms pa med na/ 'jigs pa skye zhing / goms pa yod na yid la dga' ba skye bar gsungs so//
