Thus, when you examine from within meditative equipoise, with a subtle part of your mind, the individual, the self, the person, or the “I” who is resting in meditative equipoise that appears to your mind, not even an atom of it exists; there will be pure emptiness in its wake. Then, allowing this generic image of pure vacuity to appear clearly in your mind, rest single-pointedly in meditative equipoise without bringing to your mind anything else in the form of conceptual elaboration. When your apprehension of this pure vacuity, a nonimplicative negation, wanes a little, apply analysis as before while abiding within meditative equipoise and continue to meditate single-pointedly. This is the way to maintain the space-like meditative equipoise. It is stated that when you first ascertain things in this way, if you have no familiarity with the view, fear will arise; if you do have familiarity, joy will arise.
c. [Illusion-like post-equipoise]
rjes thob kyi rnam gzhag ston pa ni/
To present the features of the post-equipoise stage, the text says:
skyes bu khams drug 'dus pa'i phyir/ / yang dag ma yin/[100] zhes gsungs/

d.div: [100] sde dge_4858_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rgyal po la gtam du bya ba rin po che'i phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_81_shog_110_na1
[1193] Nāgārjuna, Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī), 1.81ab, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 110a1.

f.d: mnyam gzhag de las langs nas brtags pa na/ bdag nyid kyi shes pa ma rig pa'i gdon gyis bzung ba'i dbang gis phyin ci log tu snang ba'i skyes bu ni med mod/ 'on kyang skyes bu'am/ gang zag gam/ nga tsam zhig ni nges par yod la/ yod tshul yang mtho yor la mi dang / thag khra la sbrul du btags pa ltar/ skyes bu zhes/ rang gi khams drug gam phung po lnga tshogs tsam la btags pa'i ming tsam/ brda tsam/ rtog pas btags tsam dang / yang dag pa ma yin pa sgyu ma lta bu'i stong pa rten 'brel du shar ba tsam la nges shes bskyed nas bsgom zhing / mdo sde zab mo'i dbyangs kyis kyang dran par bya ste/

When you rise from the meditative equipoise and examine, you will have this realization: although what appears to my mind has no existence — the person that is perceived in a distorted way because of my mind being possessed by the demon of ignorance — there is certainly, nonetheless, the individual, the person, or the mere “I.” Its mode of existence is, however, akin to a man imputed onto a cairn or a snake onto a striped rope. Thus the “person” is a mere label designating a mere collection of your own six elements or five aggregates, a mere convention, a mere conceptual imputation, something unreal and illusion-like, emptiness arising as dependent origination. Cultivate such an ascertainment and meditate. You should also contemplate it through chanting the profound scriptures.

ting nge 'dzin rgyal po las/
sgyu ma byed pa dag gis gzugs sprul te/ / rta dang glang po shing rta sna tshogs byas/ / de la ji ltar snang ba gang yang med/ / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/ /
ji ltar bu mo gzhon nu'i rmi lam na/ / bu pho byung zhing shi ba des mthong nas/ / byung nas dga' zhing shi nas mi dga' ltar/ / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/ /
ji ltar mtshan mo chu yi zla ba dag / dwangs shing rnyog pa med pa'i chu nang snang / / chu zla stong pa gsog ste gzung du med/ / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/ /
ji ltar sos ka'i nyi ma phyed dus na/ / skyes bu skom pas gdungs shing 'gro ba yis/ / smig rgyu dag la chu yi phung por mthong / / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/ /
smig rgyu la yang chu ni yod ma yin/ / sems can rmongs pa de la 'thung 'dod de/ / mi bden chu ni btung bar yod mi nus/ / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/ /
ji ltar chu shing rlon pa'i sdong po la/ / snying po 'dod phyir skyes bus de gshegs kyang / / nang dang phyi rol kun na snying po med/ / chos rnams thams cad de bzhin shes par gyis/[101] / zhes so//

The King of Meditations Sutra says:
The illusionist conjures images of horses, elephants, and all sorts of chariots, yet none are real the way they appear to be. Like this, understand all phenomena.
Just as a young woman, in a dream, sees her son being born and dying, and she is happy when he is born and sad when he dies, so should you understand all phenomena.
Just as at night the moon’s reflection appears in water that is clear and unmuddied, [537] yet this water-moon is empty and unreal, ungraspable, so should you understand all phenomena.
Just as at midday in a summer heat, a traveler who is tormented by thirst sees mirages as bodies of water, so should you understand all phenomena.
In a mirage, no water exists at all; although deluded beings wish to, there can be no drinking of unreal water; so should you understand all phenomena.
Just as people chop through the live trunk of a plantain tree thinking it has a core yet there is no core anywhere, outside or inside, so should you understand all phenomena.[1194]

d.div: [101] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin gyi rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 9_shog_26_ba2
[1194] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 9, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 26b2.

f.d: d. [The selflessness of phenomena]

de ltar rang rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i gang zag gi bdag med la goms pa nyams 'og tu chud pa na/ sdud pa las/
bdag ci 'dra ba de 'drar sems can thams cad shes/ / sems can thams cad ci 'dra de 'drar chos kun shes/[102] / zhes gzhan gang zag dang chos kyi bdag med sgom tshul bstan pa'i phyir/

Now, when you have gained some experience in your familiarity with the selflessness of the person, then, as stated in the following in Condensed Perfection of Wisdom, meditate on selflessness of other persons and phenomena:
Just like yourself, understand all sentient beings to be the same; just like all sentient beings, understand all phenomena to be the same.[1195] To indicate this, the text says:

d.div: [102] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin sna tshogs/ ka_'phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa sdud pa tshigs su bcad pa/ shog_3_na6
[1195] Prajñāpāramitāsañcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, shes rab sna tshogs, ka, 3a6.

f.d:
ji lta bar// de bzhin khams ni re re yang / / 'dus phyir yang dag nyid du min/[103] /[31]
gsungs pa ji bzhin btsal ba na/ / mnyam gzhag mnyam par 'jog mkhan sogs// rdul phran tsam yang ma rnyed pa/ / de tshe g.yeng med rtse gcig tu// nam mkha' lta bu'i mnyam gzhag skyong / /[32] zhes bshad do//

div.b: 31cd “Likewise, each element too is in turn a composite and hence has no real existence.”

div.div: 32 In accordance with this statement, when you search, not even a minute particle will be found of the meditative equipoise, the one who is in equipoise, and so forth. At that point, maintain the space-like equipoise without distraction and single-pointedly.

d.div: [103] sde dge_4858_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_81_shog_110_na1
[1196] Nāgārjuna, Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī), 1.81cd, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109b7.

f.d: de yang skye 'phags thams cad dang / phyi nang gi sa'i khams dang / de bzhin du chu dang / me dang / rlung dang / rnam par shes pa'i khams ni re re ba dang / yang 'dus pa sogs 'khor 'das kyi chos thams cad/ rang cag rnams kyi blo la snang ba de nges par byas nas/ sngar skyes bu'i snang tshul dang 'dzin tshul brtags nas mnyam par 'jog pa ji lta bar/ gtan la phab ste/ bden par grub pa rdul tsam yang ma rnyed pa de'i tshe/ ma rnyed pa ni rnyed pa'i mchog dang / ma mthong ba mthong ba dam par gsungs pa bzhin sems kyi don dam pa'i ngo bo mthong bas sems ngo 'phrod pa yin pas de kha'i ngang la g.yeng ba med par rtse gcig tu/ bden grub bkag tsam chos nyid nam mkha' lta bu'i mnyam gzhag skyong ngo / /

Thus, with respect to all phenomena of samsara and nirvana — all ordinary beings and āryas, both the outer and inner elements of earth, likewise water, fire, wind, and consciousness, individually as well as their collection and so forth — ascertain how they appear to your mind. And just as you examined the mode of appearance and mode of apprehension in relation to the person and rested your mind in meditative equipoise, here too, establish their [abiding nature]. [538] When, as a result, you have not found even the minutest particle that possesses true existence, at that point, as in the statements “Not finding is the supreme finding” and “Not seeing is the supreme seeing,”[1197] you have seen the mind’s true nature and have recognized the mind. So, without any distraction, rest single-pointedly in that awareness and maintain meditative equipoise on this pure negation of true existence, the space-like true nature of phenomena.

d.div: [1197] Kamalaśīla’s Lamp for the Middle Way (Madhyamakāloka, Toh 3887 Tengyur, dbu ma, sa, 168b4) cites a passage from Perfectly Gathering the Teachings Sutra that reads “Not seeing all phenomena is the perfect seeing”; Dharmasaṃgītisūtra, Toh 238 Kangyur, mdo sde, zha, 68b6.

f.d: yang na bdag tu 'dogs pa'i gzhi phra ba rlung sems shin tu phra bar gsungs shing / gdams ngag pa rnams kyang sems kyi gnas lugs gtan la 'bebs pa la sems ngo sprod par bzhed pa ltar smras pa/

Alternatively, as the extremely subtle wind and mind are stated to be the subtle basis of the designation of self, and also as the upholders of pith instructions understand establishing the abiding nature of the mind to constitute introducing the mind’s nature, I say:

yang na mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngang / / gzugs su ma grub stong sang nge // sgrib med sna tshogs 'char zhing 'phro/ / 'gag med gsal zhing rig pa'i rgyun//[33] chad pa med par 'jug pa'i sems/ / ltos med snang zhing 'dzin pa yi// zhen yul mgon po zhi ba lhas/ / rgyun dang tshogs zhes bya ba ni//[34]
'phreng ba dmag sogs bzhin du brdzun/[104] / zhes gsungs lung dang rigs pa yis// snang tshul ltar du ma grub pa'i/ / ngang du rtse gcig mnyam par zhog /[35] ces so//

div.div: 33–34 Alternatively, while in meditative equipoise, observe your mind as thus characterized: pure vacuity because it does not exist as physical; unobscured as diverse appearances arise to it; and unceasing, a luminous and aware continuum that is uninterrupted in its engagement. Such a mind appears and is conceived as independent, but with respect to such objects of clinging, the guardian Śāntideva states:

35 “The so-called continuums and collections, just like rosaries, armies, and so on, are false.”[1198] So through scripture such as this and reasoning, establish this truth of how things do not exist as they appear and rest your mind single-pointedly in this meditative equipoise.

d.div: [104] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_101_shog_27_ba1
[1198] Guide to the Bodhisattva Way (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 9.101, Toh 3872 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 27b1.

f.d:
yang na zla ba'i zhabs kyis/
sems nyid kyis ni sems can 'jig rten dang / / snod kyi 'jig rten shin tu sna tshogs 'god/[105] / ces sems snod bcud thams cad kyi rtsa bar bstan pas/ sems kyi gzhi rtsa chod na 'phrul gzhan dang mi 'dra bas 'di ltar bya ste/

Alternatively, Candrakīrti says:
It is the mind that constructed the vast diversity of both the domain of sentient beings and their universe.[1199] This explains that the mind is the root of all the worlds and their inhabitants, so if you are able to cut the root basis of the mind, the impact would be unlike employing any other technique. For this, you should proceed in the following manner.

d.div: [105] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_89_shog_208_ba2
[1199] Entering the Middle Way (Madhyamakāvatāra) 6.89 Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 208b2.

f.d:
sngar gyi rgyun mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngang nas rang sems la brtags pa na gzugs gang du yang ma grub pas stong sang nge ba/ nyi ma la sprin lta bu'i sgrib pa med pa/ mi 'gyu dgu 'gyu/ mi dran dgu dran sna tshogs 'char zhing phyir 'phro ba/ mar me shi ba lta bu'i 'gag pa med pa gsal zhing rig pa'i rgyun chad pa med par breng chags su 'jug pa'i sems de/ rang sems 'dzin pa'i blo la gang la yang ltos pa med pa rang dbang du snang zhing / snang ba ltar 'dzin pa'i zhen yul la ma snang ba ltar gyi sems de/ mgon po zhi ba lhas spyod 'jug tu/
rgyun dang tshogs zhes bya ba ni/ / 'phreng ba dmag sogs bzhin du brdzun/[106] / zhes 'phreng ba'i cha shas re re nas srad bur brgyus pa la/ 'phreng ba zhes btags tsam dang / go mtshon thogs pa'i skyes bu re re nas 'dus pa la dmag ces ming rkyang btags tsam ma gtogs bden par ma grub/ ces gsungs pa'i lung dang rigs pa yis/ snang tshul ltar du ma grub par nges pa'i/ ngang du rtse gcig tu mnyam par zhog cig /

If, while maintaining the continuity of your earlier meditative equipoise, you examine your mind, since it does not exist in a material way, it will appear as pure vacuity, like a sun that is unobscured by, for instance, clouds. Yet all sorts of diverse forms and all sorts of diverse thoughts arise in it and it moves outward as well. Unlike the flickering of a flame, it is unceasing; and it operates fluidly with an uninterrupted continuum of that which is luminous and aware. Now this mind appears to you as if it is totally independent of the subject that apprehends it. [539] With respect to such a mind — the object clung to just as perceived, or this mind as it appears to you — the guardian Śāntideva says:
The so-called continuums and collections, just like rosaries, armies, and so on, are false.[1200] So on the basis of scriptures and reasoning, ascertain how “rosary” is merely imputed onto a composite where individual beads are strung on a string, and how “army” is just a name merely imputed onto a collection of individual men bearing arms. Apart from this there is nothing truly existent. Rest single-pointedly in meditative equipoise with the ascertainment that your mind does not exist in accord with how it appears to you.

d.div: [106] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_101_shog_27_ba1
[1200] See note 1198 above.

f.d:
de ltar yang brgyad stong pa las/
sems la sems ma mchis te/ sems kyi rang bzhin ni 'od gsal ba'o/[107] / zhes sems la rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i sems ma mchis te/ sems kyi rang bzhin 'od gsal ba stong pa nyid do/ /zhes gsungs shing / dkon brtsegs las kyang /
sems ni dus gsum gyi sangs rgyas thams cad kyis kyang ma gzigs mi gzigs gzigs par mi 'gyur ro/[108] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines says:
The mind is devoid of mind, for the nature of mind is clear light.[1201] This states that there is no intrinsically existing mind in the mind, for the nature of the mind is clear-light emptiness. And in the Heap of Jewels too it says:
The mind has never been seen, is not being seen, and will not be seen by all the buddhas of the three times.[1202]

d.div: [107] sde dge_12_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_'phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa brgyad stong pa/ bam po dang po/ le'u/ 1_shog_3_na3

[108] sde dge_46_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ka_'phags pa sgo mtha' yas pa rnam par sbyong ba bstan pa'i le'u zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ shog_70_ba4_'di yin nam snyam tshig ji bzhin ma brnyed pas dpyad dgos/
[1201] Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā, chap. 1, Toh 12 Kangyur, brgyad stong, ka, 3a3.
[1202] Presenting the Thorough Cleansing of Limitless Avenues Sutra (Anantamukhapariśodhananirdeśaparivarta), Toh 46 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ka, 70b4.

f.d:
rje mar pas kyang sems kyi chos nyid ji lta ba bzhin nges nas sgom pa la sems stong pa nyid la sbar zin gyi tha snyad mdzad de/ ji skad du
shar chu bo gang+gA'i 'gram du phyin/ / rje mai trI chen po'i bka' drin gyis/ / gzhi chos nyid skye ba med pa rtogs/ / sems stong pa nyid la sbar zin byas/ / don spros bral gnyug ma'i ngo bo mthong / / sku gsum ma dang mngon sum mjal/ / mi kho bo'i spros pa de nas chod/[109] / ces gsungs shing / 'gro mgon phag grus kyang /
'khor 'das gnyis kyi rtsa ba sems/ / sems gdod nas dag pa de bzhin nyid/ / gdod nas zhi zhing ma skyes pas/ / sems ye nas spros pa'i mtha' dang bral/[110] / zhes gsungs so//

Also Lord Marpa labels ascertaining the mind’s true nature as it is and meditating on it as “grabbing the emptiness of mind with one’s bare hands.” He says:
I went to the banks of the River Ganges in the east. There through the kindness of the great Lord Maitripa, I realized the ground, the unborn reality, and grabbed with bare hands the emptiness of mind. I saw the primordial nature, reality free from elaboration; I met face to face with my mother, the three buddha bodies. From then on, this man’s elaborations were severed.[1203] Also, Drogön Phakmo Drupa says:
Mind is the root of both samsara and nirvana; mind’s primordial purity is true suchness; Since it is primordially peaceful and unborn, mind is utterly free of elaborated extremes.[1204]

d.div: [109] sgra bsgyur mar pa lo tsA'i rnam thar mthong ba don yod/ 134_yig phreng _3_si khron mi rigs dpe skrun khang nas 1990_lor dpar du bskrun pa/
[110] rin chen rgyan 'dra zhes bya ba/ phag gru rdo rje rgyal po'i gsung 'bum/ ga_shog_2_ba2
[1203] Tsangnyön Heruka, Meaningful to Behold, 134.
[1204] Phakdru Dorjé Gyalpo, Like a Precious Ornament, 2b2.

f.d: mdor na bdag cag gi dge ba'i bshes gnyen thams cad mkhyen pa ma yin pa la yin par grags pa lta bu min pa/ don dang mthun pa'i thams cad mkhyen pa sangs rgyas ye shes zhabs kyi zhal snga nas kyi zhal gdams 'god pa/

In brief, I present in the following the oral instruction of my spiritual mentor, the omniscient Sangyé Yeshé, who is true to the meaning of his name and not like the case where someone who is not omniscient but is reputed to be. The text says: [540]

mdor na bdag gi dge ba'i bshes/ / don dang mthun pa'i thams cad mkhyen// sangs rgyas ye shes zhal snga nas/ /[36]
gang shar rnam rtog 'dzin par yongs rig na/ / don dam chos dbyings gzhan la ltos med 'char// shar ba'i ngang du rig pa zhugs pa la/ / rtse gcig mnyam par 'jog pa e ma ho/[111] /[37]
zhes gang shar rnam rtog 'dzin pa ste/ gang shar rtog pas btags pa tsam du rig na/ don dam chos nyid rkyen gzhan la ma ltos par blo yul du 'char te 'jug par/
tha snyad bden pa thabs su gyur pa dang / / don dam bden pa thabs byung 'gyur ba ste/[112] / zhes gsungs pa bzhin no/ /

36 In brief, as my spiritual mentor, the omniscient Sangyé Yeshé, who is in accord with reality, states:
37 “When you are fully aware that whatever appears is conceived by thoughts, then the ultimate expanse dawns independently of anything else. When your awareness enters into what has thus dawned, you rest in single-pointed meditative equipoise — E ma ho!”[1205]
He says that when you recognize whatever you perceive as “conceived by thoughts” — that is to say, viewing whatever arises as conceptual imputations — then the ultimate truth, the true nature, will dawn within the sphere of your awareness without dependence on any other condition. This is as stated in the following in Entering the Middle Way:
The conventional truth is the means, while the ultimate truth is its end.[1206]

d.div: [111] mkhas grub sangs rgyas ye shes kyi gsung 'bum/ le tshan ca/ gsung mgur chab shog/ dris lan sogs phyogs gcig tu sdebs pa/ shog_67_ba6
[112] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_80_shog_207_na2
[1205] Khedrup Sangyé Yeshé, Collection of Experiential Songs, Letters, and Replies to Queries, 67b6.
[1206] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra, 6.80ab, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 207a2.

f.d: shar ba'i ngang du rig pa zhugs pa ste/ chos nyid blo yul du shar ba de dang / yul can shes pa rtse gcig tu sbyar nas mnyam par 'jog pa ni ngo mtshar ba'o/ / zhes gsungs pa'i rkang pa phyi ma gnyis kyi don dang mthun par/

“When your awareness enters into what has thus dawned,” that is say, when you rest your mind in meditative equipoise through single-pointed fusion of the true nature — which has dawned within the sphere of your awareness — with the subject awareness, this is indeed most wonderful. In the same vein as these last two lines,

dam pas kyang // stong pa'i ngang du rig pa'i mdung skor bya/ / lta ba la thogs thug med do ding ri ba/[113] /[38]
zhes sogs gsungs pa'i dgongs pa gcig tu gnas so//

38 Dampa Sangyé says: “Whirl the spear of awareness within emptiness; the view, O people of Dingri, is unobstructed.”[1207] These statements and their likes make the same point.
The intention of statements such as these remains the same.

d.div: [113] pha dam pa sangs rgyas kyi zhal gdams ding ri brgyad cu pa/ shog_17_ba4_gdams ngag mdzod/
[1207] Dampa Sangyé, Hundred Verses of Advice, verse 51, 17a4.

f.d: [mjug ]
2.3. The concluding practice

gsum pa rjes ni phyag rgya chen po la mnyam par bzhag pa'i dge ba rnams bla na med pa'i byang chub tu bsngo ba ste/ rtsa bar/ 'di la sbyor dngos rjes gsum las/ zhes dngos su bstan pa/ 'jug gang du sbyor tshul khong na gnas kyang mi gsal ba mtshams 'dir sbyor rgyu yin cing / slan chad sa mtshams phyed pa'i phyir rtsa bar 'god na'ang /

The third, the concluding practice, is dedicating the virtues of meditative equipoise on mahāmudrā to unexcelled enlightenment. The root text has the line “Here, of the three — preparation, main practice, and conclusion” [in verse 3], explicitly mentioning a concluding practice, yet where exactly it goes was left implicit and unclear. It is to be applied here at this juncture. Thus to delineate the boundary, I present here the root text:

rjes ni phyag chen bsgoms pa las/ / byung ba'i rnam dkar ci mchis pa// dus gsum dge tshogs rgya mtshor bcas/ / bla med byang chub chen por bsngo//[39]
zhes sbyar kyang rung ngo //

39 At the conclusion, the virtues that have emerged from meditating on mahāmudrā together with the ocean of virtues of all three times, dedicate these all to the great, unexcelled enlightenment. [541]
This is how the root text can be correlated [to the outline].

da ni phyag rgya chen po la mnyam par bzhag pa'i mnyam gzhag las langs nas rjes thob tu nyams len ji ltar skyong tshul dang / slar yang mnyam par 'jog pa'i tshe dgag bya'i don spyi 'phyug med du nges par bya ba dang / mnyam rjes ci yang rung pa'i skabs su mtha' gzhan du dogs pa'i dogs pa bsal ba rnams phyogs gcig tu bstan pa'i phyir 'di ltar/

Now to present together in one place (1) how to maintain your practice in the post-equipoise period after you have risen from meditative equipoise on mahāmudrā, (2) how to ascertain inerrantly the generic concept of the object of negation when you return to meditative equipoise, and (3) how to dispel doubts that might arise either in relation to meditative equipoise or the post-equipoise state,

de ltar goms nas tshogs drug gi / yul du snang ba ci shar yang // snang tshul zhib mor rtogs shig dang / / gnas tshul rjen par lhang gis 'char// gang shar ngos 'dzin lta ba'i gnad//[40]
mdor na rang sems la sogs pa/ / gang gang snang ba'i don der ni// ma 'dzin de de'i gnas tshul de/ / nges par gyis la rtag tu skyongs//[41] 'di ltar shes nas 'khor 'das kyi/ / chos kun rang bzhin gcig tu sbyor/ /
ces smras so//

the text says:
40 Thus, having gained familiarity [with this practice], realize precisely the mode of appearance of any object that appears within the field of your six senses, and its mode of being will dawn naked and vivid. Recognizing whatever appears is the key to the view.
41 In brief, whatever appears — be it your own mind or something else — do not grasp but ascertain its mode of being and always maintain that awareness. Knowing this, bring all phenomena of samsara and nirvana into a single nature.

de ltar mnyam gzhag tu goms par byas nas/ rjes thob tu mig shes sogs tshogs drug gi yul du gzugs la sogs pa'i snang ba ci shar yang ji ltar snang ba'i tshul la zhib mor 'byed pa'i rnam dpyod kyis legs par rtogs shig dang / de ltar brtags pas bden par snang yang / gsog dang gsob dang rmi lam dang chu nang gi zla gzugs ltar snang yang rang dbang gi snying po med pa'i rten 'byung gi gnas tshul rjen lhang gis 'char zhing / de la brten nas chos nyid la nges pa je cher 'gro ste/ rje mi tras/
gang shar ngos 'dzin lta ba'i gnad/[114] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro//

Thus, having cultivated familiarity [with emptiness] during meditative equipoise, whatever appearances might arise during the post-equipoise period, such as of form and so on, within the field of your six senses, such as visual perception, examine carefully with discerning intellect as to how they appear to your mind. When you examine in this way, the truth of their dependent origination — how although they appear to you as if they possess true existence, like something hollow, like an effigy, like a dream, or like the moon’s reflection in water, they are devoid of independent essence — will dawn upon you starkly and vividly. Through this your ascertainment of the true nature will grow greater. This is as Lord Mitrayogi says:
Recognizing whatever appears is the key point of the view.[1208]

d.div: [114] mi tra dz+wa ki la lhag pa'i lha 'phags mchog thugs rje chen pos dngos su gnang ba'i snying po don gsum du grags ba'i gdams pa'i rtsa tshig las drangs/ rtsa tshig 'di cha tshang deb 'di nang yod pa dngul chu d+harma b+haDa'i gsung snying po don gsum gyi zin bris nang bzhugs/

[1208] “Root Lines of Instruction on the Three Essential Points” (Snying po don gsum gyi rtsa tshig) verse 5a. This is part of a short five-stanza text attributed to the Indian master Mitrayogi (written also as Mitrajvaki), who visited Tibet in the twelfth century at the invitation of Trophu Lotsāwa Jampa Pal. On this root text, see page 36.

f.d: da ni mang du yang ci zhig dgos mdor bsdu na rang cag tshu rol mthong ba rnams la rang gi sems la sogs pa chos can gang dang gang zhig snang ba'i tshul de nyid dgag bya'i snang tshul yin pas/ snang ba'i don der zhen cing ma 'dzin par/ / de dang de'i gnas tshul snang ba ltar du grub pa bkag tsam nges par gyis la mnyam gzhag nam mkha' lta bu dang / de las langs nas bkag pa'i shul na ci 'dug bltas pa na ming tsam/ btags tsam gyi bya byed rten 'brel bsnyon med du 'char ba'i rjes thob kyi rnal 'byor res 'jog gis rtag tu skyong ba yin no/ / mnyam rjes skyong tshul 'di ltar shes par byas nas/ 'khor 'das kyi chos ma lus pa kun gyi'ang bden pa bkag tsam gyi don dam pa'i rang bzhin dbyer mi phyed par gcig tu sbyar nas mnyam par 'jog pa dang / rjes thob tu kun rdzob pa'i rang bzhin snang tsam sgyu ma lta bur sbyar nas goms par byed dgos te/

What need is there to say more? Let me sum this up in a succinct way. For us near-sighted ordinary beings, [542] it is precisely the way in which this or that subject — our mind and so on — appears to us that is itself the way we perceive the object of negation. So instead of clinging to perceived things and grasping at them, ascertain the ultimate mode of being of this or that phenomenon — namely, the simple negation of their existing in accord with how they appear to the mind. In this way, rest in space-like meditative equipoise. And when you rise from meditative equipoise and observe what remains in the aftermath of negation, what will appear undeniably to you is the world of dependent origination of everyday activity on the nominal level of mere labels and mere conceptual imputations. This is the yoga of post-equipoise, and you constantly maintain these two in alternation: [the yoga of space-like meditative equipoise and the yoga of illusion-like post-equipoise]. Knowing thus how to maintain meditative equipoise and post-equipoise, rest in meditative equipoise wherein the ultimate natures of all phenomena of samsara and nirvana — the simple negation of their true existence — are indivisibly subsumed into a single truth. And during the post-equipoise state, relate to everything as mere conventional realities, as mere appearances, and as illusion-like. In this way, you should meditate.
de skad du yang 'phags pa lhas/ /[42] dngos po gcig gi lta po gang / / de ni kun gyi lta por bshad// gcig gi stong nyid gang yin pa/ / de ni kun gyi stong nyid yin/[115] /[43] zhes gsungs so//

div.b: 42 Here, Āryadeva says: “The viewer of one thing is stated to be the viewer of all, and the emptiness of one is the emptiness of all.”

d.div: [115] sde dge_3846_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsha_slob dpon 'phags pa lha/ bzhi brgya pa/ rab byed/ 8_sh+loka_16_shog_9_ba6
[1209] Four Hundred Verses (Catuḥśataka) 8.16, Toh 3846 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsha, 9b6.

f.d: 'o na chos nyid la mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngor/ rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba'i chos rnams ming rkyang btags yod tsam du snang ngam zhe na smras pa/
Do the phenomena of dependent origination appear as mere names and conceptual existences within the perspective of meditative equipoise? In response, I say:

de ltar chos nyid la/ / tshul bzhin mnyam par bzhag pa'i ngor// yod med la sogs 'khor 'das kyi/ / spros pa'i mtha' dang bral mod kyi//[44]
zhes brjod par bya ste/

div.div: 43 Thus, within the perfect meditative equipoise on this ultimate nature of reality, you are free from the elaborated extremes of existence and nonexistence and of samsara and nirvana.

f.d:
rje btsun mid las/
don dam bden pa'i dbang du ni/ / bgegs las sangs rgyas nyid kyang med/ / sgom pa po dang bsgom bya dang / / bgrod bya sa dang lam rtogs med/ / 'bras bu sku dang ye shes med/ / de phyir mya ngan 'das pa med/ / ming dang tshig gis btags pa tsam/ khams gsum brtan dang g.yo bar bcas/ / gdod nas ma grub skye ba med/ / gzhi med lhan cig skyes pa med/ / las dang las kyi rnam smin med/ / de phyir 'khor ba'i ming yang med/ / mthar thug don la de ltar snang /[116] / zhes pa dang /

Lord Milarepa says:
From the standpoint of ultimate truth, there are no obstacles, no karma, and no buddhahood; there is no meditation, no object of meditation, no grounds to traverse, no paths to realize, no fruition of buddha bodies and no gnosis, and therefore there is no nirvana. All are merely imputed by labels and words. [543] The three worlds, the stationary and the moving, have primordially no existence or arising; they have no basis and nothing innately arisen; there are no karma and no fruitional effects. Therefore not even the name samsara exists. This is how they appear within the final reality.[1210]

d.div: [116] rje mi la'i mgur 'bum/ tshe ring mched lnga'i drod nyul ba dang zhus lan gyi rim pa/ shog_482_nas _483_yig phreng _17_sgom pa po med bsgom bya med/ /bgrod bya sa dang lam rtags med//
[1210] Milarepa, Hundred Thousand Songs, 482.

f.d: smra bsam brjod med shes rab pha rol phyin/[117] /zhes sogs dang / mkhas grub khyung pos kyang / snang srid rang grol sgyu ma rmi lam bzhin/[118] /zhes sogs gsungs pa ltar ro//

And there is the line “The perfection of wisdom is beyond speech, thought, and expression,”[1211] and the scholar-siddha Khyungpo Naljor says, “Mundane appearances are self-liberating, like illusions or dreams.”[1212]

d.div: [117] smra bsam brjod med shes rab pha rol phyin/ / zhes pa 'di sgra gcan 'dzin gyi yum la bstod pa las yin par dgas po'i thar rgyan wa Na nas deb gzugs su dpar du bskrun pa shog grangs _248_yig phreng drug par gsal/
[118] 'dir mkhas grub 'khyung po gsungs pa 'khyung po rnal 'byor la go dgos la de'i gsung de gang las drangs dpe ma brnyed pas 'tshol zhib byed zhu ma thub/

[1211] This is the first line of a well-known praise of the perfection of wisdom attributed to the Buddha’s son Rahula and traditionally chanted, in Tibetan Buddhism, before the Heart Sutra. The full stanza reads: “The perfection of wisdom is beyond speech, thought, and expression. / Unborn and unceasing, it shares the nature of space. / It is experienced firsthand by the yogi’s gnosis. / To this mother of the conquerors of all three times, I pay homage.”
[1212] Source not located.

f.d:
'o na de ltar yin na las 'bras sogs gtan med dam zhe na/ don dam du med pas med go mi chod pas/ las 'bras sogs shin tu yod ces brjod pa/
de las langs nas brtags pa'i tshe/ / ming rkyang btags yod tsam zhig gis// bya byed rten 'brel bsnyon med par/ / rmi lam smig rgyu chu zla dang // sgyu ma lta bur ngang gis 'char/ /[45]
zhes smras pa ltar/ rje mid las kyang /
e ma sems can med gyur na/ / dus gsum sangs rgyas ci las byung / / rgyu med 'bras bu mi srid las/ / kun rdzob bden pa'i dbang du ni/ / 'khor ba dang ni mya ngan 'das/ / thams cad yod ces thub pas gsungs/ / yod pa dngos por snang ba dang / / med pa stong pa'i chos nyid gnyis/ / ngo bo dbyer med ro gcig pas/ / rang rig gzhan rig yod min te/ / thams cad zung 'jug yangs pa yin/[119] / zhes gsungs so/ /

If that is so, does this mean karma and its effects and so forth are utterly nonexistent? To state that karma and its effects and so forth do very much exist, since the absence of ultimate existence is not the same as absence of existence, the text says:
44 Yet when you arise from that equipoise and examine, it is undeniable that actions, agents, and dependent originations of mere labels and mere concepts naturally appear — like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon in water, or like a magician’s illusion.
Along the same lines, Lord Milarepa also says:
Alas! If there were no sentient beings, whence would come the buddhas of three times? A result without a cause is impossible, and so, from the standpoint of conventional truth, samsara as well as nirvana — everything — exists, the Sage stated. Existence, the appearance of entities, and nonexistence, emptiness, which is their true nature — the nature of these two is indivisible and of one taste. Thus there is no [differentiation between] self-cognition and other cognition. Everything is a vast union.[1213]

d.div: [119] rje mi la'i mgur 'bum/ tshe ring mched lnga'i drod nyul ba dang zhus lan gyi rim pa/ shog_483_yig phreng _4
[1213] Milarepa, Hundred Thousand Songs, 483.

f.d:
yod tshul yang ming tsam btags tsam du yod pas tshim par byas nas 'jog pa yin te/ 'phags mchog klu sgrub zhabs kyis/
gzugs kyi dngos po ming tsam phyir/ / nam mkha' yang ni ming tsam mo/[120] / zhes gsungs pa'i phyir/

As for their mode of existence, this is to be defined on the basis of being satisfied with their existence at the level of mere labels and mere designations. The supreme ārya, Nāgārjuna, for example, states:
Because physical entities are mere labels, space too is a mere label.[1214]

d.div: [120] sde dge_4158_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_slob dpon klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_99_shog_80_ba3
[1214] Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī) 1.99, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 80b3.

f.d: des na 'phags pa yab sras bzhed pa'i lta ba phyag rgya chen po'i go don mthar thug pa ni btags yod ming rkyang zhes pa 'di yin pas gsal bar bshad na/ dper na khang pa ka ba bzhi pa zhig gi nang na ka ba yod par ni 'dod dgos te/ de na ka ba bzhi yod pa'i phyir/ de'i ka ba de ni ka ba bzhi po so sor rjes su 'gro ba'i spyi yang yin no/ /

Thus the final import of the mahāmudrā view as upheld by Ārya Nāgārjuna and his spiritual son [Āryadeva] comes to what is described as “imputed existence, just nominal.” Let me explain this clearly. To give an example, it must be acknowledged that a pillar does exist in a house with four pillars, because there are four pillars. [544] And “pillar” is a universal that pervades each of the four individual pillars.

'o na ka ba rdzas spyi de'i mtshan gzhi ci yin zhes btsal na bzhi po de re re nas de'i mtshan gzhir mi rung / /bzhi po tshogs pa'ang de'i mtshan gzhi min/ bzhi po so so ba dang / tshogs tsam pa las don gzhan du gyur pa'i de'i mtshan gzhi yang bstan rgyu med do/ / des na de'i nang gi ka ba rdzas spyi de ni ka ba bzhi po'i steng du ka ba zhes ming gis btags tsam ste/ ming gis btags tsam des tshim nas 'jog pa ma gtogs btsal na mi rnyed pas btags yod ming rkyang zhes bya ste chos thams cad la mtshungs so/ /

Now if one were to search for the identity of the substance of this universal “pillar” by inquiring what exactly it is, none of the four pillars individually is a suitable candidate, nor is the four collectively. Yet, apart from the four pillars individually and their collection, there is nothing else that can be identified as a candidate either. Thus the substance of this universal “pillar” is nothing but a name imputed on those individual pillars, and nothing apart from what is posited on the basis of being satisfied with the mere designation by label can be found if one searches [beyond this]. This is what is called “imputed existence, just nominal,” and it is true also of every other phenomenon.

da ni bsal bya'i dogs pa 'di yod de/ lugs 'di dang 'brel ba'i snga phyi'i yi ge 'god pa po sogs 'ga' zhig /so skye'i shes pa thams cad 'khrul shes dang / de'i rgyu mtshan gyis so skye'i blo la snang pa gang shar thams cad rang bzhin gyis grub par snang zhing 'char zhes zer bzhin du/ da lta'i snang tshul 'di las gzhan pa'i dgag bya'i snang tshul bden grub rwa rong nge ba zhig 'dzin par 'dod pa ni/ rang cag so skye'i blo la snang ba/ snang ba ltar ma grub zer ma nus pas nongs par 'dug pa/ de ltar na rang rgyud pa'i mkhas pa rnams kyis gzugs sogs blo gnod med la snang ba'i dbang gis yod par zhal gyis bzhes pa la/ dpal ldan zla bas dgag pa ji ltar mdzad pa'i tshul legs par soms shig/ / 'on kyang tshur mthong gi dbang shes lnga la yul lnga tshugs thub tu ma grub bzhin du tshugs thub tu grub par snang bas 'khrul shes dang / yul lnga rang mtshan du grub par snang ba'i cha la tshad ma dang de'i rgyu mtshan gyis de dag tha snyad du 'jog pa'i tshad mar 'jog pa sogs ni shes dgos so/ /

Now the following doubt needs to be clarified. Some earlier and later writers connected with this tradition [of Geden mahāmudrā], while saying that all cognitions of ordinary beings are deluded and that, as such, whatever is perceived is perceived as possessing intrinsic nature, they also assert a mode of perceiving the object of negation that is distinct from our everyday mode of perception — some kind of “true existence” springing like horns from its head! This error seems to derive from their inability to state that what is perceived by our ordinary mind does not exist as it appears to us. In view of this, they should ponder well Candrakīrti’s refutation of Svātantrika Mādhyamikas’ assertions that form and so forth exist by virtue of their appearance to an undefective mind. This said, it is necessary also to understand (1) how [according to Svātantrika] the five sense consciousnesses are mistaken in that they perceive the five sensory objects to exist self-sufficiently although they do not, (2) how the five are veridical with respect to their perception of things as existing by virtue of intrinsic characteristics, and (3) how, because of that, they are accepted as valid cognitions that posit things on the conventional level.

yang mang po zhig gang zag mi 'gog /gang zag bden grub 'gog par gsungs snyam du mnyam gzhag tu gang zag ling po zhig bzhag nas/ blos byas kyi gang zag bden grub zhig 'gog pa'i ngal ba byed pa ni ches mi 'thad de rtag mthar 'gyur pa'i phyir ro/ / gzhan yang brjod par bya ba du ma 'dug na'ang mangs pas 'jigs pa'i phyir de tsam mo/ /

Many others, recalling how it is said that the person is not negated but only the truly existent person, proceed in their meditative equipoise to set aside the whole person, leaving it untouched, and strive hard to negate merely some mentally contrived “truly existing person.” This is completely wrong, for it leads to the extreme of eternalism. Although there is much more to discuss, fearing excessive length, this will suffice.

de ltar bsgoms pas rtag chad kyi mtha' dang bral ba'i lam bzang mngon du 'gyur tshul bstan pa/
snang bas stong pa mi sgrib cing / / stong pas snang ba mi 'gog pa// stong dang rten 'byung don gcig pa'i/ / lam bzang de tshe mngon sum 'gyur/ /[46]
zhes smras te/

To indicate how, as you practice in this manner, the excellent path free of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism will manifest, the text says: [545]
45 When appearance does not obscure emptiness and when emptiness does not obstruct appearance, the excellent path — where emptiness and dependent origination share the same meaning — will then manifest .

'di dang mthun par rje thams cad mkhyen pas/
snang ba rten 'brel bslu ba med pa dang / / stong pa khas len bral ba'i go ba gnyis/ / ji srid so sor snang ba de srid du/ / da dung thub pa'i dgongs pa rtogs pa med/ /
nam zhig res 'jog med par cig car du/ / rten 'brel mi bslur mthong ba tsam nyid nas/ / nges shes yul gyi 'dzin stangs kun 'jig na/ / de tshe lta ba'i dpyad pa rdzogs pa lags/[121] / zhes pa dang / 'jug par yang /
de bzhin chos rnams thams cad stong na yang / / stong nyid dag las rab tu skye bar 'gyur/ / bden pa gnyis su'ang rang bzhin med pa'i phyir/ / de dag rtag pa ma yin chad pa'ang min/[122] / zhes dang / mgon po klu sgrub kyis kyang /
chos rnams stong pa nyid shes nas/ / rgyu dang 'bras bu 'thad pa gang / / ngo mtshar las kyang 'di ngo mtshar/ / rmad byung las kyang 'di rmad byung /[123] / zhes gsungs pa ltar go sla'o//

Along the same lines, the omniscient Jé Tsongkhapa says:
As long as the two understandings — of appearance, undeceiving dependent origination, and of emptiness, the absence of all positions — remain separate, then you have not realized the intent of the Sage.
However, if at some point, not in alternation but at once, the instant you see that dependent origination is undeceiving, this dismantles the entirety of the object of grasping at certitude, at this point your analysis of the view is complete.[1215] Entering the Middle Way says:
Likewise although all things are empty, they do arise from emptiness in a robust way. Since no intrinsic nature exists in either of the two truths, phenomena are neither eternal nor annihilated.[1216] The guardian Nāgārjuna too states:
Having understood this emptiness of phenomena and yet cause and effect remain tenable, this is more amazing than amazing! This is more wondrous than wondrous![1217] The meaning here is easily understood.

d.div: [121] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ kha_lam gtso rnam gsum/ gsung thor bu/ shog_194_ba1
[122] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma la 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_38_206_na2
[123] sde dge_1800_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ngi _slob dpon klu sgrub/ byang chub sems kyi 'grel pa/ shog_41_ba4
[1215] Three Principal Elements of the Path, verses 11–12. See page 53 above.
[1216] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra, 6.38, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 206a2.
[1217] Commentary on the Awakening Mind (Bodhicittavivaraṇa) verse 88, Toh 1801 Tengyur, rgyud, ngi, 41b4.

f.d: de ltar zhi gnas kyi rta la bskyon nas phyag chen bskyangs pas stong pa nyid la dmigs pa'i dpyad stobs kyis lus sems shin sbyangs kyi bde bas zin pa'i ting nge 'dzin nam thob pa na sbyor lam drod thob pa yin no/ /

When, through maintaining the practice of mahāmudrā by saddling it astride the horse of tranquil abiding, you achieve meditative concentration permeated by the bliss of physical and mental pliancy derived through the force of analysis focused on emptiness, you have reached the heat stage of the path of preparation.[1218]

d.div: [1218] Heat is first of the four stages within the path of preparation (within the fivefold paths of accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, and no-more training), the remaining three being peak, forbearance, and supreme Dharma.

f.d:
bka' brgyud gong ma 'ga' zhig ni phyag chen gyi lam la rnal 'byor bzhi'i rnam gzhag mdzad de/ sems la rtse gcig tu dmigs pas rtse gcig dang / sems spros bral du rtogs pas spros bral dang / snang sems ro gcig tu rtogs pas ro gcig dang / mtshan bcas kyis sgom du med pas sgom med de bzhi yin la/ sa mtshams rje rgod tshang pa ni dang po mos spyod/ gnyis pa mthong lam/ gsum pa sa gnyis pa nas sa bdun pa'i bar/ bzhi pa dag sa sogs kyi ngo bor bzhed/ zhang rin po che ni/
phyag rgya chen po gcig chod la/ / rmongs pas sa lam rtsi pa 'khrul/ / 'on kyang rmongs pa dga' ba'i phyir/ / mtshan nyid theg pa'i sa lam rnams/ / 'dir yang dod po rtsi bar bya/[124] / gsung zhing / rtsi tshul rje rgod tshang pa dang 'dra'o//

Some past Kagyü masters present the mahāmudrā path within the framework of four yogas: (1) Since you focus single pointedly on the mind, there is single-pointedness. (2) Since you realize the mind as free of elaborations, there is freedom from elaboration. (3) Since you realize appearance and the mind as being of a single taste, there is single taste. And (4) since you cannot meditate on it with signs, there is nonmeditation. In terms of correlating these to the grounds and paths, the master Götsangpa holds that the first yoga correlates to the [path of] imaginative engagement,[1219] the second yoga to the path of seeing, the third yoga to the second up to the seventh bodhisattva ground, and the fourth yoga to the pure grounds.[1220] Shang Rinpoché says:
With respect to all-accomplishing mahāmudrā, the ignorant make the error of counting grounds and paths. [546] Yet to please the ignorant, I too will delineate here the equivalents of the Philosophy Vehicle’s grounds and paths.[1221] As for how this delineates [the grounds and paths], it is similar to that of the master Götsangpa.

d.div: [124] 'tshol zhib byas kyang ma rnyed/

[1219] The “path of imaginative engagement” (mos spyod kyi lam) is the first two paths in the five-path schema — the paths of accumulation and preparation. At this level, the practitioner’s engagement with emptiness is mediated by imagination and concepts rather than direct. Götsangpa Gönpo Dorjé (1189–1253) was an early master of the Drukpa Kagyü, a student of Tsangpa Gyaré and the guru of Yangönpa.

[1220] The “pure grounds” (dag sa) are the eighth, ninth, and tenth bodhisattva grounds, so called because by the eighth ground the bodhisattva has eliminated the afflictions together with their roots. Within the five paths schema, the first of the ten bodhisattva grounds is attained when the meditator reaches the third path, the path of seeing, marked by direct realization of emptiness for the first time.
[1221] Lama Shang, Ultimate Supreme Path, 71. See also translation in Roberts, Mahāmudrā and Related Instructions, 122–23.

f.d:
spros bral sa dang por mdzad pa la/ gzhung lugs pa 'gas de mi 'thad de/ rjes thob tu yon tan brgya phrag bcu gnyis med pa'i phyir zhes brgal ba la/ zhang rin po che ni/
khyung rtsal sgong shun nang nas rdzogs/ / sgong shun bral na nam 'phang spyod/ / sku gsum yon tan sems la rdzogs/ / sgyu lus zhig na gzhan don 'char/[125] / zhes gsungs la/ 'jig rten mgon po'i gsung nas/
khyed kyi khyab pa de nges pa'i bstan bcos kyi lung rnyed na kho bos rta bzang po ster/ sa bcu pa'i mdo las gsungs pa ni skye ba phyi ma'i dbang du mdzad pa yin gsung /[126] gsung dgos pa can 'di rigs kyi yin pa 'dra/ rje btsun sa paN gyis/ dge slong nam mkha' 'bum gyi dri lan du/
'bri stag dang phyag rgya ba'i chos lugs 'di rgyud dang sde snod gang dang mi mthun pa gda'/ 'di yang dag pa'i lam ma lags sam snyam du sems/ tshig 'di nyid gzhan du ma 'phel ba zhig mdzod/[127] ces gsungs pa'ang mchis so/ /

For this correlation of freedom from elaboration to the first bodhisattva ground, some textual experts object. They say that this is incorrect because the twelve sets of hundredfold higher qualities[1222] do not appear in the post-meditative equipoise state. Shang Rinpoché writes in response:
A garuḍa’s powers are already complete within the egg; as soon as it hatches, its flying powers are displayed. The qualities of the three buddha bodies are already complete within the mind; as soon as the illusory body is dismantled, the welfare of others unfolds.[1223] In response, we find the following statement of Jikten Gönpo:
If you can find a scriptural citation from a treatise to establish your entailment, I will give you a good horse; what is stated in the Ten Grounds Sutra is from the point of view of future lives.[1224] Perhaps because of such critiques, we also find the following statement from the exalted Sakya Paṇḍita in his response to queries from the monk Namkha Bum:
In the spiritual traditions of the Drigungpa, Taklungpa, and [other] mahāmudrā advocates, one finds things that do not seem to accord with either the tantra or [sutra] basket. I consider this an imperfect path. Please be sure, however, you do not to share my words with others.[1225]

d.div: [125] phyag rgya chen po lam zab mthar thug_zhang skyes med rin po che'i gsung / rtsib ri dpar ma pod kha/ 22_na6
[126] skyob pa 'jig rten mgon po'i gsung 'di gang nas drangs 'tshol zhib byed kyang ma rnyed/
[127] bka' gdams pa nam mkha' 'bum gyi zhus lan/ sa skya paN+Di ta'i gsung 'bum/ na_32_na2_sa skya bka' 'bum pod lnga pa/ na_244_na2

[1222] This is reference to a set of twelve qualities, according to the Ten Grounds Sutra, that a bodhisattva obtains on the bodhisattva grounds in an increasing number, with a hundredfold on the first ground, a thousandfold on the second, and so on. For a detailed list of these qualities, see Tsongkhapa, Illuminating the Intent (trans.), 527–30.
[1223] Lama Shang, Ultimate Supreme Path, 66; Roberts (trans.), 211, 114.
[1224] Source not located.

[1225] Replies to Kadampa Namkha Bum’s Questions, 511. This comes as part of Sapaṇ’s response to a list of fourteen questions from the Kadampa monk. In question number 13, the monk asks, “Is this mahāmudrā teaching of Drigungpa, Taklungpa, and so on, erroneous or not?” There are slight variations in the wording among the different editions of Sakya Paṇḍita’s collected works. Some editions read “With respect to the Drigungpa, Taklungpa, and [other] mahāmudrā advocates, there appear to be all sorts, some in accord with the tantras and sutra baskets and others not. Whether or not they are correct paths you should analyze well.” The final sentence “Please be sure. . .” does not appear in all editions — only in the Shalu and the Luphu editions.

f.d: 'on kyang 'phags pa'i skye bo rnams kyi mdzad pa rnam thar so so skye bo rnams kyi yul las 'das shing chos dang / skyes bu dam pa la brten pa'i sdig pa shin tu mi bzad pas phyogs 'dzin gyi sdang shugs dor nas dag snang nor bu'i 'od kyis khyab par mdzad du gsol zhes chos kyi rgyal mtshan gsol ba 'debs so//

This said, the enlightened activities of ārya beings remain beyond the comprehension of ordinary beings; and furthermore, since there is the danger of creating most grave negative karma in relation to the Dharma and sublime beings, I, Chökyi Gyaltsen, appeal to you: please reject the power of antagonistic sectarianism and spread everywhere the jewel light by which everything is seen as pure.
gsum pa [brtsams pa las byung ba'i dge ba bsngo ba ]ni
3. Dedicating the virtues derived from the composition

'di ltar/
de skad smra ba mang thos spong ba pa/ / blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan zhes bya ste// dge bas 'gro kun zhi sgo gnyis pa dang / / bral ba'i lam 'dis myur du rgyal gyur cig /[47]
ces dam bca' mthar phyin pa'i tshul dang / brtsams pa'i dge ba 'gro ba rnams sgrib gnyis kyi g.yul las rgyal ba'i phyir bsngo ba'o//

This is as follows:
46 These were uttered by a renunciant who has heard widely, someone who is called Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen. From this virtue may all beings swiftly become victorious through this path, for there is no second path to peace.
This states how the promise [to compose] has been fulfilled and dedicates the virtues derived from composing the text to all beings gaining victory in their battle against the two obscurations. [547]

smras pa/
mdo rgyud rgya mtsho bsrubs pa'i snying po mchog/ / rgya bod mkhas grub yongs kyi dgongs pa'i gnad/ / grub mchog dam pa ma lus gshegs pa'i lam/ / phyag chen bstan pa'i nyi ma deng 'dir shar/ /

Thus I say:
It is the supreme essence churned from the ocean of sutras and tantras, the essential point of the intention of all masters of India and Tibet, the path traversed by all sublime supreme siddhas — may the sun of mahāmudrā teaching shine here today.

d.div: ma rig 'khrul pa'i myos chus yid drangs nas/ / 'jigs rung srid pa'i btson khang ra bar tshud/ / sdug bsngal gsum gyis mnar ba'i lus can rnams/ / ngal gso'i bsti gnas dga' ba'i tshal 'di yin/ /

With their minds consumed by the intoxicant of ignorant delusion, beings trapped in the terrifying prison of cyclic existence and tormented by the three classes of suffering — for them, mahāmudrā is a pleasure grove, a source of true respite.
mtha' dag 'gro la lam bzang mtshon pa'i mig / skyes chen dam pa rnams kyi bzhed pa'i srol/ / phyag chen ma 'dres gsal ba mdzes pa'i gzugs/ / 'char byed gang 'di nor bu'i me long nyid/ /

This is the eye that sees the excellent path for countless beings. This is the tradition upheld by the great sublime beings. That which reflects the beautiful form of such mahāmudrā, undiluted and clear, is indeed a jewel mirror.
'di nang chos brgyad 'ching ba'i sgrog bcad de/ / dben pa'i gnas su ting 'dzin bde ba la/ / 'dod dgur spyod pa'i skal ldan mang po la/ / 'khrul med lam bzang 'doms pa'i bla ma'ang yin/ /

For those many fortunate ones who, having cut the fetters of the eight worldly concerns, remain immersed freely in the bliss of meditative concentration in solitude, this is also a guru who teaches the flawless excellent path.
tshul 'dir 'bad las byung ba'i dge ba'i tshogs/ / bsil zer thur mas phye ba'i kun+da ltar/ / mchog tu dkar ba gang zhig bsags pa de/ / ma rnams sgrol phyir byang chub chen por bsngo/ /

Through the collection of virtue arisen from this effort, like jasmine opened by the spoon-like cool rays of the moon, whatever supremely white karma I may have amassed I dedicate toward great awakening so I may help free my mothers.
de yi mthu las 'gro ba ma lus pa/ / yid kyi bum bzang mdo sngags zung 'brel gyi/ / phyag chen legs bris a mr-i tas gang ste/ / zung 'jug bde ba che la longs spyod shog/

Through the power of this, may the mind vases of all beings without exception be filled with the celestial ambrosia of mahāmudrā, which unites sutra and tantra, and may they enjoy the great bliss of union.

f.d: Colophon

ces dge ldan bka' rgyud kyi bka' srol phyag rgya chen po'i rtsa ba rgyas par bshad pa yang gsal sgron me zhes bya ba 'di yang rang gi slob ma lam 'di la nges pa rnyed nas sgrub pa snying por byed pa gnas bcu rab 'byams pa dge 'dun rgyal mtshan gyis chos brgyad kyi shun pas ma gos pa'i sgrub pa'i me tog gis yang dag par mchod nas/ rtsa tshig 'di la rtsom pa po rang nyid kyis 'grel pa rgyas shing mtha' chod pa/ nyams su blang bya'i don gyi snying po gsal zhing 'dril ba lung rigs kyi rgyab rten tshad ma dang 'brel zhing snyan rgyud kyi gdams pas rgyan pa zhig cis kyang zhu zhes nan cher bskul ba la brten nas/ phyag rgya chen po so so'i grub pa'i mtha' rgya mtsho'i pha rol tu son pa'i spong ba pa blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan gyis chos grwa chen po bkra shis lhun po'i gtsug lag khang du mgyogs par sug bris su bgyis pa'o/ /

This extensive explanation of the root text of mahāmudrā of the tradition of the precious Geden lineage entitled Lamp So Bright was composed at the behest of my student Gendun Gyatso, a rabjampa[1226] who is learned in the ten texts, one who has found conviction in this path and takes it as the heart of his meditative practice. Making a perfect offering of spiritual practice untainted by the husks of the eight worldly concerns, he asked me: “Please, as the author of the root text, write your own a commentary on this root text — a commentary that is extensive, decisively comprehensive, wherein the key points of the practice are clear and organized, the background support of valid scriptural citations and reasoning are provided, and it is adorned with the oral instructions of the ear-to-ear transmission.” Because of his persistent urging, I, Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen, a renunciant who has traveled to the shores of the seas of the individual mahāmudrā traditions, have written this quickly in the scripture hall of the great Dharma seat of Tashi Lhunpo.

d.div: [1226] Literally, “learned in myriad texts,” rab ’byams pa, like the more well-known title geshé, is an academic title connoting mastery of classical texts.

f.d: 'dis kyang bstan pa rin po che mi nub pa'i rgyal mtshan du gyur cig/ // sarba mang+ga laM//
Through this, may the precious teaching be a victory banner that is never damaged. Sarva maṅgalaṃ.[1227]

d.div: [1227] A Sanskrit phrase meaning “May auspiciousness prevail everywhere!”

f.d: @#/ /dge ldan bka' brgyud phyag rgya chen po'i nyams 'khrid rje blo bzang bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan dpal bzang po'i gsung gis bskul ba bzhugs/ /

d.b: 12. An Experiential Guide to Mahāmudrā of the Sacred Geden Lineage

f.d: shar skal ldan rgya mtsho/
Shar Kalden Gyatso
@#/ /na mo ma hA mu tra ya/
Namo mahāmudrāya.

d.div: blo bzang rgyal ba'i sprul ba'i zlos gar las/ / kun khyab kun gyi rang bzhin chos kyi dbyings/ / rjen par 'doms mkhas rgyal dbang thams cad mkhyen/ / dge mtshan gter gyur bla mas bdag skyongs shig /

Through your play as Conqueror Losang Drakpa’s emanation, you are most skilled in explaining to others, in a direct way, the ultimate expanse, the pervasive nature of everything. Omniscient conqueror, treasury of goodness, my guru, pray nurture me.

f.d: 'dir phyag rgya chen po'i nyams 'khrid 'chad pa la gnyis/ brgyud pa'i lo rgyus bshad pa dang / ji ltar nyams su len pa'i tshul lo/ /
The experiential guide to mahāmudrā presented here has two parts: the origin of the lineage [of this practice] and the way to undertake the practice.
brgyud pa'i lo rgyus bshad pa dang /
1. Origin of the lineage of this practice

dang po ni/ rgyal ba rdo rje 'chang gis rje btsun 'jam dbyangs/ des rje rin po che/ des rtogs ldan 'jam dpal rgya mtsho/ des mnyam med ba so ba/ des rje btsun chos kyi rdo rje/ des rgyal ba blo bzang don grub/ des chos 'di'i khungs tsam khrid yig sogs du mar gsungs/ rdzogs par ni mkhas grub sangs rgyas ye shes/ bla ma des kyang chos 'di'i che brjod mang du mdzad/ thugs la 'khrungs tshul gyi nyams mgur yang mang du mdzad/ des paN chen thams cad mkhyen pa/ bla ma 'dis chos 'di'i rtsa tshig/ de'i rgyas bshad yang gsal sgron me/ bla brgyud gsol 'debs sogs brtsams nas gnas bcu rab 'byams pa dge 'dun rgyal mtshan/ ha ldong dka' bcu ba shes rab seng ge/ bsam blo chos rje tshul khrims rgya mtsho sogs sgom chen pa du ma la ma sbas par lhugs par gdams pas/ de rnams kyis kyang thugs nyams su bstar bas ji lta ba bzhin rtogs/ gzhan yang dge ldan du 'di'i nyams 'khrid rab byung pa rab tu mang ba zhig la bstsal ba'i tshe yang / tshal rab 'byams pa dge 'dun chos ldan dang / 'pha' ra byang chub sems dpa' sogs kyi rgyud la zla re zla gnyis tsam la sems gnas khyad par can 'khrungs/ de la brten nas de dus kyi chos nyan phal cher tshe 'di blos btang nas sgrub pa snying bor mdzad pas/ deng sang rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug sha stag go/

The first is as follows. Conqueror Vajradhara taught it to Mañjuśrī, he to precious Jé Tsongkhapa, he to Tokden Jampal Gyatso, he to Basowa, he to the revered Dharmavajra, and he to Conqueror Losang Döndrup. The latter spoke of the sources of this teaching in numerous guidebooks; he, however, taught it in its entirety to Khedrup Sangyé Yeshé. This guru, in turn, expressed elevated praise of this teaching far and wide. He also composed numerous experiential songs relating to the arising of its realization within him. He taught it to the omniscient Panchen, who authored the root text for this teaching, its extensive explanation Lamp So Bright, and the prayer to its lineage gurus. Having composed these texts, Panchen transmitted it, concealing nothing and without reservation, to many great meditators, such as Gendun Gyaltsen, a rabjampa in the ten topics, Sherab Sengé, one from Hamdong learned in the ten treatises, and Tsultrim Gyatso, the Dharma master from Samlo. On their part too, because they put it into practice, they realized the teaching exactly as it is. Furthermore, when Panchen gave an experiential guidance on this teaching to many monks at Ganden Monastery, extraordinary levels of mental stillness arose in the mindstreams of disciples like Gendun Chöden, Tsal Rabjampa Gendun Chöden, Phara Bodhisattva [550], and others. Because of this, many among those who attended the teaching gave up the concerns of this life and embraced meditative practice as the heart commitment of their life. Today, they have all become accomplished yogis.
gnyis pa nyams su len pa'i tshul ni/
2. The way to undertake the practice

gnas dben par lus rnam snang gi chos bdun dang ldan pas/ sems rnam g.yeng sogs kyis ma bslad par dga' spro'i ngang nas 'di ltar/ dal 'byor don che/ rnyed dka'/ 'chi ba mi rtag pa/ las rgyu 'bras/ 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs/ nges 'byung gi bsam pa/ byams snying rje/ byang chub kyi sems rnams blo sbyong dang lam rim dang / bdag gis sbyar ba'i 'khrid yig ltar bskyang / de nas skyabs 'gro'i 'khrid dben sa bka' brgyud kyi 'khrid nas 'byung ba ltar ram/ khol phyung du bris pa ltar dang / rdo rje sems pa'i sgom bzlas/ ltung bshags/ maN+Dal/ bla ma'i rnal 'byor gyi 'khrid rnams logs nas 'byung ba ltar bskyang la/ gsol 'debs gang mang byas nas bla ma rang la bstims pas byin gyis brlabs par bsams shing /

In a place of solitude, adopting the sevenfold posture of meditation,[1228] ensure that your mind is not tainted by distraction and the like. With a joyful mind, contemplate the great value of the life of leisure and opportunity and the difficulty of obtaining it, death and impermanence, karma and its effects, the faults of samsara, the thought of renunciation, loving kindness and compassion, and the awakening mind. Undertake these contemplations as found in the texts on mind training, the stages of the path, or as explained in my own guidebook.[1229] Then undertake the practice of going for refuge, either as found in the guides from the Ensa oral transmission or as found in texts composed specifically on refuge, and Vajrasattva meditation and recitation, the Confession of Downfalls, mandala offering, and guru yoga in accord with how they are presented in their respective guides. Then, having made supplications many times, dissolve the guru into yourself and imagine that you receive blessing from this.

d.div: [1228] On the sevenfold posture, see pages 461–63.
[1229] Shar Kalden Gyatso is here referring probably to his Mahayana Mind Training Dispelling the Darkness of the Mind.

f.d: snang ba ban bun du gyur ba'i ngang de la rnam rtog gang gis kyang bcas bcos mi byed par sngar 'das kyi rjes mi gcod/ ma 'ongs pa'i sngon mi bsu/ da lta 'gyu ba gang yang med pa'i ngang du cung zad mnyam par gzhag go/

Then, within this state where all appearances have become somewhat indistinct, do nothing by way of contrivance of conceptualization, such as entertaining the hopeful thought “If only I could accomplish such and such immediate and ultimate goals” or having anxious thoughts like “What if such and such undesirable events befall me?” Neither chasing the past nor anticipating the future, rest your mind in equipoise in the present, with no movement at all.[1230]

d.div: [1230] From the start of this paragraph up to the end of the explanation of the sixth analogy of resting your mind on page 695 was adopted verbatim from Panchen’s Lamp So Bright, 660–63.

f.d:
de ltar 'jog pa'i tshe brgyal ba dang / gnyid log pa lta bu'i yid la byed pa thams cad bkag pa ma yin par sems g.yo med du gnas pa de nyid ma g.yengs pa ste cung zad kyang brjed pa med pa'i dran pa'i rgyang so tshugs par byed/ de ltar dmigs pa la dran pa'i thag pas bcings kyang / dran pa nyams na sems 'gyu ba'am rnam rtog 'phro nyen che bas/ dran pa'i shugs ji zhan du song na/ sems gzhan du 'gyu ba'am mi 'gyu ba rig pa'i shes bzhin bya ra ba lta bu bsdoms nas 'jog dgos te/ dbu ma snying bo las/
sems kyi glang chen log 'gro ba/ / dmigs pa'i ka ba brtan po la/ / dran pa'i thag pas nges bcings te/ / shes bzhin lcags kyus rim dbang bya/[1] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro/ /

At the time of resting your mind in this way, unlike the total cessation of all mental engagement during fainting or falling asleep, post the sentry of mindfulness ensuring the mind that is abiding unwavering remains undistracted — that is to say, it is not lost to even the slightest forgetfulness. Even though you may tie the meditation object with the rope of mindfulness, if your mindfulness weakens, there is great danger that thoughts involving the mind’s movement could proliferate. So you need to place your mind [on the focal object] by stationing the watchman of meta-awareness, monitoring whether your mind has wandered elsewhere due to a weakening of the force of mindfulness. This is as stated in the following in Essence of the Middle Way:
This wandering elephant of mind, tie it firmly to a sturdy post, its object, with the rope of mindfulness and gradually tame it with the hook of meta-awareness.[1231] [551]

d.div: [1] sde dge_3855_bstan/ dbu ma/ dza_slob dpon legs lda 'byed/ dbu ma'i snying po'i tshig le'ur byas pa/ le'u/ 3_shog_4_na6
[1231] Bhāviveka, Madhyamakahṛdaya, 3.16, Toh 3855 Tengyur, dbu ma, dza, 4a6 (critical edition, 62).

f.d: mdor na ting nge 'dzin skyon med sgrub pa dran shes kyi skyong tshul las ma 'das shing / de yang dran pa gtso bo yin te/ de byung na shes bzhin dran pa'i 'bras bur gsungs pas zhar la 'ong ngo / / de'i rnam rtog gzhan 'gags nas/ sems rig cing gsal ba nges byung na de ka'i ngo bo la/ dran pa hrim gyis bsgrims la rtse gcig tu gcer gyis ltos shig /de ltar bltas pa na 'gyur ba'am rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa/ de dang de nyid ngos zin par bya ste/ de ltar byed pa ni shes bzhin la rag las so// yang na ni 'dul ba lung las mda' mkhan dang ral bskor mkhan 'thab tshul gsungs pa ltar/[2] dran shes stobs bskyed nas thog rdzis su rnam rtog ci dang ci skyes pa de 'phral du rbad rbad bcad de 'phro mthud mi mjug pa'o/ /

In brief, the cultivation of flawless meditative absorption constitutes nothing but the maintenance of mindfulness and meta-awareness. Here too, mindfulness the key: when mindfulness is present, meta-awareness arises as a byproduct, for meta-awareness has been described as a result of mindfulness. At that point, when all other thoughts have ceased and that aware and clear mind is perceived, fasten your mindfulness with a firm focus on its nature and starkly observe it with single-pointedness. Observing in this manner, note whatever movement or thought arises and recognize it as just this or that. Doing this depends, of course, on meta-awareness. Alternatively, as explained in a Vinaya text, meditate in way in which an archer and a swordsman fight in a duel: applying the force of your mindfulness and meta-awareness, tread on whatever thoughts arise, instantly cutting them down and thus preventing them from gaining momentum.

d.div: [2] 'dul ba lung las mda' mkhan dang ral bskor mkhan 'thab tshul gsungs pa zhes pa 'di paN chen blo bzang chos rgyan gyi phyag chen yang gsal sgron mer yang gsungs mod de'i khungs ngos 'dzin ma thub/

f.d:
rnam rtog 'phro bcad pa'i mthar 'gyu ba med par gnas pa de'i tshe dran shes ma shor bar khong grims la 'phral du lhod chags pa zhig byas la mnyam bzhag gi ngang du glod dgos te/ ma cig gis/
hrim gyis sgrims la lhod kyis glod/ / sems kyi 'jog sa de na gda'/[3] / zhes dang /

d.div: [3] ma gcig kyi gsung / hrim gyis sgrims la lhod kyis glod/ /sems kyi 'jog sa de na gda'/ /zhes pa 'di yang paN chen gyis phyag chen rtsa 'grel gnyis kar drangs mod de'i khungs 'tshol zhib byed kyang rnyed son ma byung /
[1232] Source of Machik’s quote not located.

f.d:
gzhan yang ji skad du bram ze chen pos kyang /
'jur bus bcings pa'i sems nyid ni/ / glod na grol bar the tshom med/[4] / ces gsungs pa ltar khong grims la lhod chags pa zhig byas te/ 'di tsam las bsgrims drags nas rgod pa skye bar 'dug snyam pa las cung zad glod/ 'di tsam las/ glod drags na bying ba skye ba 'dug snyam pa las cung zad bsgrim na ran par 'gyur bas de gnyis kyi mtshams su rnam rtog gi 'gyu ba las sems glod/ gnas cha byung res kyi bying zon byas nas 'jog dgos te/

Also, the Great Brahman, Saraha, says:
This mind, bound in its own entanglement, when relaxed becomes free, no doubt.[1233] So, as suggested in the above, inwardly alert, stay relaxed. And when you sense your mind becoming too alert, such that excitation may arise, relax a little; and when you sense your mind becoming too relaxed, such that mental laxity may arise, strengthen your alertness a little. This way you will find just the right balance. So between those two extremes, relax your mind from the movements of thought, and watch out for occurrence of mental laxity every time stability arises.

d.div: [4] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod kyi glu/ shog_73_na4
[1233] Saraha, Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti), Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 73a4.

f.d:
slob dpon tsan+d+ra gau mis/
brtson pa bsten na rgod pa 'byung 'gyur zhing / / de spangs na ni zhum pa skye bar 'gyur/ / 'di yis rigs par mnyam 'jug rnyed dka' na/ / bdag gi sems dkrugs pas ni ci zhig bgyi/[5] / zhes 'byung ba bzhin no/ / de dag gi dus su rnam rtog la thog rdzis byas pa dang / rnam rtog gang dang gang skyes pa de'i ngo bo bltas pa de dang de'i tshe rnam rtog de dag rang yal du song ba'i stong sang 'char/ de bzhin du sems g.yo med du gnas pa'i tshe'ang brtags pa na ma bsgribs stong sang gsal hrig ge pa/ snga phyi gnyis khyad par med par mthong ba de la gnas 'gyu 'dres pa yin zhes sgom chen pa rnams la grags shing tha snyad mdzad do//

Master Candragomin writes:
If effort is applied excitation arises; if shunned slackness occurs. When it is hard to find a proper balance, my mind is perturbed, so what should I do?[1234] During these times when you are trampling on the thoughts or looking at the face of each thought as it arises, right there and then, the thoughts will vanish on their own accord, giving rise to the dawning of a pure vacuity. Similarly, when you examine the mind as it remains without wavering, you will see an unobstructed pure vacuity, a vivid clarity, with no differentiation between the earlier and the latter instances. This is known to the great meditators as “the merging of stillness and movement,” and they refer to it by such a phrase. [552]

d.div: [5] sde dge_1159_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_slob dpon tsan dra go mi/ bshags bstod/ shog_205_na6
[1234] Praise in the Form of a Confession (Deśanāstava), Toh 1159 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 205b5.

f.d:
yang na sems gnas pa skyong tshul 'di ltar bya ste/ rnam rtog ci 'dra zhig skyes kyang mi 'gog par gang du 'gyu gang la 'gyu ngos zin par byas te rnam rtog de'i ngo bo la blta zhing 'jog la/ de ltar bzhag pas mthar 'gyu ba [6]'gags nas gnas pa ni rgya mtsho chen por rdzings nang du yun ring bor bzung ba'i bya brtson ni/ rgya mtsho'i nang du 'phur ba'i dpe dang mtshungs pa yin pa'i phyir te/ do ha las/
ji ltar gzings nas 'phur ba'i bya rog ni/ / phyogs rnams bskor nas slar yang der 'bab bzhin/[7] / zhes gsungs pa ji bzhin bskyangs par bya ste/

Alternatively, you could engage in the following method for stilling the mind: Whatever thought arises, do not suppress it but note where it comes from and where it moves to and rest your mind by simply looking at the nature of that thought. As you rest your mind in this way, movement will eventually cease and your mind will become still. This is analogous to the flights of a bird long captive aboard a ship sailing across a vast ocean. The Dohā Treasury of Songs says:
It’s like the raven that takes off from a ship, flies to every direction, and lands there again.[1235] Maintain your meditation exactly as described here.

d.div: [6] ma dper mthar 'gyur ba 'gags nas gnas pa ni zhes byung yang 'gyu ba 'gag nas zhes rjes 'jug ra med par byas na legs par snang mod 'dir ma bcos par rang sor bzhag yod/
[7] sde dge_2273_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_sa ra ha/ do ha mdzod ces bya ba phyag rgya chen po'i man ngag_shog_123_na6
[1235] Saraha, Dohā Treasury of Songs (Dohākoṣagīti), Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 73a4.

f.d:
yang dgon pas/
blo rnam rtog la skyon du mi lta zhing / / mi rtog pa ched du mi sgom par/ / sems rang lugs su zhog la rgyang so tshugs dang / / sgom zhi gnas kyi steng du phebs pa zhig 'ong gi[8] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro//

So Yangönpa says:
Not viewing the thoughts as faults, not deliberately meditating on nonconceptuality, rest your mind in its natural mode and post a sentry, and your meditation will reach tranquil abiding.[1236]

d.div: [8] rgyal ba yang dgon pa rgyal mtshan dpal gyi gsung 'bum/ ka_phyag rgya chen po lhan cig skyes sbyor gyi thon chos/ shog_11_na2_blo rtog pa la skyon du ma blta bar/ /mi rtog pa ched du ma bsgom par/ /sems rang lugs su zhog la rgyangs so tshugs dang / /sgom zhi gnas kyi thil du phebs pa cig 'ong gis//
[1236] Yangönpa, Parting Teaching on Mahāmudrā Innate Union, 11a2.

f.d:
gzhan yang deng sang gi gdul bya rnams kyis sems kyi bzhag thabs drug gi sgo nas bskyangs na gdams pa'i rgyal bor 'gyur ro/ / ji ltar zhe na/
sprin dang bral ba'i nyi bzhin bzhag / khyung chen mkha' la lding bzhin bzhag/ / rgya mtsho chen po'i gzings bzhin bzhag/ / bu chung lha khang lta bzhin bzhag / mkha' la bya 'phur rjes bzhin bzhag / ras bal brdal ba bzhin du bzhag / sems kyi bzhag thabs 'di dag gis/ / rnal 'byor don dang ldan par 'gyur/[9] / zhes pa ste/

Furthermore, if today’s trainees maintain their meditation practice by means of the six methods of resting the mind, theirs will be a king among instructions. How are they done? It is said:
Rest it like the sun free from the clouds. Rest it like a great garuḍa soaring in the sky. Rest it like a ship on the great ocean. Rest it like a small child looking inside a temple. Rest it like the tracks of a bird flying in the sky. Rest it like fluffed cotton wool. By these methods of resting the mind, your yoga will be meaningful.[1237]

d.div: [9] 'di gzhung gzhan zhig nas drangs sam shar skal ldan rgya mtsho rang nyid kyis sdom du mdzad zhu dka'/
[1237] A similar citation is found in Dakpo Tashi Namgyal’s Moonbeams of Mahāmudrā, 329, with Milarepa cited as its source.

f.d: dang po ni/ dper na sprin dang bral ba'i nyi ma de gsal zhing dwangs par gnas pa ltar/ sems kyi rang bzhin 'od gsal ba de la mtshan 'dzin gyi rnam rtog dang bying rgod sogs kyis ma bsgribs par 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as the sun when free of clouds remains supremely bright and brilliant, in the same manner, rest your mind in the luminous nature of mind unobscured by conceptual apprehension of signs, by mental laxity and excitation, and so forth.

gnyis pa ni/ dper na nam mkha' lding ni nam mkhar rgyu ba'i tshe gshog pa ldeb pa sogs rtsol ba ha cang mi dgos par rang shugs kyis rgyu ba bzhin du/ sems ha cang grims pa ha cang lhod drags pa ma yin par/ khong grims pa'i gsal cha'i ngar dang ldan zhing 'phral lhod chags pas dran shes kyi rgya dang ma bral bar skyong ba'o/ /

Just as a garuḍa flying across the sky does so naturally, soaring high without needing much exertion of flapping its wings, in the same manner, maintain your meditation without straying outside the seal of mindfulness and meta-awareness — in such a way that your mind is neither too alert nor too relaxed but possesses vibrant clarity due from being alert at the core yet relaxed on the surface.

gsum pa ni/ dper na rgya mtsho chen po rlung gis bskyod kyang khar rlabs cung zad byung yang gting g.yo bar mi nus pa bzhin du/ sems dmigs pa la 'jog pa'i tshe rnam rtog phra mo 'gas cung zad g.yos kyang / rnam rtog rags pas cung zad kyang ma g.yos par 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as waves rise a little on the surface when a great ocean is stirred by winds, but the sea is not moved in its depths, in the same manner, rest your mind in such a way that even if some subtle level of thought does elicit movement when you place your mind on the meditation object, it is not swayed even slightly by the coarse levels of thought. [553]

bzhi pa ni/ dper na bu chung lha khang la blta ba'i tshe/ ri mo'i cha shas phra ba la rtog dpyod mi 'jug cing cha rags pa bkra ba la mi g.yeng bar lta ba bzhin/ sems dmigs pa la 'jog pa'i sgo lnga'i dbang shes kyi yul yid du 'ong mi 'ong ci shar yang rtog dpyod chags sdang mi byed par dmigs pa la rtse gcig tu 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as a small child looking inside a temple does not consider the details of the murals but stares undistracted at the large vibrant patterns, in the same manner, when your mind is focused on the meditation object, whatever objects — attractive or unattractive — may appear to your five senses, simply rest your mind single-pointedly on the meditation object without judgment and without emotions of attachment or aversion.

lnga ba ni/ dper na bya nam mkhar 'phur ba'i rjes mi 'byung ba ltar/ tshor ba bde sdug btang snyoms ji 'dra zhig byung yang chags sdang rmongs gsum gang gi'ang dbang du mi gtong bar mnyam par 'jog pa'o/ /

Just as birds cruising across the sky leave no track, in the same manner, whatever feelings you might be experiencing, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, rest your mind in equipoise without giving in to any of the three poisons of the mind — attachment, aversion, and delusion.

drug pa ni/ dper na ras bal brdal ba'i tshe 'jam zhing khong lhod lhod por yod pa bzhin du/ mnyam par 'jog pa'i sems dug gsum mngon gyur pa dang bying rgod kyi rtsub reg dang bral bar byas te mnyam par 'jog pa yin no//

Just as when cotton wool is fluffed it becomes softer and freer, in the same manner, when you rest your mind in equipoise, you do so free of manifest levels of the three poisons and the rough and hard textures of mental laxity and excitation.

de ltar bskyangs pa las lag rjes 'di lta bu zhig 'byung ste/ mnyam gzhag gi ngo bo gang gis kyang ma bsgribs pa dwangs shing shin tu gsal ba dang / gzugs can gyi dngos po gang du yang ma grub pas stong sang nam mkha' lta bu yin pa la/ yang bzang ngan gyi yul lnga ci byung yang me long dwangs pa la gzugs brnyan ltar gsal hril ge pa cir yang 'char bas/ 'di yin 'di min gyi ngos bzung dang bral ba'i nyams 'char/ 'di 'dra ba'i ting nge 'dzin ji ltar brtan yang lus sems shin sbyangs kyi bde bas ma zin na 'dod sems rtse gcig pa dang / des zin na ting nge 'dzin zhi gnas su gsungs shing / mngon shes rdzu 'phrul sogs yon tan mang bo'i 'byung khungs yin pa dang / khyad par theg pa gsum ka'i 'phags lam rnams kyang 'di la brten nas 'thob pa yin no/ / ting nge 'dzin 'di la bka' rgyud pa rnams kyis gsal stong 'dzin med kyi ting nge 'dzin gyi tha snyad byed cing nyams len gyi mthil du mdzad do//

What imprints will emerge from maintaining meditative equipoise in the way presented above? When you maintain meditative equipoise in this way, the following will unfold: You will experience the nature of your meditative equipoise as unobscured by anything, as lucid and utterly clear. As it does not exist in any physical way, it is a pure vacuity like space, yet like reflections appearing in an unblemished mirror, whatever objects it encounters — good or bad — appear clearly and vividly. It is undefinable by any identifications of “it is this” or “it is not that.” Now, however stable such a meditative concentration may be, if it is not imbued with physical and mental pliancy, it is said to be a single-pointedness of mind belonging to the desire realm. A meditative concentration imbued with [physical and mental pliancy, on the other hand] is described as tranquil abiding. Tranquil abiding will be the source of numerous higher qualities such as clairvoyance and other supernatural feats. In particular, all the paths of the three vehicles are attained on the basis of tranquil abiding.[1238] Kagyüpas use the phrase “meditative concentration characterized by clarity, vacuity, and nonapprehension” to describe such a concentration, and they embrace it as a core practice.

d.div: [1238] Here ends the lengthy section Kalden Gyatso brings verbatim (except for verse 24 of the root text, which our author leaves out) from Panchen’s Lamp So Bright, beginning on page 692.

f.d: sgom thog nas lta ba 'tshol 'dod pa rnams kyis 'dis mtshon pa'i ting nge 'dzin gang rung zhig la myong ba ma skyes kyi bar du lta ba mi 'tshol la/ ting nge 'dzin la gnas cha brtan po thob pa'i mtshams shig nas lta ba 'tshol ba yin/ lta thog nas sgom 'tshol 'dod pa rnams bla ma x[10] rang la bstims pa'i mjug de nyid du bdag gi 'dzin tshul la brtags pa yin no/ / sgo de gnyis gang nas 'jug kyang lta ba tshol ba'i tshul ni 'di ltar/
